source: Short definitions written for DKLA by an agent swarm on 11-12 November 2026 (policy, six term judges, six miss-finders, a minimalist, a completionist and an arbiter, two sense auditors, gloss writers and legal checkers, and a final reader); where a Cornell LII Wex entry exists it is the source and is linked (CC BY-SA 4.0).

terms.label: abandonment
terms.gloss: Voluntarily giving up a right, claim, argument, or property with no intent to reclaim it; an argument not pressed on appeal is treated as abandoned.

terms.label: abatement
terms.gloss: Reducing or ending something by legal order, such as correcting a workplace hazard. In old pleading, a plea in abatement objected to a defect, like bad service, without contesting the merits.

terms.label: abeyance
terms.gloss: Temporary suspension; a matter "held in abeyance" is put on hold until something else is decided.

terms.label: abrogate
terms.gloss: To abolish or cancel a law, treaty right, or rule, as when Congress overrides a treaty or a statute replaces a common-law rule.

terms.label: abscond
terms.gloss: To flee or hide to avoid legal process, such as arrest, a lawsuit or creditors.

terms.label: absolute immunity
terms.gloss: Complete protection from a lawsuit, or claimed protection from being forced to testify, covering acts within a protected role however wrongful, unlike qualified immunity, which can be overcome.

terms.label: absolute privilege
terms.gloss: A complete defense to defamation for statements made in certain settings, such as court proceedings or legislative debate, even if false or made with ill will.

terms.label: abstention
terms.gloss: A federal court's decision to decline or postpone deciding a case it has power to hear, out of respect for state courts or related state proceedings.

terms.label: abstract of title
terms.gloss: A summary of the public records affecting a piece of land, such as sales, mortgages, and liens, used to trace and show who owns it.

terms.label: abuse of discretion
terms.gloss: A deferential standard of review: an appeals court overturns a trial judge's judgment call only if it was clearly unreasonable, legally mistaken, or unsupported.

terms.label: abuse of process
terms.gloss: The civil wrong of misusing a court procedure, such as a subpoena, attachment, or arrest, for an improper purpose it was not designed to serve.

terms.label: acceleration (of a debt)
terms.gloss: A creditor's right, usually under a contract term, to demand the entire remaining debt at once after a default, instead of in later installments.

terms.label: accept (an offer)
terms.context: \b(offers?|offeror|offerees?|counter-?offers?|bids?|acceptances?|mailbox|purchase orders?|quotations?|quotes?|terms of the offer|by performance|by promise|unilateral contracts?|bilateral contracts?|revok\w*|revocation|silence|goods|cargo\w*|shipments?)\b
terms.gloss: To agree to an offer's terms in the way the offer invites, which forms a contract; a reply that changes the terms is usually a counteroffer instead.

terms.label: acceptance
except: acceptance of a permissible agency construction
acceptance of certain reasonable agency constructions
acceptance of a reasonable agency answer
acceptance of certain united states assistance
terms.gloss: Agreeing to the terms of an offer, which forms a contract. In a sale of goods, a buyer that accepts delivered goods loses the right to reject them, though it may sometimes revoke acceptance.

terms.label: accessory before the fact
terms.gloss: A person who helps plan or encourages a crime but is not present when it is committed.

terms.label: accommodation shipment (UCC)
terms.gloss: Goods a seller ships while telling the buyer they do not match the order, offered only as a favor. Under UCC § 2-206 that shipment is a new offer, not an acceptance.

terms.label: accord and satisfaction
terms.gloss: An agreement to accept a different performance, often a smaller payment, to settle a disputed debt (the accord), plus that performance (the satisfaction), which ends the original claim.

terms.label: account stated
terms.gloss: A claim that a debtor agreed, expressly or by not objecting in time, that a statement of the balance owed was correct, so the creditor can sue on that balance.

terms.label: accounting (court remedy)
terms.gloss: A court-ordered remedy requiring someone who handled another's money or property, such as a partner, agent, or trustee, to disclose the full figures and pay over what is owed.

terms.label: accredited investor
terms.gloss: An investor who meets SEC income, wealth, or professional tests, so companies may sell securities to them in private offerings exempt from full registration.

terms.label: accrue
terms.gloss: For a legal claim, to come into existence, usually when the injury happens; the deadline for filing suit generally starts running then.

terms.label: acquiescence
terms.gloss: Silent or passive acceptance of someone else's conduct. A party that fails to object may be treated as having accepted it.

terms.label: acquittal
terms.gloss: A finding by a judge or jury in a criminal case that the defendant is not guilty; it bars a second prosecution for the same offense.

terms.label: acquittance
terms.gloss: An old term for a written release confirming that a debt has been paid or that the debtor is discharged from it.

terms.label: act of God
terms.gloss: A natural event no one could foresee or prevent, such as a flood or earthquake; it can excuse a party from liability or from performing a contract.

terms.label: act of state doctrine
terms.gloss: A doctrine under which U.S. courts generally refuse to judge the lawfulness of a foreign government's official acts done within its own territory.

terms.label: acting officer
terms.gloss: An official who temporarily performs the duties of a vacant office, such as a department head, until someone is permanently appointed and confirmed.

terms.label: action (lawsuit)
terms.gloss: A lawsuit: a case one party brings against another in court. Here it does not mean an act or deed.

terms.label: action on the case
terms.gloss: An old common-law lawsuit for indirect or consequential harm, as opposed to trespass, which covered direct, forcible injury. Modern negligence claims grew from it.

terms.label: actionable
terms.gloss: Giving grounds for a lawsuit: conduct the law lets someone sue over, if it is proven. Not the business sense of 'practical' or 'ready to act on'.

terms.label: active negligence
terms.gloss: An older indemnity term for a party's own direct carelessness causing harm, which could bar it from shifting the loss to another under a general indemnity clause.

terms.label: actual authority
terms.gloss: Power a principal actually gives an agent, in words or by implication, to act for the principal, so that the agent's acts bind the principal.

terms.label: actual controversy
terms.gloss: A real, present dispute between parties with opposing interests, which federal courts require before deciding a case, including a request for a declaratory judgment.

terms.label: actual damages
terms.gloss: Money awarded to make up for losses actually suffered and proved (also called compensatory damages), as opposed to nominal, statutory or punitive damages.

terms.label: actual innocence
terms.gloss: Being factually innocent of the crime, not merely having a conviction overturned for a legal flaw. Some compensation laws and court doctrines require proof of it.

terms.label: actual knowledge
terms.gloss: Real, personal awareness of a fact. Constructive or imputed knowledge is knowledge the law treats someone as having because they should have known, or because their agent knew.

terms.label: actual malice
terms.gloss: In defamation since New York Times v. Sullivan (1964), knowing a statement was false or recklessly disregarding whether it was. In older cases and privilege rules, spite or an improper motive.

terms.label: ad hoc
terms.gloss: Latin for "for this": done for one particular case or purpose rather than under a general rule.

terms.label: ad valorem
terms.gloss: Latin for 'according to value': a tax or duty set as a percentage of an item's value rather than a fixed amount.

terms.label: additional insured
terms.gloss: A person or company, other than the buyer of an insurance policy, added to the policy so that it is also covered.

terms.label: additional or different terms (UCC § 2-207)
terms.gloss: Terms in a reply that add to, or differ from, the offer. At common law they make the reply a counteroffer; under UCC § 2-207 a contract can still form, and rules decide which terms count.

terms.label: ADEA
terms.gloss: The Age Discrimination in Employment Act, a federal law forbidding employment discrimination against workers aged 40 and over.

terms.label: adequacy of representation
terms.gloss: The requirement that those speaking for a group in a lawsuit will fairly protect its interests. In class actions it tests the named representatives and their lawyers for conflicts and competence.

terms.label: adequate assurance of performance
terms.gloss: When one party reasonably doubts the other will perform, it may demand written assurance and suspend its own performance until it gets it. Failing to give assurance can count as repudiation.

terms.label: adequate remedy
terms.gloss: A remedy, usually money damages, that fully makes up for a harm; courts grant special relief such as injunctions or mandamus only when no adequate remedy exists.

terms.label: adequate remedy at law
terms.gloss: Money damages or another ordinary remedy that would fully fix the harm. Courts of equity traditionally grant injunctions only when none exists.

terms.label: adhesion contract
terms.gloss: A standard-form contract drafted by the stronger party and offered on a take-it-or-leave-it basis, with no chance to bargain over terms.

terms.label: adjudicate / adjudication
terms.gloss: To decide a legal dispute and the parties' rights in it, as a court does. When an agency adjudicates, it applies the law to particular parties' facts, unlike rulemaking.

terms.label: adjudication (by an agency)
terms.context: (rulemaking|rule-making|formal adjudication|informal adjudication|agency adjudication|administrative adjudication|adjudicatory (hearings?|proceedings?|setting|procedures?|order|control|process)|Londoner|Bi-Metallic|(policy|policymaking|announced|standards?) (\w+ )?through adjudication|rather than adjudication|individual adjudication|adjudication powers)
terms.gloss: An agency deciding a specific case about particular parties, much as a court does, rather than making general rules for the future. Formal adjudication uses trial-type hearings.

terms.label: adjudicative facts
terms.gloss: Facts about the particular parties and events in a dispute (who did what, where, and when), as opposed to general facts that inform a policy or rule.

terms.label: adjustment of status
terms.gloss: The process by which a noncitizen already in the United States becomes a lawful permanent resident (gets a green card) without leaving the country.

terms.label: charge of discrimination
terms.gloss: The complaint a worker must first file with the EEOC or a state agency before suing under Title VII and similar anti-discrimination laws.

terms.label: administrative forfeiture
terms.gloss: Forfeiture of seized property by a government agency without a court case, allowed when no one files a timely claim contesting it.

terms.label: administrative hearing
terms.gloss: A trial-like hearing before an agency official, who takes evidence and argument before ruling on matters such as benefits, licenses, or penalties.

terms.label: administrative law
terms.gloss: The law governing government agencies: how they make rules, decide cases, and are reviewed by courts, largely under the Administrative Procedure Act.

terms.label: administrative law judge (ALJ)
terms.gloss: A hearing officer within a government agency who holds trial-like hearings and issues decisions, which the agency's leaders can usually review and change.

terms.label: Administrative Procedure Act (APA)
terms.gloss: The 1946 federal law setting the basic procedures agencies must follow to make rules and decide cases, and letting courts set aside unlawful agency action.

terms.label: administrator (of an estate)
terms.gloss: A person appointed by a court to manage and settle a dead person's estate when there is no will or no named executor able to serve.

terms.label: administrator ad prosequendum
terms.gloss: A person a court appoints only to bring a lawsuit for a dead person's estate or survivors, such as a wrongful-death claim, not to manage the whole estate.

terms.label: administratrix / executrix
terms.gloss: Older terms for a woman who manages a dead person's estate: an executrix is named in the will; an administratrix is chosen by a court, usually when there is no will.

terms.label: admiralty
terms.gloss: Maritime law, covering ships, shipping, and sea commerce. Federal courts hear these cases under special rules, traditionally without a jury.

terms.label: admission (evidence)
terms.gloss: A party's own statement or concession that a fact is true, which the other side can use against it as evidence. 'Admitting' evidence also means letting the factfinder consider it.

terms.label: adversarial (adversary system)
terms.gloss: Describes the American way of deciding disputes: opposing sides, not the judge, gather and present evidence and argument, and a neutral judge or jury decides.

terms.label: adverse party
terms.gloss: The party on the opposite side of a case from a given party, whose interests are opposed to that party's.

terms.label: adverse possession
terms.gloss: A way to gain ownership of land by openly, continuously, and exclusively occupying it without the owner's permission for a period set by law, often 10 to 20 years.

terms.label: adverse selection
terms.gloss: The tendency of people likelier to need insurance to buy it while healthier people hold off, pushing up average costs and premiums.

terms.label: adverseness
terms.gloss: The requirement that a case involve parties with genuinely opposed interests, so a court decides a real dispute rather than giving an advisory opinion.

terms.label: advice and consent
terms.gloss: The Senate's constitutional role in approving the President's nominations for major offices and, by a two-thirds vote, treaties.

terms.label: advisory opinion
terms.gloss: A court's answer to a legal question when there is no real dispute before it. Federal courts may not give them under Article III, though some state courts may.

terms.label: advisory verdict
terms.gloss: A jury's finding that the judge may consider but need not follow, because the judge, not the jury, decides the issue.

terms.label: affiant
terms.gloss: The person who makes and signs a sworn written statement (an affidavit).

terms.label: affidavit
terms.gloss: A written statement of facts that the writer swears or affirms is true, signed before an official such as a notary, and usable as evidence.

terms.label: affirm
terms.gloss: Of a higher court: to uphold a lower court's decision, leaving its result in place. The opposite is to reverse.

terms.label: affirmation of fact (warranty)
terms.gloss: A seller’s factual statement about goods that becomes part of the basis of the bargain. Under UCC § 2-313 it creates an express warranty, unlike mere opinion or sales talk.

terms.label: affirmative defense
terms.gloss: A defendant's own reason for defeating a claim even if the plaintiff's allegations are true, such as a privilege or the statute of limitations. The defendant must raise and usually prove it.

terms.label: affirmed in part, reversed in part
match: affirmed in part and reversed in part
terms.gloss: An appeals court ruling that upholds some of the lower court's decisions and overturns or sets aside others, rather than deciding the whole judgment one way.

terms.label: Affordable Care Act
terms.gloss: The 2010 federal health-insurance law, including insurer coverage rules, an individual coverage requirement, insurance exchanges and premium tax credits.

terms.label: newly discovered evidence
terms.gloss: Evidence found after trial that could not have been found earlier with reasonable diligence; if likely to change the result, it can justify a new trial or relief from judgment.

terms.label: age of majority
terms.gloss: The age, usually 18, at which a person becomes a legal adult, able to make binding contracts.

terms.label: agency
terms.gloss: A government body, such as the EPA or SEC, created by statute to carry out a law, often by making rules and deciding disputes; in private law, "agency" is the agent-principal relationship.

terms.label: agency guidance
terms.gloss: Informal agency documents, such as letters, manuals or FAQs, explaining how the agency reads its rules. They generally lack the force of law.

terms.label: agency (principal and agent)
terms.gloss: A relationship in which one person, the agent, acts on behalf of and under the control of another, the principal. Not a government agency.

terms.label: agent
terms.gloss: A person authorized to act for another (the principal), whose authorized acts, such as signing contracts or receiving legal papers, legally bind the principal.

terms.label: aggravated indecent assault
terms.gloss: A Pennsylvania felony of penetrating another person's genitals or anus, other than by intercourse, without consent, including when the person is unconscious or was drugged to prevent resistance.

terms.label: aggrieved
terms.gloss: Harmed in a legal right or interest. Statutes often let only an "aggrieved" person sue or seek review, a standing requirement.

terms.label: aiding and abetting
terms.gloss: Knowingly helping or encouraging someone else to commit a wrong. The helper can be held liable along with the main wrongdoer.

terms.label: alias process (summons)
terms.gloss: A second summons or other court paper issued after the first was not successfully served. Here 'alias' does not mean a false name.

terms.label: alibi
terms.gloss: A defense that the accused was somewhere else when the crime happened, so could not have committed it; an alibi witness testifies to that.

terms.label: alien
terms.gloss: The legal term for a person who is not a citizen or national of the country; for federal diversity jurisdiction, a citizen of a foreign country.

terms.label: Alien Tort Statute
terms.gloss: A 1789 federal law (28 U.S.C. § 1350) letting foreign citizens sue in U.S. courts for civil wrongs that violate the law of nations or a U.S. treaty.

terms.label: alienation (of property)
terms.gloss: Transfer of property to someone else; a "restraint on alienation" limits an owner's power to sell or give the property away, and the law disfavors such restraints.

terms.label: alimony
terms.gloss: Court-ordered payments from one spouse or ex-spouse to the other for support during or after separation or divorce.

terms.label: All Writs Act
terms.gloss: 28 U.S.C. § 1651, which lets federal courts issue any orders, such as mandamus, needed to protect or carry out their jurisdiction.

terms.label: allegation
terms.gloss: A statement of fact a party asserts, usually in a pleading, and must later prove; on a motion to dismiss, courts assume well-pleaded factual allegations are true.

terms.label: allotment (Indian land)
terms.gloss: Under federal Indian policy from about 1887 to 1934, a parcel of reservation land assigned to an individual tribal member; leftover 'surplus' land was often opened to non-Indian settlers.

terms.label: alter ego
terms.gloss: A company or person so controlled by another that a court treats the two as one, disregarding the separate corporate form, often to make the owner pay the company's debts.

terms.label: alternative ground
terms.gloss: A second, independent reason that would support the same result; an appeals court may affirm a judgment on any ground the record supports.

terms.label: ambiguity
terms.gloss: Language is ambiguous when it can reasonably be read more than one way. Courts then turn to context, outside evidence, or interpretive rules to pick the meaning.

terms.label: amended pleading
terms.gloss: A revised complaint, answer, or other pleading that replaces the original; under Rule 15 a party may amend once early on as of right, and afterward with consent or the court's permission.

terms.label: amend / amendment
terms.gloss: A formal change to a pleading, statute, regulation, contract or constitution. To amend is to make that change, for example by filing an amended complaint.

terms.label: American Bar Association (ABA)
terms.gloss: The national voluntary association of lawyers, which writes model ethics rules, accredits law schools, and rates judicial nominees.

terms.label: Americans with Disabilities Act
terms.gloss: The 1990 federal law forbidding discrimination against people with disabilities in jobs, government services, and businesses open to the public, and requiring reasonable accommodations.

terms.label: amicus curiae (plural: amici)
terms.gloss: Latin for 'friend of the court': a nonparty allowed to file arguments because it has an interest in the case or useful expertise.

terms.label: amount in controversy
terms.gloss: The money at stake in a lawsuit, as claimed by the plaintiff. For a federal diversity case it must today exceed $75,000, not counting interest and costs.

terms.label: announced the judgment of the Court
terms.gloss: Phrase used when the lead opinion states the Court's result but a majority does not join all of its reasoning; the parts lacking majority support speak only for a plurality.

terms.label: annulment
terms.gloss: Cancelling a legal act or decision so it has no legal effect, as when a high court annuls a lower court's judgment. A marriage annulment treats the marriage as void from the start.

terms.label: answer (pleading)
terms.gloss: The defendant's formal written response to a complaint, admitting or denying each allegation and raising any defenses.

terms.label: antecedent debt
terms.gloss: A debt that already existed before the new promise or transfer in question. Whether taking a note or security for it counts as giving value was a recurring commercial-law question.

terms.label: antenuptial (prenuptial) agreement
terms.gloss: A contract made before marriage setting each spouse's property rights, and sometimes support, if the marriage ends by divorce or death. Also called a prenuptial agreement.

terms.label: Anti-Injunction Act
terms.gloss: Usually 28 U.S.C. § 2283: federal courts may not halt state-court proceedings unless Congress authorizes it, it aids their jurisdiction, or it protects their judgments. A separate tax version bars suits restraining tax collection.

terms.label: antitrust
terms.gloss: The law, chiefly the Sherman and Clayton Acts, forbidding monopolization and agreements that unreasonably restrain competition, such as price-fixing. Injured private parties can sue for triple (treble) damages.

terms.label: APA § 553 (informal rulemaking)
terms.gloss: The Administrative Procedure Act provision on informal rulemaking: published notice, a chance for public comment, and a concise statement of basis and purpose, with exemptions such as interpretive rules.

terms.label: APA § 701 (limits on judicial review)
terms.gloss: The Administrative Procedure Act provision withholding judicial review where a statute precludes it (701(a)(1)) or the action is committed to agency discretion by law (701(a)(2)).

terms.label: APA § 702 (right of review)
terms.gloss: The Administrative Procedure Act provision letting a person harmed by agency action, or aggrieved within the meaning of a statute, sue for review; it also waives sovereign immunity for relief other than money damages.

terms.label: APA §§ 554, 556–557 (formal hearings)
terms.gloss: The Administrative Procedure Act sections for trial-type agency hearings: a presiding officer, evidence and cross-examination, decision on the record, and separated functions. They govern formal adjudication and formal rulemaking.

terms.label: APA § 706 (judicial review)
terms.gloss: The Administrative Procedure Act section (5 U.S.C. § 706) telling courts when to set aside agency action, such as action that is arbitrary and capricious or unsupported by substantial evidence.

terms.label: apparent authority
terms.gloss: An agent's power to bind the person or company it acts for, because that party led an outsider to reasonably believe the agent had permission, even though it did not.

terms.label: appeal
terms.gloss: Asking a higher court to review a lower court's decision for legal error; the higher court may affirm (uphold), reverse, or vacate (set aside) it, often remanding for further proceedings.

terms.label: appealable
terms.gloss: Able to be appealed now. Most court orders become appealable only when the case ends in a final judgment.

terms.label: appearance (special or general)
terms.gloss: Formally taking part in a case before a court. A special appearance contests the court's power over the defendant without accepting it; a general appearance accepts that power.

terms.label: appellant
terms.gloss: The party that brings an appeal, usually the one that lost below; the opposing party is the appellee (or respondent).

terms.label: appellate court
terms.gloss: Relating to appeals: an appellate court reviews a lower court's decision for legal error on the existing record rather than holding a new trial.

terms.label: Appellate Division (New York)
terms.gloss: New York's intermediate appeals court, which reviews trial-court rulings; above it is the New York Court of Appeals, the state's highest court.

terms.label: appellate jurisdiction
terms.gloss: A court's power to review and revise another court's decision, as opposed to original jurisdiction to hear a case first.

terms.label: appellee
terms.gloss: The party responding to an appeal, usually the side that won in the lower court. The party bringing the appeal is the appellant.

terms.label: Appointments Clause
terms.gloss: The constitutional provision on filling federal offices: the President appoints principal officers with Senate consent, and Congress may let the President, courts, or department heads appoint lesser officers.

terms.label: appropriation
terms.gloss: A law in which a legislature sets aside public money for a particular purpose; under the Constitution, federal money may be spent only as Congress appropriates it.

terms.label: arbitrability
terms.gloss: Whether a particular dispute falls within an agreement to arbitrate, and so must go to an arbitrator instead of a court.

terms.label: arbitrary and capricious (review)
terms.gloss: The usual test courts apply to agency decisions: the agency must have considered the relevant factors and explained a rational link between the facts and its choice.

terms.label: arbitration
terms.gloss: Resolving a dispute outside court before a private decision-maker (an arbitrator) chosen by the parties, usually under a contract clause; the award is usually binding and courts review it very narrowly.

terms.label: arising under (federal-question jurisdiction)
terms.context: \b(aris(ing|es|e)|arose) under (federal law|the Constitution|the laws of the United States|federal|a federal|treat(y|ies))|well-pleaded|\b1331\b
terms.gloss: Describes a case whose claim is created by federal law or necessarily depends on a substantial federal question. Federal courts may hear such cases.

terms.label: arm's length
terms.gloss: Describes a deal between independent parties each acting in its own interest, with no special relationship or duty to look out for the other.

terms.label: arrears
terms.gloss: Overdue payments that were owed and not paid on time, such as unpaid child support.

terms.label: Article I
terms.gloss: The part of the Constitution that creates Congress, lists its powers, and sets the steps for making a law: passage by both houses and presentment to the President.

terms.label: Article I court (legislative court)
terms.gloss: A tribunal Congress creates outside the regular federal judiciary, such as the Tax Court, whose judges lack life tenure. The cases it may decide are limited.

terms.label: Article II
terms.gloss: The part of the Constitution that creates the presidency, giving the President executive power, the power to appoint officers, and the duty to see the laws faithfully carried out.

terms.label: Article III
terms.gloss: The part of the U.S. Constitution that creates the federal courts and limits them to real 'cases' and 'controversies', so a plaintiff there must show an actual injury.

terms.label: as-applied challenge
terms.gloss: A claim that a law is unconstitutional only as used against this particular person or conduct, leaving it enforceable in other situations.

terms.label: as is
terms.gloss: Sold in its present condition: the buyer takes the property with any defects, and the seller makes no promises about its quality.

terms.label: assault
terms.gloss: Intentionally threatening or attempting violence so that someone fears immediate harmful contact; it is both a crime and a civil wrong. Many criminal codes also use the word for actually injuring someone.

terms.label: assent
terms.gloss: Agreement to a contract's terms, shown by words or conduct and judged by how a reasonable person in the other party's position would understand it.

terms.label: assign (transfer a right)
terms.gloss: To transfer a right one holds, such as a right to payment under a contract or a legal claim, to someone else (the assignee), who can then enforce it.

terms.label: assignment (of rights)
terms.gloss: A transfer of a contract right or other legal claim from its holder (the assignor) to someone else (the assignee), who can then enforce it.

terms.label: assignment of income
terms.gloss: A tax doctrine that income is taxed to whoever earns it or owns the property producing it, even if the right to receive it is handed to someone else, such as a relative.

terms.label: assizes
terms.gloss: Periodic court sessions held in English counties by judges traveling from London on circuit, to try civil and criminal cases before local juries.

terms.label: associational standing
terms.gloss: An organization's right to sue on behalf of its members when they could sue themselves, the case relates to the group's purpose, and individual members need not take part.

terms.label: assume without deciding
terms.gloss: When a court accepts a point as true for argument's sake, without ruling on it, because the case comes out the same either way.

terms.label: assumpsit
terms.gloss: An old common-law lawsuit for breaking a promise or for money owed. It developed into the modern claims for breach of contract and for restitution.

terms.label: assumption of risk
terms.gloss: A defense that the injured person knowingly and voluntarily accepted a known danger, which can reduce or bar their recovery.

terms.label: at home (general jurisdiction)
terms.gloss: The test for general jurisdiction: a corporation may be sued on any claim only where its ties make it essentially at home, normally its state of incorporation or principal place of business.

terms.label: at law (vs. in equity)
terms.gloss: Belonging to the historic courts of law, which mainly awarded money damages and used juries, as opposed to courts of equity, which issued orders like injunctions without juries.

terms.label: at will
terms.gloss: Able to be ended by either side at any time, for a good reason, a bad reason, or none, though not for an illegal reason such as discrimination. Most U.S. jobs are at will by default.

terms.label: attachment (of property)
terms.gloss: A court order seizing or freezing a defendant's property, often before trial, so it can later pay a judgment or give the court power over the case.

terms.label: attaint (writ)
terms.gloss: An old English writ for challenging a jury's false verdict before a larger jury of twenty-four. If it succeeded, the verdict was reversed and the original jurors were punished.

terms.label: attestation
terms.gloss: Formal witnessing or certification that a document was properly signed or is authentic.

terms.label: attorney-client privilege
terms.gloss: The rule protecting confidential communications between a lawyer and client, made to get legal advice, from forced disclosure.

terms.label: attorney's fees
terms.gloss: Money paid for a lawyer's work. Under the American rule each side pays its own, unless a statute, contract, or court rule shifts fees to the other side.

terms.label: attorney general
terms.gloss: The chief lawyer of a government: the U.S. Attorney General heads the Justice Department, and each state has its own attorney general.

terms.label: Attorney General's Manual on the APA
terms.gloss: A 1947 Justice Department guide to the Administrative Procedure Act, which courts often consult as an authoritative early reading of the statute.

terms.label: attorney-in-fact
terms.gloss: Someone authorized in writing to act for another person, usually under a power of attorney. Not necessarily a lawyer.

terms.label: auditor (court-appointed)
terms.gloss: A person a court appoints to examine complicated accounts, hear witnesses and report preliminary findings. The judge or jury still makes the final decision.

terms.label: Auer deference
terms.gloss: Courts' practice of accepting an agency's reasonable reading of its own ambiguous regulation. Kisor v. Wilkie (2019) kept it but limited it to genuinely ambiguous rules.

terms.label: authentication
terms.gloss: Showing that a document or item is genuine, what it is claimed to be; also, signing or otherwise adopting a record to show it is yours.

terms.label: automatic stay
terms.gloss: The freeze on most collection efforts and lawsuits against a debtor that takes effect automatically, without a court order, as soon as a bankruptcy case is filed.

terms.label: award
terms.gloss: A sum of money or other relief that a court, jury, or arbitrator orders one party to give another; in arbitration, the arbitrator's final decision itself.

terms.label: back pay
terms.gloss: Wages an employee should have earned but did not because of an unlawful firing or discrimination, which a court or agency can order the employer to pay.

terms.label: bad faith
terms.gloss: Dishonest or deliberately improper conduct, such as knowingly pressing a baseless claim or refusing an obligation without reason; it can justify sanctions, fee awards, or extra damages.

terms.label: bail
terms.gloss: Money or conditions a court sets so an arrested person can be released before trial while ensuring they come back to court; the Eighth Amendment bars excessive bail.

terms.label: bailment
terms.gloss: Handing personal property to someone to hold for a purpose, such as storage or shipping, without giving up ownership. The holder is the bailee; the owner is the bailor.

terms.label: balloon payment
terms.gloss: A large final payment that pays off the rest of a loan or purchase price after a series of smaller installments.

terms.label: bankruptcy
terms.gloss: A federal court process for people or businesses that cannot pay their debts. Assets are either sold to pay creditors or the debts are reorganized, and remaining debt is usually discharged (wiped out).

terms.label: bankruptcy court
terms.gloss: A unit of each federal district court that hears bankruptcy cases; its judges serve 14-year terms without Article III protections, which limits what they may finally decide (Stern v. Marshall).

terms.label: bankruptcy estate
terms.gloss: All the debtor's property interests when a bankruptcy case begins, gathered into one estate administered under the bankruptcy court's supervision to pay creditors.

terms.label: preference (bankruptcy)
terms.gloss: A payment a debtor made to a creditor shortly before bankruptcy, usually within 90 days, that the bankruptcy trustee can take back to share fairly among all creditors.

terms.label: bar (to a claim)
terms.gloss: To bar a claim is to block it legally, as a deadline, an earlier judgment, or an immunity can. The blocking rule itself is called a bar.

terms.label: bargain (contract)
terms.gloss: An agreement in which each side gives something in exchange for the other's promise or performance; in contract law a bargained-for exchange supplies consideration.

terms.label: bargaining unit
terms.gloss: A group of employees with shared job interests that a single union represents in negotiating with an employer, as determined under labor law.

terms.label: Baron (judge)
terms.gloss: The title of a judge of the old English Court of Exchequer.

terms.label: basic assumption
terms.gloss: A fact or condition both parties took for granted when contracting. If it was mistaken, or an unexpected event destroys it, mistake, impracticability, or frustration may excuse performance.

terms.label: Batson challenge
terms.gloss: An objection that the other side used peremptory strikes to remove jurors because of race; under Batson v. Kentucky the striking party must then give a race-neutral reason.

terms.label: bearer (instrument)
terms.gloss: Whoever holds a bond, note, or check made payable 'to bearer' rather than to a named person. Such paper can be transferred just by handing it over.

terms.label: below (the lower court)
terms.gloss: Lawyers' shorthand for the lower court or earlier stage of the same case: an argument "raised below" was first made to the trial court or agency.

terms.label: bench trial
terms.gloss: A trial decided by a judge alone, with no jury, so the judge finds the facts as well as applying the law.

terms.label: beneficial interest
terms.gloss: The right to enjoy property's benefits, such as its use or income, even though someone else, like a trustee or nominal holder, holds the legal title.

terms.label: beneficiary
terms.gloss: Someone entitled to benefits under a trust, will, insurance policy, or contract, often while another person (such as a trustee) controls the property; loosely, anyone a law is meant to help.

terms.label: bequeath
terms.gloss: To give property, traditionally personal property such as money or belongings, to someone in a will; the gift is called a bequest.

terms.label: bequest
terms.gloss: A gift of personal property, such as money or belongings, made by will; to "bequeath" is to leave property that way.

terms.label: best efforts / reasonable efforts
terms.gloss: A contract duty, express or implied, to try diligently and in good faith to achieve the agreement's goal, without promising success.

terms.label: bicameralism
terms.gloss: The requirement that both houses of Congress, the House and the Senate, pass the same bill before it goes to the President and can become law.

terms.label: bilateral contract
terms.gloss: A contract formed by an exchange of promises, each side promising to do something, unlike a unilateral contract, which is accepted by performing.

terms.label: bilateral monopoly
terms.gloss: A market with only one possible seller and one possible buyer, such as an injunction holder and the party bound by it bargaining over a release; such bargaining often breaks down.

terms.label: bill (in equity)
terms.gloss: The old name for the plaintiff's opening pleading in a court of equity, roughly what is now called a complaint.

terms.label: bill (legislation)
terms.gloss: A proposed law introduced in a legislature. It becomes a statute only if both houses pass it and the President or governor signs it, or a veto is overridden.

terms.label: bill of attainder
terms.gloss: A law that singles out a named person or group and punishes them without a trial. The Constitution forbids both Congress and the states to pass one.

terms.label: bill of exceptions
terms.gloss: Exceptions are formal objections to a trial judge's rulings, or to a court-appointed official's report; a bill of exceptions sets them out in writing so a higher court can review them.

terms.label: bill of exchange
terms.gloss: A signed written order directing someone to pay a fixed sum of money to another, on demand or on a set date. A check is a modern example.

terms.label: bill of lading
terms.gloss: A document a carrier gives a shipper listing goods accepted for transport; it serves as a receipt and can control who may claim the goods.

terms.label: bill of particulars
terms.gloss: A more detailed written statement of the charges or claims, which a court can order so the other side knows exactly what it must answer or defend against.

terms.label: Bill of Rights
terms.gloss: The first ten amendments to the Constitution, protecting individual rights such as speech, jury trial, and due process.

terms.label: bill of sale
terms.gloss: A written document that transfers ownership of goods from seller to buyer.

terms.label: binder (insurance)
terms.gloss: A short, temporary insurance contract giving coverage right away until the full policy is issued.

terms.label: block grant
terms.gloss: A lump sum of federal money given to a state for a general purpose, leaving the state wide freedom in how it runs the program.

terms.label: boilerplate
terms.gloss: Standardized, preprinted contract language used over and over, such as the fine print on the back of a form.

terms.label: bona fide
terms.gloss: Latin for 'in good faith': genuine and honest. A bona fide purchaser buys for value without notice of others' claims and is often protected against them.

terms.label: bond
terms.gloss: A written promise, often backed by a surety, to pay a sum if an obligation is not met, such as one a litigant posts to cover the other side's losses.

terms.label: breach
terms.gloss: Failing to do what a contract or legal duty requires, without a legal excuse. A breach gives the other side a right to a remedy, such as damages.

terms.label: breach of contract
terms.gloss: Failing, without legal excuse, to perform a promise in an enforceable contract. The usual remedy is money damages that leave the injured party as well off as performance would have.

terms.label: breach of promise to marry
terms.gloss: An old lawsuit against a person who broke off an engagement to marry, treating the engagement as a binding promise; many states have since abolished it.

terms.label: breach of warranty
terms.gloss: A claim that goods or property did not live up to a promise about their quality or condition, whether the seller made the promise or the law implied it.

terms.label: brief (written argument)
terms.gloss: A party's written argument to a court, setting out the facts and legal reasons for the ruling it wants. 'Briefing' is the exchange of these papers.

terms.label: bubble concept
terms.gloss: An EPA approach treating a whole plant as one pollution source, as if under a bubble, so changes inside it need no new permit unless total emissions rise.

terms.label: bucket shop
terms.gloss: An illegal business, common around 1900, that took bets on stock or commodity price changes without actually buying or selling anything.

terms.label: burden of persuasion
terms.gloss: A party's duty to convince the factfinder that its version is true to the required degree, such as more likely than not. If the evidence is evenly balanced, that party loses.

terms.label: burden of production
terms.gloss: A party's duty to offer enough evidence on a point for the factfinder to consider it; otherwise the judge can decide the point against them. It can shift between sides.

terms.label: burden of proof
terms.gloss: A party's duty to prove a disputed fact, by producing evidence and persuading the factfinder. If the evidence leaves the factfinder unconvinced, that party loses on the point.

terms.label: business efficacy
terms.gloss: The principle, from the English case The Moorcock, that a court may imply a contract term the parties left out if it is needed to make the deal work as they plainly intended.

terms.label: business-records exception
terms.gloss: A rule letting records kept in the regular course of business be used as evidence, despite the usual bar on out-of-court statements, if a qualified witness or certification shows how they were kept.

terms.label: but-for cause
terms.gloss: A cause without which the result would not have happened: if the act had not occurred, the harm would not have occurred either.

terms.label: by operation of law
terms.gloss: Automatically, because a legal rule says so, without anyone agreeing to it or taking any action.

terms.label: bylaws
terms.gloss: The internal rules a corporation or other organization adopts to run its affairs, such as how directors are chosen and when officers are indemnified.

terms.label: cancellation of removal
terms.gloss: Immigration relief letting certain noncitizens in deportation proceedings stay and become lawful permanent residents if they meet strict requirements.

terms.label: canon of construction
terms.gloss: A standard rule of thumb judges use to interpret legal texts, such as giving every word effect or reading unclear contract terms against the drafter.

terms.label: capable of repetition, yet evading review
match: capable of repetition, yet evading review
capable of repetition yet evading review
terms.gloss: An exception to mootness (a dispute that has ended, so a ruling would change nothing): courts may still decide disputes too brief to finish in court that are likely to recur for the same party.

terms.label: capacity (legal)
terms.gloss: The legal ability to do a binding legal act, such as make a contract or will, or bring a suit. Minors and people with serious mental impairments may lack it.

terms.label: capital offense
terms.gloss: A crime for which the death penalty may be imposed.

terms.label: capital punishment
terms.gloss: The death penalty: execution as punishment for a crime; a capital case is one where death is a possible sentence.

terms.label: caption
terms.gloss: The heading of a court filing or opinion that names the court, the parties, and the case number, such as 'Smith v. Jones.'

terms.label: capture (prize)
terms.gloss: The wartime seizure of a ship at sea by the captors; courts decided whether a capture was lawful or whether the captors owed the owner damages.

terms.label: case or controversy
terms.gloss: Article III's limit that federal courts decide only real, live disputes between parties with a genuine stake in the outcome, not hypothetical questions or requests for advice.

terms.label: cash on delivery
terms.gloss: Payment terms requiring the buyer to pay when the goods are delivered, so payment and delivery happen at the same time.

terms.label: cashier’s check
terms.gloss: A check a bank draws on its own funds, so the bank itself guarantees payment rather than the customer's account.

terms.label: cassation
terms.gloss: Review by France's highest court for civil and criminal cases, or a similar civil-law court, limited to errors of law. It can annul a lower judgment and send the case to another court.

terms.label: catchall (residual clause)
terms.gloss: General words, often at the end of a list in a statute or contract, such as "or other," meant to cover similar things not specifically named.

terms.label: causation
terms.gloss: The required link between a defendant's conduct and the plaintiff's harm, usually both factual cause (the harm would not have happened otherwise) and proximate, or legal, cause.

terms.label: cause of action
terms.gloss: A recognized legal basis for suing: a set of facts that, if proven, entitles the plaintiff to a court-ordered remedy. One complaint can plead several.

terms.label: censure
terms.gloss: A formal public reprimand, such as a court's official condemnation of a lawyer's misconduct, imposed as a sanction.

terms.label: reasonable certainty (damages)
terms.gloss: The rule that damages must be proved with reasonable certainty; losses that are mere guesswork are "speculative" and cannot be recovered.

terms.label: certified question
terms.gloss: A legal question one court formally sends to another, usually a state's highest court, to answer before the sending court decides the case, typically because no clear precedent exists.

terms.label: certiorari
terms.gloss: A higher court's order agreeing to review a lower court's decision. The U.S. Supreme Court grants it to choose the small share of cases it will hear.

terms.label: cession
terms.gloss: A formal transfer of land or governing authority, such as a tribe giving up land to the United States by treaty.

terms.label: challenge for cause
terms.gloss: A request to remove a potential juror for a specific reason, such as bias or a tie to a party. Unlike peremptory challenges, which need no reason, they are unlimited in number.

terms.label: challenge to the array
terms.gloss: An objection to the whole pool of potential jurors, claiming it was assembled improperly, rather than an objection to any single juror.

terms.label: chancellor (equity judge)
terms.gloss: The judge of a court of equity (chancery), which grants remedies like injunctions rather than money damages. Some states, such as Delaware, still use the title.

terms.label: chancery
terms.gloss: A court of equity, which historically gave remedies such as injunctions that ordinary law courts could not. England's Court of Chancery was the model; Delaware still has one.

terms.label: change of position
terms.gloss: Reliance that alters a party's situation, such as spending money or giving up rights. It can make undoing a deal unfair and can support estoppel.

terms.label: changes-being-effected (CBE) regulation
terms.gloss: An FDA rule letting a drug maker strengthen its label warning right away, before FDA approval, based on newly acquired information, subject to FDA later rejecting the change.

terms.label: Chapter 11 bankruptcy
terms.gloss: The part of the Bankruptcy Code under which a business usually keeps operating while it reorganizes its debts under a court-approved plan.

terms.label: Chapter 93A
terms.gloss: Massachusetts's consumer-protection statute, which forbids unfair or deceptive business practices and allows damages, sometimes multiplied, plus attorney's fees.

terms.label: charitable trust
terms.gloss: A trust for a public purpose, such as education, research, or relief of poverty, rather than for particular people; the state attorney general can enforce it.

terms.label: chattel
terms.gloss: Movable personal property, such as goods or animals, as opposed to land and buildings.

terms.label: checks and balances
terms.gloss: The constitutional design giving each branch of government ways to limit the others, such as the presidential veto, Senate confirmation, and judicial review.

terms.label: Chenery doctrine
terms.gloss: The rule that a court judges an agency action only by the reasons the agency gave when it acted, not by new reasons its lawyers offer later.

terms.label: Chenery II
terms.gloss: SEC v. Chenery Corp. (1947): an agency may announce new policy through case-by-case adjudication instead of rulemaking, a choice largely left to its informed discretion.

terms.label: Chevron deference
terms.gloss: The former rule that courts accept an agency's reasonable reading of an unclear statute it administers. The Supreme Court overruled it in Loper Bright (2024).

terms.label: Chevron step one and step two
terms.gloss: Under the Chevron test, overruled in 2024, step one asked whether Congress had clearly answered the question; if not, step two asked whether the agency's reading was reasonable.

terms.label: child support
terms.gloss: Money a parent is legally required to pay toward a child's living expenses, usually under a court order or separation agreement.

terms.label: chilling effect
terms.gloss: The discouragement of lawful activity, especially free speech, caused by fear of legal consequences.

terms.label: choice of law
terms.gloss: The rules a court uses to decide which state's or country's law governs a dispute. A choice-of-law clause is the contracting parties' own pick.

terms.label: c.i.f. (cost, insurance, and freight)
terms.gloss: A shipping term: the price covers the goods plus insurance and freight to a named destination port. The seller performs by shipping the goods and handing over the shipping documents.

terms.label: circuit
terms.gloss: One of the thirteen federal appeals courts (the First through Eleventh, D.C. and Federal Circuits); "the Ninth Circuit" means that region's court of appeals.

terms.label: circuit court
terms.gloss: In many states, the main trial court. Until 1912 the federal system also had circuit courts, trial courts separate from today's federal courts of appeals.

terms.label: circuit split
terms.gloss: Disagreement among federal courts of appeals on the same legal question; resolving such conflicts is a main reason the Supreme Court agrees to hear a case.

terms.label: circumstantial evidence
terms.gloss: Evidence that proves a fact indirectly, by supporting an inference, rather than through direct observation. It can be as convincing as direct evidence.

terms.label: CISG (U.N. Sales Convention)
match: convention on contracts for the international sale of goods
terms.gloss: The U.N. Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods, a treaty governing sale-of-goods contracts between businesses in different member countries unless they opt out.

terms.label: citizenship (for diversity)
terms.context: \b((alabama|alaska|arizona|arkansas|california|colorado|connecticut|delaware|florida|georgia|hawaii|idaho|illinois|indiana|iowa|kansas|kentucky|louisiana|maine|maryland|massachusetts|michigan|minnesota|mississippi|missouri|montana|nebraska|nevada|new hampshire|new jersey|new mexico|new york|north carolina|north dakota|ohio|oklahoma|oregon|pennsylvania|rhode island|south carolina|south dakota|tennessee|texas|utah|vermont|virginia|washington|west virginia|wisconsin|wyoming|delaware|district of columbia|state)\W+(citizens?|citizenship)|(citizens?|citizenship) of (alabama|alaska|arizona|arkansas|california|colorado|connecticut|delaware|florida|georgia|hawaii|idaho|illinois|indiana|iowa|kansas|kentucky|louisiana|maine|maryland|massachusetts|michigan|minnesota|mississippi|missouri|montana|nebraska|nevada|new hampshire|new jersey|new mexico|new york|north carolina|north dakota|ohio|oklahoma|oregon|pennsylvania|rhode island|south carolina|south dakota|tennessee|texas|utah|vermont|virginia|washington|west virginia|wisconsin|wyoming|delaware|district of columbia|state)|divers\w*|domicil\w*|1332|incorporat\w*|principal place of business|removal|remov\w*|nerve center|forum[- ]defendant|citizen of (a|another|the same|different|any|each|both|its|that)|citizens of (different|the same|another|a different|both|each)|complete|alienage|subject matter jurisdiction|subject-matter jurisdiction|federal jurisdiction|amount in controversy)\b
terms.gloss: For diversity jurisdiction, a person is a citizen of the state where they are domiciled; a corporation is a citizen of its state of incorporation and of its principal place of business.

terms.label: civil case
terms.gloss: A lawsuit to enforce private or public rights, usually for money damages, an injunction, or a civil penalty, as opposed to a criminal prosecution brought by the government to punish a crime.

terms.label: civil code
terms.gloss: A state's comprehensive written collection of private-law statutes on subjects like contracts, property and family; California's Civil Code is an example.

terms.label: civil law (legal system)
terms.gloss: The legal system of continental Europe and Latin America, descended from Roman law and based on comprehensive written codes rather than judge-made precedent.

terms.label: civil liability
terms.gloss: Responsibility to pay damages or provide another remedy in a private lawsuit, as distinct from criminal punishment.

terms.label: civil penalty
terms.gloss: A money penalty for violating a statute or regulation, imposed by a court or agency in a civil rather than criminal proceeding.

terms.label: civil rights
terms.gloss: Legal guarantees of equal treatment and personal freedom, and the statutes enforcing them, such as 42 U.S.C. § 1983, which lets people sue state and local officials who violate constitutional rights.

terms.label: claim preclusion (res judicata)
terms.gloss: The rule that a final judgment on the merits bars the same parties from suing again on the same claim, including grounds they could have raised the first time.

terms.label: claimant
terms.gloss: The person or business making a claim, whether in a lawsuit, an arbitration, an insurance or benefits proceeding, or against an estate or fund; often the counterpart of a plaintiff.

terms.label: claim
terms.gloss: A demand for a legal remedy resting on a set of facts and a legal theory, such as a breach-of-contract or negligence claim; one lawsuit can contain several claims.

terms.label: class action
terms.gloss: A lawsuit in which one or a few people sue on behalf of a larger group with similar claims. Once a court certifies the class, the judgment generally binds its members.

terms.label: Class Action Fairness Act (CAFA)
terms.gloss: A 2005 statute opening federal court to class actions over $5 million with at least 100 members whenever any class member and any defendant are citizens of different states, with some exceptions.

terms.label: class arbitration
terms.gloss: Arbitration in which one claimant proceeds on behalf of a group, like a class action; the Supreme Court allows it only where the parties affirmatively agreed to it.

terms.label: class certification
terms.gloss: A court's order letting a lawsuit proceed as a class action, after finding the proposed class and its representatives meet Rule 23's requirements. Decertification undoes that order.

terms.label: class period
terms.gloss: In a securities class action, the span of time during which investors bought or sold the stock and so are included in the class.

terms.label: Clayton Act
terms.gloss: A 1914 federal antitrust statute. Its Section 4 lets a person injured by an antitrust violation sue for three times its actual damages plus attorney fees.

terms.label: Clean Air Act
terms.gloss: The main federal air-pollution law, under which EPA sets national air-quality standards and states write plans to meet them.

terms.label: clear and convincing evidence
terms.gloss: A middle standard of proof: the claim must be shown to be highly probable, more than 'more likely than not' but less than beyond a reasonable doubt.

terms.label: clear evidence (preemption)
terms.gloss: The Wyeth v. Levine standard: a state failure-to-warn claim is preempted only by clear evidence that FDA would have rejected the warning; Merck made this a question for the judge.

terms.label: clear-statement rule
terms.gloss: A rule that courts will not read a statute to produce a major result, such as overriding states' traditional powers or waiving immunity, unless Congress said so in unmistakable terms.

terms.label: clearly erroneous (clear error)
terms.gloss: A deferential standard for reviewing a trial judge's findings of fact: the appeals court keeps them unless it is firmly convinced a mistake was made.

terms.label: clearly established law
terms.gloss: The qualified-immunity test: an official is liable only if existing case law made it clear to a reasonable official that the specific conduct was unlawful.

terms.label: clickwrap agreement
terms.gloss: An online agreement formed when a user clicks a button such as "I agree" after being shown the terms.

terms.label: closely drawn
terms.gloss: The test for campaign contribution limits: the government must show a sufficiently important interest and limits closely drawn to avoid needlessly restricting free association.

terms.label: closing (real estate)
terms.gloss: The final step of a sale, especially of real estate, when the buyer pays the price and the seller hands over the deed or other transfer documents.

terms.label: closing argument
terms.gloss: Each side's final speech to the judge or jury after the evidence is in, explaining why the evidence supports its position.

terms.label: Code of Federal Regulations
terms.gloss: The official collection of federal agencies' final regulations, organized by subject into numbered titles; '12 C.F.R. § 560.2' means title 12, section 560.2.

terms.label: codefendant
terms.gloss: One of two or more defendants sued or charged together in the same case.

terms.label: codicil
terms.gloss: A later written amendment to a will that adds to or changes it without replacing it.

terms.label: codify / uncodified
terms.gloss: To codify is to write rules into a statute or code, often restating earlier case law; an uncodified provision is enacted law left out of the official code.

terms.label: cognizable
terms.gloss: Recognized by law as a kind of claim or harm that a court can hear and remedy.

terms.label: cognizance
terms.gloss: An older word for a court's authority to hear and decide a particular kind of case, close to what is now called subject-matter jurisdiction.

terms.label: collateral attack
terms.gloss: A challenge to a judgment made in a separate, later case rather than by appeal. It usually succeeds only for basic defects, such as the first court's lack of jurisdiction.

terms.label: collateral order doctrine
terms.gloss: A narrow exception to waiting for the end of a case to appeal: an important, conclusive ruling, separate from the main dispute, that could not be fixed later can be appealed at once.

terms.label: security (for a debt)
terms.gloss: Collateral or a guarantee, such as a mortgage, pledge, bond or co-signer, given to make sure a debt or obligation will be paid.

terms.label: collective action (FLSA)
terms.gloss: A group lawsuit by workers for unpaid wages under the Fair Labor Standards Act. Unlike a class action, each worker must opt in by filing written consent.

terms.label: collective bargaining
terms.gloss: Negotiation between an employer and a union representing its workers over wages and working conditions; the resulting collective-bargaining agreement binds both sides.

terms.label: collusion
terms.gloss: Secret cooperation between supposed adversaries, such as arranging a suit to create federal jurisdiction or a settlement that favors lawyers or defendants over absent class members.

terms.label: color of law
terms.gloss: Acting with the apparent authority of government, as an official does, even when misusing or exceeding that authority. Federal civil-rights suits under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 require action under color of state law.

terms.label: colorable
terms.gloss: Plausible or arguable on its face: strong enough to deserve serious consideration, even if it may not ultimately prove correct.

terms.label: Colorado River abstention
terms.gloss: A doctrine letting a federal court, in exceptional circumstances, pause or dismiss its case in favor of a parallel state-court suit over the same dispute.

terms.label: comity
terms.gloss: The respect one court or government gives to another's laws and decisions out of courtesy rather than legal obligation, such as federal restraint toward state courts.

terms.label: Commander in Chief
terms.gloss: The President's constitutional role as head of the armed forces (Article II, § 2), a source of military authority but not unlimited power at home.

terms.label: Commerce Clause
terms.gloss: Article I's grant of power to Congress to regulate commerce with foreign nations, among the states (interstate commerce), and with Indian tribes; the basis of much federal regulation.

terms.label: commercially reasonable
terms.gloss: Done the way a sensible businessperson in that trade would act; the UCC uses this standard for steps like a seller's resale after a buyer breaks the contract.

terms.label: commingling
terms.gloss: Mixing money or property that should be kept separate, such as a trustee's or lawyer's own funds with funds held for others.

terms.label: committed to agency discretion
match: committed to agency discretion by law
terms.gloss: A narrow exception to court review: some agency choices, such as whether to bring an enforcement action, are left to the agency because no legal standard exists to judge them by.

terms.label: committee report
terms.gloss: A written explanation of a bill by the congressional committee that studied it; courts consult it as legislative history to understand a statute's purpose.

terms.label: common carrier
terms.gloss: A business that offers to carry goods, passengers, or messages for the general public, and so must serve all comers on reasonable, nondiscriminatory terms.

terms.label: common law
terms.gloss: Law developed by judges through decisions in individual cases, rather than law enacted by a legislature.

terms.label: common nucleus of operative fact
terms.gloss: A shared core of facts underlying two claims. When a state claim and a federal claim share one, a federal court may hear both together.

terms.label: common plan or scheme
terms.gloss: An evidence-rule exception letting a prosecutor show other bad acts because they reveal one overall design the defendant followed, not merely bad character.

terms.label: commonality (Rule 23(a)(2))
terms.gloss: The class-action requirement that members share a common question whose answer will resolve an issue central to every member's claim in one stroke.

terms.label: Commonwealth (as a party)
terms.gloss: The official name of some states, such as Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, Kentucky and Virginia. In a criminal case, "the Commonwealth" is the prosecuting government, like "the State" or "the People."

terms.label: community property
terms.gloss: In some states, such as California and Arizona, property acquired during a marriage (other than by gift or inheritance), which belongs equally to both spouses no matter who earned it.

terms.label: companion case
terms.gloss: A separate case decided by the same court at the same time as a related one, often argued together and raising the same or overlapping issues.

terms.label: comparable sales
terms.gloss: An appraisal method that values property by the prices paid for similar properties sold around the same time and place.

terms.label: comparative fault
terms.gloss: Dividing responsibility for harm by percentage among the parties, including the injured person, instead of letting any fault by the plaintiff bar recovery entirely.

terms.label: compensatory damages
terms.gloss: Money meant to make up for the actual loss or harm the plaintiff suffered, as opposed to money meant to punish the wrongdoer.

terms.label: competent evidence
terms.gloss: Evidence the law allows a court to consider because it is relevant and admissible. 'Competent' here does not mean skilled or convincing.

terms.label: complainant
terms.gloss: The person who brings a complaint to a court, agency, or police; in a criminal case, the alleged victim who reported the crime; in old equity practice, the plaintiff.

terms.label: complaint
terms.gloss: The document a plaintiff files to start a lawsuit, setting out the facts, the legal claims, and what the plaintiff asks the court to order.

terms.label: complete defense
terms.gloss: A defense that, if proved, defeats the claim entirely, rather than only reducing the damages or liability.

terms.label: composition with creditors
terms.gloss: An agreement between a debtor and several creditors that each will accept a partial payment as full settlement. The creditors' promises to one another supply the consideration.

terms.label: compromise
terms.gloss: To settle a disputed claim by agreement, each side giving up part of what it wanted, so the dispute ends without a court deciding who was right.

terms.label: compulsory counterclaim
terms.gloss: A defendant's claim against the plaintiff arising from the same transaction or events. It must be raised in the same lawsuit or it is usually lost.

terms.label: compulsory joinder
terms.gloss: The rule (Federal Rule 19) requiring certain absent persons to be added to a lawsuit when it cannot fairly go on without them; if they cannot be added, it may be dismissed.

terms.label: concealment
terms.gloss: Actively hiding a material fact; in fraud law it can count as a misrepresentation, and fraudulently concealing a claim can pause the statute of limitations.

terms.label: concerted activity
terms.gloss: Employees acting together for mutual aid or protection, such as organizing a union or jointly raising workplace complaints. The National Labor Relations Act protects it from employer interference.

terms.label: conciliation
terms.gloss: An informal effort to settle a dispute, such as the EEOC's required attempt to persuade an employer to remedy discrimination before the agency sues.

terms.label: conclusion of law
terms.gloss: A court's ruling on what the law requires, given the facts. At the pleading stage, bare legal conclusions in a complaint are not assumed true.

terms.label: conclusory
terms.gloss: Stating a conclusion, such as 'the defendant acted unlawfully,' without the specific facts that would support it. Courts give such statements little or no weight.

terms.label: concurrence (concurring opinion)
terms.gloss: A separate opinion by a judge who agrees with the result but adds or substitutes reasons. To concur is to agree with the result.

terms.label: concurrence in the judgment
match: concurred in part and in the judgment
concurred in the judgment in part
terms.gloss: A judge's vote agreeing with the outcome but not with the majority's reasoning, usually explained in a separate opinion. The judge does not join the majority's explanation.

terms.label: condemnation (taking of property)
terms.gloss: Not criticism: the government's forced taking of private property for a public use, such as a road, which the Constitution requires it to pay for fairly.

terms.label: condemnation (forfeiture)
terms.gloss: In admiralty and customs cases, a court's judgment declaring seized property, such as a ship or cargo, forfeited to the government or its captors. Not a taking for public use.

terms.label: condition (contract)
terms.gloss: In contract law, an event that must happen before a party has to perform, unless the condition is excused or waived; if it fails, the duty it guards never arises.

terms.label: condition precedent
terms.gloss: An event that must happen before a party's duty to perform under a contract arises. If it never occurs, the duty never becomes due.

terms.label: conditional acceptance
terms.gloss: A reply that agrees only if the offeror accepts new or different terms; it is treated as a counteroffer, not an acceptance.

terms.label: conditional legislation
terms.gloss: A law that takes effect, or changes, only when an official finds that a stated condition exists. It was an early way courts approved giving power to the executive.

terms.label: conditional privilege
terms.gloss: In defamation, a defense protecting statements made for a legitimate purpose, such as an employer explaining a firing. Unlike absolute privilege, it is lost if abused or made with malice.

terms.label: conference report
terms.gloss: A report from the joint House-Senate committee that settles differences between the two chambers' versions of a bill. Courts often treat it as especially reliable evidence of what Congress meant.

terms.label: confirm (an arbitration award)
terms.gloss: To turn an arbitrator's award into an enforceable court judgment, or to ask a court to do so.

terms.label: confiscatory
terms.gloss: Confiscation is taking private property without paying for it; a confiscatory rate or price is so low it effectively does the same, raising due-process or takings objections.

terms.label: conflict of interest
terms.gloss: A situation in which a lawyer, fiduciary, or official has competing loyalties or a personal stake that could compromise duties owed to another.

terms.label: confrontation (right)
terms.gloss: The right to face and cross-examine the witnesses against you. The Sixth Amendment guarantees it in criminal trials, and due process sometimes requires it at hearings.

terms.label: restitution of conjugal rights
terms.gloss: The rights spouses have to each other's company. An old English suit for 'restitution of conjugal rights' asked a court to order a spouse who had left to return.

terms.label: registration-based jurisdiction
terms.gloss: The theory, upheld in Mallory (2023), that where state law so provides, a company registering to do business in a state consents to be sued there on any claim.

terms.label: consent decree
terms.gloss: An order of a court or agency whose terms the parties agreed to, usually to settle a case. Unlike a private settlement, it can be enforced directly as an order.

terms.label: consent to jurisdiction
terms.gloss: A defendant's agreement, stated outright or implied from its conduct, to let a court exercise personal jurisdiction over it even without the usual connections to the forum.

terms.label: consent to suit
terms.gloss: Agreement to be sued: for a government, usually a statute waiving its sovereign immunity; for a private party, accepting a court's power to hear claims against it.

terms.label: consequential damages
terms.gloss: Compensation for indirect losses that flow from a breach, such as profits lost while a machine sat unrepaired. Recoverable only if foreseeable when the contract was made.

terms.label: conservatorship
terms.gloss: Putting a conservator, appointed by a court or a regulator, in charge of a person's or company's property and affairs to protect and manage them, as with a failing financial firm.

terms.label: consideration (contract)
terms.gloss: What each side gives or promises in exchange for the other's promise. Without such a bargained-for exchange, a promise usually is not an enforceable contract.

terms.label: consignment
terms.gloss: An arrangement in which an owner (consignor) delivers goods to another (consignee) to sell or carry, keeping ownership meanwhile; "consignee" also means simply the person a shipment is sent to.

terms.label: consolidation
terms.gloss: Combining related lawsuits so they are handled together for efficiency, while each keeps its own claims.

terms.label: conspicuous (contract term)
terms.gloss: Written or displayed so that a reasonable person would notice it, such as in large or bold type; some terms, like warranty disclaimers, count only if conspicuous.

terms.label: conspiracy
terms.gloss: An agreement between two or more people to do something unlawful; it can be a crime or, as in antitrust and civil-rights law, a basis for civil liability.

terms.label: constitutional avoidance
terms.gloss: The principle that when a statute can reasonably be read two ways, courts choose the reading that avoids serious doubts about its constitutionality.

terms.label: construction (interpretation)
terms.gloss: Interpretation: deciding what a statute, contract, or other legal text means and how it applies. Not building.
