terms.label: constructive discharge
terms.gloss: Treating an employee's resignation as a firing because the employer made working conditions so intolerable that a reasonable person would have felt forced to quit.

terms.label: constructive fraud
terms.gloss: Conduct the law treats as fraud even without intent to deceive, such as abusing a position of trust, or a debtor's transfer of property for too little value that harms creditors.

terms.label: constructive notice
terms.gloss: Knowledge the law treats a person as having because a reasonably careful person would have learned it, for example from a public record or posted terms, whether or not they did.

terms.label: constructive trust
terms.gloss: A court-ordered remedy, not a real trust: someone who wrongfully or unjustly obtained property must hold it for, and turn it over to, the person who should have it.

terms.label: construe
terms.gloss: To interpret a legal text, such as a statute or contract, and decide its meaning; "construed against the drafter" means doubts are resolved against whoever wrote it.

terms.label: consumer reporting agency
terms.gloss: Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, a business that compiles reports on people's credit or background and supplies them to others for lending, insurance, or hiring decisions.

terms.label: contempt of court
terms.gloss: Disobeying a court order or disrupting court. Civil contempt pressures someone to comply, such as daily fines until they obey; criminal contempt punishes past defiance.

terms.label: contingent fee
terms.gloss: A lawyer's fee payable only if the client wins, usually a percentage of the recovery.

terms.label: contingent interest
terms.gloss: A property interest that will take effect only if some uncertain condition is met, such as surviving another person.

terms.label: continuance
terms.gloss: A court's postponement of a hearing, trial, or deadline to a later date.

terms.label: continuing objection
terms.gloss: An objection a lawyer makes once to a whole line of questions or evidence, which the court treats as repeated each time, keeping the issue alive for appeal.

terms.label: contra proferentem
terms.gloss: A rule for reading contracts: an unclear term is interpreted against the party that drafted it.

terms.label: contraband
terms.gloss: Goods that are illegal to possess, import or export, such as illegal drugs or smuggled items. Police may seize contraband they find.

terms.label: contract
terms.gloss: A promise or set of promises the law will enforce, usually formed by offer, acceptance and consideration. "Contractual" means arising from or set by a contract.

terms.label: Contract Disputes Act
terms.gloss: The 1978 federal statute governing claims between the government and its contractors, decided first by a contracting officer, then by a contract appeals board or the Court of Federal Claims.

terms.label: contract formation
terms.gloss: The creation of a binding contract, generally requiring offer, acceptance and consideration (or a substitute), as distinct from later questions of performance.

terms.label: contract price
terms.gloss: The price the parties agreed to in their contract, the usual starting point for measuring damages and restitution.

terms.label: contribution (among wrongdoers)
terms.context: \bcontribution,? (or|and) indemn|indemn\w*,? (or|and) contribution|right (to|of) contribution|contribution claims?|bar on contribution|whether contribution|for contribution
terms.gloss: A defendant's right to make others responsible for the same harm pay their fair share of what it has paid, or must pay, the injured person. Not a donation.

terms.label: contribution limit
terms.gloss: A cap on how much a person or group may give to a candidate, party or committee. Buckley v. Valeo upheld such caps to prevent corruption and its appearance.

terms.label: contributory infringement
terms.gloss: Liability for knowingly helping someone else infringe, for example by intentionally inducing a buyer to misuse a trademark or by supplying products to someone known to be infringing.

terms.label: contributory negligence
terms.gloss: The plaintiff's own carelessness helping cause the injury. In a few places it still bars recovery entirely; most states now just reduce the award (comparative negligence).

terms.label: control-group test
terms.gloss: A rule limiting a corporation's attorney-client privilege to senior managers who control its response to legal advice; Upjohn rejected it and protected lower employees' communications too.

terms.label: conversion (tort)
terms.context: \b(fraud\w*|negligen\w*|contract|unjust enrichment|fiduciary|trespass|malpractice|tortious|infringement|replevin|unfair competition|misconduct|possessory|counterclaimed|breach|conversion (claims?|judgment|award|instruction|cases)|(malicious|fraudulent|willful) conversion|constituted conversion|defeated conversion|massachusetts conversion|conversion of (the|a) (horse|mature crop))\b
terms.gloss: Not a change of form: the civil wrong of seriously interfering with another person's movable property, such as taking, keeping, or destroying it as if it were your own. The owner can recover its value.

terms.label: convey / conveyance
terms.gloss: To convey is to transfer ownership of land or other property, usually by a deed. The transfer itself is a conveyance.

terms.label: conviction
terms.gloss: A court's formal judgment that a person is guilty of a crime, after a guilty plea or a guilty verdict.

terms.label: coordinated expenditure
terms.gloss: Spending made in cooperation with a candidate or campaign. The law treats it as a contribution, so contribution limits apply.

terms.label: copyright
terms.gloss: The legal right of an author or owner to control copying, publication, and adaptation of an original creative work, such as a book.

terms.label: corporate waste
terms.gloss: Directors' giving away company assets, or spending them for no real benefit, on terms no reasonable businessperson would accept. Shareholders may sue over it on the company's behalf.

terms.label: corporation
terms.gloss: A business entity created under state law that is a legal person separate from its shareholders; for diversity it is a citizen of its state of incorporation and its principal place of business.

terms.label: corpus (of a trust)
terms.gloss: The money or property held in a trust, which the trustee manages for the beneficiaries.

terms.label: corroborating evidence
terms.gloss: Evidence that supports or confirms other evidence, such as a document or another witness backing up a witness's account.

terms.label: cost-benefit analysis
terms.gloss: Weighing a regulation's expected costs against its expected benefits, often in dollar terms, to decide whether it is worth adopting.

terms.label: cost of completion
terms.gloss: A measure of contract damages: what it would cost to finish or fix the promised work, as opposed to how much the breach reduced the property's market value.

terms.label: costs (court costs)

terms.gloss: Court-related expenses, such as filing fees and transcript charges, that the losing party usually must repay the winner. They normally do not include lawyers' fees.

terms.label: cotenant
terms.gloss: One of two or more people who own or rent the same property at the same time, each entitled to use and possess the whole.

terms.label: counsel
terms.gloss: The lawyer or lawyers representing a party in a case; "counsel" is the formal word courts use.

terms.label: right to counsel of choice
terms.gloss: A party's qualified right to be represented by the lawyer it picks. Courts may override it, for example by disqualifying a lawyer for misconduct or a conflict of interest.

terms.label: counsel of record
terms.gloss: The lawyer formally listed in the court file as representing a party, who receives filings and answers to the court for the case.

terms.label: count (in a complaint or indictment)
terms.gloss: One separately stated claim in a complaint, or one separately charged crime in an indictment. Each count can succeed or fail on its own.

terms.label: counterclaim
terms.gloss: A claim a defendant brings against the plaintiff within the same lawsuit, making the defendant a plaintiff on that claim.

terms.label: counteroffer
terms.gloss: A reply to an offer that proposes different terms. It rejects the original offer, which can then no longer be accepted, and makes a new offer in its place.

terms.label: course of dealing
terms.gloss: The pattern of the parties' earlier transactions with each other, which courts use to interpret or fill gaps in their current contract.

terms.label: course of performance
terms.gloss: How the parties have actually carried out this contract on repeated occasions, which courts use as evidence of what its terms mean.

terms.label: court-martial
terms.gloss: A military court that tries members of the armed forces for offenses against military law, under the Uniform Code of Military Justice.

terms.label: court of appeals
terms.gloss: An intermediate appellate court; in the federal system, one of thirteen circuit courts between the district courts and the Supreme Court. New York's Court of Appeals is that state's highest court.

terms.label: Court of (Federal) Claims
terms.gloss: A federal court that hears money claims against the United States, such as contract and takings claims. Today's Court of Federal Claims succeeded the old Court of Claims.

terms.label: Court of Exchequer
terms.gloss: An old English common-law court, originally for royal revenue cases, which by the 1800s heard ordinary civil cases such as Hadley v. Baxendale.

terms.label: court of law
terms.gloss: A court of justice, as in the Constitution's Appointments Clause. Historically, a common-law court that awarded money damages with juries, as opposed to a court of equity (chancery).

terms.label: covenant
terms.gloss: A formal promise in a contract, deed, or lease to do or not do something, such as a promise not to compete or a loan agreement's financial conditions.

terms.label: cover (UCC § 2-712)
terms.context: \b2[.-]71[1-3]\b|substitute (goods|purchases)|between cover and|cover (price|damages|purchases|and)|proving cover|interest on cover|buyer covered
terms.gloss: A buyer's good-faith purchase of substitute goods after the seller fails to deliver. The buyer may then recover the extra cost over the contract price, plus other proven losses.

terms.label: coverture
terms.gloss: The old common-law rule that a married woman's legal identity merged into her husband's, limiting her power to own property, make contracts, or sue.

terms.label: cracking (gerrymandering)
terms.gloss: Drawing district lines that split a group of voters across several districts so they cannot form a majority anywhere.

terms.label: credibility
terms.gloss: Whether a witness should be believed. Deciding credibility is the job of the jury or trial judge, not an appeals court.

terms.label: creditor
terms.gloss: A person or business that is owed money; a judgment creditor is one who has won a court judgment for the debt and can enforce it.

terms.label: criminal intent
terms.gloss: The guilty state of mind a crime requires, such as purpose or knowledge, in addition to the wrongful act; also called mens rea.

terms.label: cross-appeal
terms.gloss: An appeal by the party on the other side of an appeal, asking the higher court to change parts of the decision that went against it.

terms.label: cross-claim
terms.gloss: A claim by one party against a co-party on the same side, such as one defendant suing another defendant, arising from the same events as the original case.

terms.label: cross-complaint
terms.gloss: In California and some other states, a pleading in which a defendant asserts its own claims within the same lawsuit, against the plaintiff, a co-defendant, or a new party.

terms.label: cross-examination
terms.gloss: Questioning of a witness by the opposing party to test their testimony; direct examination is questioning by the side that called the witness, and redirect follows cross.

terms.label: culpable
terms.gloss: Blameworthy. Culpability measures how much fault a person bears, from carelessness to deliberate wrongdoing.

terms.label: cure (a defect or breach)
terms.gloss: To fix a defect or breach so it no longer counts against a party, such as a seller replacing nonconforming goods (UCC § 2-508) or a party correcting a procedural defect.

terms.label: custody
terms.gloss: A parent's legal right and duty to care for a child, or the government's physical control over a detained person. It can also mean simply having control of property or evidence.

terms.label: cy pres
terms.gloss: French for "as near as possible": using leftover funds for the next-best purpose, such as giving unclaimed class settlement money to a charity tied to the class's interests.

terms.label: damages
terms.gloss: Money a court orders one party to pay another to make up for a legal wrong, such as a breach of contract or an injury.

terms.label: dangerous and unusual weapons
terms.gloss: Under District of Columbia v. Heller (2008), a category of weapons outside the Second Amendment's protection, which the government may ban or tightly regulate.

terms.label: de facto
terms.gloss: Latin for 'in fact': existing in reality even if not formally or legally recognized, as opposed to de jure, 'by law.'

terms.label: de facto officer doctrine
terms.gloss: A rule treating official acts as valid when done by someone holding an office under apparent authority, even if that person's appointment or election later proves defective.

terms.label: de minimis
terms.gloss: Latin for "about minimal things": too small or trivial for the law to take into account.

terms.label: de novo
terms.gloss: Latin for 'anew': a court reviewing a question de novo decides it fresh, giving no deference to the earlier decision.

terms.label: deadly force
terms.gloss: Force likely to cause death or serious injury; under Tennessee v. Garner, police may use it on a fleeing suspect only with probable cause that the suspect poses a significant threat of serious harm.

terms.label: debtor
terms.gloss: A person or business that owes money to another (the creditor); in bankruptcy, the person or company whose case it is.

terms.label: decedent
terms.gloss: A person who has died, especially one whose estate is being settled.

terms.label: deceit
terms.gloss: The civil wrong of fraud: knowingly misrepresenting a fact to induce someone to rely on it, where that person does rely and is harmed.

terms.label: declarant
terms.gloss: A person who made a statement offered as evidence, especially an out-of-court statement or a written sworn declaration; hearsay rules limit such statements because the declarant is not cross-examined.

terms.label: declaration (sworn statement)
terms.gloss: A written statement of facts that the signer declares true under penalty of perjury, usable as evidence in place of a sworn affidavit without a notary.

terms.label: declaration under penalty of perjury
terms.gloss: A signed written statement declared true under penalty of perjury; federal law lets it substitute for a sworn, notarized affidavit.

terms.label: declaratory judgment (relief)
terms.gloss: A court ruling that states the parties' legal rights or the meaning of a law or contract, without ordering anyone to pay or act.

terms.label: Declaratory Judgment Act
terms.gloss: The federal law letting courts declare the parties' legal rights in a real dispute without ordering damages; it adds a remedy but not new power to hear cases.

terms.label: decree
terms.gloss: A court's judgment or order, a word used especially in equity, divorce, and probate cases. A final decree ends the case in that court.

terms.label: dedication (of land)
terms.gloss: A landowner's gift of land, or a right to use it, to the public, such as a road, which becomes effective when the government accepts it.

terms.label: deed
terms.gloss: A signed written document that transfers ownership of land, or an interest in it, from one person (the grantor) to another (the grantee).

terms.label: deed in lieu of foreclosure
terms.gloss: A borrower's voluntary transfer of mortgaged property to the lender to settle the loan and avoid a foreclosure proceeding.

terms.label: deed of trust
terms.gloss: A document pledging real estate as security for a loan, used in some states instead of a mortgage. A neutral trustee can sell the property if the loan goes unpaid.

terms.label: deemed consent
terms.gloss: Consent the law treats as given because a party did certain things, even if it never actually agreed, such as consent to a court's jurisdiction triggered by specified activities.

terms.label: defamation
terms.gloss: A false statement of fact, communicated to others, that harms someone's reputation. Written forms are libel; spoken forms are slander.

terms.label: default
terms.gloss: Failing to do what a contract or the law requires, such as missing a loan payment or not answering a lawsuit. A defendant who defaults can lose by default judgment.

terms.label: default judgment
terms.gloss: A judgment entered against a defendant who failed to respond to the lawsuit or otherwise defend it, without a trial on the merits.

terms.label: default rule (gap filler)
terms.gloss: A rule that applies only when the parties, or lawmakers, have not provided otherwise. In contracts, such rules supply terms the agreement leaves open.

terms.label: defaulting (breaching) party
terms.gloss: The party who failed to perform its contract; traditionally it could not sue on the contract, though restitution may let it recover the value of benefits it provided.

terms.label: defendant
terms.gloss: The party being sued in a civil case, or the person charged with a crime in a criminal case.

terms.label: defense
terms.gloss: A reason a party sued or prosecuted should not be held liable, by denying the facts alleged or by showing an excuse such as consent or the statute of limitations; also, that side of a case.

terms.label: deference
terms.gloss: Giving weight to another decisionmaker's judgment, as when appeals courts respect a trial court's findings or courts accept an agency's reasonable reading.

terms.label: deficiency (debt)
terms.gloss: The part of a debt still unpaid after the lender takes back and sells the property securing it. A deficiency judgment makes the borrower personally liable for that remainder.

terms.label: delegation
terms.gloss: Handing authority to someone else, especially Congress giving an agency or the President power to act under a statute. The nondelegation doctrine limits how much Congress may hand off.

terms.label: demand note
terms.gloss: A promissory note payable whenever the holder asks for payment, rather than on a fixed date.

terms.label: demeanor (of a witness)
terms.gloss: A witness's manner while testifying, such as tone, hesitation and body language, which judges and juries may use in deciding whether to believe the witness.

terms.label: demise (lease)
terms.gloss: In property law, a lease or other transfer of the right to possess property for a time. Not death.

terms.label: demurrer
terms.gloss: A response arguing that even if the complaint's facts are true, they give no legal claim. Federal courts replaced it with the motion to dismiss; some states still use it.

terms.label: department head (Appointments Clause)
terms.gloss: The head of an executive department, such as a Cabinet secretary. The Appointments Clause lets Congress give department heads the power to appoint inferior officers.

terms.label: dependent / independent covenants
terms.gloss: Older terms for how contract promises relate. If dependent, one side must perform before demanding the other's performance; if independent, each must be performed regardless, so either side can sue without performing first.

terms.label: deportation
terms.gloss: The government's formal expulsion of a noncitizen from the country; current federal law calls it "removal."

terms.label: deposit receipt
terms.gloss: A real-estate form acknowledging a buyer's deposit and setting out the terms of the purchase, often serving as the written sale contract.

terms.label: deposition
terms.gloss: Sworn questioning of a witness or party by lawyers outside court before trial, recorded word for word, to gather facts and preserve testimony.

terms.label: derivative suit
terms.gloss: A suit a shareholder brings on the corporation's behalf to enforce the corporation's own rights when its managers will not. Any recovery generally goes to the corporation.

terms.label: descent
terms.gloss: The passing of a dead person's property to their heirs under inheritance law, rather than under a will.

terms.label: desertion
terms.gloss: Unjustified abandonment of a duty: in family law, a spouse's leaving the marriage (a traditional divorce ground); at sea, a sailor's leaving the ship mid-voyage.

terms.label: design defect
terms.gloss: In products liability, a flaw in a product's basic plan that makes every unit unreasonably dangerous, often shown by a safer, practical alternative design.

terms.label: detinue
terms.gloss: An old form of lawsuit to recover specific personal property that someone wrongfully keeps, or its value.

terms.label: detrimental reliance
terms.gloss: Reasonably acting, or not acting, in dependence on another's promise in a way that leaves you worse off. It can make a promise enforceable without a bargain (promissory estoppel).

terms.label: devise
terms.gloss: A gift made in a will, traditionally of land or buildings; the person receiving it is the devisee. Modern statutes often use the word for any gift by will.

terms.label: dictum (plural dicta)
terms.gloss: A remark in a judicial opinion that was not needed to decide the case, so later courts are not bound to follow it.

terms.label: dilatory
terms.gloss: Intended or tending to cause delay; dilatory tactics stall a case rather than address its merits, and courts can refuse or sanction them.

terms.label: diminution in value
terms.gloss: A way to measure damages by how much less the property or result is worth because of the breach, instead of what fixing it would cost.

terms.label: direct-action statute
terms.gloss: A state law, as in Louisiana, letting an injured person sue the wrongdoer's liability insurer directly, without first winning a judgment against the insured.

terms.label: direct appeal
terms.gloss: An appeal taken through the ordinary route from the judgment itself, sometimes straight to the Supreme Court, as opposed to a later collateral challenge or a petition for review.

terms.label: direct-benefit estoppel
terms.gloss: A rule that someone who never signed a contract, but knowingly takes a direct benefit under it, can be held to its terms, such as an arbitration clause.

terms.label: direct evidence
terms.gloss: Evidence that proves a fact by itself if believed, such as an eyewitness account or an open statement of motive, as opposed to circumstantial evidence, which requires an inference.

terms.label: directed judgment
terms.gloss: An order that judgment be entered for a party without a jury's decision because the evidence permits only one result, or an appeals court's instruction to enter it.

terms.label: directed verdict
terms.gloss: A judge's ruling that takes a case from the jury and decides it, because the evidence could reasonably support only one result. Federal courts now call it judgment as a matter of law.

terms.label: directory (vs. mandatory)
terms.gloss: Describes a requirement, often a deadline, that officials should follow but whose breach does not invalidate the action taken, unlike a mandatory requirement.

terms.label: disaffirm (a contract)
terms.gloss: To cancel a contract one has a legal right to escape, such as one made as a minor or under duress, by refusing to be bound by it.

terms.label: disallowance (of a claim)
terms.gloss: In bankruptcy, the court's rejection of a creditor's claim against the estate, so that claim shares in nothing when the estate's assets are paid out.

terms.label: disapprove (a precedent)
terms.gloss: For a court, to reject an argument or an earlier decision's reasoning as wrong; a higher court that disapproves a precedent signals it should not be followed, short of formally overruling it.

terms.label: disbarment
terms.gloss: Revocation of a lawyer's license to practice law, the most severe professional discipline.

terms.label: discharge (of a duty or debt)
terms.gloss: Release from a legal obligation, so the duty to perform or pay no longer exists, whether by performance, agreement, changed circumstances, or a bankruptcy order.

terms.label: disclaimer
terms.gloss: A statement denying responsibility, such as a contract term excluding implied warranties or saying the buyer relies on no outside statements; warranty disclaimers generally must be clear and conspicuous.

terms.label: discontinue (a count)
terms.gloss: In older practice, a plaintiff's withdrawal of one claim, or count, from the case.

terms.label: discovery (pretrial)
terms.gloss: The formal pretrial process in which each side can require the other to hand over documents and answer questions, including under oath, about the case.

terms.label: proportionality (discovery)
terms.gloss: The limit, now in Rule 26(b)(1), that discovery must be proportional to the needs of the case, weighing stakes, importance, access to information and burden against benefit.

terms.label: discretion
terms.gloss: A judge's, agency's, or official's freedom to choose among lawful options. A higher court overturns a discretionary ruling only for abuse of discretion, such as a clearly unreasonable choice or a legal error.

terms.label: discretionary review
terms.gloss: Review a higher court may choose to grant or refuse, as when the Supreme Court grants or denies certiorari. No party has a right to it.

terms.label: discriminatory intent
terms.gloss: A purpose to treat someone worse because of a protected trait such as race or sex. It must be proved for disparate-treatment and equal-protection claims.

terms.label: disgorgement
terms.gloss: A remedy forcing a wrongdoer to give up the profits gained from the wrong, measured by what the wrongdoer gained rather than what the victim lost.

terms.label: dishonor (of a check)
terms.gloss: A bank's or other payer's refusal to pay a check, note, or similar instrument when it is presented for payment.

terms.label: dismiss (a case or claim)
terms.context: \b(dismissals?|claims?|counts?|suits?|lawsuits?|cases?|actions?|complaints?|petitions?|appeals?|counterclaims?|charges?|indictments?|bill|proceedings?|plaintiffs?|defendants?|parties|party|with prejudice|without prejudice|for lack|for want|for failure|as moot|moot|12\(b\)|41\(|jurisdiction\w*|motions?|court|judge|district|forum non conveniens|voluntar\w*|involuntar\w*)\b
terms.gloss: A court's ending of a lawsuit or claim without a full trial, for example for lack of jurisdiction or failure to state a claim; dismissal "without prejudice" allows refiling, "with prejudice" does not.

terms.label: disparate impact
terms.gloss: Discrimination shown by results: a policy neutral on its face that falls much more heavily on a protected group and lacks enough justification, whatever the intent.

terms.label: disparate treatment
terms.gloss: Treating people or things differently. In discrimination law it means intentional unequal treatment because of a protected trait, unlike disparate impact, which targets neutral rules with unequal effects.

terms.label: dispensing power
terms.gloss: A claimed royal or executive power to excuse people from obeying a statute. England abolished it in 1689, and American courts have held the President has no such power.

terms.label: disposition
terms.gloss: How a court finally resolves a case, motion, or appeal, such as affirming, reversing, vacating, or dismissing.

terms.label: dispositive
terms.gloss: Decisive: enough by itself to settle a question, or the whole case. A dispositive motion, such as one for summary judgment, seeks to end the case.

terms.label: disqualification (of judge or lawyer)
terms.gloss: Removing a judge or lawyer from a case because of a conflict of interest or possible bias, often on a party's motion.

terms.label: dissent
terms.gloss: A separate opinion by a judge who disagrees with the majority's result. It has no legal force but may influence later courts.

terms.label: dissolution
terms.gloss: The legal ending of a marriage (divorce), partnership, corporation, or other body; dissolving an injunction or stay means lifting it.

terms.label: distinguish (a precedent)
terms.gloss: To explain why an earlier decision does not control a new case because its facts or legal issue differ in a way that matters.

terms.label: distributee
terms.gloss: A person who receives a share of a dead person's estate, typically an heir entitled to it under the inheritance laws when there is no will.

terms.label: distributive share (divorce)
terms.gloss: The portion of the marital property a spouse receives when a court divides the couple's assets in a divorce.

terms.label: district attorney
terms.gloss: The local public prosecutor, usually elected, who decides whether to bring criminal charges in a county or district and tries those cases for the state.

terms.label: disturbing the peace
terms.gloss: A minor crime of disrupting public order, for example by fighting, making loud noise or threatening others; also called breach of the peace.

terms.label: diversity jurisdiction
terms.gloss: Federal courts' power to hear cases between citizens of different states, or with foreign citizens, when (today) over $75,000 is at stake. Usually no plaintiff may share a state with any defendant.

terms.label: divestiture
terms.gloss: A required sale or giving up of assets, a business or an ownership stake, often ordered to cure an antitrust violation such as an unlawful merger.

terms.label: divisible (severable) contract
terms.gloss: A contract that splits into matching pairs of part-performance and part-payment, so completing a part earns its price even if other parts fail. An entire contract must be fully performed.

terms.label: docket
terms.gloss: A court's official record of the filings and events in a case (each with a docket number); also the court's list of pending cases.

terms.label: production (discovery)
terms.gloss: In discovery, handing over documents, files or other things to the opposing side, voluntarily or because a request or court order requires it.

terms.label: documentary evidence
terms.gloss: Evidence in written or recorded form, such as letters, contracts and business records, as opposed to live witness testimony.

terms.label: Dodd-Frank Act
terms.gloss: A 2010 federal financial-reform statute passed after the 2008 financial crisis. Among much else, it created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB).

terms.label: doing business (jurisdiction)
terms.gloss: Carrying on regular, continuous business activity in a state; it can subject an out-of-state company to that state's courts or require it to register there.

terms.label: doing business as (d/b/a)
terms.gloss: Operating under a trade name rather than one's legal name, often written d/b/a. The trade name does not create a separate legal person.

terms.label: domestic relations
terms.gloss: Family law: marriage, divorce, child custody and support. Under the domestic-relations exception, federal courts will not issue divorce, alimony or custody decrees.

terms.label: domicile
terms.gloss: A person's legal home: where they live and intend to stay indefinitely. Everyone has exactly one, and it decides which state they are a citizen of for diversity jurisdiction in federal court.

terms.label: donative intent
terms.gloss: A genuine intention to make a gift, needed for a transfer to count as a gift rather than a sale, loan, or bargained exchange.

terms.label: dormant Commerce Clause
terms.gloss: The principle that the Constitution's grant of commerce power to Congress also, on its own, limits state laws that discriminate against or unduly burden interstate trade.

terms.label: double jeopardy
terms.gloss: The Fifth Amendment protection against being tried or punished twice for the same criminal offense.

terms.label: double recovery
terms.gloss: Collecting compensation twice for the same loss, which courts prevent even when a party wins on several legal theories.

terms.label: dower
terms.gloss: A widow's traditional right to part of her late husband's land, usually a lifetime interest in one-third. Most states have abolished or replaced it.

terms.label: drawee
terms.gloss: The party, usually a bank, that a check or draft orders to pay. The person who writes the order is the drawer; the person paid is the payee.

terms.label: drawer (of a check or bill)
terms.gloss: The person who signs a check or similar written order directing a bank or another party to pay money to someone else.

terms.label: due care
terms.gloss: The care a reasonably prudent person would use in the circumstances; failing to use it is negligence.

terms.label: due diligence
terms.gloss: The reasonable care and effort a party is expected to use in doing something, such as investigating a deal or trying to obtain financing a contract requires.

terms.label: due process
terms.gloss: The Constitution's guarantee that government will not take life, liberty, or property without fair procedures, such as notice and a chance to be heard. It also limits where defendants can be sued.

terms.label: duress
terms.gloss: Wrongful threats or pressure that leave a person no reasonable choice but to agree. A contract made under duress can usually be undone by the pressured party.

terms.label: duty (legal)
terms.gloss: A legal obligation to act, or not act, in a certain way toward another. Failing to perform a duty one owes can make one liable.

terms.label: duty of loyalty
terms.gloss: A fiduciary's obligation to act in the other person's interest rather than its own, avoiding self-dealing and conflicts.

terms.label: duty to disclose
terms.gloss: A legal obligation to reveal certain facts to the other party, so that staying silent or hiding them can count as fraud or a breach.

terms.label: earnest money
terms.gloss: A deposit a buyer pays when agreeing to buy property, showing serious intent and usually credited toward the price.

terms.label: easement
terms.gloss: A right to use someone else's land for a specific purpose, such as a path or a utility line, without owning it.

terms.label: economic-loss doctrine
terms.gloss: A rule that usually bars tort suits for purely financial losses, such as lost profits or a product's failure to work, leaving those disputes to contract and warranty law.

terms.label: economic waste
terms.gloss: In contract damages, destroying useful work to fix a minor defect. To avoid it, courts may award the drop in value instead of the full cost of rebuilding.

terms.label: EEOC
terms.gloss: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, the federal agency enforcing job-discrimination laws such as Title VII; workers usually must file a charge with it before suing.

terms.label: effects test
terms.gloss: A basis for a state's courts to hear claims against an out-of-state defendant who intentionally aimed harmful conduct at the state, knowing the injury would be felt there.

terms.label: efficient breach
terms.gloss: The theory that breaking a contract and paying the other side's damages can be better overall when performing would cost more than it is worth.

terms.label: Eighth Amendment
terms.gloss: The amendment barring excessive bail, excessive fines, and cruel and unusual punishments.

terms.label: ejectment
terms.gloss: A traditional lawsuit to recover possession of land from someone occupying it, establishing the right to possess it.

terms.label: ejusdem generis
terms.gloss: Latin for 'of the same kind': a reading rule that general words following a list cover only things similar to the listed items.

terms.label: election of remedies
terms.gloss: The rule that a party with inconsistent remedies for the same wrong, such as contract damages or the reasonable value of work done, must choose one, so it cannot recover twice.

terms.label: element
terms.gloss: One of the separate things that must be proved to win a claim or prove a crime; failing to prove any one element defeats the whole claim.

terms.label: Eleventh Amendment
terms.gloss: The amendment courts read to bar many private suits against states, especially damages suits in federal court, as a form of state sovereign immunity.

terms.label: embedded federal question (Grable)
terms.gloss: A federal issue inside a state-law claim. Under Grable, federal courts may hear the claim if the issue is necessary, disputed and substantial, and hearing it would not upset the federal-state balance.

terms.label: Emergency Court of Appeals
terms.gloss: A special World War II court of federal judges with exclusive power to decide whether wartime price regulations were valid.

terms.label: emergency powers
terms.gloss: Special authority that a government, especially the President, claims or receives by statute to act quickly in a crisis such as war or a national emergency.

terms.label: Emergency Price Control Act
terms.gloss: A 1942 wartime law letting a federal Price Administrator set maximum prices and rents, with challenges sent only to a special Emergency Court of Appeals.

terms.label: emergency temporary standard
terms.gloss: An OSHA workplace rule issued immediately, without the usual notice-and-comment process, when workers face grave danger; it is meant to last only six months while a permanent standard is adopted.

terms.label: eminent domain
terms.gloss: The government's power to take private property for public use, so long as it pays the owner just compensation.

terms.label: emoluments
terms.gloss: Salary, fees, or other benefits received from holding an office; the Constitution's Emoluments Clauses limit what officials may accept, such as gifts from foreign governments.

terms.label: emotional distress
terms.gloss: Mental or emotional suffering, such as anxiety, grief, or humiliation, caused by another's conduct. Some claims allow damages for it.

terms.label: en banc
terms.gloss: Decided by all the active judges of a court (or a large panel of them) together, instead of the usual three-judge panel, usually for especially important or conflicting questions.

terms.label: enact
terms.gloss: To pass a bill into law. An enactment is the resulting statute, and the enacted text is what courts interpret.

terms.label: encumbrance
terms.gloss: A claim or right in property held by someone other than the owner, such as a mortgage, lien, or easement, that limits the owner's use or sale of it.

terms.label: endorsement (indorsement)
terms.gloss: A signature on a check or note, usually on the back, that transfers it to someone else or makes the signer liable to pay if the main party does not.

terms.label: endorsement (insurance)
terms.gloss: In insurance, a written amendment added to a policy that changes its coverage, such as adding a vehicle or an exclusion.

terms.label: Enelow-Ettelson doctrine
terms.gloss: An old rule, overruled in Gulfstream (1988), that treated a stay of a damages suit ordered on equitable grounds as an injunction that could be appealed immediately.

terms.label: enemy combatant
terms.gloss: A person the government treats as part of or supporting forces fighting the United States in armed conflict, and claims power to detain without criminal charges.

terms.label: title (ownership)
terms.gloss: Legal ownership of property, with the right to possess and transfer it; taking or passing title means becoming, or making someone, the owner.

terms.label: enforceable / unenforceable
terms.gloss: Able to be enforced by a court; an unenforceable promise may exist, but a court will not compel performance or award damages for breaking it.

terms.label: enjoin
terms.gloss: To forbid someone, by a court order called an injunction, from doing something (or, less often, to require them to do it).

terms.label: entitlement
terms.gloss: A legal right to a benefit, such as welfare payments, that anyone meeting the eligibility rules can claim; it can count as property protected by due process.

terms.label: entry of judgment
terms.gloss: The clerk's or court's formal recording of a judgment on the docket, which makes it effective and starts deadlines for post-trial motions and appeal.

terms.label: enumerated powers
terms.gloss: The specific powers the Constitution grants Congress, mainly in Article I, Section 8, such as taxing and regulating interstate commerce. Every federal law must rest on some constitutional grant of power.

terms.label: environmental impact statement
terms.gloss: The detailed study NEPA requires an agency to prepare before a major action significantly affecting the environment, covering its effects and the alternatives.

terms.label: equal protection
terms.gloss: The Fourteenth Amendment guarantee (applied to the federal government through the Fifth) that government will not treat people differently without adequate justification, judged most strictly for race.

terms.label: equally divided court
terms.gloss: A tie vote among the judges. The lower court's decision stands, but the tie explains no reasoning and sets no precedent.

terms.label: equitable
terms.gloss: Relating to equity, the body of remedies and doctrines, such as injunctions, that grew out of England's old Court of Chancery. Equitable claims are usually decided by a judge, not a jury.

terms.label: equitable estoppel
terms.gloss: A rule barring a party from asserting a right when its own words or conduct led another person to reasonably rely on the opposite, to that person's harm.

terms.label: equitable ownership
terms.gloss: Having the real benefit of property, protected by courts of equity, while someone else holds legal title, as a buyer under a signed purchase contract does before closing.

terms.label: equitable relief
terms.gloss: A court order to do or stop doing something, such as an injunction or specific performance, rather than an award of money damages.

terms.label: balance of equities
terms.gloss: The comparative fairness and hardship to each side that a court weighs when deciding whether to grant an injunction, specific performance, or a similar order.

terms.label: equity (courts of equity)
terms.gloss: The body of law, from England's old chancery courts, that offers remedies like injunctions and specific performance when money damages would not be enough. Not fairness or ownership value.

terms.label: Erie doctrine
terms.gloss: The rule that federal courts deciding state-law claims apply state substantive law but federal procedure. Deciding which category a rule falls into is the 'Erie question.'

terms.label: ERISA
terms.gloss: The Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974, the federal law regulating private employers' pension and benefit plans; it preempts many state laws.

terms.label: legal error
terms.gloss: A trial court's mistake about the law, such as a wrong evidence ruling or jury instruction. A "reversible error" is serious enough that the appeals court must set the result aside.

terms.label: escape clause
terms.gloss: A contract or statutory provision letting a party end or avoid its obligations if specified events occur.

terms.label: escheat
terms.gloss: The passing of property to the state when its owner dies with no will and no heirs to inherit it, or when property such as a bank account is abandoned.

terms.label: escrow
terms.gloss: An arrangement in which a neutral third party holds money or documents until agreed conditions are met, then releases them.

terms.label: Establishment Clause
terms.gloss: The First Amendment clause forbidding government to establish an official religion or to favor religion in certain ways.

terms.label: estate
terms.gloss: All the property, rights, and debts left by a person who has died (or of a bankrupt debtor), managed as a unit; also, an ownership interest in land.

terms.label: estoppel
terms.gloss: A rule barring a party from taking a position that contradicts its own earlier words, conduct, or a prior ruling, when others relied on it.

terms.label: eviction
terms.gloss: The legal process by which a landlord removes a tenant from rented property, ordinarily through a court order.

terms.label: evidence
terms.gloss: Testimony, documents, objects and other material offered in court to prove or disprove a fact. "Evidentiary" means relating to evidence or the rules on what may be used.

terms.label: evidentiary hearing
terms.gloss: A court or agency hearing at which witnesses testify and evidence is taken to resolve disputed facts, rather than deciding on written papers alone.

terms.label: ex officio
terms.gloss: By virtue of holding an office; an ex officio member sits on a body automatically because of another position.

terms.label: ex parte
terms.gloss: Done at the request of one side without notice to, or participation by, the other side, such as an emergency order issued after hearing only one party.

terms.label: ex post facto law
terms.gloss: Latin for 'after the fact.' The Constitution forbids criminal laws that punish conduct that was legal when done, or that increase its punishment afterward.

terms.label: exaction
terms.gloss: A charge the government demands, such as a tax or duty. In land-use law, a condition attached to a building permit, such as giving land or paying a fee.

terms.label: exception (to a ruling)
terms.gloss: In older practice, a party's formal objection to a judge's ruling or jury instruction, noted on the record so it could be raised on appeal.

terms.label: exception (old practice)
terms.gloss: In older practice, a formal objection to a judge's ruling, recorded so it could be reviewed later on appeal, often through a bill of exceptions.

terms.label: excessive force
terms.gloss: Force by police beyond what is objectively reasonable in the circumstances of an arrest or other seizure, which violates the Fourth Amendment's ban on unreasonable seizures.

terms.label: excise tax
terms.gloss: A tax on making, selling, or using particular goods or activities, such as fuel, liquor, or coal, as opposed to a tax on property or income.

terms.label: exclusionary rule
terms.gloss: The rule that evidence the government obtains by violating a person's constitutional rights, such as through an illegal search, generally cannot be used against that person at a criminal trial.

terms.label: exclusive dealing
terms.gloss: An arrangement giving one party the sole right to sell, buy, or represent another's goods; UCC § 2-306(2) implies a duty to use best efforts.

terms.label: exclusive jurisdiction
terms.gloss: Power to hear a type of case that belongs to one court or agency alone, so no other court may decide it.

terms.label: exclusive license
terms.gloss: Permission to use a patent, trademark or other right that the owner promises not to give anyone else; sometimes the owner even gives up its own right to use it.

terms.label: exclusive remedy
terms.gloss: The only remedy the law allows for a type of claim, as when workers' compensation replaces an injury lawsuit against the employer.

terms.label: exclusivity clause
terms.gloss: A contract term promising that one party will deal only with the other, or that a landlord will not lease nearby space to a competing business.

terms.label: exculpatory
terms.gloss: Tending to clear someone of blame. Exculpatory evidence points toward innocence; an exculpatory clause releases a party in advance from liability for certain harms.

terms.label: excusable neglect
terms.gloss: A good enough reason for missing a deadline, such as an honest mistake, that lets a court allow a late filing or undo a default. Courts weigh the reason, delay, good faith, and harm to the other side.

terms.label: excuse (of performance)
terms.gloss: A legal reason that releases a party from performing, or from meeting a condition, without being in breach, such as impossibility, frustration or the other side's breach.

terms.label: execute (a document)
terms.gloss: To sign or otherwise complete a legal document, such as a contract, deed, or note, so it takes effect. A 'fully executed' contract has been signed by every party.

terms.label: execution (of a judgment)
terms.gloss: The court-ordered process of enforcing a money judgment, for example by having a sheriff seize and sell the losing party's property to pay it.
terms.context: \b(judgments?|levy|sheriff\w*|writ|stay\w* execution|postjudgment|post-judgment|execution machinery|execution sale|sought execution|attachments?|judgment debtor|property execution|body-execution|execution against|barred execution)\b

terms.label: executive agency
terms.gloss: A government agency within the executive branch that carries out laws, as opposed to a court or a part of Congress. Whether the President may freely fire its head is often disputed.

terms.label: clemency
terms.gloss: The President's or a governor's power to forgive or lessen punishment for a crime, by pardon, shortened sentence (commutation), or delay (reprieve).

terms.label: executive order
terms.gloss: A written directive from the President to executive-branch officials. It is valid only as far as the Constitution or a statute gives the President power.

terms.label: executive power
terms.gloss: The constitutional power to carry out and enforce the laws, which Article II gives the President; it includes directing and removing many officers.

terms.label: executive privilege
terms.gloss: The President's limited right to keep executive-branch communications confidential from Congress or the courts; it can give way to a strong need, such as evidence for a criminal trial.

terms.label: executor
terms.gloss: The person named in a will to manage a dead person's estate: collecting property, paying debts, and distributing what remains, under court supervision.

terms.label: executory
terms.gloss: Not yet performed: a promise or contract on which some performance still remains to be done.

terms.label: exhaustion of remedies
terms.gloss: The requirement to use every available step within an agency or grievance system before going to court. Not tiredness.
terms.context: remed\w*|administrative|grievance|PLRA|futility|failure to exhaust|lack of exhaustion|excused exhaustion|habeas|§\s*405|internal|claim presentment|exhaustion (requirement|findings?|facts|disputes?|matters)

terms.label: exhibit
terms.gloss: A document or object formally marked and offered as evidence in a case, or a document attached to a filing or contract.

terms.label: exigent circumstances
terms.gloss: An emergency that justifies skipping a usual safeguard, such as police entering without a warrant or a court allowing seizure of property before a hearing.

terms.label: expectation damages
terms.gloss: Money that puts the injured party where it would have been if the contract had been performed: roughly the value of the lost bargain, minus any costs it saved by not performing.

terms.label: expenditure limit
terms.gloss: A cap on how much a candidate, campaign or outside group may spend. Buckley struck these down as direct limits on political speech, except when accepted in exchange for public financing.

terms.label: expert testimony
terms.gloss: Testimony from a witness qualified by special knowledge, such as a doctor or engineer, who may give opinions an ordinary witness could not; the judge screens it for reliability.

terms.label: express (term, warranty, condition)
terms.gloss: Stated directly in words, spoken or written, rather than implied from conduct or circumstances, as in an express term, warranty or condition.

terms.label: express advocacy
terms.gloss: Campaign speech that explicitly urges voting for or against a clearly identified candidate, with words like "vote for" or "defeat." Buckley v. Valeo confined certain election rules to it.

terms.label: express contract
terms.gloss: A contract whose terms the parties stated in words, spoken or written, as opposed to one implied from their conduct.

terms.label: express warranty
terms.gloss: A seller's explicit promise or factual statement about the goods, such as a description or sample, that becomes part of the deal; the seller is liable if they fall short.

terms.label: expunge
terms.gloss: To erase or seal an official record, such as an arrest record, a report, or a passage in a grand-jury record, so it is treated as if it no longer exists.

terms.label: extrajudicial
terms.gloss: Outside the courts' judicial work. A judge's extrajudicial service is non-judicial work, such as sitting on a commission; an extrajudicial killing is one no court authorized.

terms.label: presumption against extraterritoriality
terms.gloss: The presumption that a federal statute applies only within the United States unless Congress clearly indicates it should reach conduct or events abroad.

terms.label: extrinsic evidence
terms.gloss: Evidence from outside a written document, such as negotiations or trade practice, used to show what its words mean.

terms.label: face value
terms.gloss: The amount written on a financial instrument, such as a note, bond, or insurance policy, or the stated amount of a claim, as opposed to what it might sell for or be worth.

terms.label: facial challenge
terms.gloss: A claim that a law or contract term is invalid in every application, on its face, rather than only as applied to the challenger's own situation.

terms.label: fact pleading (code pleading)
terms.gloss: An older pleading system, still used in some states, requiring a complaint to state the facts making up each element of a claim, rather than legal conclusions or a short general statement.

terms.label: factfinder
terms.gloss: Whoever decides the facts in a trial or hearing: the jury, or the judge when there is no jury.

terms.label: failure of consideration
terms.gloss: A defense that arises when the performance promised in exchange never happens or becomes worthless, which can excuse the other side from performing or paying.

terms.label: failure to state a claim
terms.gloss: Stating a claim means alleging facts that, if true, would give the plaintiff a legal right to relief. A complaint that fails to do so can be dismissed without a trial.

terms.label: fair hearing
terms.gloss: A hearing before a neutral decision-maker where a person can present evidence and arguments. In welfare and benefit programs, it is the formal hearing for contesting an agency decision.

terms.label: Fair Housing Act (Title VIII)
terms.gloss: Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, which bans discrimination in selling or renting housing because of race, religion, sex, and other protected traits.

terms.label: Fair Labor Standards Act
terms.gloss: The 1938 federal statute setting minimum wage, overtime pay, and child-labor rules; workers can sue together in a collective action to recover unpaid wages.

terms.label: fair market value
terms.gloss: The price a willing buyer would pay a willing seller, neither forced to deal and both reasonably informed.

terms.label: notice (due process)
terms.gloss: Being told, in time and in enough detail, what the government or opposing party claims or requires, so one can respond or comply; due process generally requires it.

terms.label: fair play and substantial justice
terms.gloss: The fairness standard from International Shoe: suing an out-of-state defendant in a state must be reasonable, not merely supported by minimum contacts, weighing the burdens and interests involved.

terms.label: fair use
terms.gloss: A defense to copyright infringement allowing limited use of protected work, such as for commentary, research, or new transformative purposes, judged by four statutory factors.

terms.label: fair warning
terms.gloss: The due-process idea that people must have reasonable advance notice of what the law forbids, or where they may be sued, before it is used against them.

terms.label: fairness hearing
terms.gloss: A court hearing where affected people may object before the judge decides whether a proposed class-action settlement or consent decree is fair, reasonable, and adequate.

terms.label: false advertising
terms.gloss: Misleading statements in advertising about one's own or a competitor's product, prohibited by the Lanham Act, FTC rules and state laws.

terms.label: false arrest
terms.gloss: A tort or civil-rights claim for being taken into custody without legal authority, such as without probable cause.

terms.label: false imprisonment
terms.gloss: The tort or crime of intentionally confining someone against their will without legal justification.

terms.label: feasibility (OSHA standards)
terms.gloss: Under the Occupational Safety and Health Act, a toxic-substance standard must be feasible: achievable with available technology and affordable without threatening the industry's survival.

terms.label: Federal Arbitration Act
terms.gloss: The 1925 federal statute (FAA) making written arbitration agreements valid and enforceable, and letting courts compel arbitration and confirm or vacate arbitrators' awards.

terms.label: Federal Circuit
terms.gloss: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, a nationwide appeals court for patent cases, money claims against the federal government, and certain other specialized matters.

terms.label: federal common law
terms.gloss: Rules made by federal judges, not by statutes, in the few areas where national interests need one uniform federal rule.

terms.label: federal enclave
terms.gloss: Land within a state over which the federal government holds governing authority, such as many military bases, so federal law rather than ordinary state law largely applies there.

terms.label: federal-question jurisdiction
terms.gloss: A question of federal law. Federal courts have 'federal-question jurisdiction' over cases arising under the Constitution, federal statutes, or treaties, usually because federal law creates the plaintiff's claim.

terms.label: federal recognition (of a tribe)
terms.gloss: The United States' formal acknowledgment of a Native American tribe as a sovereign government, giving it a government-to-government relationship and access to federal programs.

terms.label: Federal Register
terms.gloss: The daily federal publication where agencies print proposed and final rules, notices, and presidential documents. Publication there gives the public legal notice.

terms.label: Federal Rules of Civil Procedure
terms.gloss: The rules, adopted by the Supreme Court under the Rules Enabling Act and in force since 1938, that govern civil lawsuits in federal court, from pleadings and discovery to trial.

terms.label: Federal Rules of Evidence
terms.gloss: The rules governing what evidence federal courts may admit; Rule 501, for instance, leaves most privileges to judge-made common law.

terms.label: Federal Tort Claims Act
terms.gloss: The federal statute waiving the United States' sovereign immunity for many torts by federal employees acting within the scope of their jobs, with exceptions such as discretionary functions.

terms.label: Federal Vacancies Reform Act (FVRA)
terms.gloss: A 1998 federal statute setting who may temporarily serve as an acting officer when a Senate-confirmed executive post falls vacant, and for how long.

terms.label: federalism
terms.gloss: The division of power between the national government and the states, with each having its own sphere; it shapes doctrines like Erie, abstention, and limits on Congress.

terms.label: fee simple
terms.gloss: The fullest form of land ownership: the owner holds it indefinitely and may sell it, give it away, or pass it on at death.

terms.label: Federal Employers’ Liability Act (FELA)
terms.gloss: A federal statute letting injured railroad workers sue their employer for damages caused by the railroad’s negligence, in place of ordinary workers’ compensation.

terms.label: felon
terms.gloss: A person convicted of a felony, a serious crime usually punishable by more than a year in prison.

terms.label: felon in possession
terms.gloss: The federal crime, under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1), of possessing a gun after being convicted of a crime punishable by more than a year in prison.

terms.label: felony
terms.gloss: A serious crime, generally one punishable by more than a year in prison.

terms.label: fiduciary duty
terms.gloss: The duty of loyalty and care owed by a fiduciary: someone trusted to act for another, such as a trustee, agent, partner, or director, who must put the other's interests first.

terms.label: Fifth Amendment
terms.gloss: The amendment guaranteeing, among other things, due process of law against the federal government, protection against double jeopardy and self-incrimination, and just compensation for takings.

terms.label: fighting words
terms.gloss: Face-to-face insults likely to provoke immediate violence, a narrow category of speech the First Amendment does not protect.

terms.label: final agency action
terms.gloss: An agency decision ready for court challenge under the Administrative Procedure Act: it ends the agency's decisionmaking and determines rights or carries legal consequences.

terms.label: final decision (appeals)
terms.gloss: A ruling that ends the case, leaving nothing but enforcement. Under 28 U.S.C. § 1291, federal appeals generally must wait for one; most earlier orders cannot be appealed yet.

terms.label: final judgment
terms.gloss: A court decision that ends the litigation, leaving nothing for the court to do but carry it out. Generally only final judgments can be appealed.

terms.label: final-judgment rule
terms.gloss: The general rule that a party may appeal only after the trial court finishes the whole case, not from each ruling along the way.

terms.label: final rule
terms.gloss: An agency's finished, binding regulation, usually adopted after it publishes a proposed rule (a draft) and considers the public's comments on it.

terms.label: finding (of fact)
terms.gloss: A decision by a judge, jury, or agency about what the facts are, based on the evidence; appellate courts generally defer to findings of fact.

terms.label: findings of fact
terms.gloss: A court's or agency's formal decisions about what actually happened, based on the evidence. Appeals courts usually accept them unless they are clearly wrong.

terms.label: firm offer
terms.gloss: A definite offer that can be accepted to form a contract, not just an invitation to negotiate. Under the UCC, a merchant's signed written promise to keep an offer open binds for up to three months.

terms.label: FIRREA
terms.gloss: The Financial Institutions Reform, Recovery, and Enforcement Act of 1989. Passed after the savings-and-loan collapse, it overhauled regulation of thrifts and imposed stricter capital rules.

terms.label: First Amendment
terms.gloss: The part of the Bill of Rights barring government from abridging freedom of speech, press, religion, assembly, or petition. Through the Fourteenth Amendment it binds the states too.

terms.label: first assistant
terms.gloss: Under the Vacancies Act, the deputy or second-in-command of an office, who by default becomes the acting officer when the post falls vacant.

terms.label: question of first impression
terms.gloss: A legal question that no court in that jurisdiction has decided before, so there is no binding earlier decision to follow.

terms.label: fishing expedition
terms.gloss: A critical label for broad discovery requests made without a specific basis, in the hope of turning up something useful.

terms.label: fitness for review (ripeness)
terms.gloss: Part of the ripeness test: whether an issue is concrete and settled enough for a court to decide now, without waiting for further facts or agency action.

terms.label: fleeting expletive
terms.gloss: A single, unplanned curse word on a live broadcast. The FCC long declined to penalize these as indecent, then changed that policy in 2004.

terms.label: Federal Land Policy and Management Act
match: federal land policy and management act
terms.gloss: The 1976 federal law governing how public lands are managed, used, and planned, mainly by the Bureau of Land Management, including protecting possible wilderness areas.

terms.label: f.o.b. (free on board)
terms.gloss: A shipping term naming the place, such as the seller's plant or a ship, up to which the seller bears delivery costs and risk of loss; after that, the buyer does.

terms.label: Freedom of Information Act
terms.gloss: The federal law giving anyone the right to request records from federal agencies, subject to listed exemptions such as trade secrets.

terms.label: forbearance
terms.gloss: Deliberately holding back from doing something one has a right to do, such as suing or collecting a debt. In contracts, that holding back can be the price paid for a promise.

terms.label: force majeure
terms.gloss: A contract term excusing or delaying performance when an extraordinary event beyond the parties' control, such as war or natural disaster, prevents it.

terms.label: foreclosure
terms.gloss: The legal process by which a lender or lienholder enforces its claim after a default, usually by forcing a sale of the property and applying the proceeds to the debt.

terms.label: foreign corporation
terms.gloss: A corporation formed under the laws of a different state or country from the one where it is doing business or being sued. It need not be foreign to the U.S.

terms.label: foreseeability
terms.gloss: Whether a reasonable person could have anticipated a result. It limits contract damages and negligence liability, and also matters for personal jurisdiction.

terms.label: forfeiture
terms.gloss: Losing a right, property, or argument because of wrongdoing or a failure, such as government seizure of property tied to crime or a party's failure to raise an argument in time.

terms.label: formal rulemaking
terms.gloss: Agency rule-writing done through trial-like hearings on the record, required only when a statute says so; most rules use the simpler notice-and-comment process.

terms.label: forms of action
terms.gloss: The fixed categories of old common-law lawsuits, such as trespass, debt, or assumpsit. Each had its own writ and procedure, and choosing the wrong one could defeat a claim.

terms.label: forthwith
terms.gloss: An old legal word meaning immediately, or as soon as reasonably possible.

terms.label: forum
terms.gloss: The court, or the state, where a lawsuit is brought and heard. In personal-jurisdiction cases the "forum state" is the state whose courts are asked to hear the case.

terms.label: forum-defendant rule
terms.gloss: The rule that a case cannot be moved from state to federal court on diversity grounds if a properly joined and served defendant is a citizen of the state where it was filed.

terms.label: law of the forum (lex fori)
terms.gloss: The law of the place where the court hearing the case sits, as opposed to the law of another state or country connected to the dispute.

terms.label: forum non conveniens
terms.gloss: Latin for 'inconvenient forum': a court's power to dismiss a case it could hear because a court elsewhere, often abroad, is a much more suitable place for it.

terms.label: forum-selection clause
terms.gloss: A contract term choosing the court or place where the parties' disputes must be litigated. Courts usually enforce it unless enforcement would be unreasonable or unjust.

terms.label: forum shopping
terms.gloss: Choosing a court or jurisdiction because it is likely to give a better result or more favorable law, something the Erie doctrine aims to discourage between state and federal courts.

terms.label: Fourteenth Amendment
terms.gloss: The post-Civil War amendment barring states from denying due process or equal protection of the laws; its Due Process Clause limits state-court personal jurisdiction.

terms.label: Fourth Amendment
terms.gloss: The constitutional protection against unreasonable searches and seizures by government, which generally requires a warrant based on probable cause.

terms.label: franchise
terms.gloss: A license to run a business under another company's brand and system (franchisor to franchisee); in older cases, a special privilege granted by government, such as a corporate or bank charter.

terms.label: fraud
terms.gloss: Knowingly misrepresenting or concealing a material fact to induce another to rely on it, to their harm; it is a tort, a crime, and a ground to undo a contract or judgment.

terms.label: fraud on the court
terms.gloss: Misconduct that corrupts the court process itself, such as fabricated evidence or bribing a judge, rather than just deceiving the other side. It permits reopening even old judgments.

terms.label: fraudulent concealment
terms.gloss: Deliberately hiding facts or assets to deceive someone, such as hiding property from creditors. Hiding a wrong from its victim can also pause (toll) the deadline for suing.

terms.label: fraudulent conveyance
terms.gloss: A transfer of property made to cheat creditors, or for too little in return while the owner is insolvent. Creditors or a bankruptcy trustee can undo it.

terms.label: fraudulent inducement
terms.gloss: Fraud that leads someone into a contract, such as lying about a key fact; the deceived party may undo the contract or sue for damages, if its reliance was justified.

terms.label: fraudulent misrepresentation
terms.gloss: A knowingly false statement of fact, made to induce reliance, that the victim reasonably relies on to its harm. It supports a fraud claim or undoing the contract.

terms.label: suppression (fraudulent concealment)
terms.gloss: A fraud claim for hiding, or failing to disclose, an important fact one had a duty to reveal, causing the other person harm.

terms.label: freedom of contract
terms.gloss: The principle that people may make the agreements they choose and courts should enforce them, subject to limits such as public policy and unconscionability.

terms.label: frivolous
terms.gloss: Lacking any reasonable basis in law or fact; filing frivolous claims or arguments can lead to sanctions, for example under Rule 11.

terms.label: front pay
terms.gloss: Money for wages a wrongly fired or excluded worker will lose in the future, awarded instead of putting the worker back in the job.

terms.label: frustration of purpose
terms.gloss: A contract excuse: an unexpected event destroys the deal's main purpose, known to both sides, so duties end though performance remains possible. In English law, frustration also covers impossibility.

terms.label: FTC
terms.gloss: The Federal Trade Commission, an independent federal agency enforcing laws against unfair competition and unfair or deceptive business practices.

terms.label: full faith and credit
terms.gloss: The constitutional and statutory duty of each state, and of federal courts, to honor the laws, official records, and court judgments of other states.

terms.label: fundamental fairness
terms.gloss: A core due-process standard asking whether a procedure or government action is basically fair. Courts also use it to review terms like forum-selection clauses.

terms.label: fundamental right
terms.gloss: A right the Supreme Court treats as especially protected, such as speech, voting or privacy. Laws that burden it usually face strict scrutiny.

terms.label: futility
terms.gloss: An exception excusing a party from first pursuing administrative remedies (exhaustion) when doing so would clearly be pointless.

terms.label: future interest
terms.gloss: A legal interest held now in property that gives the right to possess it only later, for example after someone else's life estate ends. Some depend on a condition and may never take effect.

terms.label: garnishment
terms.gloss: A court process that collects a debt from money or property a third party holds for the debtor, such as wages owed by an employer (the garnishee).

terms.label: general appearance
terms.gloss: Taking part in a case in a way that accepts the court's power over you, which usually gives up objections to personal jurisdiction.

terms.label: general counsel / in-house counsel
terms.gloss: General counsel is an organization's chief lawyer; in-house counsel are lawyers employed by the company itself, while outside counsel are hired from law firms.

terms.label: general damages
terms.gloss: Damages for harm that naturally follows from the kind of wrong done, which anyone so wronged would suffer. Unlike special damages, they need not be specifically pleaded.

terms.label: general denial
terms.gloss: An answer that denies every allegation in the complaint at once rather than responding to each one separately.

terms.label: general issue (plea)
terms.gloss: In common-law pleading, a defendant's blanket denial of the plaintiff's whole claim, which let the defendant contest everything at trial.

terms.label: general jurisdiction (over a defendant)
terms.gloss: A court's power over a defendant for any claim at all, even one unrelated to the state. For a person, usually their home state; for a company, where it is incorporated or headquartered.

terms.label: General Term
terms.gloss: In nineteenth-century New York, the appeals session of the Supreme Court or certain city courts, where a panel of judges reviewed trial-level and Special Term decisions.

terms.label: general verdict
terms.gloss: A jury verdict that simply names the winner and any amount awarded, without stating the jury's findings on the specific disputed issues.

terms.label: generalized grievance
terms.gloss: A complaint about government shared equally by all citizens, such as an interest in lawful government, which alone does not give anyone the right to sue in federal court.

terms.label: genuine dispute of material fact
terms.context: \b(summary judgment|summary-judgment|rule 56|trial|factfinder|material facts?|jury|no genuine|raising a genuine|raised a genuine|found a genuine|remained|triable|no-genuine-dispute)\b
terms.gloss: A real disagreement, backed by evidence, about a fact that could change the outcome. If one exists, the court cannot grant summary judgment on that issue; a trial must resolve it.

terms.label: germane
terms.gloss: Closely related to the matter at hand; for example, an association may sue for its members only on interests germane to its purpose, and added duties must be germane to an office.

terms.label: gerrymander
terms.gloss: Drawing election district lines to favor one party or group; Rucho held that partisan gerrymandering claims are political questions federal courts cannot decide.

terms.label: gift over
terms.gloss: A provision in a will or trust that passes property to a second person if a stated event happens to the first, such as dying young or without children.

terms.label: going concern
terms.gloss: An operating business sold or valued as a whole, including its customers and goodwill, rather than as a collection of separate assets.

terms.label: good cause
terms.gloss: A legally adequate reason, which some laws or contracts require before acting, such as firing an employee, removing an official, excusing a missed deadline, or skipping notice and comment.

terms.label: good faith
terms.gloss: Honest intent and fair dealing without trying to defraud or take unfair advantage; many legal duties, defenses, and protections turn on whether a party acted in good faith.

terms.label: good title
terms.gloss: Valid ownership free of reasonable doubt or defects, which a seller can actually transfer to a buyer.

terms.label: goods
terms.gloss: In sale-of-goods law (UCC Article 2), things that are movable when identified to a contract for sale, as opposed to land, services or money.

terms.label: goodwill
terms.gloss: The value of a business's reputation and customer relationships beyond its physical assets. A seller of a business often promises not to compete to protect the goodwill sold.

terms.label: governmental immunity
terms.gloss: A government's protection from being sued or held liable without its consent. The term is often used for local governments such as cities and counties.

terms.label: grace period
terms.gloss: Extra time after a due date during which payment or compliance is still allowed without default, such as days an insurance policy stays in force after an unpaid premium.

terms.label: Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act
terms.gloss: A 1999 federal statute that let banks, securities firms and insurers combine, and requires financial institutions to protect customers' personal information.

terms.label: grand jury
terms.gloss: A group of citizens who hear the prosecution's evidence in secret and decide whether to indict, that is, formally charge someone with a serious crime.

terms.label: grant (a motion or petition)
terms.gloss: For a court to grant a motion, petition, or request is to approve it and give the order or relief asked for; to deny it is to refuse.

terms.label: grantee
terms.gloss: The person who receives property or a right by deed or other grant; the person making the grant is the grantor.

terms.label: grantor
terms.gloss: The person who transfers property or a right by deed or other grant; the person who receives it is the grantee.

terms.label: gratuitous
terms.gloss: Given or promised for nothing in return. In contract law such a promise usually cannot be enforced, though reasonable reliance on it sometimes changes that.

terms.label: gravamen
terms.gloss: The core or most important part of a claim or complaint: what it is really about.

terms.label: grievance
terms.gloss: A formal complaint pursued through an internal dispute system, such as a union contract's grievance-and-arbitration procedure or a prison's complaint process.

terms.label: gross income
terms.gloss: In tax law, all income from whatever source, except what the tax code specifically excludes, before deductions; the starting point for figuring taxable income.

terms.label: gross negligence
terms.gloss: Extreme carelessness showing reckless disregard for others' safety or interests; more blameworthy than ordinary negligence and often not excusable by contract.

terms.label: guaranteed issue / community rating
terms.gloss: Insurance rules requiring insurers to sell coverage to anyone (guaranteed issue) and to charge people in an area the same price regardless of health (community rating).

terms.label: guaranty
terms.gloss: A promise to pay another person's debt or perform their obligation if they fail to; the person making it is the guarantor.

terms.label: guardian
terms.gloss: A person appointed by a court with legal power to care for, or act and sue for, someone who cannot act alone, such as a child or incapacitated adult.

terms.label: guardian ad litem
terms.gloss: A person a court appoints to protect the interests of a child or an incapacitated person within a particular lawsuit.

terms.label: Gun Control Act of 1968
terms.gloss: The main federal law regulating the firearms trade, licensing dealers and barring certain people, such as felons, from having guns.

terms.label: habeas corpus
terms.gloss: A court order requiring the government to bring a detained person before a judge and justify the detention; also the lawsuit asking for that order.

terms.label: hard-look review
terms.gloss: Careful court review of whether an agency seriously examined the relevant data, alternatives, and objections and explained its choice, rather than acting arbitrarily.

terms.label: harmless error
terms.gloss: A trial mistake that an appeals court finds did not affect the outcome, so it is no reason to reverse the judgment.

terms.label: harmonious-reading canon
