terms.gloss: Reckless conduct showing conscious disregard of a known, serious risk to others. It is worse than ordinary carelessness and often supports punitive damages.

terms.label: war powers
terms.gloss: Constitutional authority over war, split between Congress (declaring war, raising and funding forces) and the President (commanding them); the 1973 War Powers Resolution limits unauthorized deployments.

terms.label: warrant
terms.gloss: A court order, issued by a judge on a showing of probable cause, authorizing officers to search a place, seize property, or arrest a person.

terms.label: warranty
terms.gloss: A seller's promise or guarantee about the quality, condition or facts of something sold. It can be stated expressly or implied by law.

terms.label: warranty deed
terms.gloss: A deed in which the seller guarantees good title to the land and promises to defend the buyer against others' claims to it.

terms.label: weight of evidence
terms.gloss: How convincing the evidence is, as judged by the factfinder; a judge may order a new trial if a verdict goes against the clear weight of the evidence.

terms.label: well-pleaded complaint rule
terms.gloss: The rule that a case arises under federal law, for federal-court jurisdiction, only if the plaintiff's own claim, not an expected defense, rests on federal law.

terms.label: whistleblower
terms.gloss: An employee who reports wrongdoing by an employer or coworker, inside the company or to authorities; many laws protect them from retaliation.

terms.label: will
terms.gloss: A legal document, signed with required formalities, in which a person directs who gets their property after death and who will manage the estate.

terms.label: willful
terms.gloss: Done deliberately and knowingly, not by accident or mere carelessness; under some statutes, such as the FCRA, it also covers reckless disregard. Willful violations often bring larger penalties or extra damages.

terms.label: willing buyer and willing seller
terms.gloss: The fair-market-value test: the price a reasonably informed buyer and seller would agree on, with neither forced to make the deal.

terms.label: wire fraud
terms.gloss: Federal crimes of using the mail (mail fraud) or interstate phone, radio, or internet communications (wire fraud) to carry out a scheme to cheat people.

terms.label: with prejudice
terms.gloss: Final: a dismissal or ruling that bars the party from ever bringing the same claim again. 'Prejudice' here has nothing to do with bias.

terms.label: without prejudice
terms.gloss: Leaving the door open: a dismissal or denial that does not stop the party from refiling the claim or renewing the request later. 'Prejudice' here has nothing to do with bias.

terms.label: work product
terms.gloss: Materials prepared by or for a party in anticipation of litigation, such as a lawyer's notes and memos. The other side can get them only by showing substantial need and no other source.

terms.label: workers' compensation
terms.gloss: A state insurance system that pays employees hurt on the job regardless of fault, usually in exchange for barring them from suing the employer.

terms.label: workmanlike
terms.gloss: Done with the ordinary skill and care expected of a competent tradesperson; building contracts often carry an implied promise of workmanlike performance.

terms.label: writ
terms.gloss: A formal written court order commanding a person, official, or lower court to do, or stop doing, a specific act.

terms.label: writ of error
terms.gloss: An older form of appeal in which a higher court reviewed only legal mistakes shown in the lower court's record, not the facts.

terms.label: writ of prohibition
terms.gloss: An order from a higher court directing a lower court not to act beyond its authority in a case.

terms.label: written confirmation (UCC)
terms.gloss: Under the UCC, a writing sent after an oral deal confirming its terms. Between merchants it can satisfy the statute of frauds, and under § 2-207 it may propose added terms.

terms.label: wrongful death
terms.gloss: A lawsuit, created by statute, letting a dead person's family or estate recover for losses from a death caused by another's wrongful act.

terms.label: wrongful termination
terms.gloss: Firing an employee in violation of a contract, statute or public policy, an exception to the usual rule that employers may fire at-will employees for any reason.

terms.label: yellow-dog contract
terms.gloss: An employment agreement in which the worker promises not to join, or to leave, a labor union. The Norris-LaGuardia Act of 1932 made such promises unenforceable in federal courts.

terms.label: zone of interests
terms.gloss: A test asking whether a plaintiff's interest is among those the statute was meant to protect or regulate, so that the plaintiff may sue under it.

terms.label: zoning
terms.gloss: Local laws dividing land into districts and controlling what uses and buildings are allowed in each.

terms.label: gratuity
terms.gloss: A gift or payment given as thanks rather than owed. One given to an official for an official act can amount to a bribe or kickback.

terms.label: holder (of an instrument)
terms.gloss: The person in possession of a bond, note, or check who is entitled to demand payment on it.

terms.label: for value
terms.gloss: Paying something real, usually money, to acquire a bond or note. A good-faith buyer who paid value can enforce it despite flaws in how it was issued.

terms.label: before maturity
terms.gloss: Before the bond or note came due for payment. Buying it earlier, without notice of problems, helps a buyer qualify as a protected good-faith holder.

terms.label: interest coupons
terms.gloss: Detachable slips attached to a bond, each a separate promise to pay one interest installment. Each could be cashed, or sued on, by itself.

terms.label: forgery
terms.gloss: Faking or altering a document or signature to deceive. A forged note is a defense to paying it.

terms.label: actually litigated and determined
terms.gloss: Really contested by the parties and really decided by the court. Only such issues bind later lawsuits on a different claim (issue preclusion).

terms.label: relitigate
terms.gloss: To argue again, in a new lawsuit, a claim or issue already decided. Preclusion rules forbid it.

terms.label: stranger (to a lawsuit)
terms.gloss: Someone who was not a party to a lawsuit and so generally is not bound by its judgment.

terms.label: for the use and benefit of
terms.gloss: Suing for another's use and benefit means the named plaintiff sues as a stand-in, with any recovery going to that other person.

terms.label: § 10(b)
terms.gloss: The anti-fraud section of the Securities Exchange Act, forbidding deceptive practices in connection with buying or selling securities.

terms.label: corrective disclosure
terms.gloss: A later public announcement revealing the truth behind an earlier misstatement, which typically makes the stock price drop.

terms.label: efficient market
terms.gloss: A market in which public information is quickly reflected in a stock's price, so the price embodies what is publicly known.

terms.label: fraud-on-the-market
terms.gloss: The theory that investors who trade at the market price rely on public lies reflected in that price, so reliance can be presumed for a whole class.

terms.label: truth-on-the-market defense
terms.gloss: A defense that the market already knew the truth from other public sources, so a misstatement could not have misled investors or moved the price.

terms.label: Basic Inc. v. Levinson
terms.gloss: Basic Inc. v. Levinson (1988), the Supreme Court case adopting the presumption that investors relied on public misstatements reflected in a stock's market price.

terms.label: total mix of information
terms.gloss: All the information available to investors. A fact is material if it would significantly change that overall picture for a reasonable investor.

terms.label: loss causation
terms.gloss: The requirement that the misstatement itself, not other factors, caused the investor's loss, usually shown by a price drop when the truth comes out.

terms.label: discovery stay
terms.gloss: A pause on pretrial evidence-gathering; the PSLRA requires one until the court rules on a motion to dismiss.

terms.label: Securities Litigation Uniform Standards Act
terms.gloss: A 1998 federal law that blocks most large class actions claiming securities fraud under state law, so such claims must proceed under federal securities law.

terms.label: absent class members
terms.gloss: Class members who are not named parties and do not personally take part in the case, though a class judgment can bind them.

terms.label: settlement pressure
terms.gloss: The push on a defendant facing a certified class to settle even weak claims, because one loss at trial could be enormous.

terms.label: interference (tort)
terms.gloss: Short for tortious interference: wrongfully disrupting another's contracts or business relationships.

terms.label: Rule 12(b)(1)
terms.gloss: The federal rule letting a party ask the court to dismiss a case because the court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction over that kind of case.

terms.label: contacts (with a state)
terms.gloss: A defendant's connections with a state, such as sales, advertising, or visits. Enough deliberate contacts let that state's courts hear claims against it.

terms.label: purposeful (contacts)
terms.gloss: Deliberate: contacts the defendant itself chose to create with the state, not ones caused by others or by chance.

terms.label: Calder v. Jones
terms.gloss: Calder v. Jones (1984): California could hear a libel suit against out-of-state writers who aimed a story at California, knowing the harm would be felt there.

terms.label: Walden v. Fiore
terms.gloss: Walden v. Fiore (2014): jurisdiction must rest on the defendant's own contacts with the state, not just on the plaintiff living or being injured there.

terms.label: coextensive with due process
terms.gloss: Reaching as far as the Constitution allows. Then the only question for jurisdiction is the constitutional due-process limit.

terms.label: transfer (of a case)
terms.gloss: Moving a pending case to a different court where it can properly be heard, instead of dismissing it.

terms.label: interest of justice
terms.gloss: A broad standard letting a court do what fairness requires, here transferring a case filed in the wrong court instead of dismissing it.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 1631
terms.gloss: A federal statute letting a court that lacks jurisdiction transfer the case to a court that has it, if that serves the interest of justice.

terms.label: lease-purchase
terms.gloss: An agreement to rent goods with payments that let the renter buy them at the end, often for a token price. Courts may treat it as a sale.

terms.label: purchase option
terms.gloss: The right to buy the goods at the end of the lease. A 'nominal' option costs only a token sum, making the lease effectively a sale.

terms.label: addendum
terms.gloss: A written addition to a contract that adds or changes terms.

terms.label: completion certificate
terms.gloss: A signed form acknowledging that installation was finished. The seller argued it proved the buyer had accepted the goods.

terms.label: rejection (of goods)
terms.gloss: A buyer's refusal of delivered goods as not conforming to the contract. Under the UCC it must be timely and properly communicated or it fails.

terms.label: repossession
terms.gloss: The seller or lender taking back goods when the buyer fails to pay.

terms.label: public sale
terms.gloss: A publicly announced auction of repossessed goods. The money raised is credited against the debt.

terms.label: proceeds
terms.gloss: Money received from selling property, such as the money from an auction of repossessed goods.

terms.label: county court
terms.gloss: A trial court for a county, often handling smaller cases. In Mississippi, appeals from it go to the circuit court.

terms.label: manifest error
terms.gloss: A clear, obvious mistake. Under this standard an appeals court overturns a trial judge's factual findings only for that kind of error.

terms.label: offset
terms.gloss: Subtracting money the other side owes you from what you owe them.

terms.label: affirmative damages
terms.gloss: Money awarded to a defendant on its own claim, beyond simply defeating the claim against it.

terms.label: presiding justice / judge
terms.gloss: The senior judge who leads a court or panel and runs its proceedings.

terms.label: exclusive rights
terms.gloss: Rights given to one party alone. Because only it can sell, courts often imply a duty to make reasonable efforts.

terms.label: reasonable efforts
terms.gloss: A contract duty to make a genuine, sensible effort to perform, such as promoting a product, without guaranteeing success.

terms.label: Wood v. Lucy
terms.gloss: Wood v. Lucy, Lady Duff-Gordon (N.Y. 1917): an exclusive dealing contract implies a promise to use reasonable efforts, so it is not one-sided or illusory.

terms.label: delegation of duties
terms.gloss: Handing one's contract duties to someone else to perform. The original party usually stays liable if the substitute fails.

terms.label: certainty of damages
terms.gloss: The rule that lost profits are recoverable only if the loss itself is reasonably certain, even though its exact amount may be estimated.

terms.label: expert (witness)
terms.gloss: A witness with special knowledge, such as a statistician, allowed to give opinions that help the jury.

terms.label: relevance
terms.gloss: Evidence is relevant if it makes a fact that matters more or less likely. Relevant evidence can still be excluded.

terms.label: admissibility
terms.gloss: Whether evidence may legally be shown to the judge or jury under the rules of evidence.

terms.label: Federal Rule of Evidence 403
terms.gloss: Lets a judge exclude relevant evidence when the risk of unfair prejudice, confusion, or misleading the jury substantially outweighs its usefulness.

terms.label: unfair prejudice
terms.gloss: The danger that evidence will sway the jury for improper reasons, for example by looking more conclusive than it really is.

terms.label: foundation (evidence)
terms.gloss: The preliminary showing that evidence is reliable and is what it claims to be, required before it can be admitted.

terms.label: renewal option
terms.gloss: The tenant's right to extend the lease for more years on stated terms.

terms.label: public liability insurance
terms.gloss: Insurance that pays claims by members of the public injured on the premises, protecting the business and the landlord.

terms.label: aggregate (insurance limit)
terms.gloss: The policy's cap on total payouts for all claims combined, as opposed to the limit per person or per accident.

terms.label: reinsurer
terms.gloss: An insurance company that insures other insurers, taking on part of their risk.

terms.label: surrender (of premises)
terms.gloss: Giving up possession of leased property to the landlord, ending the tenancy.

terms.label: account annexed
terms.gloss: An old Massachusetts form of suit for money owed, with an itemized bill of the goods or services attached to the complaint.

terms.label: fair value (of services)
terms.gloss: The reasonable worth of work actually done, which may be owed even though the job could not be finished.

terms.label: nonperformance
terms.gloss: Failing to do what a contract required. Raised as a defense, it means the other side never finished its part of the deal.

terms.label: partial performance
terms.gloss: Doing part of what a contract required. When finishing becomes impossible, the worker may still be paid for the value of what was done.

terms.label: visitor visa / overstay
terms.gloss: Permission to visit the U.S. temporarily. Staying past its end date (an overstay) makes a person deportable.

terms.label: removal (deportation)
terms.gloss: The legal term for deportation: being ordered to leave the United States.

terms.label: Department of Homeland Security
terms.gloss: The federal department whose immigration agencies arrest noncitizens and bring deportation charges.

terms.label: continuous physical presence
terms.gloss: Living in the U.S. without significant breaks for a required period, such as ten years, to qualify for cancellation of removal.

terms.label: discretionary relief
terms.gloss: Relief the government may grant but need not, even when a person meets all the conditions.

terms.label: nonpermanent resident
terms.gloss: A noncitizen without lawful permanent residence (a green card), including someone living in the U.S. unlawfully.

terms.label: Board of Immigration Appeals
terms.gloss: The Justice Department's appeals body that reviews immigration judges' decisions.

terms.label: Matter of Camarillo
terms.gloss: A 2011 Board of Immigration Appeals decision holding that a notice to appear stops time even without a hearing date and time.

terms.label: Chevron (case)
terms.gloss: Chevron v. NRDC (1984): courts deferred to an agency's reasonable reading of an unclear statute it administers. The Supreme Court overruled it in 2024.

terms.label: charging instrument
terms.gloss: The document that formally accuses someone and starts the proceedings against them.

terms.label: Internal Revenue Service
terms.gloss: The federal tax-collection agency.

terms.label: certified mail
terms.gloss: Mail that gives the sender proof of mailing and delivery. Whether it satisfies a requirement of personal service can be disputed, as in Grable.

terms.label: embedded federal issue
terms.gloss: A state-law claim that turns on a substantial, disputed federal question. Under Grable, such a claim can sometimes be heard in federal court.

terms.label: Smith v. Kansas City Title & Trust
match: smith v. kansas city title & trust
terms.gloss: A 1921 case allowing federal jurisdiction over a state-law suit that depended on whether a federal statute was constitutional.

terms.label: Merrell Dow v. Thompson
terms.gloss: Merrell Dow v. Thompson (1986): no federal jurisdiction over a state negligence claim merely because it relies on a federal standard with no federal remedy.

terms.label: original meaning
terms.gloss: What the words of a law or the Constitution meant to the public when adopted; an approach to interpreting them.

terms.label: Tennessee v. Garner
terms.gloss: A 1985 case holding police may not use deadly force on a fleeing suspect unless needed to stop escape and the suspect poses a serious danger.

terms.label: monetary relief
terms.gloss: Money awards, such as damages or backpay, as opposed to court orders to do or stop doing something.

terms.label: sampling and extrapolation
terms.gloss: Deciding a sample of claims and projecting the results across the whole class instead of hearing each claim.

terms.label: rigorous analysis
terms.gloss: The careful review a court must give before certifying a class, checking that Rule 23's requirements are actually met, even if that touches the merits.

terms.label: Daubert
terms.gloss: The test from Daubert v. Merrell Dow (1993) for whether expert testimony is reliable enough to be admitted.

terms.label: pattern-or-practice
terms.gloss: A claim that discrimination was the employer's standard operating procedure, not isolated acts. Proving it shifts burdens in individual claims.

terms.label: federal savings bank
terms.gloss: A federally chartered savings institution (a thrift) governed by federal banking law.

terms.label: loan modification
terms.gloss: Changing a loan's terms, such as the payment amount, usually to help a struggling borrower.

terms.label: installments
terms.gloss: Regular scheduled payments, such as monthly mortgage or pension payments.

terms.label: Land Court
terms.gloss: A specialized Massachusetts court for real-estate matters, including proceedings that come before a foreclosure.

terms.label: return date
terms.gloss: The deadline by which a defendant must respond or appear in a court proceeding.

terms.label: Home Owners’ Loan Act
terms.gloss: A 1933 federal law governing federal savings associations. Its regulations once displaced many state laws on their lending.

terms.label: agreement to agree
terms.gloss: A deal to make a future agreement on terms still to be settled. Usually unenforceable because key terms are missing.

terms.label: indefinite (agreement)
terms.gloss: Too vague about essential terms for a court to tell what was promised or to enforce it.

terms.label: essential terms
terms.gloss: Key deal terms such as price, quantity, or duration. If they are left open, there is usually no enforceable contract.

terms.label: fraudulent intent
terms.gloss: A purpose to deceive at the time of acting.

terms.label: federal prediction (of state law)
terms.gloss: A federal court's best guess of how a state's highest court would decide an unsettled state-law question. It does not bind state courts.

terms.label: amortize
terms.gloss: To spread a debt, such as missed loan payments, over a series of future installments.

terms.label: Office of Thrift Supervision
terms.gloss: A federal agency, abolished in 2011, that regulated savings banks and thrifts.

terms.label: occupy a field (preemption)
terms.gloss: To take over a whole area of regulation, so that state laws in that area are displaced (field preemption).

terms.label: trial list
terms.gloss: The court's calendar of cases scheduled to go to trial.

terms.label: board of directors
terms.gloss: The people elected by shareholders to manage a corporation. Their formal decisions are recorded as resolutions.

terms.label: stock split / stock dividend
terms.gloss: Extra shares issued to existing shareholders in proportion to what they already own, without new payment.

terms.label: pension
terms.gloss: Regular payments made to a retired worker, often monthly for life.

terms.label: gift
terms.gloss: Something given freely, with nothing expected in return. A bare promise to make a gift is generally not enforceable.

terms.label: interest (on a judgment)
terms.gloss: Extra money added to an award to make up for the delay in being paid.

terms.label: inducement
terms.gloss: Causing someone to act. A promise that induces reasonable reliance can become enforceable.

terms.label: Restatement § 90
terms.gloss: The Restatement of Contracts' promissory estoppel rule: a promise that foreseeably induces substantial reliance is binding if needed to avoid injustice.

terms.label: Ricketts v. Scothorn
terms.gloss: Ricketts v. Scothorn (Neb. 1898): a grandfather's promise of money was enforced after his granddaughter quit her job relying on it.

terms.label: commissioner (court officer)
terms.gloss: A court officer who drafts proposed opinions or rulings that the judges may adopt.

terms.label: incorporated
terms.gloss: Organized as a corporation under a state's law. That state and the headquarters state are where a company is 'at home'.

terms.label: supervisory control
terms.gloss: A Montana high-court power to correct a lower court's clear legal error right away in urgent cases, without waiting for an ordinary appeal.

terms.label: underlying action
terms.gloss: The original lawsuit from which a side proceeding, such as an emergency appeal, arose.

terms.label: International Shoe
terms.gloss: International Shoe v. Washington (1945): a state may hear suits against an out-of-state defendant with minimum contacts there, consistent with fair play and substantial justice.

terms.label: arise out of or relate to
match: arise out of or relate to
terms.gloss: The requirement that a claim be connected to the defendant's activities in the state. Ford held 'relate to' does not demand strict causation.

terms.label: relatedness
terms.gloss: Whether a claim is connected closely enough to a defendant's in-state activities to support specific jurisdiction.

terms.label: World-Wide Volkswagen
terms.gloss: World-Wide Volkswagen v. Woodson (1980): a local car dealer and distributor could not be sued in Oklahoma just because a customer drove a car there.

terms.label: Bristol-Myers Squibb
terms.gloss: Bristol-Myers Squibb v. Superior Court (2017): California courts could not hear out-of-state plaintiffs' drug-injury claims with no connection to California.

terms.label: Goodyear v. Brown
terms.gloss: Goodyear v. Brown (2011): a corporation is subject to all-purpose (general) jurisdiction only where it is essentially at home.

terms.label: Daimler AG v. Bauman
terms.gloss: Daimler AG v. Bauman (2014): substantial in-state business alone does not make a company 'at home' for general jurisdiction.

terms.label: BNSF Railway v. Tyrrell
terms.gloss: BNSF Railway v. Tyrrell (2017): applied Daimler to reject general jurisdiction in Montana over a railroad doing substantial business there.

terms.label: Keeton v. Hustler
terms.gloss: Keeton v. Hustler Magazine (1984): a magazine regularly sold in New Hampshire could be sued there for libel.

terms.label: Burger King v. Rudzewicz
terms.gloss: Burger King v. Rudzewicz (1985): a franchisee who deliberately contracted with a Florida company could be sued in Florida.

terms.label: Asahi Metal v. Superior Court
terms.gloss: Asahi (1987): Justice O'Connor's plurality said merely putting a product into the stream of commerce is not enough for jurisdiction.

terms.label: carrier
terms.gloss: A business that transports goods for others for a fee.

terms.label: servant
terms.gloss: An old legal term for an employee acting for an employer.

terms.label: paid into court
terms.gloss: Deposited money with the court as an offer to satisfy the claim. If the plaintiff then wins no more, it usually must pay the later costs.

terms.label: remote (damages)
terms.gloss: Too distant or unusual a consequence of a breach to make the breaching party pay for it.

terms.label: contemplation (of the parties)
terms.gloss: What both parties could reasonably have had in mind, when contracting, as a likely result of a breach (the Hadley test).

terms.label: Victoria Laundry
terms.gloss: Victoria Laundry v. Newman Industries (1949): an English case refining Hadley, allowing ordinary lost profits the breaching party should have foreseen.

terms.label: OSHA standard
terms.gloss: A binding workplace rule, such as a maximum exposure level, set under the OSH Act. Emergency standards are temporary.

terms.label: Secretary of Labor
terms.gloss: The Cabinet official heading the Department of Labor, who issues OSHA standards.

terms.label: feasible
terms.gloss: Capable of being done. Under the OSH Act, achievable with available technology at a cost the industry can bear.

terms.label: material impairment
terms.gloss: A significant harm to health or physical capacity, which OSHA standards aim to prevent.

terms.label: parts per million (ppm)
terms.gloss: A measure of concentration: how many units of a substance are in each million units of air.

terms.label: NIOSH
match: national institute for occupational safety and health
terms.gloss: The federal research agency that studies workplace hazards and recommends exposure limits.

terms.label: carcinogen
terms.gloss: A substance that can cause cancer.

terms.label: action level
terms.gloss: An exposure level below the legal limit that triggers monitoring and medical checks.

terms.label: engineering controls
terms.gloss: Physical workplace changes, such as ventilation or enclosed systems, that cut exposure at the source.

terms.label: dermal
terms.gloss: Through the skin.

terms.label: epidemiology
terms.gloss: The study of disease patterns in human populations, used to link exposures to illness.

terms.label: latency
terms.gloss: The long delay between exposure to a substance and the appearance of a disease such as cancer.

terms.label: confounding factors
terms.gloss: Other factors that could explain an observed illness, clouding conclusions about cause and effect.

terms.label: Postal Service
terms.gloss: The federal agency that delivers the mail.

terms.label: postal matter exception
terms.gloss: The FTCA exception keeping federal immunity for claims arising from lost, miscarried, or negligently transmitted mail.

terms.label: no-set-of-facts standard
terms.gloss: An old pleading test: dismiss only if the plaintiff could prove no set of facts supporting the claim. Replaced by plausibility in 2007.

terms.label: absurd consequence
terms.gloss: A result so illogical that Congress could not have meant it, which courts avoid when choosing between readings.

terms.label: labor union
terms.gloss: An organization that represents workers in negotiating pay and working conditions with their employer.

terms.label: shop steward
terms.gloss: A worker who represents the union to fellow employees and management at the workplace.

terms.label: collective bargaining
terms.gloss: Negotiation between an employer and the union representing its workers over a labor contract.

terms.label: bargaining order
terms.gloss: An NLRB order requiring the employer to recognize the union and negotiate with it.

terms.label: recognition (of a union)
terms.gloss: An employer's acceptance of a union as its workers' bargaining representative.

terms.label: good-faith reasonable doubt (labor law)
terms.gloss: An employer's genuine, evidence-based uncertainty that a union still has majority support, needed to poll workers or withdraw recognition.

terms.label: employer poll
terms.gloss: An employer-run vote asking workers whether they still want the union.

terms.label: successor employer
terms.gloss: A new owner continuing the business with mostly the same workers. It must bargain with the existing union.

terms.label: majority support
terms.gloss: Support from more than half of the employees in the bargaining unit, which a union needs to keep representing them.

terms.label: enforce (an agency order)
terms.gloss: When a court enforces an agency order, it makes the order legally binding, so disobeying it becomes contempt of court.

terms.label: union dues
terms.gloss: Fees workers pay the union for representation.

terms.label: circumstantial evidence
terms.gloss: Indirect evidence from which a fact can be inferred, rather than direct proof.

terms.label: overtime
terms.gloss: Extra pay, at one and a half times the regular rate, for hours over 40 in a week.

terms.label: exemption
terms.gloss: Being freed from a rule that otherwise applies, such as an employee exempt from overtime pay or an agency rule exempt from notice and comment.

terms.label: Wage and Hour Division
terms.gloss: The Labor Department office that enforces federal minimum-wage and overtime law.

terms.label: opinion letter
terms.gloss: An agency's written answer explaining how the law applies to particular facts. It is guidance, not binding law.

terms.label: Administrator’s Interpretation
terms.gloss: A Wage and Hour Division guidance document stating how the agency reads the law for a whole category of workers.

terms.label: Paralyzed Veterans doctrine
terms.gloss: A D.C. Circuit rule that an agency had to use notice and comment to significantly change a definitive interpretation. Perez rejected it.

terms.label: force and effect of law
terms.gloss: Legally binding, like a statute.

terms.label: Vermont Yankee
terms.gloss: Vermont Yankee v. NRDC (1978): courts may not require agencies to use more procedures than the APA demands.

terms.label: Auer v. Robbins
terms.gloss: Auer v. Robbins (1997): courts defer to an agency's reasonable reading of its own unclear regulation. Kisor (2019) narrowed it.

terms.label: Seminole Rock
terms.gloss: Bowles v. Seminole Rock (1945), the origin of courts' deference to agencies' interpretations of their own regulations.

terms.label: Christensen v. Harris County
terms.gloss: Christensen v. Harris County (2000): no deference to an agency interpretation that conflicts with a regulation's clear text.

terms.label: Supreme Court Rule 15.2
terms.gloss: The Supreme Court rule requiring a party opposing review to raise its objections in its opposition brief or risk losing them.

terms.label: Secretary of the Interior
terms.gloss: The Cabinet official heading the Interior Department, which manages federal lands and Indian affairs.

terms.label: divest
terms.gloss: To take away ownership, such as stripping the government of title to land it holds.

terms.label: Carcieri v. Salazar
terms.gloss: Carcieri v. Salazar (2009): the Secretary may take land into trust only for tribes that were under federal jurisdiction in 1934.

terms.label: Fair Credit Reporting Act
terms.gloss: The federal law requiring consumer reporting agencies to follow reasonable procedures for accuracy and giving consumers certain rights.

terms.label: fees and costs
terms.gloss: Attorney's fees and litigation expenses the losing defendant may be ordered to pay.

terms.label: concrete (injury)
terms.gloss: A real, not abstract, injury. Article III standing requires one, though it need not be physical or financial.

terms.label: imminent (injury)
terms.gloss: About to happen. A threatened injury must be certainly impending to give standing.

terms.label: named plaintiff
terms.gloss: The person who actually files a class action on behalf of the group.

terms.label: intangible injury
terms.gloss: A non-physical harm, such as to reputation or privacy.

terms.label: private rights
terms.gloss: Rights belonging to an individual, such as property or contract rights, as opposed to duties owed to the public at large.

terms.label: TransUnion v. Ramirez
terms.gloss: TransUnion v. Ramirez (2021): narrowed standing for bare statutory violations, requiring concrete harm for each class member seeking damages.

terms.label: permissible exposure limit (PEL)
terms.gloss: The highest average workplace exposure OSHA allows, usually measured over an eight-hour shift.

terms.label: short-term exposure limit (STEL)
terms.gloss: A cap on exposure over a short period, typically 15 minutes, to limit spikes.

terms.label: Office of Management and Budget
terms.gloss: The White House office that oversees the federal budget and reviews agency regulations.

terms.label: hybrid rulemaking
terms.gloss: Agency rulemaking that adds hearing-like procedures to ordinary notice and comment, as the OSH Act requires.

terms.label: linear no-threshold model
terms.gloss: A risk model assuming any dose, however small, carries some cancer risk in proportion to the dose.

terms.label: dose-response
terms.gloss: How the likelihood or severity of harm changes as exposure increases.

terms.label: senior status
terms.gloss: Semi-retirement for federal judges, who keep hearing cases with a lighter workload.

terms.label: record as a whole
terms.gloss: The entire evidentiary record, including evidence that cuts against the agency's conclusion.

terms.label: wrongful discharge
terms.gloss: Firing an employee in breach of contract or law. Damages are the promised pay minus what the employee earned, or could have earned, elsewhere.

terms.label: comparable (substantially similar) employment
terms.gloss: For mitigation, a job of the same kind and quality. A fired employee need not take different or inferior work to reduce damages.

terms.label: Evidence Code
terms.gloss: A state statute collecting its rules of evidence, as in California. Its section 455 requires letting parties be heard before a court takes judicial notice.

terms.label: will (testament)
terms.gloss: A legal document saying who gets a person's property at death. It must be signed (executed) with required formalities.

terms.label: remainder
terms.gloss: The interest of whoever gets property after an earlier holder's lifetime use ends.

terms.label: lifetime use
terms.gloss: The right to use property only for one's life (a life estate), after which it passes to someone else.

terms.label: Lawrence v. Fox
terms.gloss: Lawrence v. Fox (N.Y. 1859): the landmark case letting a third party sue on a promise made to someone else for that third party's benefit.

terms.label: use permit
terms.gloss: Official local-government permission to develop or use land in a particular way, often granted subject to conditions and for a limited time.

terms.label: legitimate public purpose
terms.gloss: A proper government goal, such as safety or environmental protection; the takings test used at the time asked whether a land-use decision substantially advanced such a goal.

terms.label: posttrial motion
terms.gloss: A request made after the verdict asking the trial judge to enter judgment for the losing side anyway or to order a new trial.

terms.label: historical analogue
terms.gloss: For jury-right questions, the kind of case from 18th-century English courts that a modern claim most resembles; suits like those tried at law then get a jury now.

terms.label: premium
terms.gloss: The regular payment a policyholder makes to an insurance company to keep the coverage in force.

terms.label: policy reserve
terms.gloss: The savings value built up inside a life insurance policy, which the owner could borrow against or use to keep coverage going if premiums stopped.

terms.label: paid-up insurance
terms.gloss: A smaller life insurance policy needing no further premiums, which an owner could get by using the policy's built-up value after stopping payments.

terms.label: blue note
terms.gloss: In Slocum, the insurer's printed promissory note form: signing it with a partial cash payment extended time to pay the rest of the premium on stated terms.

terms.label: suspense account
terms.gloss: A holding account where a business parks money it has received but not yet applied to any obligation, pending some further step.

terms.label: binding instructions
terms.gloss: Pennsylvania's term for a judge's instruction telling the jury it must find for one side, much like a directed verdict.

terms.label: arrest of judgment
terms.gloss: An old common-law step by which a judge refused to enter judgment on a verdict because the pleadings showed a legal defect, such as a claim the law does not recognize.

terms.label: demurrer to evidence
terms.gloss: An old procedure where one side admitted all the other side's evidence as true and asked the court to rule that, even so, it was legally insufficient.

terms.label: sufficiency of the evidence
terms.gloss: Whether the evidence, taken in the light most favorable to one side, is enough for a reasonable jury to find for that side; a question of law for the judge.

terms.label: nonpreclusive
terms.gloss: Not barring a later lawsuit; a nonpreclusive ending leaves the claimant free to sue again.

terms.label: franchise (film)
terms.gloss: In Partmar, a long-term contract giving a theatre the right to show a distributor's new films on set terms and fees.

terms.label: first-run
terms.gloss: The first public showing of a new film in an area, which earned the most money; distributors licensed it to favored theatres.

terms.label: separate trial
terms.gloss: An order splitting a case so some claims or issues are tried on their own, before or after the rest.

terms.label: failure of proof
terms.gloss: A party's not producing enough evidence to prove what it had to prove, so it loses on that point.

terms.label: prejudicial (error)
terms.gloss: Harmful enough to have affected the outcome; only prejudicial errors justify reversal or a new trial.

terms.label: draft
terms.gloss: A written order by one person (the drawer) telling another (the drawee) to pay money, like a check; the drawee becomes bound by 'accepting' it.

terms.label: negotiable / nonnegotiable
terms.gloss: Whether a written promise or order to pay meets the formal rules that let it be freely transferred like money; special presumptions apply only to negotiable ones.

terms.label: value received
terms.gloss: A traditional phrase in notes and pleadings stating that the signer got something of value in exchange, meaning the promise was supported by consideration.

terms.label: Code of Civil Procedure (New York)
terms.gloss: New York's old statute setting the rules for civil lawsuits, including pleading and attachment; it was replaced in 1921.

terms.label: First / Third Department
terms.gloss: Regional divisions of New York's Appellate Division, the intermediate appeals court that reviews the trial-level Supreme Court.

terms.label: charter (a vessel)
terms.gloss: To hire a ship, barge or tug from its owner for a voyage or a period of time.

terms.label: stevedore
terms.gloss: A dockworker hired to load and unload cargo ships.

terms.label: guarantee
terms.gloss: A promise to pay someone else's debt if that person does not pay.

terms.label: memorandum (court filing)
terms.gloss: A written argument filed with the court explaining a party's position on a motion and the law supporting it.

terms.label: limited remand
terms.gloss: An appeals court sending a case back to the trial court for one specific task, such as making a finding, while keeping the appeal open.

terms.label: publish (a deposition)
terms.gloss: To open a sealed deposition transcript and formally make it part of the court's record so the court can consider it.

terms.label: favorable inferences
terms.gloss: On summary judgment, the court must assume every reasonable conclusion from the evidence that helps the party opposing the motion.

terms.label: execution (signing a document)
terms.gloss: Signing a document, and doing whatever else is needed, such as delivery, to make it legally effective.

terms.label: charge-back
terms.gloss: A deduction or reversal a supplier makes against money owed to a distributor, for example to recover disputed credits or fees.

terms.label: representations and warranties
terms.gloss: Statements of fact and promises written into a contract itself; a party may rely on them and sue if they prove false.

terms.label: justifiable reliance
terms.gloss: A required element of fraud: the victim must actually and reasonably have relied on the false statement when deciding to act.

terms.label: fraudulent scheme
terms.gloss: A deliberate plan to cheat someone. In Illinois a broken promise about the future is usually not fraud, but it can be if made as part of such a scheme.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 1920
terms.gloss: The federal statute listing the litigation expenses, such as filing fees, transcripts, copies and court-appointed interpreters, that a federal court may order the loser to pay.

terms.label: court reporter fees
terms.gloss: Charges for the stenographer who records testimony at depositions or hearings and prepares the transcript.

terms.label: circulation to the full court
terms.gloss: A Seventh Circuit practice: before a panel creates a split with another circuit, it sends the opinion to all active judges to see if any want en banc review.

terms.label: Ninth Circuit (numbered federal circuits)
terms.gloss: One of the thirteen federal courts of appeals, most covering a region of the country; each hears appeals from the federal trial courts below it and sits just below the Supreme Court.

terms.label: maintenance (child support)
terms.gloss: Regular payments a parent makes, often under a divorce judgment, toward a child's living expenses; also called child support.

terms.label: incorporated into the judgment
match: incorporated the agreement into its judgment
terms.gloss: When a court adopts the parties' settlement as part of its own judgment, so the terms can be enforced as a court order.

terms.label: KRS (Kentucky Revised Statutes)
terms.gloss: Kentucky Revised Statutes, the official collection of Kentucky's state laws.

terms.label: kickback
terms.gloss: An illegal secret payment demanded or paid in return for steering or keeping a business deal; a form of bribe.

terms.label: reasonable grounds for insecurity
terms.gloss: Under UCC § 2-609, a real reason to doubt the other side will perform; it lets a party demand written assurance and pause its own performance meanwhile.

terms.label: disclosed principal
terms.gloss: When an agent makes a contract and the other side knows whom the agent is acting for; normally only that principal, not the agent, is bound to pay.

terms.label: time is of the essence
terms.gloss: A contract term making deadlines strict, so that even a short delay counts as a serious breach.

terms.label: aggrieved seller / party
terms.gloss: The party harmed by the other side's breach, who is entitled to remedies.

terms.label: windfall
terms.gloss: A gain beyond what makes a party whole; courts avoid remedies that leave the injured party better off than if the contract had been performed.

terms.label: Federal Trade Commission Act
terms.gloss: The 1914 law that created the FTC; section 5 bans unfair methods of competition, and section 6 gives the agency investigative powers and some power to make rules, whose reach is disputed.

terms.label: effective date
terms.gloss: The date a new law or regulation starts to apply.

terms.label: delegation (of lawmaking power)
terms.gloss: Congress handing its lawmaking power to an agency; it is allowed only if Congress gives an 'intelligible principle' to guide the agency.

terms.label: cross-motion
terms.gloss: A motion filed by the opposing side asking for the same kind of ruling in its own favor, such as both sides seeking summary judgment.

terms.label: Loper Bright
terms.gloss: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024), the Supreme Court decision overruling Chevron: courts must decide for themselves what a statute means, without deferring to the agency.

terms.label: cease-and-desist order
terms.gloss: An order, issued by an agency after a hearing, requiring a company to stop a specific unlawful practice.

terms.label: procedural (housekeeping) rule
terms.gloss: An agency rule about its own internal processes, such as how it runs proceedings, as opposed to a rule creating binding duties for the public.

terms.label: National Petroleum Refiners
terms.gloss: National Petroleum Refiners Ass'n v. FTC (D.C. Cir. 1973), an appeals-court decision holding that the FTC could issue binding substantive rules about unfair trade practices.

terms.label: party-limited relief
terms.gloss: A remedy that protects only the parties who sued, as opposed to relief, such as setting a rule aside, that works for everyone.

terms.label: obligation implied by law
terms.gloss: A duty to pay that a court imposes to prevent unfairness, even though no one agreed to it; another name for quasi-contract.

terms.label: agreed facts
terms.gloss: Facts both sides formally accept as true, so the court decides only the legal questions without hearing evidence.

terms.label: inequitable / equitable reason
terms.gloss: Unfair in the sense courts of equity care about; an 'equitable reason' is a fairness-based justification for making someone pay or act.

terms.label: deduction (tax)
terms.gloss: An amount the tax law lets a taxpayer subtract from income before computing tax, such as qualifying business expenses.

terms.label: refund suit
terms.gloss: A lawsuit by a taxpayer who has paid a disputed tax and sues the government to get it back.

terms.label: joint return
terms.gloss: A single income tax return filed together by a married couple.

terms.label: ordinary and necessary business expenses
terms.gloss: The tax-law test for deducting business costs: expenses that are common and helpful in the taxpayer's trade or business, not personal.

terms.label: discovery deposition
terms.gloss: A deposition taken before trial to learn facts, rather than to preserve testimony for use at trial; the questioning side often does not test the witness as it would at trial.

terms.label: improvidently granted
terms.gloss: Done unwisely or in error. The Supreme Court 'dismisses as improvidently granted' when it decides it should not have taken a case.

terms.label: oil-and-gas lease
terms.gloss: A contract letting a company drill for and sell oil and gas from someone's land in exchange for royalties.

terms.label: putative class action
terms.gloss: A lawsuit filed as a class action that a court has not yet approved, or 'certified', to proceed on behalf of the class.

terms.label: Class Action Fairness Act (CAFA)
terms.gloss: A 2005 federal law letting large class actions (over $5 million in total, at least 100 members, and any class member and defendant from different states) be filed in or moved to federal court.

terms.label: notice of removal
terms.gloss: The document a defendant files to move a case from state court to federal court, stating why the federal court has jurisdiction.

terms.label: short and plain statement
terms.gloss: The basic federal pleading standard: allege the key points briefly and clearly, without detailed proof.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 1446
terms.gloss: The federal statute setting the procedure for removing a case from state to federal court, including what the notice of removal must contain.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 1254
terms.gloss: The statute letting the Supreme Court review, by certiorari, cases 'in the courts of appeals'.

terms.label: presumption against removal
terms.gloss: A rule that courts, when in doubt, should send removed cases back to state court; the Court held it does not apply to CAFA cases.

terms.label: poor vehicle (for review)
terms.gloss: A case considered as a means for a court to decide a legal question; a 'poor vehicle' has features making it a bad case for deciding the issue.

terms.label: certificate of appealability
terms.gloss: Permission a prisoner must get before appealing the denial of a habeas petition; the Court has treated a request for one as a case it can review.

terms.label: evade review
terms.gloss: Escape court review because the issue never reaches a court in a form it can decide, for example because parties avoid testing the disputed rule.

terms.label: racially restrictive covenant
terms.gloss: A deed or agreement barring sale or rental of property to people of a particular race; the Supreme Court later held courts may not enforce them (Shelley v. Kraemer, 1948).

terms.label: frontage
terms.gloss: The length of a property's border along a street; the covenant's validity was measured by the share of street frontage whose owners signed.

terms.label: representative action
terms.gloss: A lawsuit in which some people sue or are sued on behalf of others with the same interest, whose rights the judgment then binds; a class action.

terms.label: defendant class
terms.gloss: A group of defendants sued as a class, with some representing the rest; rarer than a class of plaintiffs.

terms.label: consortium (business)
terms.gloss: A group of companies that join together to carry out a large project.

terms.label: consolidated trial
terms.gloss: A single trial combining several related lawsuits that share common questions.

terms.label: continuous and systematic
terms.gloss: The level of ongoing business activity in a state that allows its courts to hear any claim against a company, even one unrelated to that state.

terms.label: jurisdiction by necessity
terms.gloss: A proposed rule letting a court hear a case, despite weak contacts, because no other court is available to the plaintiff; the Supreme Court has not adopted it.

terms.label: payor / payee
terms.gloss: The payor is the party making a payment, for example by writing a check; the payee is the party receiving it.

terms.label: criminal contempt
terms.gloss: Punishment, such as a fine, imposed by a court for willfully disobeying its orders, treated like a criminal penalty.

terms.label: Court of Chancery (Delaware)
terms.gloss: Delaware's court of equity, which hears most disputes about the internal affairs of Delaware corporations, without a jury.

terms.label: sequestrator
terms.gloss: The court-appointed official who carries out a sequestration order by taking control of the defendant's property.

terms.label: stop-transfer order
terms.gloss: An instruction on a corporation's records forbidding any transfer of particular shares, freezing them in place.

terms.label: Pennoyer v. Neff
terms.gloss: An 1878 Supreme Court case holding that a state's courts have power only over people and property physically within its borders; International Shoe later loosened it.

terms.label: pragmatic finality (Cox Broadcasting)
terms.gloss: The Supreme Court's practical test, from Cox Broadcasting v. Cohn, for treating a state-court ruling as 'final' enough to review even though the case is not over.

terms.label: adjudicatory authority
terms.gloss: A court's power to decide a case in a way that binds a particular party; personal jurisdiction.

terms.label: Burnham v. Superior Court
terms.gloss: A 1990 Supreme Court case upholding jurisdiction over a person served with papers while briefly in the state, with the Justices split on the reasons.

terms.label: Mallory v. Norfolk Southern
terms.gloss: A 2023 Supreme Court case upholding a state law treating a company's registration to do business there as consent to be sued there.

terms.label: general contractor
terms.gloss: The main contractor who runs a whole construction or repair job and hires and pays any subcontractors, usually charging a fee for overhead and profit.

terms.label: aggregation (of claims)
terms.gloss: Adding together the claims of all class members to see whether the total meets a jurisdictional amount, such as CAFA's $5 million.

terms.label: named plaintiff / class representative
terms.gloss: The person who files a class action on behalf of the group; the unnamed members are the absent people the suit claims to represent.

terms.label: overburden
terms.gloss: The soil and rock lying on top of a deposit, such as gravel, which must be stripped off to mine it.

terms.label: market value
terms.gloss: The price property would bring in a sale between a willing buyer and a willing seller.

terms.label: prevailing opinion
terms.gloss: The opinion that decides the case, even if, as in Groves, fewer than a majority of all the court's judges joined it.

terms.label: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)
terms.gloss: The federal agency that carries out national environmental laws, such as the Clean Air Act, by writing and enforcing regulations.

terms.label: air pollutant
terms.gloss: Under the Clean Air Act, any physical, chemical, biological or radioactive substance emitted into the air; the Court held this covers greenhouse gases.

terms.label: ambient air
terms.gloss: The outdoor air around us, as opposed to air inside buildings or equipment.

terms.label: endangerment (finding)
terms.gloss: The EPA's scientific judgment whether a pollutant 'may reasonably be anticipated to endanger public health or welfare'; a yes requires it to regulate.

terms.label: petition (for rulemaking)
terms.gloss: A formal request asking an agency to issue, change or repeal a rule; the APA gives interested persons the right to file one.

terms.label: procedural right
terms.gloss: A right given by statute to a particular procedure, such as petitioning and getting court review; when it protects a concrete interest, standing rules are relaxed somewhat.

terms.label: special solicitude
terms.gloss: Extra leniency in standing analysis that Massachusetts v. EPA gave states suing to protect their territory and sovereign interests.

terms.label: quasi-sovereign interest
terms.gloss: A state's interest in the health, well-being and environment of its people and territory as a whole, apart from property it owns.

terms.label: proprietary interest
terms.gloss: An interest a state has simply as an owner of property, like any private landowner.

terms.label: Massachusetts v. Mellon
terms.gloss: A 1923 case holding that a state cannot sue the federal government to protect its citizens from the operation of a federal law.

terms.label: Georgia v. Tennessee Copper
terms.gloss: A 1907 case letting Georgia sue to stop out-of-state factory fumes damaging its territory, recognizing a state's interest in its land and air.

terms.label: Heckler v. Chaney
terms.gloss: A 1985 case holding that an agency's decision not to bring an enforcement action is presumed to be unreviewable by courts.

terms.label: nonenforcement
terms.gloss: An agency's choice not to take enforcement action in a particular case.

terms.label: FDA v. Brown & Williamson
terms.gloss: A 2000 case holding that the FDA lacked power to regulate tobacco, given Congress's history of treating tobacco separately.

terms.label: SCRAP (United States v. SCRAP)
terms.gloss: A 1973 case that found standing for students on a long, loose chain of causation; it is often cited as the outer limit of standing.

terms.label: attenuated (causation)
terms.gloss: Stretched thin; an attenuated causal chain has so many intervening steps that the link between action and harm is too weak.

terms.label: imminence
terms.gloss: For standing, the requirement that a future injury be certainly impending or substantially likely, not speculative.

terms.label: advance notice (of proposed rulemaking)
terms.gloss: An early agency announcement asking for public input on whether and how to write a rule, before it publishes an actual proposed rule.

terms.label: Lujan / Spokeo / TransUnion
terms.gloss: Leading Supreme Court standing decisions (1992, 2016, 2021) requiring a plaintiff to show a concrete, particularized injury.

terms.label: closing
terms.gloss: The final step of a real-estate sale, when the buyer pays and the seller hands over the deed.

terms.label: delivery (of a document)
terms.gloss: Handing over a signed document with the intent that it take legal effect; some documents bind only once delivered.
terms.context: \b(formal delivery|accounts of delivery|delivery of the paper|delivery of the deed|deed)\b

terms.label: intoxication (contract defense)
terms.gloss: Drunkenness; it lets a person escape a contract only if it left them unable to understand what they were agreeing to.

terms.label: avoidance (of a contract)
terms.gloss: Undoing a voidable contract, for example because of incapacity or fraud, so the party is no longer bound.

terms.label: Supreme Court of Appeals
terms.gloss: The name of Virginia's highest court until 1971 (now the Supreme Court of Virginia); West Virginia's highest court still uses the name.

terms.label: anchor (tenant)
terms.gloss: A large store, like a department store, that draws shoppers to a mall and usually occupies a big end space.

terms.label: negative duty
terms.gloss: A duty not to do something; such orders are easy for courts to supervise compared with orders to perform work.

terms.label: exclusive agency
terms.gloss: An arrangement in which only one agent may act for the principal in a given field; in Wood, only Wood could market Lady Duff-Gordon's name and designs.

terms.label: endorsement (commercial)
terms.gloss: A famous person's public approval of a product, which makes it sell; here, Lady Duff-Gordon's name attached to others' designs.

terms.label: well-pleaded allegations
terms.gloss: The factual statements in a complaint, which a court must accept as true when deciding whether the complaint states a claim.

terms.label: implied promise
terms.gloss: A promise the court finds in a contract from its terms and purpose, though not written in so many words.

terms.label: Special Use Valuation
terms.gloss: A federal estate-tax rule letting family farms be valued at farm-use value rather than market value, if heirs agree to keep farming them.

terms.label: unequivocal acceptance (mirror-image rule)
terms.gloss: The rule that an acceptance must agree to the offer's exact terms without conditions; a response that changes or leaves terms open is not an acceptance.

terms.label: conditional assent
terms.gloss: A reply that agrees only if the other side accepts some change; it is not an acceptance but in effect a counteroffer.

terms.label: undivided (share)
terms.gloss: A co-owner's fractional share of the whole property, not of any specific part of it.

terms.label: North Dakota Century Code
terms.gloss: The official collection of North Dakota's state statutes.

terms.label: original proceeding
terms.gloss: A case started directly in a higher court, such as a request for a writ ordering a lower-court judge to stop, rather than an appeal.

terms.label: concurred in part and dissented in part
match: concurred in part and dissented in part
terms.gloss: A judge's split vote: agreeing with some of the court's decision and disagreeing with the rest.

terms.label: Hanson v. Denckla
terms.gloss: A 1958 case holding that jurisdiction requires the defendant itself to have purposefully reached into the state, not just someone else's actions.

terms.label: Hess v. Pawloski
terms.gloss: A 1927 case upholding a state law treating a nonresident driver's use of its roads as consent to be sued there over accidents.

terms.label: down payment
terms.gloss: The part of the price a buyer pays up front when signing, held toward the purchase.

terms.label: adjourned
terms.gloss: Postponed to a later date.

terms.label: waive a condition
terms.gloss: A party for whose sole benefit a contract condition exists may give it up and insist on going ahead with the deal.

terms.label: admissible evidence
terms.gloss: Evidence a court may legally consider; second- or third-hand reports of what someone said are often not admissible.

terms.label: broker
terms.gloss: An agent who arranges deals between buyers and sellers, such as a real-estate broker, for a commission.

terms.label: shipping articles
terms.gloss: The written employment contract a ship's crew signs, stating the voyage, the work, and the wages.

terms.label: unforeseen circumstances (Restatement § 89)
terms.gloss: Under Restatement § 89, a fair change to a contract can bind without new consideration if prompted by circumstances the parties did not anticipate when contracting.

terms.label: New York General Obligations Law
terms.gloss: New York's statute on contracts and debts. Its § 5-1103 lets a signed written change to a contract bind even without new consideration.

terms.label: counterfactual
terms.gloss: A hypothetical 'what if' version of events, such as what would have happened without the breach, used to test reasoning or measure loss.

terms.label: costs (court costs)
terms.gloss: Court expenses, such as filing and transcript fees, that the losing side may be ordered to pay. They usually do not include lawyers' fees.

terms.label: after-discovered (newly discovered) evidence
terms.gloss: Evidence found after trial that could not reasonably have been found earlier. It justifies a rehearing or new trial only if likely to change the result.

terms.label: underwriters
terms.gloss: Insurers who agreed to bear the risk of loss; here, the companies insuring the tug.

terms.label: strict proof
terms.gloss: An old pleading formula demanding that the plaintiff prove an allegation. It neither admits nor denies it, so courts treat it as an improper answer.

terms.label: on its own initiative (sua sponte)
terms.gloss: Done by the judge without any party asking, also called sua sponte.

terms.label: Rule 8(d) (former; failure to deny)
terms.gloss: Former federal rule, now Rule 8(b)(6): an allegation not properly denied counts as admitted, except allegations about the amount of damages.

terms.label: admitted (in pleading)
terms.gloss: In pleading, an allegation the defendant does not properly deny is treated as admitted: accepted as true without proof.

terms.label: admitted (to practice in a court)
terms.gloss: Not licensed to practice as a lawyer before that particular court. Each federal court admits lawyers separately.

terms.label: publicity given to private life
terms.gloss: A privacy claim for publicly revealing embarrassing private facts that are not of legitimate public concern.

terms.label: civil conspiracy
terms.gloss: An agreement by two or more people to commit an unlawful act that harms someone. It makes each liable for the others' wrong but requires an underlying tort.

terms.label: prospective jurors
terms.gloss: People summoned for jury service who are being screened, before any are chosen to sit on the jury.

terms.label: relief from judgment
terms.gloss: Undoing or modifying a final judgment after it is entered, for reasons such as mistake, fraud, or new evidence (federal Rule 60).

terms.label: public controversy
terms.gloss: A real public debate. Voluntarily joining one can make a person a 'public figure' who must prove actual malice to win defamation-type claims.

terms.label: generally applicable law
terms.gloss: A law that applies to everyone rather than targeting religion. Religious belief usually does not excuse breaking it.

terms.label: Gasperini v. Center for Humanities
terms.gloss: Gasperini v. Center for Humanities (1996): federal courts hearing state claims use the state's test for excessive damages, applied through federal procedure.

terms.label: noneconomic damages cap
terms.gloss: A state law limiting damages for non-financial harms such as pain, suffering, and emotional distress.

terms.label: constitutional guideposts (punitive damages)
terms.gloss: The Supreme Court's three tests for whether punitive damages are unconstitutionally excessive: how blameworthy the conduct was, the ratio to actual harm, and comparable penalties.

terms.label: reprehensibility
terms.gloss: Blameworthiness. How bad the defendant's conduct was is the most important factor in judging whether punitive damages are too high.

terms.label: Philip Morris v. Williams
terms.gloss: Philip Morris USA v. Williams (2007): a jury may not use punitive damages to punish a defendant for harm done to people who are not parties to the case.

terms.label: weight of the evidence
terms.gloss: Which side the evidence more convincingly favors. A judge may order a new trial when a verdict goes against its clear weight.

terms.label: Rule 47(a) (juror questioning)
terms.gloss: The federal rule letting the trial judge decide how prospective jurors are questioned, by the judge personally or by the lawyers.

terms.label: Rule 60 (relief from judgment)
terms.gloss: The federal rule allowing relief from a final judgment for listed reasons, such as mistake, newly discovered evidence, fraud, or other justifying cause.

terms.label: outrageous conduct
terms.gloss: Conduct so extreme it goes beyond all bounds of decency, a required element of intentional infliction of emotional distress.

terms.label: body execution (civil arrest)
terms.gloss: Enforcing a money judgment by jailing the debtor rather than seizing property, historically to pressure payment or disclosure of hidden assets.

terms.label: insolvent's oath
terms.gloss: A jailed debtor's sworn statement of having no property to pay the debt; after creditor notice and examination, it can win release.

terms.label: prejudgment arrest
terms.gloss: Jailing a defendant before any judgment, to keep them from fleeing or hiding assets while the case is pending.

terms.label: saving construction
terms.gloss: Reading a statute narrowly so that it stays constitutional, instead of striking it down.

terms.label: fraudulent transfer
terms.gloss: Moving property to someone else, such as a spouse, to put it beyond creditors' reach. The law lets creditors undo such transfers.

terms.label: product disparagement
terms.gloss: A claim for false statements that damage the reputation of a business's product and cause it financial loss; also called trade libel.

terms.label: New York Times v. Sullivan
terms.gloss: The 1964 case holding that public officials, later public figures too, suing over false statements must prove actual malice: knowing falsity or reckless disregard.

terms.label: historical fact
terms.gloss: A finding about what actually happened or what someone actually knew, as opposed to a legal conclusion. Appeals courts normally defer to trial judges on these.

terms.label: independent review
terms.gloss: An appeals court examining the record itself without deferring to the trial court, required in First Amendment cases for findings like actual malice.

terms.label: incitement
terms.gloss: Speech intended and likely to provoke imminent lawless action, which falls outside First Amendment protection.

terms.label: quantum of proof
terms.gloss: How much evidence is needed to win, such as a preponderance or clear and convincing evidence.

terms.label: arising out of or relating to
match: arising out of or relating to
terms.gloss: The link specific jurisdiction requires: the lawsuit must come from, or be closely connected to, the defendant's activities in that state.

terms.label: Revell v. Lidov
terms.gloss: Revell v. Lidov (5th Cir. 2002): posting an article online, readable in Texas but not aimed at Texas, did not allow a Texas libel suit.

terms.label: Ford Motor Co. v. Montana Eighth Judicial District Court
terms.gloss: Ford v. Montana Eighth Judicial District (2021): a claim can 'relate to' a company's in-state activity without strict proof that activity caused the injury.

terms.label: Fielding v. Hubert Burda Media
terms.gloss: An earlier Fifth Circuit case on when a publication's circulation in a state supports personal jurisdiction there.

terms.label: Montreal Convention
terms.gloss: An international treaty governing airline liability for passenger injuries on international flights, with a two-year deadline to sue.

terms.label: limitations period (statute of limitations)
terms.gloss: A legal deadline for filing a lawsuit. Once it passes, the claim is usually barred no matter its merit.

terms.label: bankruptcy stay
terms.gloss: The automatic freeze on lawsuits against a debtor that begins when a bankruptcy case is filed.

terms.label: reporter (case reporter)
terms.gloss: A published series of court decisions, such as F.3d. A citation's volume and page number point to where an opinion appears.

terms.label: under oath
terms.gloss: Having sworn to tell the truth, so that lying becomes perjury.

terms.label: objective unreasonableness
terms.gloss: A standard judging conduct by what a reasonable lawyer would have done, regardless of what this lawyer actually believed.

terms.label: conscious avoidance
terms.gloss: Deliberately closing one's eyes to a high probability of a fact. The law treats it like actual knowledge.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 1927
terms.gloss: A federal statute making a lawyer personally pay the extra costs caused by unreasonably and vexatiously multiplying court proceedings.

terms.label: 18 U.S.C. § 505
terms.gloss: A federal criminal law against forging a judge's signature or a court's seal.

terms.label: court registry
terms.gloss: An account held by the court clerk into which fines or disputed funds are paid.

terms.label: deterrence
terms.gloss: Discouraging future misconduct, by these lawyers and others; the main aim of Rule 11 sanctions.

terms.label: deposit
terms.gloss: Money paid up front toward the price. A buyer who does not get what was promised may sue to get it back.

terms.label: quasi-fiduciary
terms.gloss: A relationship resembling a fiduciary one, in which one side relies heavily on the other's care, such as hotel and guest or carrier and passenger.

terms.label: Hadley v. Baxendale
terms.gloss: Hadley v. Baxendale (1854): contract damages are limited to losses that naturally follow a breach or that both sides could foresee when contracting.

terms.label: natural and probable consequences
terms.gloss: Losses that ordinarily and predictably flow from a breach. Under Hadley, these are recoverable.

terms.label: living wage ordinance
terms.gloss: A local law requiring businesses with city contracts to pay their workers a set wage, usually above the state or federal minimum.

terms.label: Labor Code (California)
terms.gloss: California's main employment statute, covering wages, hours, vacation pay, and penalties for violations.

terms.label: waiting-time penalties
terms.gloss: A California penalty of up to 30 days' wages when an employer willfully fails to pay all wages owed when employment ends.

terms.label: remedial purpose
terms.gloss: A law's aim of correcting a problem or protecting a group; courts read such laws generously to achieve that aim.

terms.label: penal law
terms.gloss: Criminal laws imposing punishment, which must be stated more precisely than economic regulation.

terms.label: legal opinion (testimony)
terms.gloss: Testimony about what the law means. Witnesses cannot give it because deciding the law is the judge's job.

terms.label: designated deposition representative
terms.gloss: A person an organization names to testify for it at a deposition on specified topics, whose answers count as the organization's testimony.

terms.label: Civil Code § 1559
terms.gloss: California's statute letting a third party enforce a contract made expressly for its benefit.

terms.label: prevailing wage
terms.gloss: Laws requiring contractors on public work to pay at least the standard local wage for that kind of work.

terms.label: Labor Commissioner
terms.gloss: The California official who enforces wage laws and collected penalties before PAGA let employees sue for them.

terms.label: persuasive interpretation
terms.gloss: An agency's reading of a law that courts may adopt because it is well reasoned, though they are not bound by it.

terms.label: contingent nonpayment risk
terms.gloss: The risk lawyers take when they will be paid only if they win, which can justify a higher fee award.

terms.label: employee handbook
terms.gloss: A company's written guide to its policies. Whether it creates a binding contract depends on its wording, including any disclaimers.

terms.label: American Arbitration Association
terms.gloss: A private nonprofit organization that runs arbitrations under its own procedural rules.

terms.label: constructive awareness
terms.gloss: Awareness the law assumes a person had because they reasonably should have known, even if they did not actually know.

terms.label: hostile working conditions
terms.gloss: Workplace harassment, based on traits such as sex or race, so severe or pervasive that it changes the conditions of employment; a form of illegal discrimination.

terms.label: negligent training and supervision
terms.gloss: A claim that an employer carelessly failed to train or oversee an employee who then harmed someone.

terms.label: minority (being under 18)
terms.gloss: Being under the age of legal adulthood. Minors can generally cancel (disaffirm) their contracts.

terms.label: age certificates
terms.gloss: State-issued work certificates letting 16- and 17-year-olds take any lawful job, instead of certificates tied to one specific job.

terms.label: bilateral consideration
terms.gloss: Each side giving something in exchange, here mutual promises to arbitrate that must bind both sides.

terms.label: cruise-ticket venue cases
terms.gloss: Cases such as Carnival Cruise Lines v. Shute enforcing fine-print clauses on tickets that fix where passengers may sue.

terms.label: read against the drafter
terms.gloss: The rule (contra proferentem) that unclear contract language is read against the party that wrote it.

terms.label: Erie (Erie Railroad v. Tompkins)
terms.gloss: Erie Railroad v. Tompkins (1938): federal courts hearing state-law claims must apply state substantive law, though they follow federal procedure.

terms.label: Industrial Commission
terms.gloss: The South Carolina agency that decided workers' compensation claims.

terms.label: Guaranty Trust Co. v. York
terms.gloss: Guaranty Trust Co. v. York (1945): under Erie, federal courts should apply state rules that would significantly affect the outcome, so results match state court.

terms.label: Herron v. Southern Pacific
terms.gloss: Herron v. Southern Pacific (1931): a federal judge could direct a verdict despite a state rule leaving the issue to the jury.

terms.label: comment on the evidence
terms.gloss: Federal judges may tell jurors their own view of the evidence and witnesses, while leaving the final decision to the jury.

terms.label: balancing (of interests)
terms.gloss: Weighing competing interests, here state interests in uniform results against the federal interest in its own judge-jury system.

terms.label: international union (and locals)
terms.gloss: The national union organization; its 'locals' are local chapters. The international is not automatically liable for what local members do.

terms.label: picketing
terms.gloss: Union members standing outside a workplace to publicize a dispute and discourage others from working or doing business there.

terms.label: Labor Management Relations Act
terms.gloss: The 1947 federal labor law (Taft-Hartley). Its § 303 lets businesses harmed by unlawful secondary boycotts sue unions for damages.

terms.label: secondary pressure (secondary boycott)
terms.gloss: Union pressure on a neutral company, not the employer in the dispute, to stop dealing with that employer. Federal law restricts it.

terms.label: primary labor dispute
terms.gloss: A dispute directly between a union and the employer it targets, where pressure is generally lawful.

terms.label: post-trial motions
terms.gloss: Requests after the verdict, such as for judgment as a matter of law or a new trial, asking the judge to change or set aside the result.

terms.label: Hurn v. Oursler
terms.gloss: A 1933 case letting federal courts hear a state claim only if it was another 'ground' for the same cause of action, a test Gibbs replaced.

terms.label: strikers
terms.gloss: Workers refusing to work to pressure an employer during a labor dispute.

terms.label: Exxon Mobil v. Allapattah
terms.gloss: Exxon Mobil v. Allapattah (2005), interpreting 28 U.S.C. § 1367, the 1990 supplemental-jurisdiction statute that codified and partly changed Gibbs's approach.

terms.label: loss of society
terms.gloss: Damages for losing the companionship, love, and support of a close family member who was killed or severely injured.

terms.label: Medical Liability and Insurance Improvement Act
match: medical liability and insurance improvement act
terms.gloss: Texas's 1977 malpractice-reform law, which capped most damages against doctors at $500,000, apart from medical expenses.

terms.label: damages cap
terms.gloss: A legal ceiling on how much money can be awarded; here, a state statute limiting malpractice damages.

terms.label: excessiveness (of damages)
terms.gloss: Whether a damages award is so large it must be reduced.

terms.label: federal interpleader statutes (§§ 1335, 1397, 2361)
terms.gloss: The federal interpleader statutes: § 1335 grants jurisdiction with minimal diversity and $500 at stake, § 1397 sets venue, and § 2361 allows nationwide service and injunctions.

terms.label: multiple liability
terms.gloss: The risk that a stakeholder pays the same money twice, or more than it owes in total, to rival claimants in separate suits.

terms.label: prescription (Louisiana)
terms.gloss: Louisiana's term for the deadline to sue, its version of a statute of limitations.

terms.label: duty to defend
terms.gloss: A liability insurer's contractual obligation to defend its insured against lawsuits, separate from paying claims.

terms.label: Sandiganbayan
terms.gloss: The Philippines' special anticorruption court.

terms.label: Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act
terms.gloss: The 1976 federal law giving foreign states immunity from suit in U.S. courts, subject to listed exceptions.

terms.label: nonjoinder
terms.gloss: Failure to bring a required party into the lawsuit.

terms.label: equity and good conscience
terms.gloss: Rule 19(b)'s test: whether fairness allows the case to proceed without an absent required party, weighing prejudice, protective measures, adequacy, and alternatives.

terms.label: enforcement of a foreign judgment
terms.gloss: Asking a U.S. court to give effect to a judgment from another country's court so it can be collected here.

terms.label: piecemeal suits
