terms.gloss: Separate lawsuits each deciding part of a dispute, rather than one case resolving all claims together.

terms.label: policy limits (per person / per occurrence)
terms.gloss: Insurance limits: the most the insurer pays for one injured person, and the most for all claims from a single accident.

terms.label: exclusion (insurance)
terms.gloss: A clause in an insurance policy listing situations it does not cover.

terms.label: Strawbridge v. Curtiss
terms.gloss: Strawbridge v. Curtiss (1806): read the diversity statute to require complete diversity, so no plaintiff may share citizenship with any defendant.

terms.label: Section 90 (promissory estoppel)
terms.gloss: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 90: a promise that foreseeably induces reliance is enforceable if needed to avoid injustice.

terms.label: expectation (damages measure)
terms.gloss: The contract-damages measure that puts the injured party where it would have been had the promise been kept.

terms.label: result promise
terms.gloss: A doctor's specific promise to achieve a particular outcome, enforceable as a contract even without negligence.

terms.label: exceptions (objections to rulings)
terms.gloss: Formal objections to a trial judge's rulings, such as jury instructions, preserved for review on appeal. 'Overruling' them rejects them.

terms.label: defensive practice (defensive medicine)
terms.gloss: Doctors ordering extra tests or avoiding risky treatments mainly to avoid lawsuits.

terms.label: Hawkins v. McGee
terms.gloss: Hawkins v. McGee (1929), the 'hairy hand' case: a doctor who guaranteed a perfect hand owed the difference between the promised and actual result.

terms.label: double counting
terms.gloss: Counting the same loss twice, as by awarding both the full expected benefit and the costs needed to obtain it.

terms.label: stationary source
terms.gloss: A fixed source of pollution, such as a power plant or factory, as opposed to cars and trucks.

terms.label: best system of emission reduction
match: best adequately demonstrated system of emission reduction
terms.gloss: Section 111's yardstick: EPA picks the best proven pollution-cutting method, considering cost, and limits must reflect what it achieves.

terms.label: performance standards
terms.gloss: Emission limits a source must meet, set by what the best system can achieve, while leaving the method of compliance to the source.

terms.label: § 111(d) (existing sources)
terms.gloss: The Clean Air Act provision covering pollutants from existing plants not handled by other programs: EPA sets the guideline and states write plans to apply it.

terms.label: Clean Power Plan
terms.gloss: EPA's 2015 rule to cut power-plant carbon emissions, largely by shifting electricity generation from coal to gas and renewables. It never took effect.

terms.label: heat rate
terms.gloss: How much fuel a plant burns to make a unit of electricity. Improving it means burning less fuel and emitting less.

terms.label: generation shifting
terms.gloss: Cutting emissions by moving electricity production from dirtier plants (coal) to cleaner ones (gas, wind, solar) rather than making each plant cleaner.

terms.label: allowances and credits
terms.gloss: Tradable permits: a plant over its limit can buy them from cleaner producers instead of cutting its own emissions.

terms.label: cap-and-trade
terms.gloss: A system setting a total emissions limit and letting polluters buy and sell permits to emit within it.

terms.label: Affordable Clean Energy rule
terms.gloss: EPA's 2019 replacement rule, limited to efficiency improvements at individual coal plants.

terms.label: gap-filling provision
terms.gloss: A provision covering what other programs leave out; § 111(d) is a backstop for pollution not regulated elsewhere.

terms.label: Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS)
terms.gloss: The former federal agency (until 2003) that enforced immigration law for the Attorney General.

terms.label: Immigration and Nationality Act
terms.gloss: The 1952 federal law that is the core of U.S. immigration and citizenship law.

terms.label: good moral character
terms.gloss: A statutory requirement that an applicant has lived lawfully and honestly during the required period.

terms.label: extreme hardship
terms.gloss: Suffering beyond the ordinary hardships of deportation, to the person or close citizen or permanent-resident relatives.

terms.label: voluntary departure
terms.gloss: Permission to leave the country on one's own by a deadline, avoiding a formal deportation order.

terms.label: discharged from committee
terms.gloss: Taken away from the committee that would normally study a measure and sent straight to the full chamber for a vote.

terms.label: recorded vote
terms.gloss: A vote in which each member's position is officially recorded, rather than a voice vote.

terms.label: petition for review
terms.gloss: The way to challenge an agency order, like a deportation order, directly in a federal court of appeals.

terms.label: Refugee Act of 1980
terms.gloss: The 1980 law setting U.S. procedures for admitting refugees and granting asylum.

terms.label: impeachment (removal power)
terms.gloss: Congress's power to remove officials: the House brings charges (impeaches) and the Senate holds the trial.

terms.label: aggrandize
terms.gloss: To enlarge one branch's power at another's expense, a separation-of-powers concern.

terms.label: naturalize
terms.gloss: To grant citizenship to a noncitizen.

terms.label: impartial tribunal
terms.gloss: A neutral decision-maker with no stake in the outcome, a basic fairness protection.

terms.label: Whitman v. American Trucking
terms.gloss: Whitman v. American Trucking (2001): upheld a broad delegation to EPA because Congress gave an 'intelligible principle' to guide it.

terms.label: Gundy v. United States
terms.gloss: Gundy v. United States (2019): upheld letting the Attorney General decide sex-offender registration rules for older offenders, over a sharp nondelegation dissent.

terms.label: bid / bidding
terms.gloss: A formal offer answering a government's invitation, here to lease township land. Public bidding laws require awards on the advertised terms.

terms.label: solicitation (for bids)
terms.gloss: The government's published invitation for bids, stating the terms.

terms.label: gross receipts
terms.gloss: A business's total revenue before any costs or expenses are subtracted.

terms.label: Law Division
terms.gloss: The New Jersey Superior Court's general civil and criminal trial court.

terms.label: Contract Clause
terms.gloss: The Constitution's ban on states passing laws that impair existing contracts.

terms.label: bargaining power
terms.gloss: Each side's relative strength in negotiating. Between equals, agreed terms are presumed fair.

terms.label: customary international law
terms.gloss: International rules that bind nations because nearly all of them consistently follow them out of a sense of legal duty, even without a treaty.

terms.label: genocide
terms.gloss: Killing or seriously harming members of a national, ethnic, racial or religious group with intent to destroy that group in whole or in part.

terms.label: Genocide Convention
terms.gloss: The 1948 UN treaty defining genocide as an international crime and requiring nations to prevent and punish it, whether committed by officials or private people.

terms.label: war crimes
terms.gloss: Serious violations of the laws of armed conflict, such as murdering, torturing or taking hostage civilians or captured fighters.

terms.label: Geneva Conventions
terms.gloss: Four 1949 treaties setting the basic rules for humane treatment of wounded soldiers, prisoners of war and civilians during armed conflict.

terms.label: Common Article 3
terms.gloss: A provision in all four Geneva Conventions setting minimum humane-treatment rules for civil wars, binding every side, including rebel forces.

terms.label: Protocol II
terms.gloss: A 1977 add-on treaty to the Geneva Conventions that expands protections for people caught up in civil wars.

terms.label: recognition (of a state)
terms.gloss: A government's formal acknowledgment that an entity is a country, or that a group is its lawful government.

terms.label: extrajudicial killing
terms.gloss: A killing by government agents without the legal process of a court judgment, such as a summary execution.

terms.label: summary execution
terms.gloss: Killing a person on the spot, without any trial or court judgment.

terms.label: joint action
terms.gloss: A test treating a private person as acting for the government when he willfully acts together with officials in the challenged conduct.

terms.label: implied action
terms.gloss: A right to sue that a court infers from a law or legal norm even though no statute expressly creates one.

terms.label: United Nations Headquarters Agreement
terms.gloss: The 1947 U.S.-UN treaty governing the UN's New York headquarters, including protections for UN representatives and invited visitors.

terms.label: invitee (United Nations)
terms.gloss: Here, a person officially invited by the United Nations to come to New York for its business.

terms.label: doing-business jurisdiction
terms.gloss: Jurisdiction over an out-of-state defendant based on its carrying on regular business in the state.

terms.label: prize (law of prize)
terms.gloss: Relating to 'prize' law, the old body of law governing the wartime capture of enemy ships and cargo at sea.

terms.label: Filártiga v. Peña-Irala
terms.gloss: A 1980 Second Circuit case letting Paraguayans sue a former Paraguayan official in U.S. court under the Alien Tort Statute for torturing their relative.

terms.label: Baker v. Carr
terms.gloss: A 1962 Supreme Court case listing the factors that make an issue a 'political question' courts should leave to Congress or the President.

terms.label: Civil Rights Act of 1957
terms.gloss: The first federal civil-rights law since Reconstruction; among other things it let the U.S. Attorney General sue to stop interference with voting.

terms.label: Section 1971
terms.gloss: The federal voting-rights statute (then 42 U.S.C. §1971) barring intimidation of voters and letting the Attorney General sue for orders preventing it.

terms.label: Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp.
terms.gloss: A 1949 Supreme Court case allowing immediate appeal of orders that conclusively settle an important issue separate from the merits and could not be reviewed later.

terms.label: Leiter Minerals v. United States
terms.gloss: A 1957 Supreme Court case holding that the Anti-Injunction Act does not bar the United States itself from asking a federal court to halt state proceedings.

terms.label: Douglas v. City of Jeannette
terms.gloss: A 1943 Supreme Court case holding federal courts should ordinarily not stop state criminal prosecutions, leaving defendants to raise federal defenses at the state trial.

terms.label: preventive relief
terms.gloss: A court order meant to stop a legal wrong before it happens or continues, rather than compensate for it afterward.

terms.label: principal debtor
terms.gloss: The person or company that actually owes the debt, as opposed to the surety who promised to pay if they did not.

terms.label: special equity
terms.gloss: A proposed extra protection, beyond ordinary rules, for wives and others who guarantee a loved one's debts; the House of Lords rejected it.

terms.label: put on inquiry
terms.gloss: Aware of enough warning signs that the law expects one to take reasonable steps to learn the truth; otherwise one is treated as knowing what inquiry would have shown.

terms.label: confidential relationship
terms.gloss: A relationship of trust (such as solicitor and client) in which the law presumes the trusted party used undue influence in a deal benefiting him, unless shown otherwise.

terms.label: warranty by sample
terms.gloss: An express warranty created when a sample or model is part of the deal: the delivered goods must match it.

terms.label: superseding cause
terms.gloss: A later, independent event that breaks the chain of responsibility, relieving the original wrongdoer of liability for the resulting harm.

terms.label: discovery rule (accrual)
terms.gloss: The rule that a claim's filing deadline starts running only when the injured party discovered, or reasonably should have discovered, the injury.

terms.label: ostensible agency
terms.gloss: Agency the law recognizes because the principal led others to reasonably believe someone was its agent, even if no real authority was given.

terms.label: implied contractual indemnity
terms.gloss: A right, implied from a contract, to be reimbursed by the other party for losses to third parties caused by that party's breach.

terms.label: intervening cause
terms.gloss: An independent act (here, the bride's decision not to marry) that comes between the wrong and the loss and may cut off the wrongdoer's liability.

terms.label: legal sufficiency
terms.gloss: The early stage at which a court asks only whether the complaint's allegations, if true, state a claim the law recognizes.

terms.label: executory consideration
terms.gloss: Consideration consisting only of promises still to be performed, as opposed to something already given, such as a payment.

terms.label: Court of Common Pleas
terms.gloss: A traditional name for a trial court handling ordinary civil cases; here, the Massachusetts trial court.

terms.label: discharged in bankruptcy
terms.gloss: Debts a bankruptcy court has cancelled, so the creditor can no longer legally collect them.

terms.label: revived debt
terms.gloss: The old rule that a new promise can make enforceable again a debt that was once valid but became unenforceable, for example through time limits or bankruptcy.

terms.label: default clause
terms.gloss: A contract term spelling out what happens if a party fails to meet its obligations, such as missing a payment.

terms.label: nonwaiver clause
terms.gloss: A clause saying a party does not give up its contract rights by sometimes failing to enforce them, for example by accepting late payments.

terms.label: improper contacts
terms.gloss: Private, off-the-record attempts by one party to influence decisionmakers while a contested case is pending; they undermine fair adjudication.

terms.label: examiner (hearing examiner)
terms.gloss: A hearing officer (today called an administrative law judge) who hears evidence in an agency case and recommends a decision.

terms.label: de facto control
terms.gloss: Actual control in practice, regardless of who formally holds it on paper.

terms.label: diversification (of media control)
terms.gloss: The FCC's policy of spreading ownership of stations and newspapers among many owners, so the public hears more independent voices.

terms.label: integration (of ownership and management)
terms.gloss: In FCC comparative hearings, how far a station's owners would personally run it day to day, which the Commission favored.

terms.label: reasoned decision
terms.gloss: An agency decision that considers the relevant factors and explains a rational connection between the facts found and the choice made.

terms.label: legitimate expectations
terms.gloss: Reasonable reliance built up on past government treatment, such as a broadcaster's expectation that its license would be renewed.

terms.label: fairness regulation (fairness doctrine)
terms.gloss: The FCC's former 'fairness doctrine', requiring broadcasters to cover public issues and air contrasting views on them.

terms.label: The Bremen (M/S Bremen v. Zapata)
terms.gloss: A 1972 Supreme Court case holding forum-selection clauses in international commercial contracts enforceable unless unreasonable, unjust or the product of fraud or overreaching.

terms.label: 46 U.S.C. App. §183c
terms.gloss: A former federal shipping law (since recodified) barring ship owners from using ticket terms to escape negligence liability or limit passengers' right to trial in a competent court.

terms.label: percentage rent
terms.gloss: Rent based partly on a percentage of the tenant's sales, usually on top of a fixed base rent.

terms.label: Rule 65(a)(2)
terms.gloss: The federal rule letting a judge combine the preliminary-injunction hearing with the full trial, ordinarily with clear advance notice to the parties.

terms.label: agreement to negotiate
terms.gloss: A binding promise to bargain in good faith toward a final deal (here, with no one else), even though the final deal itself is not yet agreed.

terms.label: definiteness
terms.gloss: The requirement that a promise's terms be clear enough for a court to tell what was promised and whether it was broken.

terms.label: no-evidence motion
terms.gloss: A summary-judgment motion arguing the other side lacks evidence to prove an element of its case, rather than offering proof disproving it.

terms.label: Adickes v. S. H. Kress & Co.
terms.gloss: A 1970 Supreme Court case holding that the party seeking summary judgment must first show there is no genuine factual dispute.

terms.label: element (of a claim)
terms.gloss: One of the required parts of a claim or charge that must be proved to win.

terms.label: attribution (of contacts)
terms.gloss: Treating one company's activities in a state as another's (here, counting MBUSA's California business as Daimler's) for jurisdiction.

terms.label: Perkins v. Benguet Consolidated Mining Co.
terms.gloss: A 1952 case allowing Ohio to hear an unrelated claim against a Philippine mining company whose president ran it from Ohio during World War II.

terms.label: Kiobel v. Royal Dutch Petroleum Co.
terms.gloss: A 2013 Supreme Court case holding that the Alien Tort Statute generally does not reach conduct occurring entirely in other countries.

terms.label: Mohamad v. Palestinian Authority
terms.gloss: A 2012 Supreme Court case holding the Torture Victim Protection Act allows suits only against individuals, not organizations or corporations.

terms.label: willful or wanton
terms.gloss: Intentional harm, or conduct so reckless it shows conscious indifference to an obvious danger; much worse than ordinary carelessness.

terms.label: longitudinal (path)
terms.gloss: Running lengthwise alongside the tracks, as opposed to crossing them.

terms.label: transverse crossing
terms.gloss: A place where a path crosses the tracks; Pennsylvania law could treat people there differently from those walking alongside the tracks.

terms.label: general law
terms.gloss: Under Swift v. Tyson, fields like commercial and common law that federal judges decided by their own view of the law, without following state court decisions.

terms.label: general jurisprudence
terms.gloss: Same idea as 'general law': legal questions thought to belong to no single state, which federal courts decided for themselves under Swift v. Tyson.

terms.label: independent judgment
terms.gloss: A court deciding for itself what the law is, rather than deferring to another body (state courts under Swift; agencies after Loper Bright).

terms.label: Swift v. Tyson
terms.gloss: An 1842 Supreme Court decision letting federal courts in diversity cases create their own 'general' common law instead of following state court decisions; Erie overruled it.

terms.label: Rules of Decision Act
terms.gloss: Section 34 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 (now 28 U.S.C. §1652): state 'laws' are the rules of decision in federal courts unless federal law provides otherwise.

terms.label: local usages
terms.gloss: Customs and practices recognized in a particular place.

terms.label: substantive
terms.gloss: Concerning the actual rights and duties at stake, as opposed to procedural (how a case is handled).

terms.label: Black & White Taxicab case
terms.gloss: A 1928 case in which a Kentucky company reincorporated in Tennessee to create diversity and get a federal court to enforce a deal Kentucky courts would have voided.

terms.label: incorporation
terms.gloss: Formation of a corporation under a state's or country's laws; its state of incorporation is one of its citizenships and 'homes'.

terms.label: Judiciary Article
terms.gloss: Article III of the Constitution, which creates the federal judicial power and defines its reach.

terms.label: 1937 intervention statute
terms.gloss: A 1937 law requiring that the United States be notified, and allowed to take part, when a federal statute's constitutionality is questioned in a case.

terms.label: Byrd v. Blue Ridge Rural Electric Cooperative
terms.gloss: A 1958 case holding that a strong federal interest, like the federal jury's role, can outweigh a state rule in a diversity case.

terms.label: Hanna v. Plumer
terms.gloss: A 1965 case holding a valid Federal Rule of Civil Procedure applies in diversity cases even if state practice differs.

terms.label: general demurrer
terms.gloss: A pleading objection arguing that the complaint, even if true, states no legal claim.

terms.label: demurrer for uncertainty
terms.gloss: A pleading objection arguing that the complaint is too vague or unclear to respond to.

terms.label: common source (interpleader)
terms.gloss: The old interpleader requirement that rival claims derive from the same origin, such as one contract or one title.

terms.label: independent liability
terms.gloss: A separate obligation the stakeholder owes one claimant regardless of who wins the fund, which traditionally barred interpleader.

terms.label: adverse title
terms.gloss: A claim of ownership conflicting with the landlord's; 'antecedent' means it supposedly existed before the lease began.

terms.label: clouded title
terms.gloss: Ownership made doubtful by an outstanding claim, which can make property hard to sell or borrow against.

terms.label: citizenship (for diversity)
terms.gloss: The state a party belongs to for diversity jurisdiction: for a person, the state where they live permanently; for a corporation, both its state of incorporation and its principal place of business.

terms.label: United Mine Workers v. Gibbs
terms.gloss: A 1966 case letting federal courts hear state claims sharing a 'common nucleus of operative fact' with a federal claim, with discretion to decline.

terms.label: Aldinger v. Howard
terms.gloss: A 1976 case refusing to let a plaintiff add a state claim against a county, a party Congress then seemed to have excluded from civil-rights suits.

terms.label: Zahn v. International Paper Co.
terms.gloss: A 1973 case requiring each class member in a diversity class action to meet the amount-in-controversy minimum.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. §1359
terms.gloss: A federal law denying jurisdiction where a party was improperly or collusively made or joined to create jurisdiction.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. §1447(c)
terms.gloss: The remand statute: procedural defects in removal must be raised within 30 days, but lack of subject-matter jurisdiction requires remand whenever discovered.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. §1447(d)
terms.gloss: The statute generally barring appeals of orders sending removed cases back to state court.

terms.label: properly joined and served
terms.gloss: A defendant actually named in the suit and formally served with papers; only such local defendants trigger the bar on removal.

terms.label: nonjurisdictional
terms.gloss: Not affecting the court's basic power to hear the case, so the defect is lost (waived) if not raised in time.

terms.label: Thermtron Products v. Hermansdorfer
terms.gloss: A 1976 case holding that a remand on grounds the statute does not authorize can be reviewed despite the general bar on reviewing remands.

terms.label: Grubbs v. General Electric Credit Corp.
terms.gloss: A 1972 case holding that an improperly removed case tried to judgment stands if the federal court would have had original jurisdiction.

terms.label: small claims
terms.gloss: A simplified court for minor money disputes, usually without lawyers or formal rules of evidence.

terms.label: Dating Services Law (N.Y. Gen. Bus. Law §394-c)
terms.gloss: New York's statute regulating paid dating services, requiring set contract terms and capping charges when those terms are missing.

terms.label: cooling-off period
terms.gloss: A short period (here three days) during which a consumer may cancel a contract for any reason.

terms.label: substantial justice
terms.gloss: New York small-claims courts' mandate to do fair justice between the parties under the law, without strict procedural rules.

terms.label: invitation to negotiate
match: invitations for customers to make offers
terms.gloss: A preliminary communication, as most ads are, inviting people to make offers rather than being an offer that can itself be accepted.

terms.label: Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA)
terms.gloss: A federal health agency within HHS that wrote the women's preventive-care guidelines, which included contraception.

terms.label: grandfathered plans
terms.gloss: Older health plans exempt from some ACA requirements because they existed before the law and have not changed significantly.

terms.label: accommodation (contraceptive mandate)
terms.gloss: The arrangement letting an objecting religious employer notify the government, after which its insurer or plan administrator provided contraceptive coverage separately.

terms.label: complicity
terms.gloss: Here, the religious belief that taking part in the arrangement would make them morally responsible for contraception they oppose.

terms.label: Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA)
terms.gloss: A 1993 federal law barring the government from substantially burdening religious exercise unless that is the least restrictive way to further a compelling interest.

terms.label: Burwell v. Hobby Lobby Stores
terms.gloss: A 2014 Supreme Court case holding RFRA exempted closely held for-profit companies with religious objections from the ACA contraceptive mandate.

terms.label: Zubik v. Burwell
terms.gloss: A 2016 Supreme Court case sending challenges to the religious accommodation back to lower courts, urging the parties to find a compromise.

terms.label: closely held (corporation)
terms.gloss: Owned by a small number of people, often a family, with shares not publicly traded.

terms.label: Perez v. Mortgage Bankers Association
terms.gloss: A 2015 Supreme Court case reaffirming that courts cannot add procedural requirements for agency rules beyond what the APA demands.

terms.label: substantial burden
terms.gloss: Under RFRA, government pressure serious enough to make a person act against, or pay a heavy price for, their religious beliefs.

terms.label: compelling interest
terms.gloss: A government goal of the highest importance, needed to justify burdening a protected right.

terms.label: less restrictive alternatives
terms.gloss: Other ways the government could reach its goal that burden religion less; RFRA requires using the least restrictive one.

terms.label: inter partes review
terms.gloss: A Patent Office proceeding, created in 2011, in which anyone may challenge an issued patent's validity before a panel of administrative patent judges.

terms.label: Patent Trial and Appeal Board
terms.gloss: The Patent Office's tribunal of administrative patent judges that decides patent challenges such as inter partes review.

terms.label: administrative patent judges (APJs)
terms.gloss: The 200-plus judges of the Patent Trial and Appeal Board who decide patent challenges; appointed by the Secretary of Commerce.

terms.label: Director (of the PTO)
terms.gloss: The head of the Patent and Trademark Office, appointed by the President with Senate confirmation.

terms.label: institution (of review)
terms.gloss: The Patent Office's decision to begin (institute) an inter partes review of a patent.

terms.label: anticipated (patent)
terms.gloss: Invalid because a single earlier patent, application or publication already disclosed the claimed invention.

terms.label: Judge Advocate General
terms.gloss: The senior military lawyer of a service branch, who oversees its military justice system.

terms.label: Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces
match: court of appeals for the armed forces
terms.gloss: The highest military appeals court, made up of civilian judges, which reviews decisions of the services' criminal appeals courts.

terms.label: Ryder v. United States
terms.gloss: A 1995 Supreme Court case granting a new appeal to a Coast Guard member because improperly appointed civilian judges had heard his case.

terms.label: Weiss v. United States
terms.gloss: A 1994 Supreme Court case holding that military officers already appointed need no second appointment to serve as military judges.

terms.label: Morrison v. Olson
terms.gloss: A 1988 Supreme Court case upholding the independent-counsel law and treating the court-appointed independent counsel as an inferior officer.

terms.label: special trial judge
terms.gloss: A judge appointed by the Tax Court's Chief Judge to help hear cases; can decide some small cases and propose decisions in others.

terms.label: superfluous (surplusage)
terms.gloss: Having no effect; courts avoid readings that would make any words of a statute pointless.

terms.label: structural (objection)
terms.gloss: Concerning the Constitution's allocation of power among the branches, rather than an individual's personal rights.

terms.label: Glidden Co. v. Zdanok
terms.gloss: A 1962 case in which the Supreme Court considered, though raised late, whether judges of certain courts could validly sit and decide cases.

terms.label: executive department
terms.gloss: A major unit of the executive branch; the Freytag majority read 'Departments' in the Appointments Clause as Cabinet-level departments.

terms.label: Cabinet
terms.gloss: The heads of the major executive departments (Secretaries of State, Treasury and so on), who advise the President.

terms.label: legislative tribunals (Article I courts)
terms.gloss: Courts created by Congress under Article I, such as the Tax Court, whose judges lack Article III's life tenure and salary protection.

terms.label: life tenure
terms.gloss: Article III judges' right to keep their posts 'during good behavior', in effect for life unless impeached.

terms.label: national ambient air quality standards (NAAQS)
terms.gloss: Nationwide limits the EPA sets on how much of certain common pollutants, such as ozone, may be in the outdoor air.

terms.label: margin of safety
terms.gloss: An extra cushion below the level known to be harmful, to protect against uncertain or unknown health risks.

terms.label: requisite
terms.gloss: Required: under the Clean Air Act, a standard must be just as strict as needed to protect public health, no more and no less.

terms.label: Subpart 2 (Clean Air Act Part D)
terms.gloss: Ozone-specific Clean Air Act rules added in 1990, with severity classes, deadlines and required controls for areas failing the ozone standard.

terms.label: Subpart 1 (Clean Air Act Part D)
terms.gloss: The Clean Air Act's general, more flexible rules for areas whose air fails a national standard.

terms.label: elephants in mouseholes
terms.gloss: Justice Scalia's image: Congress does not make fundamental changes to a regulatory scheme through vague or minor provisions.

terms.label: Article I Vesting Clause
terms.gloss: Article I, section 1: 'All legislative Powers herein granted shall be vested in a Congress', the textual basis of the nondelegation doctrine.

terms.label: J.W. Hampton, Jr. & Co. v. United States
terms.gloss: A 1928 case holding Congress may delegate power if it lays down an 'intelligible principle' to guide the official.

terms.label: Panama Refining Co. v. Ryan
terms.gloss: A 1935 case striking down a delegation letting the President ban 'hot oil' shipments with no standard to guide him.

terms.label: Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States
terms.gloss: A 1935 case striking down New Deal 'codes of fair competition' as an unconstitutional delegation of lawmaking power.

terms.label: technology-forcing
terms.gloss: Setting goals stricter than current technology can meet, to push industry to develop better pollution controls.

terms.label: General Business Law (New York)
terms.gloss: New York's collection of statutes regulating businesses and consumer dealings; its section 394-c governs paid dating and social-referral services.

terms.label: waste (damages for)
terms.gloss: Money for 'waste': damage or misuse by someone holding land, such as a tenant, that lowers its value for the owner.

terms.label: lineal relatives
terms.gloss: Relatives in a direct line of descent, such as parents, children and grandparents, as opposed to brothers, sisters or cousins.

terms.label: reserved (a question)
terms.gloss: Deliberately left a question undecided, to be resolved later or in another case.

terms.label: primary standards
terms.gloss: National air-quality standards set to protect public health; 'secondary' standards protect public welfare, such as crops, visibility and buildings.

terms.label: supplemental state claims
terms.gloss: State-law claims a federal court may hear alongside federal claims because they arise from the same events.

terms.label: comparative hearing (FCC)
terms.gloss: An FCC proceeding weighing rival applicants for the same broadcast license against each other, to pick the one that would best serve the public.

terms.label: FOIA Exemption 4
terms.gloss: The FOIA exception that lets an agency refuse to release trade secrets and confidential commercial or financial information it obtained from a business.

terms.label: proxy (stand-in litigant)
terms.gloss: A stand-in who acts for someone else. A person who sues as a proxy for someone already bound by a judgment is bound by it too.

terms.label: proportionality (discovery)
terms.gloss: The limit that discovery must be worth its cost: courts weigh the stakes, the parties' resources and access to information, and the burden against the likely benefit.

terms.label: discoverable
terms.gloss: Obtainable by the other side in pretrial discovery; information can be discoverable even if it could not be used as evidence at trial.

terms.label: subsequent remedial measures
terms.gloss: Repairs or safety changes made after an incident. Evidence rules bar using them at trial to prove earlier fault, so people are not discouraged from making fixes.

terms.label: copyrightability
terms.gloss: Whether material is the kind of original expression copyright can protect at all; ideas, systems and methods of operation are not protected.

terms.label: method of operation
terms.gloss: A way of operating something, such as a system of commands; the Copyright Act excludes methods of operation from protection, though original expression about them may be protected.

terms.label: transformative use
terms.gloss: In fair use, a use that adds a new purpose or meaning rather than merely substituting for the original; transformative uses are more likely to be fair.

terms.label: 42 U.S.C. § 1985(3)
terms.gloss: A Reconstruction-era civil-rights law letting people sue for damages when two or more persons conspire to deprive them of the equal protection of the laws.

terms.label: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
terms.gloss: A 2009 Supreme Court decision requiring complaints to allege facts making a claim plausible, and holding officials liable only for their own misconduct, not their subordinates'.

terms.label: inspector general
terms.gloss: An independent internal watchdog within a federal department that investigates misconduct and waste and reports its findings to the department and Congress.

terms.label: Bivens action
terms.gloss: A damages suit against federal officers for violating the Constitution, named for Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents (1971), where the Supreme Court first allowed one without a statute.

terms.label: Davis v. Passman
terms.gloss: A 1979 Supreme Court case letting a congressional staffer sue a congressman for damages for sex discrimination under the Fifth Amendment.

terms.label: Carlson v. Green
terms.gloss: A 1980 Supreme Court case letting a prisoner's estate sue federal prison officials for damages for deliberate indifference to his medical needs under the Eighth Amendment.

terms.label: deliberate indifference
terms.gloss: Knowing of a serious risk to a prisoner's or detainee's health or safety and consciously disregarding it; more than carelessness, less than intent to harm.

terms.label: new context (Bivens)
terms.gloss: A claim that differs meaningfully from the three cases in which the Supreme Court allowed damages suits against federal officers; courts are very reluctant to allow a remedy in a new context.

terms.label: special factors (Bivens)
terms.gloss: Reasons suggesting that Congress, not the courts, should decide whether to allow a damages suit, such as national-security concerns or the existence of other remedies.

terms.label: imply a damages remedy
terms.gloss: For courts to create a right to sue for money damages that no statute provides, by inferring it from the Constitution itself.

terms.label: alternative remedial structure
terms.gloss: Some other way to address the wrong, such as an injunction, habeas or an administrative process, whose existence can counsel courts against creating a damages remedy.

terms.label: Prison Litigation Reform Act (PLRA)
terms.gloss: A 1996 federal law restricting prisoner lawsuits, for example by requiring prisoners to use prison grievance systems first; it created no new damages action.

terms.label: intracorporate-conspiracy doctrine
terms.gloss: The rule that employees or agents of one organization, acting for it, cannot conspire with each other, because together they count as a single actor.

terms.label: clearly established (law)
terms.gloss: The qualified-immunity test: officials can be sued only if existing law made it clear to any reasonable official that the specific conduct was unlawful.

terms.label: 1871 Act (Civil Rights Act of 1871)
terms.gloss: The Reconstruction law also called the Ku Klux Klan Act, the source of today's § 1983 and § 1985(3) suits against officials and conspirators.

terms.label: Westfall Act
terms.gloss: A 1988 federal law making a suit against the United States the only remedy for most torts by federal employees, while expressly preserving suits for constitutional violations.

terms.label: unreasonably dangerous
terms.gloss: In product liability, more dangerous than an ordinary user would expect; a product defect of that kind supports strict liability.

terms.label: Court of Special Appeals (Maryland)
terms.gloss: Maryland's intermediate appeals court (renamed the Appellate Court of Maryland in 2022), which sits below the state's highest court.

terms.label: consumer goods
terms.gloss: Goods bought mainly for personal, family or household use, which consumer-protection laws often treat more protectively than business purchases.

terms.label: UCC § 2-314
terms.gloss: The UCC section creating the implied warranty of merchantability: goods sold by a merchant must be fit for their ordinary purpose.

terms.label: UCC § 2-316
terms.gloss: The UCC section allowing sellers to exclude or limit implied warranties if they follow its rules, for example by using conspicuous language.

terms.label: Maryland § 2-316.1
terms.gloss: Maryland's consumer-protection addition to its UCC: sellers of consumer goods or services cannot disclaim implied warranties or their remedies.

terms.label: identified (to the contract)
terms.gloss: The point when specific goods are designated as the ones the contract covers; the UCC treats things movable at that point as goods.

terms.label: predominant-purpose test
terms.gloss: The test for contracts mixing goods and services: if the main purpose is a sale of goods, the UCC applies; if services predominate, it generally does not.

terms.label: inadvertence (inadvertent use)
terms.gloss: Carelessness or inattention by the injured person, such as failing to notice a defect; in strict liability it does not by itself bar recovery.

terms.label: double costs
terms.gloss: Twice the ordinary court costs, ordered against a party who brought a frivolous appeal as a penalty.

terms.label: leaseback
terms.gloss: A deal in which an owner sells property and then leases it back from the buyer, keeping the use of it while freeing up money.

terms.label: repudiate
terms.gloss: To reject or disown an agreement or deal, making clear one will not go through with it.

terms.label: memorialization (memorial of a deal)
terms.gloss: A written record of an agreement already reached; parties may intend a writing merely to record their deal rather than to create it.

terms.label: writing requirement (statute of frauds)
terms.gloss: The statute of frauds rule that some contracts, including sales of goods for $500 or more, cannot be enforced without a writing signed by the party being sued.

terms.label: UCC § 2-201(3)(c)
terms.gloss: The exception to the UCC's writing requirement: an oral contract for goods is enforceable to the extent the goods have been paid for and the payment accepted, or received and accepted.

terms.label: unequivocally referable
terms.gloss: New York's requirement that the payment or conduct relied on be explainable only by the claimed contract, not by some other arrangement.

terms.label: permanent-employee contract (tenure)
terms.gloss: A tenured teaching contract: after a probationary period, the teacher could be dismissed only for cause through procedures set by statute.

terms.label: Penal Code § 995 (California)
terms.gloss: A California criminal-procedure provision letting a defendant ask the court to set aside the charges before trial, for example because the evidence presented was insufficient.

terms.label: Civil Code §§ 1689 and 1567 (California)
terms.gloss: California provisions letting a party rescind (undo) a contract whose consent was obtained by duress, menace, fraud, undue influence or mistake.

terms.label: Civil Code § 1575 (California)
terms.gloss: The California section defining undue influence, including taking unfair advantage of another's weakness of mind or grossly oppressive use of their distress.

terms.label: menace (contract law)
terms.gloss: In California contract law, a threat of unlawful harm to a person, property or character used to force consent; like duress, it makes a contract rescindable.

terms.label: actual fraud
terms.gloss: Intentional deception, such as knowingly false statements or concealment made to induce someone into a contract, as opposed to constructive fraud.

terms.label: insider
terms.gloss: A company officer, director or employee, or someone they confide in, with access to important company information that has not yet been made public.

terms.label: mineral rights
terms.gloss: Ownership of the minerals beneath land, which can be bought, sold or leased separately from the surface.

terms.label: stock option
terms.gloss: A right granted to an officer or employee to buy company shares at a fixed price within a set period.

terms.label: tippee (tip)
terms.gloss: A tippee is someone who receives confidential inside information (a 'tip') from an insider and trades on it; the insider who tipped can be made to repay the tippee's profits.

terms.label: ultimate issue
terms.gloss: The central question the factfinder must decide, such as whether a statement was misleading; witness opinions on it were traditionally restricted.

terms.label: nonexpert (lay) opinion
terms.gloss: Opinion testimony from an ordinary witness based on personal perception, rather than from an expert with specialized knowledge.

terms.label: nonjury (bench) proceeding
terms.gloss: A trial decided by a judge alone, without a jury.

terms.label: inside information
terms.gloss: Important, nonpublic information about a company obtained through a position of trust; trading on it is insider trading.

terms.label: material information
terms.gloss: Information a reasonable investor would consider important in deciding whether to buy or sell.

terms.label: double liability
terms.gloss: Having to pay twice for the same wrong, for example once into a court-supervised fund and again to private plaintiffs.

terms.label: section 21(e) (Securities Exchange Act)
terms.gloss: The provision letting the SEC ask a federal court for an injunction to stop violations of the securities laws.

terms.label: ancillary relief
terms.gloss: Extra court-ordered remedies that support the main relief, such as return of profits alongside an injunction.

terms.label: legal interest
terms.gloss: A right the law recognizes, such as ownership or a contract right, that entitles its holder to sue.

terms.label: prohibitory injunction
terms.gloss: A court order forbidding someone from doing something, as opposed to one requiring them to act.

terms.label: superior equity
terms.gloss: A stronger claim in fairness to the same money or property than another claimant has; for example, defrauded sellers might deserve ill-gotten profits more than anyone else.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 46(c)
terms.gloss: The federal statute on how circuit courts sit in panels and when the full court hears a case en banc.

terms.label: duty-free
terms.gloss: Not subject to customs duty, the tax on imported goods; duty-free shops sell untaxed goods to international travellers.

terms.label: bribery (bribe)
terms.gloss: Offering or paying something of value to an official to improperly influence an official act; a crime in virtually every legal system.

terms.label: ICSID (International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes)
match: international centre for settlement of investment disputes
terms.gloss: A World Bank institution in Washington that administers arbitrations between foreign investors and states.

terms.label: proprietary claim
terms.gloss: A claim based on ownership of property ('that is mine'), as opposed to one based on a contract promise.

terms.label: proprietary authority (government as proprietor)
terms.gloss: The government's power, like a private owner's, to manage its own property and operations, such as deciding who may enter a military base, as distinct from its power to regulate the public.

terms.label: joined to the merits
terms.gloss: Postponed so that preliminary objections, such as to jurisdiction, are decided together with the main dispute rather than first.

terms.label: memorial and counter-memorial
terms.gloss: In international arbitration, a party's main written pleading setting out facts, law and evidence; the counter-memorial is the other side's written answer.

terms.label: transnational public policy
terms.gloss: Basic principles shared across the international community, such as condemning corruption, that international tribunals apply beyond any single nation's law.

terms.label: recognition of foreign awards
terms.gloss: A national court's acceptance of an arbitration award made abroad so it can be enforced there; refusal on public-policy grounds is narrow.

terms.label: collateral (to a contract)
terms.gloss: Side or incidental, not central to the bargain, so that an illegal part could be cut away while the rest survives.

terms.label: arbitration clause
terms.gloss: The contract term requiring disputes to go to arbitration; it is treated as separate from the main contract and can survive the main contract's invalidity.

terms.label: cost shifting
terms.gloss: Making the losing side pay the winner's legal and arbitration costs.

terms.label: section 12(a)(5) (Massachusetts Arbitration Act)
terms.gloss: The provision letting a court vacate an award because there was no valid arbitration agreement, unless that issue was already decided against the challenger or it took part without objecting.

terms.label: Swiss Federal Supreme Court
terms.gloss: Switzerland's highest court, which hears final appeals in civil, criminal and public-law cases.

terms.label: contractual penalty (civil law)
terms.gloss: In Swiss law, an agreed sum a party must pay if it breaches, payable even without proof of loss but reducible by a judge if excessive.

terms.label: Swiss Code of Obligations
terms.gloss: Switzerland's main statute governing contracts, torts and commercial law.

terms.label: article 163(3) (Swiss Code of Obligations)
terms.gloss: The Swiss provision requiring a judge to reduce a contractual penalty that is excessively high.

terms.label: forfeiture (FCC fine)
terms.gloss: In FCC law, a money penalty imposed on a broadcaster for violating broadcast rules.

terms.label: Federal Communications Commission (FCC)
terms.gloss: The federal agency that licenses broadcasters and enforces communications rules, including the ban on indecent broadcasts.

terms.label: FCC v. Pacifica Foundation
terms.gloss: A 1978 Supreme Court decision upholding FCC action against an afternoon radio broadcast of George Carlin's repeated expletives, stressing that narrow context.

terms.label: patent offensiveness
terms.gloss: Obvious, plain offensiveness measured by contemporary community standards for broadcasting, a required element of indecency.

terms.label: safe-harbor hours
terms.gloss: The late-night hours (10 p.m. to 6 a.m.) when the FCC does not enforce its broadcast-indecency rules, because children are less likely to be watching.

terms.label: content discrimination
terms.gloss: Government treating speech differently because of its subject or message, which triggers close First Amendment scrutiny.

terms.label: feasible (feasibility)
terms.gloss: Capable of being done. Under the OSH Act, a standard is feasible if industry can achieve it technologically and economically without threatening its long-term viability.

terms.label: gross misapplication
terms.gloss: A clear and serious error in applying the right standard; only that would lead the Supreme Court to redo a court of appeals' review of the evidence.

terms.label: immune
terms.gloss: Legally protected from being sued or held liable.

terms.label: withholding (tax)
terms.gloss: An employer's deduction of income tax from an employee's pay, sent directly to the government.

terms.label: artful-pleading doctrine
terms.gloss: The rule that a plaintiff cannot keep a necessarily federal claim out of federal court by dressing it up in state-law labels; the court looks at the claim's real nature.

terms.label: anticipated (federal) defense
terms.gloss: A defense the defendant is expected to raise; under the well-pleaded-complaint rule, a federal defense alone cannot create federal-question jurisdiction.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 1340
terms.gloss: The statute giving federal district courts jurisdiction over civil cases arising under the internal-revenue (tax) laws.

terms.label: Rules 52(b) and 59(e)
terms.gloss: Federal rules letting a party ask the trial court, within a short deadline after judgment, to amend its findings (52(b)) or to alter or amend the judgment (59(e)).

terms.label: § 1912 and Appellate Rule 38
terms.gloss: Provisions letting a federal appeals court award damages, fees and extra costs against a party who brings a frivolous appeal.

terms.label: reinsurance certificate
terms.gloss: Here, a document telling the policyholder that a new insurer had taken over the original insurer's obligations under his policy.

terms.label: foreign insurer
terms.gloss: An insurance company incorporated in another state or country; in state law 'foreign' means out-of-state.

terms.label: registered-mail process
terms.gloss: Court papers notifying a defendant of a suit (process) sent by registered mail rather than handed over in person.

terms.label: impairment of contractual obligation (Contract Clause)
terms.gloss: A claim under the Constitution's Contract Clause that a state law unconstitutionally weakened the obligations of an existing contract.

terms.label: remedial statute
terms.gloss: A law changing procedures or remedies, such as where one may sue, rather than the underlying rights; such laws can usually apply to existing contracts.

terms.label: visitation
terms.gloss: A noncustodial parent's court-ordered right to spend time with the child.

terms.label: spousal support (separate maintenance)
terms.gloss: Court-ordered payments from one spouse to support the other; separate maintenance is such support while spouses live apart without divorcing.

terms.label: express or implied consent (Rule 15(b))
terms.gloss: Agreement shown by words or by conduct; a party who lets in evidence on a new issue without objecting may be treated as consenting to try it.

terms.label: best interests (of the child)
terms.gloss: The standard for custody decisions: the court chooses the arrangement that best serves the child's welfare.

terms.label: tender-years presumption
terms.gloss: An old rule presuming young children belong with their mother, now largely abandoned.

terms.label: notice of right to sue
terms.gloss: EEOC letters, often called right-to-sue letters, that allow a worker to file a Title VII lawsuit in court within a set time.

terms.label: 42 U.S.C. § 1981
terms.gloss: A Reconstruction-era statute guaranteeing all persons the same right to make and enforce contracts, including employment contracts, regardless of race.

terms.label: logical relationship (joinder test)
terms.gloss: The flexible test for whether claims arise from the same series of events: they are connected enough that handling them together makes practical sense.

terms.label: Rules 20(b) and 42(b)
terms.gloss: Rules letting the court order separate trials or other protective measures when joined parties or claims would cause delay, confusion or prejudice.

terms.label: federal (land) patent
terms.gloss: The federal government's official document granting title to public land to a private owner.

terms.label: direct challenge (direct appeal)
terms.gloss: Challenging a judgment within the same case, by motion or appeal, as opposed to attacking it later in a different lawsuit (a collateral attack).

terms.label: sovereign
terms.gloss: Having supreme, independent governing authority; each state has power over people and property within its own borders.

terms.label: sister state
terms.gloss: Another state of the United States, viewed in relation to the state whose judgment is at issue.

terms.label: procedural irregularity
terms.gloss: A mistake in how a proceeding was carried out that does not destroy the court's basic power; it usually can be corrected only by a direct challenge.

terms.label: weight of authority
terms.gloss: What most courts that have considered the question have held.

terms.label: tariff schedule
terms.gloss: The official list of import categories and the customs duty rate charged on each, today the Harmonized Tariff Schedule.

terms.label: Customs (U.S. Customs Service)
terms.gloss: The federal agency, now U.S. Customs and Border Protection, that classifies imported goods and collects duties on them.

terms.label: ruling letter (customs)
terms.gloss: A written Customs decision telling a particular importer how specific goods will be classified; it binds Customs for that transaction but is not a general rule.

terms.label: Court of International Trade
terms.gloss: The federal trial court in New York that hears challenges to customs and international-trade decisions.

terms.label: force of law
terms.gloss: Binding legal effect on the public generally, like a statute, rather than only on one transaction.

terms.label: Skidmore (persuasiveness)
terms.gloss: Skidmore v. Swift & Co. (1944): courts give an agency's interpretation weight according to its power to persuade, considering its thoroughness, reasoning, consistency and expertise.

terms.label: § 4(f) and § 138 (parkland protection)
terms.gloss: Federal transportation-law provisions barring use of public parkland for a federally funded highway unless no feasible and prudent alternative exists and harm is minimized.

terms.label: feasible and prudent (alternative)
terms.gloss: The statutory test: parkland may be used only if no other route is both buildable as a matter of sound engineering and prudent, meaning free of truly unusual problems or extraordinary costs.

terms.label: mental processes (of decision-makers)
terms.gloss: An official's private reasoning in reaching a decision; courts ordinarily may not probe it by questioning the decision-maker.

terms.label: APA § 706
terms.gloss: The APA provision listing the grounds on which courts set aside agency action, such as arbitrariness, lack of substantial evidence (§ 706(2)(E)), or facts warranting a trial de novo (§ 706(2)(F)).

terms.label: presumption of regularity
terms.gloss: The assumption that officials performed their duties properly unless shown otherwise.

terms.label: administrative record
terms.gloss: The documents and materials the agency actually had before it when it decided, which courts use to review the decision.

terms.label: concession (contract)
terms.gloss: A contract letting a private business operate on government property on the government's terms, such as a cafeteria inside a military base.

terms.label: Greene v. McElroy
terms.gloss: A 1959 Supreme Court case setting aside the revocation of an engineer's security clearance without confrontation, because no explicit presidential or congressional authorization existed.

terms.label: stigma (infamy)
terms.gloss: A public mark of disgrace, such as being branded disloyal, that can damage reputation and job prospects and may require due-process protections.

terms.label: right/privilege distinction
terms.gloss: The old idea that government may withdraw 'privileges', like a government job, without due process because they are not 'rights'.

terms.label: justice of the peace
terms.gloss: A local judicial officer handling minor civil and criminal matters; Marbury's D.C. post carried a five-year term.

terms.label: commission (of office)
terms.gloss: The official signed and sealed document that evidences a person's appointment to public office.

terms.label: failure to appear, plead or defend
match: failure to appear, plead or defend
terms.gloss: Never showing up in the case or filing any response to the complaint, which lets the court enter a default against that party.

terms.label: coparty
terms.gloss: A party on the same side of a lawsuit as another, such as two plaintiffs or two defendants.

terms.label: coplaintiff
terms.gloss: Another plaintiff suing in the same case.

terms.label: same transaction or occurrence
terms.gloss: The test for whether claims are related enough to be joined: they arise from the same event or connected series of events.

terms.label: ancillary
terms.gloss: Secondary to and dependent on a main claim already in the case, rather than standing on its own.

terms.label: affirmative claim
terms.gloss: A claim asking for relief against someone, as opposed to a defense against a claim someone else made.

terms.label: federal judicial district
terms.gloss: The area served by one federal trial court (district court); a state has one to four districts.

terms.label: Appeals Court
terms.gloss: Massachusetts's intermediate appeals court, between the trial courts and the Supreme Judicial Court.

terms.label: direct review
terms.gloss: Here, the state's highest court taking a case straight from the trial court, skipping the intermediate appeals court.

terms.label: Chief Judge
terms.gloss: The presiding judge of a court, with administrative duties; in New York, the head of the Court of Appeals.

terms.label: Vice-Chancellor
terms.gloss: In nineteenth-century England, a judge of the Court of Chancery, the court that granted equitable remedies such as specific performance.

terms.label: Lord Justice
terms.gloss: Title of a judge on England's Court of Appeal.

terms.label: joined (an opinion)
terms.gloss: A judge 'joins' an opinion by signing on to it, agreeing with its reasoning.

terms.label: exclusive federal jurisdiction
terms.gloss: A rule that only federal courts, not state courts, may hear a type of claim, such as Sherman Act antitrust claims.

terms.label: claim-splitting
terms.gloss: Suing on part of a claim and saving the rest for a later suit, which preclusion law usually forbids.

terms.label: full and fair opportunity
terms.gloss: The usual preclusion test: a party is bound by an earlier ruling only if it had a real chance to litigate the issue there.

terms.label: pendent state claims
terms.gloss: State-law claims added to a federal case because they arise from the same facts as the federal claim (now 'supplemental jurisdiction').

terms.label: Rule 4(k)(1)(A)
terms.gloss: Federal rule making a federal court's reach over out-of-state defendants generally the same as that of the state courts where it sits.

terms.label: arising from or relating to
terms.gloss: Specific-jurisdiction requirement: the lawsuit must come out of, or be connected to, the defendant's activities in the state.

terms.label: reasonableness (jurisdiction)
terms.gloss: Final step of specific jurisdiction: even with sufficient contacts, hearing the case in that state must be fair to the defendant.

terms.label: express aiming
terms.gloss: Under the Calder effects test, deliberately targeting conduct at the forum state, more than merely being reachable there.

terms.label: Zippo sliding scale
terms.gloss: Test from Zippo Mfg. v. Zippo Dot Com (1997) judging website-based jurisdiction by how interactive and commercial a site is.

terms.label: constructively knew
terms.gloss: Should have known, so the law treats the party as knowing even if it did not actually know.

terms.label: franchise fees
terms.gloss: Here, the tax or fee a state charges companies for the privilege of doing business there.

terms.label: Rule 30(b)(6) deposition
terms.gloss: A deposition of an organization: the company must send someone prepared to answer questions on its behalf about listed topics.

terms.label: paralegal
terms.gloss: A trained assistant who does legal work under a lawyer's supervision but is not a lawyer.

terms.label: case management
terms.gloss: A judge's handling of the schedule and logistics of a lawsuit, as opposed to deciding who wins.

terms.label: substantive liability
terms.gloss: Whether a party is actually legally responsible on the claims, as opposed to procedural matters.

terms.label: extraneous prejudicial information
terms.gloss: Exceptions to the jury-secrecy rule: harmful information from outside the trial, or outside pressure on jurors, may be shown by juror testimony.

terms.label: racial animus
terms.gloss: Hostility or prejudice against people because of their race.

terms.label: deliberations
terms.gloss: The jury's private discussion and voting in the jury room after the evidence is in.

terms.label: sex-offender registration
terms.gloss: A requirement that a person convicted of certain sex crimes list their address and other information on a government registry.

terms.label: boycott
terms.gloss: In antitrust law, a group's agreement to refuse to deal with someone, which can be an illegal restraint of trade.

terms.label: board-certified
terms.gloss: A doctor certified by a specialty board as meeting its training and exam standards.

terms.label: hospital privileges
terms.gloss: A hospital's permission for a doctor to admit and treat patients there.

terms.label: consumer-protection law
terms.gloss: State laws against unfair or deceptive business practices toward consumers.

terms.label: operative complaint
terms.gloss: The current, controlling version of the complaint after any amendments.

terms.label: absent class members
terms.gloss: Class members who are not named parties and do not take part in the case, but are bound by its result.

terms.label: preliminarily approved
terms.gloss: A court's tentative OK of a class settlement so notice can go out, before a final fairness hearing.

terms.label: conditionally certified
terms.gloss: Tentatively allowed the case to go forward as a class action, subject to final approval.

terms.label: Rule 23(c)(2)(B)
terms.gloss: The class-action rule requiring, for damages classes, the best practicable notice, including individual notice to members identifiable with reasonable effort.

terms.label: individual notice
terms.gloss: Notice sent personally (for example by mail) to each person, as opposed to published or general notice.

terms.label: waiver (of a regulatory requirement)
terms.gloss: Official permission from an agency to depart from a requirement that would otherwise apply.

terms.label: reverse auction
terms.gloss: A defendant settling a class action with whichever plaintiffs' lawyers will accept the least, harming class members.

terms.label: fair, reasonable, and adequate
terms.gloss: The standard a judge applies before approving a class settlement that binds absent members.

terms.label: condemnation (eminent domain)
terms.gloss: A government's court proceeding to take private property for public use, with compensation fixed for the owner.

terms.label: commissioners (condemnation)
terms.gloss: People appointed by the court in a condemnation case to decide how much the owner should be paid.

terms.label: appropriation damage
terms.gloss: The loss an owner suffers because the government takes (appropriates) his property, including the land's value.

terms.label: restraint
terms.gloss: A court order forbidding someone, here the city, from doing something, such as entering the land.
Former federal statute giving a right of appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court when a state's highest court upheld a state law against a federal constitutional challenge.

terms.label: notice (due process)
terms.gloss: Due process requires notice reasonably likely to actually inform a person before the government affects their property, so they can be heard.

terms.label: Mullane
terms.gloss: Mullane v. Central Hanover Bank (1950): due process requires notice reasonably calculated, in the circumstances, to inform interested parties of a proceeding.

terms.label: diligent inquiry
terms.gloss: A real, careful effort to find a person or fact, such as an owner's address.

terms.label: discharge (employment)
terms.gloss: Firing an employee.

terms.label: discharge contrary to public policy
terms.gloss: A tort claim by a worker fired for a reason society forbids, such as refusing to commit a crime.

terms.label: Labor Code § 2922
terms.gloss: California statute presuming that a job with no fixed term may be ended by either side at any time ('at will').

terms.label: Tameny
terms.gloss: Tameny v. Atlantic Richfield (Cal. 1980): an employer commits a tort by firing a worker for refusing to break the law.

terms.label: agency law
terms.gloss: The law of relationships in which one person (an agent, like an employee) acts for another (a principal), including the agent's duties.

terms.label: permanent employment
terms.gloss: A promise of a 'permanent' job, which courts historically treated as at-will unless extra consideration was given.

terms.label: Civil Code § 1624
terms.gloss: California's statute of frauds, requiring a signed writing for certain contracts, such as those that cannot be performed within one year.

terms.label: sustained demurrers
terms.gloss: The court agreed the complaint failed to state a legal claim even if its facts were true.

terms.label: quasi-public
terms.gloss: Partly public in character; insurers are said to serve a quasi-public function because of their regulated role.

terms.label: emotional-distress damages
terms.gloss: Money for mental suffering, usually available in tort but rarely in contract.

terms.label: Seaman's
terms.gloss: Seaman's Direct Buying Service v. Standard Oil (Cal. 1984): a tort for denying in bad faith that a contract exists (later overruled).

terms.label: prospective / retroactive application
terms.gloss: Whether a new legal rule applies only to future cases (prospective) or also to past events and pending cases (retroactive).

terms.label: registered engineer
terms.gloss: Licensed by the state as a professional engineer; Massachusetts required engineering work to be done or overseen by a registered engineer.

terms.label: companion suit
terms.gloss: A related lawsuit between the same parties tried or decided together with the main case.

terms.label: rebuttable evidence
terms.gloss: Evidence pointing toward a conclusion that the other side may overcome with contrary proof.

terms.label: revenue-producing licensing statute
terms.gloss: A licensing law meant only to raise money; breaking it usually does not prevent collecting under a contract, unlike a law protecting the public.

terms.label: seal (engineer's)
terms.gloss: A licensed engineer's official stamp on plans showing they were prepared or approved by a registered professional.

terms.label: as security
terms.gloss: To back up a debt, giving the creditor another source of payment if the debtor does not pay.

terms.label: original parties
terms.gloss: The people who made the note or contract themselves, as opposed to later holders who received it by transfer.

terms.label: option
terms.gloss: A promise to keep an offer open that is binding because the other person paid or gave something for it.

terms.label: priority
terms.gloss: Which of two competing claims to the same property comes first and wins.

terms.label: reporter
terms.gloss: The editor who published the case in a volume of law reports, sometimes adding notes that are not part of the decision.

terms.label: jury waiver
terms.gloss: A contract term in which a party gives up the right to a jury trial.

terms.label: § 4 trial
terms.gloss: Under section 4 of the Federal Arbitration Act, a trial held to decide whether an arbitration agreement was actually made, when that is genuinely disputed.

terms.label: reasonably prudent user
terms.gloss: The law's imagined ordinary, sensible person, used to judge whether online terms were noticeable.

terms.label: disclosed agent
terms.gloss: A person acting for a known principal (here, Uber); such agents can often rely on the principal's contracts.

terms.label: secured note
terms.gloss: A promise to repay a loan backed by collateral, here a mortgage on the property, which the lender can take if unpaid.

terms.label: assumption (of a mortgage)
terms.gloss: A buyer's promise to pay the existing mortgage debt, making the buyer personally liable for it.

terms.label: taking subject to debt
terms.gloss: Receiving mortgaged property without promising to pay the loan: the lender can foreclose, but the new owner is not personally liable.

terms.label: hold harmless
terms.gloss: To promise to protect someone from loss, paying any claims or costs they face.

terms.label: recording (a deed)
terms.gloss: Filing a deed in the public land records so others are on notice of who owns the property.

terms.label: reserving rights
terms.gloss: Making clear that by acting (here, paying) one is not giving up any legal claims.

terms.label: encumbered / unencumbered
terms.gloss: Subject to a claim like a mortgage (encumbered) or free of it (unencumbered).

terms.label: equity (ownership value)
terms.gloss: The owner's share of a property's value: what it is worth minus the debts secured against it.

terms.label: renunciation
terms.gloss: Formally rejecting something, here refusing a deed so as not to be bound by it.

terms.label: Virginia Code § 11-2(4)
terms.gloss: Part of Virginia's statute of frauds requiring a signed writing for a promise to pay another person's debt.

terms.label: original undertaking
terms.gloss: A promise to pay made for one's own benefit as part of one's own deal, which is not a guarantee of another's debt.

terms.label: guarantee
terms.gloss: A promise to pay someone else's debt, or make good a promised result, if the other person fails to.

terms.label: savings and loan
terms.gloss: A bank-like institution that took deposits and made home loans; many failed in the 1980s.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 1407
terms.gloss: The multidistrict-litigation statute: lets a panel send related federal cases to one judge for pretrial work, then requires sending them back for trial.

terms.label: Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation
terms.gloss: A group of federal judges that decides when related cases nationwide are combined before one judge for pretrial proceedings.

terms.label: commercial disparagement
terms.gloss: A tort for false statements that harm a business's reputation or products and cause financial loss.

terms.label: suggest remand
terms.gloss: A transferee judge's recommendation to the multidistrict panel that a case be sent back to its original court.

terms.label: § 1404(a)
terms.gloss: Federal statute letting a court transfer a case to another district for convenience and justice.

terms.label: self-assignment / self-transfer
terms.gloss: A multidistrict judge transferring a case to his own court so he can try it, rather than returning it.

terms.label: transferee court
terms.gloss: The court to which a case is transferred.

terms.label: jurisdictional defect
terms.gloss: A flaw in the court's power to hear the case.

terms.label: improper removal
terms.gloss: Moving a case from state to federal court when federal law did not allow it.

terms.label: Troubled Assets Relief Program
terms.gloss: The 2008 federal bailout program (TARP) that gave money to banks during the financial crisis.

terms.label: appraisal
terms.gloss: A professional's estimate of a property's value, used by lenders to decide how much to lend.

terms.label: Equal Credit Opportunity Act
terms.gloss: Federal law banning lenders from discriminating against credit applicants because of race, sex, age and other traits.

terms.label: unrepresented litigant (pro se)
terms.gloss: Someone handling their own case without a lawyer; they may represent only themselves, not others.

terms.label: Twombly
terms.gloss: Bell Atlantic v. Twombly (2007): a complaint must state enough facts to make the claim plausible, not merely conceivable.

terms.label: Iqbal
terms.gloss: Ashcroft v. Iqbal (2009): applied Twombly's plausibility standard to all civil cases; bare legal conclusions are not assumed true.

terms.label: heightened pleading
terms.gloss: A rule demanding more factual detail in a complaint than usual, as Rule 9(b) does for fraud.

terms.label: Rule 9
terms.gloss: Federal rule setting special pleading requirements for certain matters, notably fraud and mistake.

terms.label: out-of-pocket loss
terms.gloss: Money actually spent or lost, such as a fee paid.

terms.label: underwriting
terms.gloss: Evaluating risks and deciding what insurance to issue and at what price.

terms.label: national-origin discrimination
terms.gloss: Treating someone worse because of the country they or their ancestors come from.

terms.label: protected group
terms.gloss: A category the discrimination laws protect, such as race, national origin, sex or age.

terms.label: adverse employment action
terms.gloss: A significant negative job action, such as firing, demotion, or a pay cut.

terms.label: Conley
terms.gloss: Conley v. Gibson (1957): a complaint survives unless no set of facts could support it, requiring only fair notice; later retired by Twombly.

terms.label: municipal liability
terms.gloss: A city's or county's own legal responsibility for violating rights, such as through an official policy.

terms.label: Rule 84 and the official forms
terms.gloss: Former Rule 84 made sample complaints (forms) in the federal rules officially sufficient; it was abolished in 2015.

terms.label: rule-amendment process
terms.gloss: The formal process (Rules Enabling Act) by which federal court rules are changed: advisory committees, Supreme Court approval, and congressional review.

terms.label: reasonable certainty / reasonable basis
terms.gloss: The standard for damages proof: enough evidence for a sensible estimate, not mathematical precision.

terms.label: remit the award
terms.gloss: To give up part of a jury award (remittitur) as a condition of avoiding a new trial.

terms.label: habilitation
terms.gloss: Services that help people with disabilities gain or keep daily living skills.

terms.label: Medicaid waiver
terms.gloss: A Medicaid program letting states pay for home and community care for disabled people; providers need a Medicaid number to bill it.

terms.label: supplemental briefing
terms.gloss: Additional written arguments a court asks the parties to file on a specific question.

terms.label: legitimate (protectable) interest
terms.gloss: Business interests a noncompete may protect, such as trade secrets, training, and customer relationships, not just avoiding ordinary competition.

terms.label: blue-pencil rule
terms.gloss: A court's power to fix an overbroad contract term; in a strict form it may only strike words, in the liberal form it may rewrite.

terms.label: National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act
match: national traffic and motor vehicle safety act
terms.gloss: The 1966 federal law directing the Department of Transportation to set mandatory safety standards for cars and equipment.

terms.label: Motor Vehicle Safety Standard
terms.gloss: A binding federal rule setting safety performance requirements for new cars; No. 202 covers head restraints, No. 208 crash protection.

terms.label: formal hearing
terms.gloss: A trial-like agency proceeding with witnesses and cross-examination, required only when a statute calls for decisions 'on the record.'
The APA sections setting trial-type procedures for formal agency hearings.
The APA section setting how courts review agency action, for example setting aside arbitrary actions (2)(A) or unsupported formal findings (2)(E).

terms.label: agency record
terms.gloss: The documents and evidence an agency gathered when making its decision, which a court reviews.

terms.label: practicability
terms.gloss: Whether a requirement can realistically be met, a statutory test for motor-vehicle safety standards.

terms.label: conference (committee)
terms.gloss: The meeting of House and Senate negotiators who reconcile different versions of a bill.

terms.label: lead time
terms.gloss: The period between issuing a rule and when it takes effect, giving industry time to comply.

terms.label: certification testing
terms.gloss: EPA testing that each new vehicle model must pass to be certified as meeting emission limits before sale.

terms.label: useful life
terms.gloss: The period, set by statute, over which a vehicle must keep meeting emission standards.

terms.label: in abeyance
terms.gloss: Put on hold, with the court delaying a decision.

terms.label: nonconformance penalties
terms.gloss: Payments that let heavy-duty engine makers sell engines slightly over the limit instead of being barred.

terms.label: passive restraint
terms.gloss: Crash protection that works without the occupant acting, such as airbags or automatic seatbelts.

terms.label: rescission (of a rule)
terms.gloss: An agency's cancellation of a rule it issued, which must itself be reasonably explained.

terms.label: phase-in
terms.gloss: Requiring compliance gradually, for a growing share of products each year.

terms.label: trap door
terms.gloss: In State Farm v. Dole, the rule's built-in escape hatch canceling the airbag/automatic-belt requirement if enough states passed qualifying seatbelt laws.

terms.label: mitigation of civil damages
terms.gloss: Letting a court reduce an injured person's damages because they were not wearing a seatbelt.

terms.label: national uniformity
terms.gloss: Having one nationwide standard rather than different state rules.

terms.label: Abbott Laboratories
terms.gloss: Abbott Laboratories v. Gardner (1967): an agency rule is ripe for court review when the issues are fit for decision and delay would cause hardship.

terms.label: hardship (ripeness)
terms.gloss: The harm a party would suffer if a court waited before deciding, one test of ripeness.

terms.label: nullification clause
