terms.gloss: In the London insurance market, the document each insurer initials to accept its share of a risk.

terms.label: cover note
terms.gloss: A temporary document confirming insurance is in place before a formal policy is issued.

terms.label: nexus
terms.gloss: A connection or link; here, between the discovery violation and the sanction imposed for it.

terms.label: OFAC
terms.gloss: The Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control, which keeps a list of terrorists, drug traffickers and others Americans generally may not do business with.

terms.label: credit report
terms.gloss: A file a credit reporting agency sells to lenders and businesses summarizing a person's credit history and other data.

terms.label: redress
terms.gloss: A remedy for an injury; for standing, a court ruling must be likely to fix or compensate the harm.

terms.label: intangible harm
terms.gloss: Non-physical, non-monetary injury, such as damage to reputation or privacy; it supports standing if it resembles a harm courts traditionally recognized.

terms.label: retrospective damages
terms.gloss: Money compensating for harm already suffered.

terms.label: citation (enforcement)
terms.gloss: A formal written charge from a regulator that a company violated a safety rule, usually carrying a fine.

terms.label: Program Policy Letter
terms.gloss: Informal written guidance the mine-safety agency issued to explain how it reads its rules, without notice-and-comment rulemaking.

terms.label: B-reader
terms.gloss: A physician certified by the federal government to classify chest x-rays for dust diseases such as black lung.

terms.label: binding norm
terms.gloss: The test asking whether an agency document actually binds the agency or the public; if it does, it may be a legislative rule needing notice and comment.

terms.label: delegated (legislative) authority
terms.gloss: Power Congress has given an agency to make rules with the force of law.

terms.label: supersession
terms.gloss: Replacement by a newer rule or document, so the old one no longer operates.

terms.label: citator
terms.gloss: A research tool (like Shepard's or KeyCite) showing whether later cases have followed, questioned or overruled a decision.

terms.label: Public Utility Holding Company Act
match: public utility holding company act of 1935
terms.gloss: A 1935 law letting the SEC break up and simplify utility holding-company empires and approve their reorganizations as fair to investors.

terms.label: preferred stock
terms.gloss: Shares paid dividends, and paid in a liquidation, ahead of common stock, usually with limited voting rights.

terms.label: common stock
terms.gloss: Ordinary ownership shares, carrying voting control and whatever value is left after everyone else is paid.

terms.label: accumulated dividends
terms.gloss: Unpaid preferred-stock dividends that pile up and must be paid before common shareholders get anything.

terms.label: general warrant
terms.gloss: A warrant naming no specific place or items, letting officers search at will; the Fourth Amendment forbids them.

terms.label: Wilkes and Entick
terms.gloss: Famous 1760s English cases condemning general warrants used against government critics; they inspired the Fourth Amendment.

terms.label: municipal policy
terms.gloss: An official city policy or custom; under § 1983 a city itself is liable only when such a policy caused the violation.

terms.label: postdeprivation remedy
terms.gloss: A legal procedure to get property back, or compensation, after the government has taken it, rather than a hearing beforehand.

terms.label: Rule 41(d) (criminal)
terms.gloss: The federal rule (now 41(f)) requiring officers who seize property under a warrant to leave a copy of the warrant and a receipt for what was taken.

terms.label: Walsh-Healey Public Contracts Act
terms.gloss: A 1936 law requiring companies with large federal supply contracts to pay at least the wages the Labor Secretary finds prevail in their industry.

terms.label: Perkins v. Lukens Steel
terms.gloss: A 1940 Supreme Court case holding that would-be government contractors had no legal right to challenge Labor Department wage determinations in court.

terms.label: Fulbright Amendment
terms.gloss: A 1952 amendment to the Walsh-Healey Act requiring formal on-the-record hearings for wage determinations and allowing affected companies to seek court review.

terms.label: litigable rights
terms.gloss: Legal rights a person can enforce by suing in court.

terms.label: proponent
terms.gloss: The party advocating a rule or position; under the APA, the proponent of a rule or order bears the burden of proof.

terms.label: rehabilitation (of evidence)
terms.gloss: Restoring the credibility of evidence or a witness after it has been attacked (impeached).

terms.label: Federal Reports Act
terms.gloss: A 1942 law coordinating federal collection of information from the public, including confidentiality protections for what is collected.

terms.label: prevailing rates (wages)
terms.gloss: The wage rates the Labor Secretary found were typically paid for similar work in the industry; Walsh-Healey contractors must pay at least these.

terms.label: reservation (in a deed)
terms.gloss: A right the seller keeps for itself when deeding land away, here an option to buy the land back.

terms.label: optionee
terms.gloss: The person who holds an option and may exercise it.

terms.label: depreciation
terms.gloss: The decline in value of property over time, here as calculated under federal tax rules.

terms.label: nonassignable
terms.gloss: Whether a right can be transferred to someone else; a nonassignable right stays with its original holder.

terms.label: indefiniteness
terms.gloss: Contract terms so vague that a court cannot tell what was promised, which can make the contract unenforceable.

terms.label: collateral agreement
terms.gloss: A separate side agreement on a related matter not covered by the writing; it can be proved if parties would naturally have made it separately.

terms.label: entire-agreement clause
terms.gloss: A clause stating that the writing is the parties' whole agreement, which bars proof of other terms.

terms.label: title company
terms.gloss: A company that searches land records, insures title, and often handles the closing of a sale.

terms.label: Corbin
terms.gloss: Arthur Corbin, Yale professor whose multivolume contracts treatise is highly influential; he favored admitting evidence of the parties' actual intent.

terms.label: cross-liability clause
terms.gloss: An insurance term treating each insured as if separately insured, so a claim by one insured against another is covered.

terms.label: plain language (plain meaning)
terms.gloss: The approach that clear contract words control and outside evidence of a different meaning is excluded; Pacific Gas rejected it as the test for admissibility.

terms.label: received conditionally
terms.gloss: Admitted provisionally, subject to being struck if later evidence fails to connect it to the case.

terms.label: progress installments
terms.gloss: Payments made in stages as construction advances.

terms.label: gratuitous undertaking
terms.gloss: A task someone takes on voluntarily, without being paid or bound to; once begun, it may still have to be performed with reasonable care.

terms.label: latent
terms.gloss: Hidden and not discoverable by reasonable inspection, like quicksand beneath a building site.

terms.label: absolute promise
terms.gloss: An unconditional promise; the promisor must perform even if it becomes much harder or costlier, unless performance becomes truly impossible.

terms.label: naked promise
terms.gloss: A bare promise with nothing given in exchange (no consideration), generally not enforceable.

terms.label: incompetent, irrelevant, and immaterial
terms.gloss: A standard all-purpose objection to evidence: not legally admissible, not related to the issues, and not significant.

terms.label: noncompetition undertaking
terms.gloss: A promise not to compete with the other party's business, here restricting use of the sold business's names and marks.

terms.label: conditional intent
terms.gloss: In Swiss law (dolus eventualis), foreseeing that conduct may cause a prohibited result and accepting that risk.

terms.label: substantiate
terms.gloss: To back up a claim with specific supporting facts or evidence; Swiss procedure requires parties to substantiate their allegations, not just assert them.

terms.label: arbitrary fact-finding
terms.gloss: The Swiss Federal Supreme Court overturns lower-court findings of fact only if clearly untenable ('arbitrary'), not merely debatable.

terms.label: Swiss Code of Obligations
terms.gloss: Switzerland's main statute on contracts and obligations; its Article 163 governs contractual penalties.

terms.label: BGE
terms.gloss: The official reports of the Swiss Federal Supreme Court's leading decisions (Bundesgerichtsentscheide).

terms.label: Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act
terms.gloss: A 1959 federal law (Landrum-Griffin Act) regulating internal union affairs; its Title IV sets rules for union officer elections, enforced through suits by the Secretary of Labor.

terms.label: Rule 24(a)
terms.gloss: The federal rule on intervention as of right: an outsider with an interest a case may impair can join unless existing parties already adequately represent that interest.

terms.label: Court of Oyer and Terminer
terms.gloss: An old name ('to hear and determine') for a county criminal court; in New Jersey it tried serious crimes and supervised grand juries until 1948.

terms.label: truth (defamation defense)
match: truth in substance and in fact
terms.gloss: A complete defense to defamation: a statement that is true in substance cannot be defamatory, so defendants plead that what they said was accurate.

terms.label: clear absence of all jurisdiction
terms.gloss: The narrow exception to judicial immunity: only acts plainly outside any authority lose protection, not acts that are merely mistaken or exceed authority.

terms.label: exercise (an option)
terms.gloss: To use an option by giving the required notice and usually paying the agreed price, which binds the other side to complete the deal.

terms.label: irrevocable offer
terms.gloss: An offer the offeror cannot take back for a set time, usually because the other side paid for that promise; a purchased option works this way.

terms.label: market price at time and place of breach
terms.gloss: The standard contract measure for failure to deliver goods or shares: market value when and where delivery was due, minus the agreed price.

terms.label: restricted (unregistered) shares
terms.gloss: Stock not registered with the SEC, so it cannot be freely resold on the public market; it is therefore valued at a discount.

terms.label: Central Valley Project
terms.gloss: A huge federal system of dams and canals in California, run by the Bureau of Reclamation, that stores and delivers water to farms and cities.

terms.label: appropriative water rights
terms.gloss: Western-state water rights earned by putting water to beneficial use, ranked by date: first in time, first in right.

terms.label: waiver of sovereign immunity
terms.gloss: A government's consent to be sued, which must be clearly expressed (for the United States, by Congress in a statute); without it, courts cannot hear claims against that government.
terms.context: \b(sovereign|immunity|390uu|McCarran|consent[- ]to[- ]suit)\b|United States needed|without a waiver|the State waiv

terms.label: McCarran Amendment
terms.gloss: A 1952 federal law letting the United States be joined in comprehensive state or federal lawsuits adjudicating everyone's water rights in a river system.

terms.label: 43 U.S.C. § 390uu
terms.gloss: A Reclamation Reform Act provision letting the United States be joined as a defendant in suits over rights under reclamation contracts, a narrow waiver of immunity.

terms.label: intended third-party beneficiary
terms.gloss: A non-party the contracting parties clearly meant to benefit and to give enforceable rights, unlike an incidental beneficiary, who merely gains and cannot sue.

terms.label: Bell v. Hood
terms.gloss: A 1946 Supreme Court case holding that a weak federal claim still gives a court jurisdiction; it should be dismissed on the merits, not for lack of jurisdiction.

terms.label: class proceedings
terms.gloss: Litigation or arbitration in which a representative sues on behalf of many similarly situated people, so one ruling binds them all.

terms.label: proposed class
terms.gloss: The group of people a plaintiff asks to represent in a class action; it becomes an actual class only if the court certifies it.

terms.label: Stolt-Nielsen
terms.gloss: Stolt-Nielsen v. AnimalFeeds (2010): a party cannot be forced into class arbitration unless there is a contractual basis for concluding it agreed to it; silence is not enough.

terms.label: gateway question
terms.gloss: A threshold issue about whether or how arbitration happens, such as whether an agreement exists; courts decide these unless the parties clearly gave them to the arbitrator.

terms.label: implied obstacle preemption
terms.gloss: Federal law overriding a state rule that stands as an obstacle to the purposes of a federal statute, even if the statute does not say so expressly.

terms.label: anti-drafter rule
terms.gloss: Another name for contra proferentem: ambiguous contract wording is read against the party who wrote it.

terms.label: escalator clause
terms.gloss: A contract term automatically raising or lowering the price as an agreed outside index changes, such as a published crude-oil price.

terms.label: two-tier price controls (old and new oil)
terms.gloss: 1973 federal rules capping the price of 'old' oil (production at prior levels) while letting 'new' oil above those levels, and matching 'released' oil, sell at market prices.

terms.label: UCC § 2-306
terms.gloss: The UCC section on output, requirements, and exclusive-dealing contracts: quantity means actual good-faith output or needs, not unreasonably out of line with estimates or past amounts.

terms.label: UCC § 2-615
terms.gloss: The UCC section excusing a seller's delay or nondelivery when performance becomes commercially impracticable because of an unforeseen event both parties assumed would not occur.

terms.label: UCC § 2-716
terms.gloss: The UCC section letting a buyer get specific performance when goods are unique or in other proper circumstances, a looser test than traditional equity.

terms.label: reopening (a closed case)
terms.gloss: Asking a court or agency to reopen a closed case or judgment so it can be reconsidered, for example because notice was defective or new facts emerged.

terms.label: Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA)
terms.gloss: The Justice Department's highest administrative tribunal for immigration cases; it reviews immigration judges' decisions before any court does.

terms.label: rescission (of an in absentia order)
terms.gloss: Cancelling a removal order entered when the person did not appear, allowed for exceptional circumstances, custody, or lack of proper notice.

terms.label: exceptional circumstances (immigration)
terms.gloss: Serious reasons beyond a noncitizen's control, such as grave illness, that excuse missing a hearing if raised within 180 days.

terms.label: Pereira
terms.gloss: Pereira v. Sessions (2018): a notice to appear lacking the hearing's time and place does not trigger the 'stop-time rule' cutting off residence time for relief.

terms.label: Niz-Chavez
terms.gloss: Niz-Chavez v. Garland (2021): a notice to appear must contain all required information in a single document, not spread over several.

terms.label: union-security clause
terms.gloss: A contract term requiring employees to join, or pay fees to, the union after hiring as a condition of keeping their jobs.

terms.label: NLRA § 10(b)
terms.gloss: The six-month time limit for filing unfair-labor-practice charges with the NLRB; older conduct generally cannot be the basis of a complaint.

terms.label: initiative / referendum
terms.gloss: Direct democracy: by initiative, voters propose and pass laws or constitutional amendments themselves; by referendum, voters approve or reject laws the legislature passed.

terms.label: redistricting / districting
terms.gloss: Redrawing the boundaries of election districts, usually after each census, so districts reflect population changes.

terms.label: Elections Clause
terms.gloss: Article I, § 4 of the Constitution: each state's 'Legislature' sets the times, places, and manner of congressional elections, but Congress may override those rules.

terms.label: Raines v. Byrd
terms.gloss: Raines v. Byrd (1997): individual members of Congress lacked standing to challenge the Line Item Veto Act because their claimed harm was abstract and widely shared.

terms.label: Coleman v. Miller
terms.gloss: Coleman v. Miller (1939): state legislators whose votes were completely nullified had standing to sue.

terms.label: Seventeenth Amendment
terms.gloss: The 1913 amendment providing for direct popular election of U.S. senators; before it, state legislatures chose them.

terms.label: one person, one vote
terms.gloss: The constitutional rule that election districts must have roughly equal populations so each person's vote carries equal weight.

terms.label: custom or usage
terms.gloss: In § 1983, a long-standing practice treated as having the force of law, such as state-enforced segregation, even without a written statute.

terms.label: joint participation
terms.gloss: When a private person acts together with state officials, the private person is treated as acting 'under color of' state law for § 1983 purposes.

terms.label: Thirteenth Amendment
terms.gloss: The 1865 constitutional amendment abolishing slavery; Congress may enforce it against private conduct, not only states.

terms.label: law-equity distinction
terms.gloss: The historic split between 'law' courts (juries, money damages) and 'equity' courts (judges, fairness remedies); some states still let judges decide fraud-in-release issues as equitable.

terms.label: concurrent jurisdiction
terms.gloss: When both state and federal courts may hear the same kind of case, letting the plaintiff choose; FELA suits can be brought in either.

terms.label: successor trustee
terms.gloss: The person named to take over managing a trust when the original trustee dies, resigns, or can no longer serve.

terms.label: individual vs. representative capacity
terms.gloss: Suing or being sued for oneself (individual capacity) versus on behalf of someone else, such as a trust (representative capacity); they count as different parties.

terms.label: licensee (broadcast)
terms.gloss: The holder of an FCC license to operate a station; it must serve the public interest as a trustee of the public airwaves.

terms.label: commencement (of an action)
terms.gloss: When a lawsuit officially begins for legal purposes, such as stopping the limitations clock; under the federal rules, filing the complaint, though some states count service on the defendant.

terms.label: Lexmark
terms.gloss: Lexmark International v. Static Control (2014): the zone-of-interests test asks whether a statute gives this plaintiff a cause of action, not whether courts should prudentially decline.

terms.label: Fairness Doctrine
terms.gloss: A former FCC policy (1949–1987) requiring broadcasters to cover controversial public issues and give fair opportunity for contrasting views.

terms.label: license renewal
terms.gloss: An agency's periodic decision whether to extend a license for a new term; the FCC renews a broadcast license only if doing so serves the public interest.

terms.label: public interest (standard)
terms.gloss: The Communications Act's test for granting or renewing broadcast licenses: the FCC must find the grant serves the 'public interest, convenience, and necessity'.

terms.label: inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance
match: inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office
inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance
terms.gloss: Standard statutory grounds for removing a protected official, first used in the FTC Act: incompetence, failing to do the job, or wrongdoing in office; policy disagreement is not among them.

terms.label: Myers
terms.gloss: Myers v. United States (1926): Congress cannot require Senate consent before the President removes an executive officer such as a postmaster.

terms.label: purely executive officer
terms.gloss: An official whose work is only carrying out the law under the President, like a postmaster; Humphrey's Executor said the President may fire these at will.

terms.label: Ethics in Government Act
terms.gloss: A 1978 post-Watergate law that, among other things, created court-appointed independent counsel to investigate high officials; those provisions lapsed in 1999.

terms.label: Special Division
terms.gloss: The three-judge panel of federal judges that appointed independent counsel and defined their jurisdiction under the Ethics in Government Act.

terms.label: conditional (duty)
terms.gloss: Of a contract duty: it arises only if a stated event happens first; if the event does not happen, the party need not perform.

terms.label: terminable at will
terms.gloss: A contract either side may end at any time for any reason, so ending it is not a breach.

terms.label: scheme requirement (promissory fraud)
terms.gloss: Illinois's rule that a false promise of future conduct is fraud only if part of a broader scheme to defraud, not a single broken promise.

terms.label: merger into the deed
terms.gloss: The doctrine that a land-sale contract's terms are absorbed into the deed at closing, so terms left out of the deed may no longer be enforceable.

terms.label: oppression or unfair surprise
terms.gloss: The two concerns of unconscionability: terms so one-sided they oppress the weaker party, or hidden terms that unfairly surprise them.

terms.label: clearance (film distribution)
terms.gloss: In film distribution, a set period after a theater first shows a movie during which nearby competing theaters may not show it.

terms.label: right to a jury trial
terms.gloss: The constitutional right, in federal civil cases under the Seventh Amendment, to have a jury decide claims of the kind historically tried in courts of law.

terms.label: historical test (jury right)
terms.gloss: The Seventh Amendment method of comparing a modern claim to 18th-century English lawsuits to see whether it would have been tried in a law court (jury) or in equity (judge).

terms.label: seniority
terms.gloss: An employee's ranking by length of service, which under a union contract decides who is laid off first and recalled first.

terms.label: duty of fair representation
terms.gloss: A union's legal duty, as the workers' exclusive bargaining agent, to represent all of them honestly and in good faith, without hostility, discrimination or arbitrary conduct.

terms.label: incidental (to equitable relief)
terms.gloss: Money awarded as a side part of an equitable remedy, such as an injunction, which historically a judge could award without a jury.

terms.label: attorney's fees and costs
terms.gloss: What a party pays its lawyers plus court expenses; normally each side pays its own unless a rule, statute or sanction shifts them to the other side.

terms.label: civil contempt / coercive sanction
terms.gloss: A penalty meant to pressure a party into obeying a court order, which ends once the party complies, as opposed to punishment for past misconduct.

terms.label: Federal Advisory Committee Act
terms.gloss: A 1972 federal law requiring advisory committees that include outsiders to hold open meetings and disclose records; groups made up entirely of federal employees are exempt.

terms.label: federal mandamus statute (28 U.S.C. § 1361)
terms.gloss: 28 U.S.C. § 1361, letting federal district courts order a federal officer to perform a clear, mandatory duty owed to the plaintiff.

terms.label: agency action
terms.gloss: Something a federal agency does, such as a rule, order or refusal, that the APA lets a court review.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 1292
terms.gloss: The statute allowing appeals before a case ends in limited situations, including orders on injunctions and legal questions a trial judge certifies under § 1292(b).

terms.label: Appellate Rule 4(a)
terms.gloss: Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4(a), setting the deadlines for filing a notice of appeal in civil cases.

terms.label: clear and indisputable right
terms.gloss: The mandamus standard: the petitioner's right to relief must be obvious, not merely arguable.

terms.label: privilege log
terms.gloss: Listing each withheld document and the privilege claimed for it, so the other side and the court can test the claim.

terms.label: generic (drug)
terms.gloss: A copy of a brand-name drug, sold under its chemical name after the patent expires, with the same active ingredient.

terms.label: bioequivalence / bioavailability
terms.gloss: Bioavailability is how much of a drug reaches the bloodstream and how fast; bioequivalence means a generic matches the brand-name drug on that measure.

terms.label: functionality (trademark)
terms.gloss: The trademark rule that a useful product feature, such as capsule colors that help patients and pharmacists, cannot be claimed as a brand identifier.

terms.label: substitution (pharmacy)
terms.gloss: A pharmacist filling a brand-name prescription with a cheaper generic, which state law allows unless the doctor forbids it.

terms.label: objective theory of contracts
terms.gloss: Contract formation depends on what a party's words and conduct would reasonably mean to the other side, not on secret intentions.

terms.label: security (for deferred payment)
terms.gloss: Collateral, such as a mortgage on the land, protecting a seller who lets the buyer pay over time.

terms.label: grazing permit
terms.gloss: A government permit letting a rancher graze livestock on public land such as a national forest; transfer was generally tied to owning qualifying land or livestock.

terms.label: time is of the essence
terms.gloss: A contract clause making deadlines strict, so performing late is a breach that can let the other side cancel.

terms.label: note and mortgage
terms.gloss: Financing where the buyer signs a promissory note for the unpaid price and gives the seller a mortgage on the land as security.

terms.label: subscribe (sign)
terms.gloss: Signed, usually at the end of a document; the statute of frauds often requires a writing subscribed by the person to be bound.

terms.label: material benefit rule
terms.gloss: The rule that a promise made in recognition of a substantial benefit already received from the promisee can be enforced despite no bargained-for exchange.

terms.label: presumption of prior request
terms.gloss: A legal fiction treating a later promise to pay for a service as if the promisor had asked for the service beforehand, supplying the missing bargain.

terms.label: executed (payment or contract)
terms.gloss: Already carried out, as opposed to "executory" (still to be performed).

terms.label: Subtitle C (RCRA)
terms.gloss: The part of RCRA creating the strict federal hazardous-waste program: tracking, permits and treatment, storage and disposal standards.

terms.label: Bevill Amendment
terms.gloss: A 1980 amendment to RCRA temporarily exempting mining and mineral-processing wastes from hazardous-waste rules until EPA studied them.

terms.label: beneficiation
terms.gloss: Mining-industry steps that concentrate ore, such as crushing, washing or separating, before the chemical processing that extracts the metal.

terms.label: hazardous characteristic
terms.gloss: A property such as ignitability, corrosivity, reactivity or toxicity that makes a waste legally "hazardous" under EPA rules.

terms.label: special wastes
terms.gloss: High-volume, low-hazard mining and mineral-processing wastes that Congress meant to keep exempt from hazardous-waste rules under the Bevill Amendment.

terms.label: mixture rule
terms.gloss: An EPA rule that a mix of listed hazardous waste with other waste is itself treated as hazardous waste.

terms.label: Simpson Amendment
terms.gloss: An RCRA provision letting EPA relax certain hazardous-waste requirements for the special wastes covered by the Bevill exemption.

terms.label: Method 1312
terms.gloss: An EPA laboratory test simulating how rain leaches contaminants out of waste, used here to screen whether a waste is low-hazard.

terms.label: Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act
match: longshoremen’s and harbor workers’ compensation act
longshoremen's and harbor workers' compensation act
longshore and harbor workers’ compensation act
longshore and harbor workers' compensation act
terms.gloss: The federal workers'-compensation law for longshoremen and other maritime workers hurt on navigable waters or adjoining dock areas.

terms.label: Sieracki–Ryan triangle
terms.gloss: The pre-1972 cycle in which an injured longshoreman sued the ship for unseaworthiness (Sieracki) and the ship then made the stevedoring employer repay it (Ryan).

terms.label: navigable waters
terms.gloss: Waters usable for commerce, such as ports and rivers, which federal maritime law governs.

terms.label: maritime employment
terms.gloss: The Longshore Act's job test: work tied to loading, unloading, building or repairing ships.

terms.label: shape-up
terms.gloss: A daily hiring line where longshoremen gather to be picked for that day's work.

terms.label: Benefits Review Board
terms.gloss: The Labor Department board that hears appeals from administrative law judges in Longshore Act and Black Lung cases.

terms.label: § 21(c) / § 921(c) (Longshore Act)
terms.gloss: The Longshore Act provision letting a person "adversely affected or aggrieved" by a Benefits Review Board order petition a federal appeals court within 60 days.

terms.label: Solicitor of Labor
terms.gloss: The Labor Department's chief lawyer, who litigates for the Department.

terms.label: experience rating
terms.gloss: Setting an employer's insurance premium based on its own past claims.

terms.label: first/last point of rest
terms.gloss: A proposed test ending coverage once unloaded cargo first comes to rest on land, and starting it when outgoing cargo leaves its last resting place before loading.

terms.label: stripping / stuffing (containers)
terms.gloss: Unloading cargo out of a shipping container (stripping) or packing cargo into one (stuffing).

terms.label: Works Progress Administration
terms.gloss: A New Deal federal agency (1935–1943) that employed millions of people on public-works relief projects.

terms.label: guarantee of prior endorsements
terms.gloss: A bank's promise, stamped on a check it collects, that earlier signatures on it are genuine; if one is forged, the bank must repay.

terms.label: for collection
terms.gloss: A bank taking a check to obtain payment for its customer from the paying bank, rather than buying it outright.

terms.label: presenter (of a check)
terms.gloss: Whoever hands a check to the drawee for payment; by doing so it warrants that it is entitled to be paid.

terms.label: recourse
terms.gloss: A right to recover a loss from someone else, such as the party who passed along a check or product that turned out to be defective.

terms.label: Erie
terms.gloss: Erie Railroad v. Tompkins (1938): federal courts must apply state law, including state court decisions, on matters the Constitution and Congress leave to the states.

terms.label: prong
terms.gloss: One part of a multi-part legal test.

terms.label: Supreme Court Rule 10
terms.gloss: The Supreme Court rule listing reasons it grants review, noting it rarely does so merely to correct factual errors or misapplied rules.

terms.label: summarily vacated
terms.gloss: Set aside a lower court's judgment without full briefing or oral argument, usually in a short unsigned opinion.

terms.label: termination for convenience
terms.gloss: A clause, common in government contracts, letting the buyer cancel a valid contract for any reason, paying the seller's costs so far, without it being a breach.

terms.label: progress payment
terms.gloss: Partial payment made as work proceeds, before the job is finished.

terms.label: overhead
terms.gloss: A business's general operating costs, like rent and administrative salaries, not tied to one particular job.

terms.label: expressly conditional acceptance
terms.gloss: Under UCC § 2-207(1), a reply is not an acceptance if it clearly says it depends on the other side agreeing to its different or added terms.

terms.label: United States Munitions List
terms.gloss: The federal list of weapons and military items whose export requires a government license.

terms.label: resentencing
terms.gloss: Imposing a new sentence after an appeal changes the convictions or the original sentence.

terms.label: frame or receiver
terms.gloss: The core housing of a gun that holds the firing parts; federal law treats it as a "firearm" itself, so it must be serialized and sold with a background check.

terms.label: serialization
terms.gloss: Marking each gun's frame or receiver with a unique serial number so it can be traced.

terms.label: artifact noun
terms.gloss: A word for a human-made object defined by its intended purpose (like "table"), which can apply even to unfinished or unassembled versions.

terms.label: knowledge (mental state)
terms.gloss: Acting "knowingly" usually requires awareness of the facts making up the offense, not awareness that the conduct is illegal.

terms.label: excess of statutory authority
terms.gloss: A claim that an agency acted beyond the power Congress gave it.

terms.label: soring
terms.gloss: Deliberately injuring a horse's legs or hooves so pain makes it lift its feet higher, exaggerating the gait prized in shows.

terms.label: Horse Protection Act
terms.gloss: The 1970 federal law banning the showing, selling or transporting of sored horses.

terms.label: APA § 555(e)
terms.gloss: The APA section requiring an agency to give prompt notice and a brief statement of reasons when it denies a request, such as a rulemaking petition.

terms.label: APA § 706(2)(A)
terms.gloss: The APA section directing courts to set aside agency action that is arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise unlawful.

terms.label: Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service
match: animal and plant health inspection service
terms.gloss: The Agriculture Department agency that enforces animal-welfare laws, including the Horse Protection Act.

terms.label: National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA)
terms.gloss: The Transportation Department agency that sets federal vehicle and tire safety standards.

terms.label: economic practicability
terms.gloss: The requirement that a safety standard be workable at reasonable cost for the industry, not merely technologically possible.

terms.label: listed species
terms.gloss: Species officially placed on the endangered or threatened list under the ESA.

terms.label: partial vs. total disability
terms.gloss: In workers' compensation, partial disability means the injured worker can still earn some wages; total means he cannot work at all, which pays more.

terms.label: special fund (Longshore Act)
terms.gloss: A Longshore Act fund, paid for by employer and insurer assessments, that takes over benefit payments after 104 weeks when a worker's pre-existing disability made the injury worse.

terms.label: Black Lung Benefits Act
terms.gloss: The federal law paying benefits to coal miners disabled by black lung disease, using procedures borrowed from the Longshore Act.

terms.label: corporal punishment
terms.gloss: Physical punishment, such as paddling, used as discipline.

terms.label: English Bill of Rights
terms.gloss: The 1689 English statute that first barred "cruel and unusual punishments", the source of the Eighth Amendment's wording.

terms.label: Virginia Declaration of Rights
terms.gloss: Virginia's 1776 declaration of rights, a model for the federal Bill of Rights, including its ban on cruel and unusual punishments.

terms.label: gross disproportionality
terms.gloss: The Eighth Amendment idea that a punishment far out of proportion to the crime is unconstitutional.

terms.label: evolving standards of decency
terms.gloss: The Supreme Court's test that the Eighth Amendment's meaning changes as society's views on acceptable punishment mature.

terms.label: Goss v. Lopez
terms.gloss: Goss v. Lopez (1975): students facing short school suspensions must get notice of the charges and a chance to tell their side.

terms.label: tenure
terms.gloss: Permanent job status, especially for teachers and professors, protecting against dismissal except for good cause and after set procedures.

terms.label: nonrenewal / nonretention
terms.gloss: A decision not to renew a fixed-term contract, such as a teacher's yearly appointment, when it ends, as opposed to firing someone during the term.

terms.label: name-clearing hearing
terms.gloss: A hearing where a public employee let go amid damaging charges can try to refute them and clear their reputation.

terms.label: blacklisting
terms.gloss: Deliberately barring a person from future jobs in a field.

terms.label: occupational liberty
terms.gloss: The due-process liberty to pursue one's chosen occupation free of government-imposed barriers.

terms.label: academic freedom
terms.gloss: Teachers' and scholars' freedom to teach, research and speak without official retaliation, protected in part by the First Amendment.

terms.label: Goldberg v. Kelly
terms.gloss: Goldberg v. Kelly (1970): welfare recipients are entitled to an evidentiary hearing before their benefits are cut off.

terms.label: Perry v. Sindermann
terms.gloss: Perry v. Sindermann (1972), decided with Roth: an established informal understanding of job security ("de facto tenure") can create a protected property interest.

terms.label: free speech (claim)
terms.gloss: A claim that the government punished someone for speech protected by the First Amendment.

terms.label: financing condition
terms.gloss: A contract term making the buyer's duty to buy depend on getting a loan on stated terms; if none is available, the buyer may cancel.

terms.label: loan commitment
terms.gloss: A lender's written promise to make a loan on stated terms.

terms.label: architect's certificate
terms.gloss: A written approval from the project architect that work meets the contract, often required before the owner must pay.

terms.label: compulsory nonsuit
terms.gloss: A judge ending a case because the plaintiff's evidence cannot support a verdict, without sending it to the jury.

terms.label: assignments of error
terms.gloss: The specific errors an appellant claims the trial court made.

terms.label: class-action waiver
terms.gloss: A contract term in which a customer gives up the right to join a class action and agrees to bring claims only individually.

terms.label: operative provision
terms.gloss: The part of a document that actually creates rights or duties, as opposed to headings, warnings or summaries that only describe them.

terms.label: delegation of arbitrability
terms.gloss: A contract term giving the arbitrator, rather than a court, the power to decide whether a dispute must be arbitrated. Courts require clear evidence the parties agreed to it.

terms.label: interest analysis
terms.gloss: A choice-of-law method that picks which place's law applies by weighing each place's connection to, and interest in, the dispute.

terms.label: lead plaintiff
terms.gloss: In a securities class action, the plaintiff the court appoints to direct the case and choose lawyers on behalf of the whole class.

terms.label: unilateral
terms.gloss: Done by one side alone, without the other side's agreement, such as a company changing its terms on its own.

terms.label: certificate of service
terms.gloss: A short signed statement filed with a court paper saying when and how copies were delivered to the other parties.

terms.label: clerk (of court)
terms.gloss: The court official who keeps the case file, records filings, enters orders and issues court papers such as writs.

terms.label: terminate (a motion)
terms.gloss: A docket housekeeping step: the clerk marks the listed motions as resolved so they no longer show as pending.

terms.label: pass-on defense
terms.gloss: A defense that a plaintiff was not really harmed by an overcharge because it passed the extra cost on to its own customers.

terms.label: took no part
terms.gloss: The judge did not participate in hearing or deciding the case, so the decision was made by the remaining judges.

terms.label: turnover order
terms.gloss: A court order directing someone holding a judgment debtor's money or property to hand it over so the judgment can be paid.

terms.label: Civil Practice Law and Rules
terms.gloss: New York's main code of civil procedure (CPLR). Article 52, including § 5225, governs collecting money judgments.

terms.label: parent (company)
terms.gloss: A company that owns or controls another company (its subsidiary). The two are usually treated as separate legal entities.

terms.label: possession or custody
terms.gloss: Actually holding property, as opposed to merely having influence or control over someone else who holds it.

terms.label: certification (to a state court)
terms.gloss: A procedure where a federal court sends an unsettled question of state law to that state's highest court for an authoritative answer, then decides the case using it.

terms.label: statutory scheme
terms.gloss: The whole set of related provisions in a statute (or statute plus regulations), read together to understand how each part fits.

terms.label: appendix (on appeal)
terms.gloss: A bound collection of the key documents from the trial-court record, filed with the briefs so the appeals court can read them.

terms.label: sports book
terms.gloss: A business that takes bets on sporting events.

terms.label: cease-and-desist demand
terms.gloss: A letter demanding that someone stop allegedly unlawful conduct, usually warning that a lawsuit will follow if they don't.

terms.label: Rule 4(f)(3)
terms.gloss: The part of Rule 4 letting a federal court order service on a defendant abroad by any method not forbidden by international agreement, such as email.

terms.label: preclusive sanctions
terms.gloss: Penalties that bar a disobedient party from presenting certain claims, defenses or evidence, which can effectively decide the case against it.

terms.label: default (on a contract)
terms.gloss: Failing to make required payments or otherwise breaking the terms of a credit or lease agreement.

terms.label: advisory committee notes
terms.gloss: Official commentary written by the committee that drafted a federal rule, which courts use to interpret the rule.

terms.label: Hague Service Convention
terms.gloss: An international treaty setting procedures for serving court papers in member countries. Where it applies, its methods generally must be used.

terms.label: reasonably calculated (notice)
terms.gloss: The due process test for notice: the method must be reasonably likely, in the circumstances, to tell the defendant about the case and allow a response.

terms.label: coextensive
terms.gloss: Having exactly the same reach. A long-arm law coextensive with due process lets a state's courts reach as far as the Constitution allows.

terms.label: but-for test (jurisdiction)
terms.gloss: A test then used by the Ninth Circuit asking whether the claim would have arisen but for the defendant's contacts with the forum state.

terms.label: purposeful interjection
terms.gloss: A factor in judging whether jurisdiction is reasonable: how much the defendant deliberately reached into the forum state's affairs.

terms.label: exceptional case (fees)
terms.gloss: Under federal trademark law, courts may award attorney fees to the winner only in exceptional cases, such as deliberate, malicious infringement.

terms.label: Criminal Rule 7(f)
terms.gloss: The Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure letting a court order the prosecution to give a bill of particulars, i.e., more detail about the charges.

terms.label: witness list
terms.gloss: A list of the people a side plans to call as witnesses. In federal criminal cases the government generally need not provide one before trial.

terms.label: findings (of fact)
terms.gloss: A judge's, jury's or agency's formal determinations of what actually happened, based on the evidence, as distinct from conclusions about the law.

terms.label: Michigan Court Rule 2.116
terms.gloss: Michigan's summary-disposition rule. (C)(10) lets a party win without trial when no genuine factual dispute exists; (I)(2) lets the court give judgment to the opposing party instead.

terms.label: McNitt Act
terms.gloss: A Michigan law (repealed 1951) under which county road commissions took over township roads in stages, including roads dedicated in recorded plats.

terms.label: road commission
terms.gloss: In Michigan, the county agency responsible for public roads, including deciding whether to accept and maintain dedicated streets.

terms.label: proprietor
terms.gloss: The owner of land. In dedication law, the owner who records a plat offering streets for public use.

terms.label: Subdivision Control Act
terms.gloss: Michigan's statute governing how land is divided into lots and plats are recorded, including the effect of dedicating streets.

terms.label: acceptance (of contract terms)
terms.gloss: Agreeing to an offer's terms, by words or by conduct such as continuing to use a service, which together with the offer forms a contract.

terms.label: withdrawal (of a dedication offer)
terms.gloss: A landowner's taking back of an offer to dedicate land to the public before it is accepted, shown by conduct inconsistent with public use.

terms.label: presumption of consistent usage
terms.gloss: An interpretive rule that the same words mean the same thing throughout a statute and in closely related statutes, unless context shows otherwise.

terms.label: statement of questions
terms.gloss: The part of an appellate brief listing the issues for the court to decide. In Michigan, an issue left out of it may be treated as abandoned.

terms.label: self-funded plan
terms.gloss: An employer health plan that pays claims from the employer's own money rather than buying insurance, often hiring a company to administer it.

terms.label: plan sponsor / administrator
terms.gloss: The employer that sets up a benefit plan (sponsor) and the party responsible for running it and deciding claims (administrator).

terms.label: preexisting condition
terms.gloss: A health problem a person had before their coverage began. Some plans excluded or delayed coverage for such conditions.

terms.label: collection action
terms.gloss: A lawsuit by a creditor, such as a hospital, to recover an unpaid debt.

terms.label: protective order / measures
terms.gloss: Court-ordered safeguards, such as a protective order, limiting how sensitive information produced in discovery may be used or disclosed.

terms.label: UCC § 2-714
terms.gloss: The UCC section measuring a buyer's damages for accepted goods that breach a warranty: usually the value as warranted minus the value as delivered.

terms.label: UCC § 2-715
terms.gloss: The UCC section allowing buyers incidental damages (handling costs) and consequential damages, such as lost profits the seller had reason to foresee.

terms.label: UCC § 2-712 (cover)
terms.gloss: The UCC section letting a buyer buy substitute goods (cover) and recover the extra cost from the seller.

terms.label: UCC § 2-607 (notice)
terms.gloss: The UCC section requiring a buyer who has accepted goods to notify the seller of a breach within a reasonable time or lose any remedy.

terms.label: tacit-agreement test
terms.gloss: An older rule that a seller owed consequential damages only if it had tacitly agreed to bear those losses. The UCC rejected it in favor of foreseeability.

terms.label: lump verdict
terms.gloss: A single damages figure from the jury that does not break the money down by category, so a court cannot tell which parts were proper.

terms.label: proxy materials
terms.gloss: The documents a company sends shareholders before a meeting so they can vote without attending. A proposal included there reaches every shareholder.

terms.label: Rule 14a-8
terms.gloss: The SEC rule requiring companies to include qualifying shareholder proposals in their proxy materials, subject to listed exclusions such as ordinary business matters.

terms.label: charter amendment
terms.gloss: A change to a corporation's charter (its founding document), which can define or limit what business the company may do.

terms.label: ordinary business exclusion
terms.gloss: The Rule 14a-8 exception letting a company omit shareholder proposals about routine day-to-day management decisions.

terms.label: no-action letter
terms.gloss: A letter from SEC staff saying it will not recommend enforcement if a company takes a described step. It is informal advice, not a binding ruling.

terms.label: corporate suffrage / democracy
terms.gloss: The idea that shareholders, as owners, should be able to vote on and propose matters of corporate policy.

terms.label: live controversy
terms.gloss: A real, ongoing dispute in which the parties still have something at stake. Federal courts can decide only those.

terms.label: General Court
terms.gloss: The official name of the Massachusetts legislature (New Hampshire's is also called the General Court).

terms.label: General Laws
terms.gloss: The official compiled statutes of a state, such as the Massachusetts General Laws.

terms.label: enfranchisement
terms.gloss: Granting the right to vote.

terms.label: federal supremacy
terms.gloss: The constitutional principle (the Supremacy Clause) that valid federal law overrides conflicting state law.

terms.label: citizenship (for diversity)
terms.gloss: For diversity jurisdiction, the state a person is domiciled in, or for a corporation its state of incorporation and principal place of business.

terms.label: Rule 12(b)(3)
terms.gloss: The Federal Rule of Civil Procedure allowing a motion to dismiss for improper venue.

terms.label: private-interest factors
terms.gloss: Considerations about the parties' own convenience, such as witness availability and travel cost, weighed in deciding whether to transfer a case.

terms.label: public-interest factors
terms.gloss: Considerations affecting the courts and community, such as court congestion and local interest in the dispute, weighed in transfer decisions.

terms.label: possession
terms.gloss: Physical control and use of property, which can be legally protected even when someone else holds title.

terms.label: counterbond
terms.gloss: A bond posted by the person holding the goods to keep or get them back while the case is decided.

terms.label: prothonotary
terms.gloss: Pennsylvania's title for the chief clerk of a civil trial court.

terms.label: wrongful detention
terms.gloss: Keeping someone else's goods without the right to do so, the core claim in a replevin action.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 1343(3)
terms.gloss: The statute giving federal district courts jurisdiction over civil-rights suits like those under § 1983.

terms.label: summary procedure
terms.gloss: A quick procedure that acts without the usual notice and full hearing, such as seizing goods on a creditor's application alone.

terms.label: deprivation
terms.gloss: Government's taking away of a protected interest (life, liberty or property). Due process requires fair procedure before or soon after.

terms.label: distraint
terms.gloss: A landlord's old self-help remedy of seizing a tenant's goods to force payment of overdue rent.

terms.label: prejudgment
terms.gloss: Before the court has decided the case, such as a writ seizing property while the dispute is still pending.

terms.label: Younger abstention
terms.gloss: From Younger v. Harris (1971): federal courts generally should not interfere with pending state court proceedings, leaving constitutional objections to the state courts.

terms.label: secured credit
terms.gloss: Lending in which the creditor holds a legal interest in specific property (collateral) it can take if the borrower does not pay.

terms.label: abode service
terms.gloss: Serving papers by leaving them at the defendant's home with a suitable adult who lives there, instead of handing them to the defendant personally.

terms.label: probate registry
terms.gloss: The probate court office that keeps records of estates and the appointment of executors.

terms.label: outcome-determinative test
terms.gloss: Test from Guaranty Trust v. York (1945): a federal diversity court follows state law if ignoring it would significantly change the case's outcome.

terms.label: inequitable administration of the laws
terms.gloss: One of Erie's concerns: unfairness when similar people get different law depending only on whether a federal court is available to them.

terms.label: primary conduct
terms.gloss: People's everyday behavior outside court, such as how they act, contract and run their affairs, as opposed to how they litigate.

terms.label: strike suits
terms.gloss: Weak shareholder lawsuits filed mainly to pressure a company into paying a settlement.

terms.label: security for expenses
terms.gloss: A rule making certain plaintiffs, such as small shareholders, post money to cover the defendant's costs if they lose.

terms.label: pleading deadline
terms.gloss: The deadline for filing a required court paper, such as the answer to a complaint.

terms.label: indebtedness
terms.gloss: Money owed; a debt.

terms.label: cross-action
terms.gloss: Texas term for a defendant's own claim against the plaintiff in the same case, the equivalent of a counterclaim.

terms.label: Judicial Code
terms.gloss: The collected federal statutes on the courts' organization, jurisdiction and procedure (then the 1911 Code; today Title 28 of the U.S. Code).

terms.label: 1789 Act (Judiciary Act)
terms.gloss: The Judiciary Act of 1789, the first federal law creating the lower federal courts and setting their jurisdiction, including removal.

terms.label: duty to plead
terms.gloss: A defendant's obligation to file an answer or other response by a deadline; removal had to be sought by that time.

terms.label: boom (log boom)
terms.gloss: A floating barrier across a river that catches and holds logs floated downstream.

terms.label: freight
terms.gloss: The payment owed to a carrier for transporting cargo.

terms.label: Title II (Communications Act)
terms.gloss: The part of the Communications Act imposing common-carrier rules, such as reasonable, nondiscriminatory rates, on telecommunications carriers.

terms.label: ancillary (Title I) authority
terms.gloss: The FCC's general power over communications services that no specific part of the Act regulates, used to impose duties reasonably related to its other responsibilities.

terms.label: universal service
terms.gloss: The policy, funded by carriers' contributions, of making telephone and related service available and affordable everywhere.

terms.label: telecommunications service
terms.gloss: Under the 1996 Act, offering pure transmission of the customer's information to the public for a fee. Such providers face common-carrier regulation.

terms.label: information service
terms.gloss: Under the 1996 Act, offering the ability to generate, process, store or retrieve information, such as internet access. Such providers escape common-carrier rules.

terms.label: declaratory ruling
terms.gloss: An agency ruling that clarifies how the law applies to a situation, to remove uncertainty.

terms.label: Federal Communications Commission
terms.gloss: The federal agency that regulates interstate communications by wire, radio, television, cable and satellite.

terms.label: judicial lottery
terms.gloss: A random draw that picks one court of appeals to hear challenges to an agency rule when petitions are filed in several circuits.

terms.label: Mead
terms.gloss: United States v. Mead (2001): Chevron deference applied only where Congress gave the agency power to act with the force of law and it used that power.

terms.label: National Guard
terms.gloss: Each state's military force, normally under the governor, which can be called into federal service under the President's command.

terms.label: federalization
terms.gloss: Calling a state's National Guard into federal service, placing it under the President's command.

terms.label: 10 U.S.C. § 12406
terms.gloss: A federal statute letting the President federalize the National Guard in listed emergencies, including when he is unable with the regular forces to execute federal law.

terms.label: regular forces
terms.gloss: The phrase in § 12406(3). The Court read it as likely meaning the regular U.S. military, not civilian federal officers.

terms.label: inherent presidential power
terms.gloss: Power claimed to come directly from the Constitution's grant of executive authority, rather than from any statute passed by Congress.

terms.label: party presentation
terms.gloss: The principle that courts decide the issues the parties actually raise and argue, rather than reaching out to decide questions on their own.

terms.label: predicate (legal precondition)
terms.gloss: A condition that must exist before a legal power can be used or a rule applies.

terms.label: Insurrection Act
terms.gloss: Federal laws letting the President use the military at home to suppress insurrections or enforce law in specified extreme circumstances.

terms.label: militia
terms.gloss: Citizen soldiers who can be called up in emergencies; the Constitution lets Congress call forth the militia, today mainly the National Guard.

terms.label: nonindictment
terms.gloss: A grand jury's refusal to charge (indict) someone the prosecutor presented a case against.

terms.label: defeasible
terms.gloss: Capable of being overcome: a defeasible presumption gives way when context or evidence points the other way.

terms.label: NPDES permit
terms.gloss: The Clean Water Act permit program that sets how much of each pollutant a facility may discharge into waters, with monitoring and reporting duties.

terms.label: permit
terms.gloss: An official license allowing an activity on stated conditions; violating the conditions breaks the law.

terms.label: notice of intent to sue
terms.gloss: Required advance warning to the violator and government before a citizen suit, giving them time to act first.

terms.label: diligent prosecution
terms.gloss: The Clean Water Act bar on citizen suits when the government is already diligently pursuing the violator in court.

terms.label: economic benefit (of noncompliance)
terms.gloss: The money a violator saved by not complying, a key factor in setting penalties so violating does not pay.

terms.label: Clean Water Act
terms.gloss: The federal law regulating pollution discharges into U.S. waters, mainly through permits, with government and citizen enforcement.

terms.label: sunk costs
terms.gloss: Resources already spent that cannot be recovered; here, the judicial effort already invested in the case.

terms.label: catalyst theory
terms.gloss: The argument that a plaintiff whose lawsuit prompted the defendant to change its behavior has prevailed, and may get attorney fees, even without a judgment.

terms.label: representation hearing
terms.gloss: An NLRB proceeding on whether, and in what group, workers will be represented by a union.

terms.label: trial examiner
terms.gloss: The official who heard evidence in an agency case and recommended a decision; the forerunner of today's administrative law judge.

terms.label: enforcement (of an agency order)
terms.gloss: NLRB orders are not self-executing; the Board asks a court of appeals to enforce them, and the court reviews the order before doing so.
terms.context: (board|challenged enforcement|compel enforcement|enforcement permissible|nonenforcement|refusal of enforcement|refusing enforcement)

terms.label: nonprobationary
terms.gloss: Past the initial trial period of employment, so entitled to full job protections against dismissal.

terms.label: competitive service
terms.gloss: Federal civil-service jobs filled by merit (often by exams) whose holders are protected against arbitrary or political firing.

terms.label: adverse action
terms.gloss: A formal personnel action against a government employee, such as removal or suspension, which triggers procedural protections.

terms.label: Civil Service Commission
terms.gloss: The former federal agency that oversaw the civil service and heard employee appeals (replaced in 1978).

terms.label: Lloyd-La Follette Act
terms.gloss: A 1912 federal law allowing removal of civil servants only for cause that will promote the efficiency of the service, with written charges and a chance to answer.

terms.label: Veterans' Preference Act
terms.gloss: A 1944 federal law giving veterans hiring preferences and extra protections, including appeal rights, against dismissal.

terms.label: Pendleton Act
terms.gloss: The 1883 law creating the merit-based federal civil service and the Civil Service Commission.

terms.label: patronage
terms.gloss: Giving government jobs as rewards for political support rather than for merit.

terms.label: expectancy
terms.gloss: A legally protected expectation, here of continued employment unless there is good cause for removal.

terms.label: name-clearing hearing
terms.gloss: A hearing allowing an employee fired on stigmatizing charges, such as dishonesty, to rebut them and clear their reputation.

terms.label: Pickering balancing
terms.gloss: From Pickering v. Board of Education (1968): a public employee's free-speech interest is weighed against the government's interest as employer in efficient operations.

terms.label: public concern
terms.gloss: Matters of political, social or community interest; speech on them gets the strongest First Amendment protection, including for public employees.

terms.label: Administrative Conference
terms.gloss: The Administrative Conference of the United States, a federal agency that studies and recommends improvements to agency procedures.

terms.label: adversarial process
terms.gloss: A process where opposing sides each present evidence and argument before a neutral decision-maker.

terms.label: Board of Equalization
terms.gloss: A state body that adjusts property-tax valuations so similar property is valued uniformly across different areas.

terms.label: assessed valuation
terms.gloss: The value a taxing authority assigns to property to calculate the property tax owed.

terms.label: assessor
terms.gloss: The local official who values property for taxation.

terms.label: adequate and independent state ground
terms.gloss: A rule that the Supreme Court will not review a state decision resting on state law sufficient to support the result, whatever the federal question.

terms.label: Londoner
terms.gloss: Londoner v. Denver (1908): due process requires a hearing when government decides a few people's taxes based on their individual circumstances.

terms.label: Tariff Act of 1922
terms.gloss: The 1922 law setting import duties; its § 315 let the President adjust rates to equalize U.S. and foreign production costs.

terms.label: duty (import tax)
terms.gloss: A tax charged on imported goods.

terms.label: dutiable
terms.gloss: Subject to an import tax; the opposite of the duty-free list.

terms.label: proclamation
terms.gloss: A formal public order issued by the President.

terms.label: Tariff Commission
terms.gloss: A federal agency (today the U.S. International Trade Commission) that investigated tariff questions and advised the President.

terms.label: Customs Court / Court of Customs Appeals
terms.gloss: Specialized federal courts for import-duty disputes: the Customs Court heard them first, and the Court of Customs Appeals reviewed its decisions.

terms.label: reciprocity (in trade)
terms.gloss: Matching treatment between countries; in Field v. Clark the President could suspend duty-free treatment for nations treating U.S. goods unequally.

terms.label: cost of performance
terms.gloss: A damages measure: what it would cost to do the promised work, as opposed to how much the work would raise the property's value.

terms.label: Groves v. John Wunder
terms.gloss: A 1939 Minnesota case awarding the cost of doing promised grading work even though it far exceeded the land's increase in value.

terms.label: change of theory
terms.gloss: Trying to switch, after trial or on appeal, to a different legal theory than the one used at trial. Courts generally forbid it.

terms.label: interim relief
terms.gloss: Temporary orders that hold things in place while a case proceeds, before a final decision on the merits.

terms.label: notice (legal)
terms.gloss: Being informed, in a legally adequate way, of something affecting your rights, such as new contract terms or a proposed government action. It is often required before rights can be lost.

terms.label: legitimate entitlement
terms.gloss: In due process law, a benefit someone has a real legal claim to under a statute, rule or contract, not a mere hope. It counts as protected property.

terms.label: statutory forbearance
terms.gloss: The FCC's power under the Communications Act to stop applying a regulation or statutory provision to carriers when it finds enforcement unnecessary.

terms.label: Roth
terms.gloss: Board of Regents v. Roth (1972): a property interest protected by due process comes from independent sources, such as statutes or contracts, giving a legitimate claim of entitlement.

terms.label: Loudermill
terms.gloss: Cleveland Board of Education v. Loudermill (1985): a public employee removable only for cause must get notice and a chance to respond before being fired.

terms.label: Sibbach
terms.gloss: Sibbach v. Wilson (1941): a Federal Rule is valid under the Rules Enabling Act if it really regulates procedure.

terms.label: Overmyer
terms.gloss: D. H. Overmyer Co. v. Frick Co. (1972): a business can validly waive in advance its right to notice and a hearing, if the waiver is voluntary, knowing and negotiated.

terms.label: La Buy
terms.gloss: La Buy v. Howes Leather Co. (1957): the Supreme Court approved mandamus to stop a district judge's practice of sending complex cases to a special master.

terms.label: Schlagenhauf
terms.gloss: Schlagenhauf v. Holder (1964): mandamus was proper to review a new, important question about ordering a defendant's medical examinations under Rule 35.

terms.label: Computer II
terms.gloss: A 1980 FCC order separating basic transmission service (regulated like telephone service) from enhanced services that process or store information (largely unregulated).

terms.label: St. Paul Mercury
terms.gloss: St. Paul Mercury Indemnity Co. v. Red Cab Co. (1938): an amount claimed in good faith counts unless it is legally certain the claim is really for less.

terms.label: Ferens
terms.gloss: Ferens v. John Deere Co. (1990): the original court's state law follows a convenience transfer even when the plaintiff itself asked for the transfer.

terms.label: Attorney General's Committee
terms.gloss: The Attorney General's Committee on Administrative Procedure, whose 1941 report on agency practices helped shape the Administrative Procedure Act.

terms.label: Division of Corporation Finance
terms.gloss: The SEC staff division that reviews company disclosure filings and answers companies' requests to exclude shareholder proposals.

terms.label: array (jury panel)
terms.gloss: The whole group of people summoned as potential jurors. Challenging the array attacks how the entire pool was chosen, not any single juror.

terms.label: interim earnings
terms.gloss: Money a wrongly fired worker earned elsewhere between the firing and reinstatement, which is subtracted from the backpay award.

terms.label: in controversy (Rule 35)
terms.gloss: Rule 35's requirement that a person's physical or mental condition be genuinely disputed in the case before a court may order an examination of it.

terms.label: reviewable
terms.gloss: Whether a higher court (or a court checking an agency) may examine and correct a decision; nonreviewability means courts may not second-guess it.

terms.label: settlement class
terms.gloss: A class certified only so that a negotiated settlement can bind its members, rather than for a trial.

terms.label: material factual dispute
terms.gloss: A real disagreement about a fact that could change the outcome; if none exists, a judge can decide the case without trial on summary judgment.

terms.label: no just reason for delay
terms.gloss: The express finding Rule 54(b) requires before a court may enter an immediately appealable final judgment on some claims or parties while others remain.

terms.label: appeal as of right
terms.gloss: An appeal the higher court must hear, as opposed to one it may choose whether to accept.

terms.label: took no part / did not participate
terms.gloss: The judge or Justice sat out the decision entirely, often because of a conflict of interest or joining the court late.

terms.label: County Court at Law
terms.gloss: A Texas county-level trial court that hears smaller civil cases, among others.

terms.label: proper lookout
terms.gloss: A driver's duty to watch attentively for traffic and hazards; failing to keep one is a common finding of negligence.

terms.label: Court of Civil Appeals (Texas)
terms.gloss: The name then used for Texas's intermediate appellate courts in civil cases, between the trial courts and the Texas Supreme Court.

terms.label: verdict winner
terms.gloss: The party in whose favor the jury decided.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 2106
terms.gloss: The federal statute letting appellate courts affirm, modify, vacate, or reverse judgments and direct any appropriate judgment or further proceedings.

terms.label: postverdict motion
terms.gloss: A motion made after the jury's verdict, such as for judgment notwithstanding the verdict or for a new trial.

terms.label: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act
terms.gloss: A 1986 federal law punishing unauthorized access to computers and damage to computer data, which also lets injured people sue.

terms.label: Rule 23(b)(2)
terms.gloss: The class-action category for cases seeking mainly injunctions or declarations that benefit the whole class at once.

terms.label: predominate (Rule 23)
terms.gloss: In a Rule 23(b)(3) class, questions common to the class must outweigh questions affecting only individual members.

terms.label: objector
terms.gloss: A class member who formally opposes a proposed class settlement or fee request in court.

terms.label: net present value
terms.gloss: Today's value of money to be received in the future, discounted because money later is worth less than money now.

terms.label: reversion (of settlement funds)
terms.gloss: In a class settlement, return of unclaimed money to the defendant, which can give the defendant an incentive to discourage claims.

terms.label: percentage method
terms.gloss: Paying class lawyers a percentage of the total value they win for the class.

terms.label: fair, adequate, and reasonable
terms.gloss: The standard a judge must find met before approving a class-action settlement that binds absent members.

terms.label: SEC Rules 10b-13 and 14d-10
terms.gloss: SEC tender-offer rules: 10b-13 barred a bidder from buying shares outside its offer during the offer; 14d-10 requires paying all tendering holders the best price paid.

terms.label: Section 27 (Exchange Act)
terms.gloss: The Securities Exchange Act provision giving federal courts exclusive jurisdiction over suits to enforce that Act.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 1738 (Full Faith and Credit Act)
terms.gloss: The statute requiring federal courts to give a state court judgment the same binding effect that the state's own courts would give it.

terms.label: factual predicate
terms.gloss: The facts underlying a claim; a settlement can release other claims that rest on the same facts as the settled case.

terms.label: in the first instance
terms.gloss: Deciding an issue first, before any other court; appellate courts usually let lower courts decide issues first.

terms.label: collateral bar
terms.gloss: Use of a judgment from one case to block claims raised in a separate case in another court.

terms.label: magistrate judge
terms.gloss: A federal judicial officer appointed by district judges who handles pretrial matters and, if the parties consent, can conduct an entire civil trial.

terms.label: regnal-year statute citation
terms.gloss: Old English statutes are cited by the year of the monarch's reign in which Parliament passed them; "27 Edward III" means the 27th year of Edward III's reign (1353).

terms.label: real and personal actions
terms.gloss: Old categories of lawsuits: real actions sought to recover land; personal actions sought debts, damages, or goods.

terms.label: error (writ of error review)
terms.gloss: Review on a writ of error, the old way a higher common-law court corrected a judgment for legal mistakes shown on the record.

terms.label: manor
terms.gloss: A landed estate held by a lord in the English feudal system, often with tenants and its own court.

terms.label: ecclesiastical jurisdiction
terms.gloss: The authority of church courts, which then decided matters such as marriage and wills; praemunire laws targeted taking cases to the Pope or other authority outside the King's courts.

terms.label: Keeper of the Great Seal
terms.gloss: The officer who held the monarch's seal and headed Chancery when there was no Lord Chancellor; in practice the same role.

terms.label: enrollment (of a record)
terms.gloss: Officially entering a decree or decision in a court's permanent records so it can be relied on later.

terms.label: conscience (in equity)
terms.gloss: Equity's traditional basis: Chancery could order a party not to use a legal right in a way that was against good conscience.

terms.label: Coke's Institutes
terms.gloss: Sir Edward Coke's multi-volume treatise on English law, published 1628 to 1644, partly after his death; Coke was the Chief Justice who opposed Chancery.

terms.label: Prince's Attorney
terms.gloss: The lawyer who managed the legal affairs of the heir to the throne, Prince Charles; here he joined the King's legal advisers.

terms.label: real-estate broker
terms.gloss: A licensed professional who arranges sales of land and buildings for a commission.

terms.label: principal (of a debt)
terms.gloss: The amount actually owed on a debt, apart from interest; here the installments paid down the price plus interest on it.

terms.label: motion to enlarge findings
terms.gloss: A request that the trial court expand or add to its written findings and conclusions; until decided, the judgment is not final for appeal.

terms.label: premature (appeal)
terms.gloss: Filed too early, before the decision is final and ready for review, so the appeal is dismissed.

terms.label: purchase money
terms.gloss: Money paid toward the price of the property being bought.

terms.label: plenary review
terms.gloss: Full, fresh review by an appeals court, giving no deference to the lower court's legal conclusions.

terms.label: reasonable efforts / best efforts
terms.gloss: A contract duty to work diligently toward a goal, here to actively promote Emerson-brand sales; "best efforts" is usually seen as more demanding than "reasonable efforts".

terms.label: implied duty (in a contract)
terms.gloss: A term a court reads into a contract though the parties did not write it, because the bargain would make little sense without it.

terms.label: implied covenant (of good faith)
terms.gloss: The unwritten promise in every contract that neither party will act in bad faith to deprive the other of the benefits of the bargain.

terms.label: honesty in fact
terms.gloss: The UCC's core meaning of good faith: actually being honest in the conduct or transaction concerned.

terms.label: verdict form
terms.gloss: The written questions the jury answers to record its decision.

terms.label: interest against the United States
terms.gloss: The rule that the U.S. need not pay interest on money it owes unless a statute or contract expressly says so (constitutional takings aside).

terms.label: construction manager
terms.gloss: A firm hired to oversee and coordinate a building project for the owner, usually for a fee, rather than to build it for a fixed price.

terms.label: one-year provision (statute of frauds)
terms.gloss: The statute-of-frauds rule requiring a signed writing for an agreement that, by its terms, cannot be performed within one year of being made.

terms.label: indefinite duration
terms.gloss: Having no fixed end date; under the one-year rule such a contract could possibly be completed within a year, so no writing is needed.

terms.label: independent expenditures
terms.gloss: Election spending supporting a candidate made without coordinating with the candidate's campaign.

terms.label: Buckley v. Valeo
terms.gloss: 1976 Supreme Court case on campaign finance which also held that FEC members with enforcement powers must be appointed by the President, not Congress.

terms.label: Senate-confirmed
terms.gloss: Appointed by the President with the Senate's approval, as the Constitution requires for principal federal officers.

terms.label: alternate juror
terms.gloss: A juror who hears the trial as a backup but does not deliberate unless a regular juror drops out; an alternate present at deliberations can taint them.

terms.label: Bowsher v. Synar
terms.gloss: 1986 Supreme Court case holding Congress cannot keep removal power over an officer (the Comptroller General) who performs executive functions.

terms.label: Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority case
terms.gloss: 1991 Supreme Court case striking down a board of members of Congress that could veto decisions of the regional airports authority, as congressional overreach into execution.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 518(a)
terms.gloss: The federal statute reserving to the Attorney General and Solicitor General the conduct of the government's cases in the Supreme Court.

terms.label: mandatory jurisdiction
terms.gloss: Cases a court must hear when properly brought, as with former direct appeals to the Supreme Court.

terms.label: Saturday Night Massacre
terms.gloss: October 20, 1973: President Nixon ordered the Watergate special prosecutor fired; the top two Justice officials resigned, and Solicitor General Robert Bork carried out the firing.

terms.label: brief in opposition
terms.gloss: The respondent's filing urging the Supreme Court not to grant certiorari.

terms.label: intervening rights
terms.gloss: Rights others gained between an unauthorized act and its later approval, which after-the-fact ratification cannot take away.

terms.label: preliminary-injunction factors
terms.gloss: What courts weigh before temporary relief: likely success on the merits, irreparable harm, the balance of hardships, and the public interest.

terms.label: federal charter
terms.gloss: Creation or authorization of a company by an act of Congress, often for a public purpose.

terms.label: securitize
terms.gloss: To bundle many loans, such as mortgages, into securities sold to investors, who receive the borrowers' payments.

terms.label: Housing and Economic Recovery Act
terms.gloss: The 2008 law creating the Federal Housing Finance Agency to regulate Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and letting it take them over as conservator.

terms.label: preferred shares
