terms.gloss: Stock that gets dividends and repayment before common stock; "senior" preferred ranks ahead of other preferred.

terms.label: liquidation preference
terms.gloss: An investor's right to be paid a set amount before common shareholders if the company is wound up.

terms.label: warrants (stock)
terms.gloss: Rights to buy a company's stock at a set price in the future.

terms.label: dividend
terms.gloss: A payment a company makes to its shareholders out of profits or capital.

terms.label: net worth sweep
terms.gloss: The 2012 change requiring Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to pay Treasury nearly all their net worth each quarter as dividends.

terms.label: sever (a provision)
terms.gloss: To cut out an unconstitutional provision while leaving the rest of the statute in force.

terms.label: anti-injunction provision (§ 4617(f))
terms.gloss: The HERA provision barring courts from restraining or affecting the FHFA's exercise of its powers as conservator or receiver.

terms.label: retrospective relief
terms.gloss: A remedy for past harm, such as returning money already paid.

terms.label: succession clause
terms.gloss: The HERA provision transferring to the FHFA, as conservator, all rights of shareholders regarding the companies.

terms.label: government-sponsored entities
terms.gloss: Privately owned companies chartered by Congress for a public purpose, like Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac in home lending.

terms.label: civil service
terms.gloss: Career government employees hired on merit and protected from politically motivated firing.

terms.label: Federal Reserve Board
terms.gloss: The Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, seven governors with fourteen-year terms who direct U.S. monetary policy and supervise banks.

terms.label: 12 U.S.C. § 242
terms.gloss: The Federal Reserve Act provision giving Governors fourteen-year terms and letting the President remove them only "for cause".

terms.label: cause (for removal)
terms.gloss: A legally sufficient reason to remove an official before the term ends; here, a substantial reason tied to the office, not policy disagreement.

terms.label: notice and an opportunity to respond
match: notice and an opportunity to respond
notice and an opportunity to defend
terms.gloss: Basic fair procedure: being told the charges and evidence and given a real chance to answer before a decision.

terms.label: title to public office
terms.gloss: The legal right to hold an office, historically tested through quo warranto rather than in equity.

terms.label: staggered terms
terms.gloss: Terms set to expire in different years so members do not all turn over at once.

terms.label: Section 78y
terms.gloss: The Exchange Act provision for review of SEC rules and final orders directly in a federal court of appeals.

terms.label: collateral (to agency review)
terms.gloss: Wholly separate from the ordinary matters an agency's review scheme handles, which can let a claim go straight to district court.

terms.label: Decision of 1789
terms.gloss: The First Congress's debate and law treating the President as able to remove the Secretary of Foreign Affairs at will, often cited for presidential removal power.

terms.label: Opinions Clause
terms.gloss: Article II clause letting the President require written opinions from principal officers of the executive departments.

terms.label: Twenty-Fifth Amendment
terms.gloss: The amendment on presidential succession and disability, letting principal officers of executive departments help declare a President unable to serve.

terms.label: intentional infliction of emotional harm
terms.gloss: A tort for outrageous conduct intentionally or recklessly causing severe emotional distress.

terms.label: American Federation of Musicians
terms.gloss: The labor union representing professional musicians in the U.S. and Canada.

terms.label: union scale
terms.gloss: The minimum pay rate set by a labor union for its members' work.

terms.label: excess of power
terms.gloss: An arbitrator deciding beyond what the parties agreed to submit; a ground for vacating an award.

terms.label: reasonable expectations (adhesion contracts)
terms.gloss: Doctrine refusing to enforce adhesion-contract terms that the weaker party would not reasonably expect.

terms.label: Arbitration Act (California)
terms.gloss: California's statute governing arbitration agreements and court enforcement or vacation of awards.

terms.label: Medicare
terms.gloss: The federal health-insurance program for people 65 and older and some people with disabilities.

terms.label: Medicaid
terms.gloss: The joint federal-state health-coverage program for people with low incomes.

terms.label: conditions of participation
terms.gloss: Rules that hospitals and other providers must meet to receive Medicare and Medicaid payments.

terms.label: zone of reasonableness
terms.gloss: Arbitrary-and-capricious review asks only whether the agency's choice was reasonable and reasonably explained, not whether the court would choose differently.

terms.label: advisory circular
terms.gloss: An FAA guidance document; here it set product test standards that federally funded airports effectively had to follow.

terms.label: 49 U.S.C. § 46110
terms.gloss: The aviation statute allowing challenges to FAA orders directly in a court of appeals within 60 days, with FAA findings conclusive if supported by substantial evidence.

terms.label: APA § 701(a)(2)
terms.gloss: The APA provision barring judicial review where agency action is committed to agency discretion by law.

terms.label: timeliness
terms.gloss: Whether something was filed or done within the legal deadline.

terms.label: reasonable-grounds exception
terms.gloss: § 46110's allowance for a late petition if there were reasonable grounds for not filing within 60 days.

terms.label: Association of Data Processing Service Organizations v. Board of Governors
match: association of data processing service organizations v. board of governors
terms.gloss: 1984 D.C. Circuit opinion (Judge Scalia) holding that substantial-evidence and arbitrary-and-capricious review demand the same factual support.

terms.label: Social Security disability insurance benefits
terms.gloss: Monthly federal payments to insured workers who cannot do substantial gainful work because of a lasting medical impairment.

terms.label: malingering
terms.gloss: Faking or exaggerating illness or injury to gain something, such as benefits.

terms.label: Appeals Council
terms.gloss: The Social Security Administration body that reviews hearing decisions; its action makes the decision final.

terms.label: substantial gainful activity
terms.gloss: Social Security's test of work involving significant effort done for pay; a claimant able to do it is not disabled.

terms.label: Social Security Act § 205(g)
terms.gloss: The provision allowing federal court review of final Social Security decisions; agency findings are conclusive if supported by substantial evidence.

terms.label: Consolidated Edison
terms.gloss: Consolidated Edison Co. v. NLRB (1938), defining substantial evidence and warning that uncorroborated hearsay does not constitute it.

terms.label: APA § 556(d)
terms.gloss: The APA provision on agency hearings: it allows documentary evidence and guarantees cross-examination where needed for a full and true disclosure of the facts.

terms.label: lay (non-expert)
terms.gloss: Not a trained professional in the field, such as a person who is not a doctor or lawyer.

terms.label: reserved leave (to enter a verdict)
terms.gloss: The trial judge let the jury's verdict stand provisionally but reserved permission for the full court to enter a different verdict if the law required.

terms.label: rule absolute
terms.gloss: Old English practice: a provisional order (rule nisi) became a "rule absolute", final and effective, if the other side failed to show sufficient cause against it.

terms.label: implied condition
terms.gloss: A condition a court reads into a contract from its nature, such as that the specific hall must still exist.

terms.label: civil law / Roman law
terms.gloss: The legal tradition based on Roman law and codes, used in continental Europe, as opposed to English common law.

terms.label: Pothier
terms.gloss: Robert-Joseph Pothier, 18th-century French jurist whose treatise on obligations heavily influenced English contract law.

terms.label: personal-service contract
terms.gloss: A contract requiring a particular person's own work, such as writing a book; that person's death or incapacity can excuse it.

terms.label: title (passing of ownership)
terms.gloss: Legal ownership; who bears a loss of sold goods can depend on whether ownership has passed to the buyer.

terms.label: risk allocation
terms.gloss: Which party bears the loss if something goes wrong, such as goods being destroyed.

terms.label: Coggs v. Bernard
terms.gloss: 1703 English case on bailments, setting the care owed by someone holding another's goods.

terms.label: malicious
terms.gloss: Done with intent to harm or with spite; here, shutting off water to harass.

terms.label: prorate
terms.gloss: To divide a payment in proportion, such as charging only for the days service was missing.

terms.label: wrongful entry
terms.gloss: Entering someone else's land without right, a form of trespass.

terms.label: make whole
terms.gloss: Compensating a plaintiff fully for losses, restoring them to where they would have been without the wrong.

terms.label: punitive award / punitive relief
terms.gloss: Punitive damages: extra money awarded to punish and deter especially bad conduct, beyond compensating the victim; generally unavailable for a plain breach of contract.

terms.label: California Fair Employment and Housing Act
match: california fair employment and housing act
terms.gloss: California's main state law banning discrimination in employment and housing.

terms.label: negligent supervision
terms.gloss: A claim that an employer carelessly failed to oversee its employees, letting them harm someone.

terms.label: first-impression question
terms.gloss: A legal question no court in that jurisdiction has decided before, so there is no precedent directly on point.

terms.label: Finley
terms.gloss: Finley v. United States (1989), holding federal courts could not add a new party on a state claim lacking its own jurisdiction; Congress overrode it in 1990 with § 1367.

terms.label: Gibbs
terms.gloss: United Mine Workers v. Gibbs (1966): federal courts may hear state claims sharing a common nucleus of facts with a federal claim, but may decline them in their discretion.

terms.label: Bauman factors
terms.gloss: Bauman v. U.S. District Court (9th Cir. 1977), listing five factors the Ninth Circuit weighs in deciding whether to issue mandamus against a trial judge.

terms.label: infant
terms.gloss: In legal usage, any minor (a person under the age of adulthood), not just a baby; a minor usually sues or is sued through an adult representative.

terms.label: not guilty (civil plea)
terms.gloss: In old civil pleading, a defendant's plea denying the wrong charged, putting the plaintiff to proof (the 'general issue'); not a criminal plea.

terms.label: Court of Common Pleas
terms.gloss: One of England's historic central courts at Westminster, which heard ordinary civil disputes between private parties.

terms.label: consequential injury
terms.gloss: Harm that follows indirectly from an act through later events, rather than striking the victim immediately; historically sued for in an action 'on the case.'

terms.label: intervening cause
terms.gloss: A later act or event between the defendant's conduct and the harm, which may or may not break the chain of responsibility.

terms.label: natural and probable consequence
terms.gloss: A result a reasonable person would expect to follow from an act, so the actor can be held responsible for it.

terms.label: patent claim
terms.gloss: The numbered sentences at the end of a patent that define exactly what the patent protects.

terms.label: independent claim
terms.gloss: A patent claim that stands on its own, defining the invention without referring to any other claim.

terms.label: dependent claim
terms.gloss: A patent claim that refers back to another claim and narrows it by adding further features.

terms.label: accused system
terms.gloss: The product a patent owner says infringes its patent.

terms.label: institutional competence
terms.gloss: Which decision-maker (judge, jury, agency, legislature) is better equipped by training and position to decide a particular kind of question.

terms.label: tacit admission
terms.gloss: Treating a party's silence in the face of an accusation it would naturally deny as an admission that the accusation is true.

terms.label: fee shifting
terms.gloss: Making the losing side pay the winner's attorney's fees, an exception to the American rule that each side pays its own.

terms.label: Advisory Committee
terms.gloss: The committee of judges, lawyers, and scholars that drafts federal procedure rules and writes official notes explaining them.

terms.label: Pavelic & LeFlore
terms.gloss: Pavelic & LeFlore v. Marvel Entertainment Group (1989), holding Rule 11 sanctions fall on the individual lawyer who signed, not the law firm.

terms.label: negligent manufacture
terms.gloss: A claim that a maker failed to use reasonable care in making a product, causing injury.

terms.label: pretrial order
terms.gloss: A court order, usually after a pretrial conference, listing the claims, defenses, and issues for trial; it controls the case from then on.

terms.label: Rule 16
terms.gloss: The federal rule governing pretrial conferences, scheduling orders, and pretrial orders.

terms.label: adverse inference
terms.gloss: An instruction letting jurors assume that evidence a party failed to produce, such as a witness it controlled, would have hurt that party.

terms.label: Graham v. John Deere
terms.gloss: Graham v. John Deere Co. (1966), the framework for judging obviousness: the prior art, differences from it, the ordinary skill in the field, and other evidence.

terms.label: invalidity
terms.gloss: A ruling that something has no legal force; for a patent, that it should never have been granted and cannot be enforced.

terms.label: licensee estoppel
terms.gloss: An old rule barring a patent licensee from challenging the validity of the patent it licensed; Lear v. Adkins (1969) abolished it.

terms.label: Lear
terms.gloss: Lear, Inc. v. Adkins (1969), which ended licensee estoppel so patent licensees may challenge the patents they pay for.

terms.label: Triplett v. Lowell
terms.gloss: Triplett v. Lowell (1936), which let a patent owner whose patent was held invalid keep suing other defendants; overruled in Blonder-Tongue.

terms.label: full and fair opportunity
terms.gloss: The requirement that a party have had a real, adequate chance to litigate an issue before being bound by its earlier loss on it.

terms.label: poaching
terms.gloss: Hiring away a competitor's employees; a 'no-poaching' rule or agreement forbids doing so.

terms.label: Wisconsin Statutes § 813.02
terms.gloss: The Wisconsin statute allowing courts to grant temporary injunctions or restraining orders while a lawsuit is pending.

terms.label: municipal court
terms.gloss: A lower trial court for smaller cases; California once had municipal courts, later merged into its superior courts.

terms.label: appellate department
terms.gloss: A panel of superior-court judges in California that hears appeals from limited civil cases, formerly those from municipal courts.

terms.label: offer
terms.gloss: A proposal that a reasonable person would understand as inviting acceptance to form a binding deal, judged by outward words and conduct rather than secret intent.

terms.label: Commercial Code § 2201
terms.gloss: California's version of UCC § 2-201, the statute of frauds requiring a signed writing for sales of goods of $500 or more.

terms.label: Restatement § 153
terms.gloss: The Restatement (Second) of Contracts rule letting a party undo a contract for its own basic, material mistake if it does not bear the risk and enforcement would be unconscionable.

terms.label: Restatement § 154
terms.gloss: The Restatement rule on when a party bears the risk of a mistake: by agreement, by knowingly acting on limited knowledge, or by a court's reasonable allocation.

terms.label: allocation of risk
terms.gloss: Whether the contract or circumstances put the danger of a particular mistake on one party, who then cannot escape the deal because of it.

terms.label: material adverse effect
terms.gloss: A significant harmful impact on the bargain for the mistaken party, a requirement for undoing a contract for mistake.

terms.label: Civil Code § 1577
terms.gloss: California's statutory definition of mistake of fact, which excludes mistakes caused by 'neglect of a legal duty.'

terms.label: Civil Code § 1692
terms.gloss: California's statute on relief after rescission, letting a court adjust the parties' positions to do complete justice.

terms.label: Vehicle Code § 11713.1(e)
terms.gloss: A California dealer-advertising provision; with related rules, it requires an advertised specific car to be identified by number and sold at the advertised price while available.

terms.label: Drennan
terms.gloss: Drennan v. Star Paving Co. (Cal. 1958), holding a subcontractor's bid could not be withdrawn after a contractor reasonably relied on it.

terms.label: Kemper and Elsinore
terms.gloss: Two California Supreme Court cases (1951 and 1960) letting contractors rescind bids containing honest clerical errors.

terms.label: accreditation
terms.gloss: Official approval by a recognized body, here the American Bar Association, that a school meets required standards; many states admit only graduates of accredited law schools to the bar.

terms.label: bar examination
terms.gloss: The licensing test a person must pass to be admitted to practise law in a state.

terms.label: demand letter
terms.gloss: A written demand for relief; under Chapter 93A it must be sent at least thirty days before suing.

terms.label: reassignment
terms.gloss: Transferring a case to a different judge.

terms.label: interests of justice
terms.gloss: A general standard asking what outcome is fair and serves the proper administration of justice.

terms.label: ward
terms.gloss: A person placed under a guardian's legal care and authority.

terms.label: cosign
terms.gloss: To sign a loan alongside the borrower, becoming responsible for paying it if the borrower does not.

terms.label: probate court
terms.gloss: The court that handles wills, estates, and guardianships.

terms.label: Unfair Trade Practices Act (Alaska)
terms.gloss: Alaska's consumer-protection law banning unfair or deceptive business practices, allowing triple damages and attorney's fees.

terms.label: unopposed
terms.gloss: Not contested by the other side, which filed no response.

terms.label: foreman (foreperson)
terms.gloss: The juror chosen to lead deliberations and speak for the jury.

terms.label: lucid interval
terms.gloss: A period of clear thinking by someone otherwise mentally incapacitated.

terms.label: refreshing recollection
terms.gloss: Showing a witness a document to jog the witness's memory; the witness then testifies from memory, and the document need not be evidence.

terms.label: Evidence Rule 612
terms.gloss: The evidence rule (Alaska's, like Federal Rule 612) on using writings to refresh a witness's memory, and the other side's right to inspect them.

terms.label: impecunious
terms.gloss: Having little or no money.

terms.label: remit
terms.gloss: To reduce a jury's damages award, as in remittitur.

terms.label: Food and Drug Administration
terms.gloss: The federal agency that regulates the safety and labeling of foods, drugs, and cosmetics.

terms.label: standard of identity
terms.gloss: An FDA rule defining what a food sold under a given name must contain, such as required ingredients and amounts.

terms.label: special dietary uses
terms.gloss: Uses of food to meet particular dietary needs, such as supplements or diet foods, which the FDA may require labels to explain.

terms.label: adulteration
terms.gloss: Making a food or drug impure, unsafe, or cheapened; 'economic adulteration' means cheapening it, as by dilution, to cheat buyers.

terms.label: over-the-counter
terms.gloss: Medicines sold without a prescription.

terms.label: APA §§ 556–557
terms.gloss: The APA sections setting trial-like procedures for formal hearings, including cross-examination needed for a 'full and true disclosure of the facts.'

terms.label: FDCA § 201(g)(1)(B)
terms.gloss: The FDCA definition of 'drug' covering articles intended to diagnose, cure, treat, or prevent disease, making intended use decisive.

terms.label: pharmacopoeia
terms.gloss: An official reference book listing drugs and their standards of strength and purity.

terms.label: Associate Justice
terms.gloss: A member of the Supreme Court other than the Chief Justice.

terms.label: Ineligibility Clause
terms.gloss: The constitutional clause barring a member of Congress from appointment to a federal office created, or whose pay was increased, during that member's term.

terms.label: vacancy
terms.gloss: An open office or seat that may lawfully be filled.

terms.label: direct injury
terms.gloss: A concrete harm to the challenger personally, already suffered or immediately threatened, required for standing to sue.

terms.label: member of the bar
terms.gloss: A lawyer admitted to practise before a particular court.

terms.label: at pleasure
terms.gloss: Serving at a superior's discretion, removable at any time without needing a reason.

terms.label: waiver of immunity
terms.gloss: A government's agreeing by law to be sued, giving up the immunity that would otherwise protect it.

terms.label: Monell
terms.gloss: Monell v. Department of Social Services (1978): local governments can be sued under § 1983 for their own policies or customs, but not merely for employing a wrongdoer.

terms.label: excessiveness review
terms.gloss: A judge's review of whether a jury's damages award is too large to stand.

terms.label: CPLR § 5501(c)
terms.gloss: New York's law requiring a new trial or reduced award when damages 'deviate materially' from reasonable compensation.

terms.label: deviates materially
terms.gloss: New York's test of whether a jury award strays significantly from awards in comparable cases, a closer check on awards than the old 'shocks the conscience' test.

terms.label: Hanna
terms.gloss: Hanna v. Plumer (1965): when a valid Federal Rule directly covers an issue, federal courts follow it even if state law differs.

terms.label: direct collision
terms.gloss: Hanna's test for whether a Federal Rule is broad enough to directly conflict with state law, so the Federal Rule controls.

terms.label: Westminster
terms.gloss: The historic seat of England's central common-law courts, whose practices guide interpretation of the Seventh Amendment.

terms.label: Unfair Competition Law
terms.gloss: California's broad statute banning any unlawful, unfair, or fraudulent business practice; each of the three is a separate 'branch' or 'prong.'

terms.label: local-controversy exception
terms.gloss: A CAFA exception requiring federal courts to send back class actions that are essentially local, with most class members and a key defendant from the state where filed.

terms.label: nondisclosure
terms.gloss: Failing to reveal information: in fraud, hiding a material fact; in litigation, failing to share required material with the other side.

terms.label: Swierkiewicz
terms.gloss: Swierkiewicz v. Sorema (2002): complaints need only Rule 8's simple notice pleading unless a rule such as Rule 9(b) demands more.

terms.label: Vess
terms.gloss: Vess v. Ciba-Geigy (9th Cir. 2003): Rule 9(b) applies to fraud-based allegations even when the claim's elements do not require fraud.

terms.label: Engalla
terms.gloss: Engalla v. Permanente Medical Group (Cal. 1997), a California Supreme Court case setting out the elements of fraud.

terms.label: extended warranty
terms.gloss: A service contract covering repairs beyond the original manufacturer's warranty period.

terms.label: single publication rule
terms.gloss: The rule treating a mass publication, like a magazine issue, as one wrong, so one lawsuit covers damages everywhere it circulated.

terms.label: criminal defamation
terms.gloss: A law making defamation a crime prosecuted by the state, not just a basis for a private lawsuit.

terms.label: holding company
terms.gloss: A company whose main business is owning stock in other companies.

terms.label: Federal Advisory Committee Act
terms.gloss: A 1972 law requiring committees that advise federal agencies or the President to have charters, open meetings, public records, and balanced membership.

terms.label: absurdity doctrine
terms.gloss: The rule that courts may depart from a statute's literal words if following them would produce an absurd result Congress could not have intended.

terms.label: Holy Trinity
terms.gloss: Church of the Holy Trinity v. United States (1892), reading a statute against its literal words to fit its 'spirit' and Congress's evident purpose.

terms.label: Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act
match: federal food, drug, and cosmetic act
terms.gloss: The main federal law regulating the safety, effectiveness, and labeling of foods, drugs, and cosmetics, enforced by the FDA.

terms.label: new drug
terms.gloss: Under the FDCA, a drug not generally recognized as safe and effective for its intended use, which needs FDA approval before sale.

terms.label: lethal injection
terms.gloss: Execution by injecting drugs that cause death.

terms.label: enforcement discretion
terms.gloss: A prosecutor's or agency's freedom to decide whether to take action against a violation; 'nonenforcement' is a decision not to.

terms.label: presumption against review
terms.gloss: Heckler's rule that an agency's decision not to enforce is presumed beyond court review unless the statute supplies standards for enforcement.

terms.label: Overton Park
terms.gloss: Citizens to Preserve Overton Park v. Volpe (1971): courts may review agency action where the statute supplies standards, such as limits on routing highways through parks.

terms.label: Dunlop v. Bachowski
terms.gloss: Dunlop v. Bachowski (1975), allowing review of the Labor Secretary's refusal to sue over a union election because the statute told him to sue upon finding probable cause.

terms.label: negative implication
terms.gloss: Reasoning that because a law says something about one case, the opposite applies to cases it leaves out.

terms.label: consent negotiations
terms.gloss: Settlement talks between an agency such as the FTC and a company, often before a formal complaint, aiming at an agreed order.

terms.label: Federal Credit Union Act
terms.gloss: The 1934 federal law authorizing and regulating federally chartered credit unions.

terms.label: credit union
terms.gloss: A member-owned, nonprofit financial cooperative that takes deposits from and lends to its members.

terms.label: common bond
terms.gloss: The shared tie, such as a common employer or association, that the law required among a federal credit union's members.

terms.label: competitive injury
terms.gloss: Harm from facing more or new competition, which can count as injury for standing.

terms.label: Air Courier
terms.gloss: Air Courier Conference v. Postal Workers (1991): postal unions fell outside the zone of interests of the postal monopoly statutes.

terms.label: Bennett
terms.gloss: Bennett v. Spear (1997), a Supreme Court case on the zone-of-interests test and who may sue under a statute.

terms.label: Surface Transportation Assistance Act
terms.gloss: A 1982 federal law whose § 405 protects truck drivers and other commercial-vehicle workers from being fired for reporting or refusing unsafe conditions.

terms.label: final order
terms.gloss: The last decision resolving a case, after which it can be appealed.
A since-repealed statute allowing direct Supreme Court appeals when a lower federal court held an Act of Congress unconstitutional.

terms.label: Arnett
terms.gloss: Arnett v. Kennedy (1974), upholding procedures for removing a federal employee where the full hearing came after removal.

terms.label: Aid to Families with Dependent Children
match: aid to families with dependent children
terms.gloss: A federal-state welfare program (1935–1996) giving cash aid to needy families with children.

terms.label: Home Relief
terms.gloss: New York's state and locally funded general welfare program for needy people outside federal programs.

terms.label: appointed counsel
terms.gloss: A lawyer provided by the government for someone who cannot afford one.

terms.label: impartial
terms.gloss: Unbiased; a decision-maker who has not prejudged the case.

terms.label: cost of service
terms.gloss: A utility's total costs of providing service, including a fair return, used to set its rates.

terms.label: discrimination or preference
terms.gloss: Utility-law bans on rates or terms that unjustly treat some customers better or worse than others.

terms.label: Florida East Coast Railway
terms.gloss: United States v. Florida East Coast Railway (1973): formal rulemaking is required only when a statute calls for rules made 'on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing.'

terms.label: area-rate regulation
terms.gloss: Setting one gas price for all producers in a region instead of a separate rate for each company, approved in the Permian Basin Area Rate Cases (1968).

terms.label: Interstate Commerce Commission
terms.gloss: A former federal agency (1887–1995) that regulated railroads, trucking, and other interstate carriers.

terms.label: Mcf
terms.gloss: Thousand cubic feet, a standard unit for measuring natural gas.

terms.label: probationary period
terms.gloss: A trial period of employment before a worker earns job protections such as tenure.

terms.label: adequate cause
terms.gloss: A legally sufficient reason, such as misconduct or incompetence, to dismiss a protected employee.

terms.label: insubordination
terms.gloss: Refusing to obey a superior's lawful instructions.

terms.label: mutually explicit understandings
terms.gloss: Clear understandings shared by employer and employee that can create a protected expectation of continued employment.

terms.label: intrastate
terms.gloss: Within a single state.

terms.label: employer contributions
terms.gloss: Payroll taxes employers pay into a state's unemployment-compensation fund.

terms.label: assessment (of tax)
terms.gloss: An official determination of the amount of tax owed.

terms.label: registered mail
terms.gloss: Mail tracked with proof of delivery, often used for legal notices.

terms.label: agent for service
terms.gloss: A person a company appoints to receive legal papers on its behalf.

terms.label: appeal tribunal
terms.gloss: An administrative body within a state agency that hears appeals, here on unemployment-tax assessments.

terms.label: corporate presence
terms.gloss: The older idea that a corporation could be sued only where it was 'present,' meaning doing business there.

terms.label: unsubstantial (appeal)
terms.gloss: Raising no substantial federal question, a ground on which the Supreme Court could dismiss an appeal without full review.

terms.label: cancellation (of contract)
terms.gloss: Ending a contract and undoing it, similar to rescission.

terms.label: failure to state a cause of action
match: failure to state a cause of action
terms.gloss: A ruling that even if all the complaint's allegations are true, they do not add up to a legal claim.

terms.label: District Court of Appeal
terms.gloss: Florida's intermediate appeals courts, between the trial courts and the Florida Supreme Court.

terms.label: fact-opinion distinction
terms.gloss: The traditional rule that only false statements of fact, not mere opinions, can support a fraud claim.

terms.label: superior knowledge
terms.gloss: Knowing much more about a subject than the other party, which can make even an opinion actionable as fraud.

terms.label: whole truth (half-truth rule)
terms.gloss: The rule that someone who chooses to speak on a subject must not give a misleadingly partial account, a 'half-truth.'

terms.label: redemption period
terms.gloss: The window after a tax or foreclosure sale during which the owner or a lender can still reclaim the property by paying what is owed plus costs.

terms.label: lienholder
terms.gloss: A creditor, such as a mortgage lender, that holds a lien: a legal claim on someone's property as security for a debt.

terms.label: security (for a debt)
terms.gloss: Property pledged to guarantee a debt, which the creditor can take and sell if the borrower does not pay.

terms.label: Mullane notice standard
terms.gloss: From Mullane v. Central Hanover Bank (1950): due process requires notice 'reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances,' to tell interested people about a proceeding and let them object.

terms.label: notice (due process)
terms.gloss: Formally telling a person that a legal proceeding or government action threatens their rights, so they can respond. Due process requires adequate notice before the government takes property or benefits.

terms.label: published notice
terms.gloss: Giving legal notice by printing it in a newspaper or posting it publicly, rather than delivering it to the person; often the least likely way to actually reach them.

terms.label: delinquent (taxes)
terms.gloss: Overdue: not paid by the legal deadline. A property 'certified delinquent' has unpaid taxes and can be sold to collect them.

terms.label: detainer notice
terms.gloss: Short for an unlawful-detainer notice: a written demand that an occupant leave property, the first step toward eviction.

terms.label: ex ante
terms.gloss: Latin for 'from before': judged from the viewpoint of the moment an action was taken, without using hindsight about how things turned out.

terms.label: contempt (of court)
terms.gloss: Disobeying or disrespecting a court's order. A court can fine or jail someone in contempt, here for not paying ordered child support.

terms.label: purge (contempt)
terms.gloss: To end a contempt sanction by doing what the court ordered, such as paying the overdue support, which earns release.

terms.label: custody (of a child)
terms.gloss: The legal right and duty to care for a child and make decisions about the child's upbringing and residence.

terms.label: custodial parent
terms.gloss: The parent or other person a child lives with, who usually receives child support from the other parent.

terms.label: right to counsel
terms.gloss: The right to have a lawyer's help. In criminal cases the Sixth Amendment guarantees a free lawyer if a defendant cannot afford one; civil cases usually have no such guarantee.

terms.label: collateral consequences
terms.gloss: Lasting legal effects of a judgment beyond the sentence itself, such as a record used against someone later; they can keep a case from becoming moot.

terms.label: probation revocation
terms.gloss: A proceeding to cancel someone's probation (supervised release instead of prison) for breaking its conditions, which can send them to prison.

terms.label: abatement (of a hazard)
terms.gloss: Fixing or removing a dangerous condition. An abatement order requires an employer to correct a workplace hazard by a deadline.

terms.label: citation (violation notice)
terms.gloss: A formal written charge from a government inspector that an employer violated a safety standard, usually with a proposed penalty and fix-by date.

terms.label: serious violation
terms.gloss: Under workplace-safety law, a violation creating a substantial chance of death or serious physical harm that the employer knew or should have known about.

terms.label: sovereign capacity
terms.gloss: Acting as the government enforcing public law, rather than as an ordinary party protecting its own private rights.

terms.label: adjunct (to a court)
terms.gloss: A helper body, such as an agency or magistrate, that finds facts for a real (Article III) court that keeps control of the final decision.

terms.label: pretrial proceedings
terms.gloss: Everything in a lawsuit before trial, such as motions, evidence exchange (discovery), and settlement talks.

terms.label: labor-law preemption
terms.gloss: The rule that federal labor law displaces state-law claims whose resolution requires interpreting a union contract; such disputes go to the contract's grievance process instead.

terms.label: term sheet
terms.gloss: A short document listing the main agreed points of a deal, which the parties later turn into a full agreement.

terms.label: uncapped (fund)
terms.gloss: With no total limit: an uncapped fund pays every qualifying claim however many there are; a capped one could run out.

terms.label: final approval
terms.gloss: The judge's ruling, after the fairness hearing, that a class settlement is fair, reasonable, and adequate, making it binding on the class.

terms.label: class (class action)
terms.gloss: The group of people with similar claims whose case is pursued together in one lawsuit by a few named representatives; all members are bound by the result.

terms.label: steering committee
terms.gloss: A group of plaintiffs' lawyers a court appoints to lead and coordinate many combined cases.

terms.label: Girsh factors
terms.gloss: The Third Circuit's nine-part checklist, from Girsh v. Jepson (1975), for judging whether a class settlement is fair, reasonable, and adequate.

terms.label: Prudential considerations
terms.gloss: Extra settlement-fairness factors from In re Prudential Insurance (3d Cir. 1998), used alongside the Girsh factors.

terms.label: Daubert challenge
terms.gloss: A request that a judge exclude expert testimony as scientifically unreliable, under the standard of Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals (1993).

terms.label: clear-sailing agreement
terms.gloss: A defendant's promise not to oppose class lawyers' fee request up to an agreed amount; courts scrutinize it for collusion.

terms.label: class counsel
terms.gloss: The lawyers appointed to represent a whole class (or subclass), who owe duties to all its members, not just named clients.

terms.label: medical monitoring
terms.gloss: A claim seeking payment for future medical testing for people exposed to a health risk who are not yet sick.

terms.label: general and individual causation
terms.gloss: General causation asks whether an exposure can cause a disease at all; individual causation asks whether it caused this particular person's illness.

terms.label: territorial exclusivity
terms.gloss: A contract right to be the only seller of a product within a defined area, protected against competing sellers there.

terms.label: transshipment
terms.gloss: In this case, selling product supplied for one bottler's area inside another bottler's exclusive territory.

terms.label: interference (tort)
terms.gloss: Short for tortious interference: wrongfully and intentionally disrupting someone's business relationships or contracts with others.

terms.label: encroachment
terms.gloss: Here, other bottlers' sales intruding into Pittsburg Pepsi's exclusive sales territory.

terms.label: probable (business) advantage
terms.gloss: An element of the interference tort: a business relationship or expectancy likely to bring future economic benefit, which the defendant disrupted.

terms.label: innocent misrepresentation
terms.gloss: A false statement of fact made honestly, without knowing it was false. It can still justify undoing (rescinding) a contract it induced.

terms.label: UCC § 2-206(1)(b)
terms.gloss: The UCC rule that an order asking for prompt shipment can be accepted by shipping; shipping non-matching goods is acceptance plus breach, unless the seller says it is only an accommodation.

terms.label: UCC § 2-302
terms.gloss: The UCC section letting a court refuse to enforce a contract, or a clause, that was unconscionable when made.

terms.label: charged with knowledge
terms.gloss: Treated by law as knowing something, such as a document one signed, whether or not one actually read or remembered it.

terms.label: summary reversal
terms.gloss: An appeals court quickly overturning a lower-court ruling without full briefing or argument, because the error is clear.

terms.label: Munsingwear vacatur
terms.gloss: From United States v. Munsingwear (1950): when a case becomes moot during appeal, the appeals court normally wipes out the lower judgment so it binds no one.

terms.label: certified copy
terms.gloss: A copy of a document officially confirmed as accurate by the office that holds the original, such as a court clerk.

terms.label: contacts (with a state)
terms.gloss: A defendant's connections with a state, such as business, sales, or presence there, that can support a court's power over it.

terms.label: purposeful (forum activity)
terms.gloss: Deliberate: a defendant who purposefully seeks a state's benefits or markets can fairly be sued there; random or one-sided contacts do not count.

terms.label: fair and reasonable (jurisdiction)
terms.gloss: The due process requirement that making a defendant defend in a state be fair, considering its burden and its connection to the state.

terms.label: Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws
terms.gloss: The American Law Institute's influential summary of rules on choosing which law applies and on court jurisdiction across states and countries.

terms.label: reciprocal-support statutes
terms.gloss: Uniform state laws letting a parent file for child support at home and have the case forwarded to a court in the other parent's state for decision and collection.

terms.label: marital domicile
terms.gloss: The home state where a married couple lived together.

terms.label: adjudicative power
terms.gloss: A court's power to decide a case binding the parties, which is a separate question from which state's law applies.

terms.label: Federal Farm Loan Act
terms.gloss: A 1916 law creating federally chartered land banks to make long-term mortgage loans to farmers, with tax-exempt bonds.

terms.label: Federal Land Banks
terms.gloss: Twelve regional banks created by the Federal Farm Loan Act, lending to farmers through cooperative borrower associations.

terms.label: Joint Stock Land Banks
terms.gloss: Privately capitalized farm-mortgage banks authorized by the Federal Farm Loan Act, operating for profit under federal supervision.

terms.label: depositary
terms.gloss: A bank designated to hold government money on deposit.

terms.label: fiscal agent
terms.gloss: A bank or body that handles financial business for the government, such as holding funds or making payments.

terms.label: Judicial Code § 24
terms.gloss: The provision of the 1911 Judicial Code then listing federal trial courts' jurisdiction, including cases arising under federal law; its successors are mainly 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331-1332.

terms.label: supremacy (federal)
terms.gloss: The Constitution's rule that valid federal law overrides conflicting state law.

terms.label: American Well Works (creation test)
terms.gloss: Holmes's 1916 test: a suit 'arises under' the law that creates the cause of action, so a state-law claim is not federal just because it raises a federal question.

terms.label: substantial federal issue
terms.gloss: Smith's test: a state-law case arises under federal law if the plaintiff's own claim necessarily turns on a real, disputed federal question.

terms.label: right of way
terms.gloss: In traffic law, the legal right of one driver to go first, which others must yield.

terms.label: opening statement
terms.gloss: A lawyer's speech at the start of trial previewing what the evidence will show; it is not itself evidence.

terms.label: discharge of the jury
terms.gloss: Ending the trial with the current jurors (a mistrial) because something unfairly prejudicial happened in front of them.

terms.label: pleaded / unpleaded
terms.gloss: Stated (or not) in the formal court papers setting out a party's claims. Evidence of an unpleaded claim may be excluded.

terms.label: aggravation (of an injury)
terms.gloss: Worsening of a condition the person already had; an accident that aggravates it can make the defendant liable for the added harm.

terms.label: invited error
terms.gloss: An error a party itself caused or welcomed at trial, which it generally cannot later complain about on appeal.

terms.label: Rule 9(g)
terms.gloss: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 9(g): items of special damage (losses not naturally flowing from the injury) must be specifically stated in the complaint.

terms.label: Form 10
terms.gloss: One of the sample complaints once appended to the Federal Rules (a short negligence complaint), showing how brief a valid complaint could be.

terms.label: Rule 54
terms.gloss: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 54, on judgments and costs, which also sets the procedure for motions seeking attorney's fees.

terms.label: in-point (decision)
terms.gloss: A precedent addressing the same legal question on similar facts, so it directly governs.

terms.label: administrative claim
terms.gloss: A written claim filed with a government agency before suing it; the FTCA requires one, and a suit may follow only after denial (or six months without a decision).

terms.label: sue and be sued
terms.gloss: Statutory language letting a government body sue, and be sued, like a business, which generally waives its immunity.

terms.label: negligent transmission (of mail)
terms.gloss: Terms in the postal exception. Miscarriage means mail going astray; negligent transmission, the Court held, means carelessness causing mail to be lost, late, damaged, or misdelivered.

terms.label: waiver of sovereign immunity
terms.gloss: A statute in which the government consents to be sued for certain claims; exceptions in it mark where immunity remains.

terms.label: immunity canon
terms.gloss: The interpretive rule that ambiguous waivers of the government's immunity are read in the government's favor.

terms.label: associated-words canon
terms.gloss: Noscitur a sociis: a word in a list is read in light of the words around it, so a broad term takes on its neighbors' narrower sense.

terms.label: customs exception
terms.gloss: The FTCA exception keeping the United States immune from claims arising from customs officers' detention of goods.

terms.label: arising out of
terms.gloss: Broad statutory phrase covering any claim that stems from or is connected to the listed events.

terms.label: slip-and-fall claim
terms.gloss: An injury claim based on tripping or slipping over a hazard on someone's property.

terms.label: Comptroller of the Currency
terms.gloss: The Treasury official who charters and supervises national banks and rules on what they may do.

terms.label: national bank
terms.gloss: A bank chartered by the federal government under the National Bank Act and supervised by the Comptroller of the Currency.

terms.label: incidental powers
terms.gloss: Powers not expressly listed in a statute but reasonably needed to carry on the business it authorizes, here banking.

terms.label: National Bank Act
terms.gloss: The 1864 federal law creating federally chartered banks and listing their powers.

terms.label: Bank Service Corporation Act
terms.gloss: A 1962 federal law letting banks jointly own service companies, but limiting those companies to providing bank services to banks.

terms.label: bank service corporation
terms.gloss: A company owned by banks to do clerical and data work for them, limited by the 1962 Act to services for banks.

terms.label: legal wrong
terms.gloss: An APA § 702 phrase: invasion of a legally protected right, one basis for seeking court review of agency action.

terms.label: personal stake
terms.gloss: A real, concrete interest in a case's outcome, required for standing so courts hear genuine disputes.

terms.label: Interstate Commerce Act
terms.gloss: The 1887 federal law regulating railroads and creating the Interstate Commerce Commission.

terms.label: "after hearing"
terms.gloss: Statutory phrase requiring some opportunity to be heard; the Court held it does not by itself trigger the APA's formal, trial-type procedures.

terms.label: verified
terms.gloss: Sworn to be true, in writing, so false statements can be punished like false testimony.

terms.label: talismanic
terms.gloss: Magic-word-like. 'No talismanic formula' means Congress need not use exact words to require something.

terms.label: legislative facts
terms.gloss: General facts about the world used to make policy for many people, as opposed to adjudicative facts about particular parties.

terms.label: prospective
terms.gloss: Applying only to the future, not to past events.

terms.label: Bi-Metallic
terms.gloss: Bi-Metallic Investment Co. v. State Board (1915): no individual hearing is required for a general policy applied to many people, unlike Londoner's few individually affected owners.

terms.label: deferential review
terms.gloss: Court review that gives the decision-maker substantial leeway and overturns only clear or unreasonable errors.

terms.label: Postmaster General
terms.gloss: The official who heads the federal postal system; then a Cabinet-level executive officer.

terms.label: Solicitor of the Treasury
terms.gloss: A Treasury Department legal officer who handled government claims and lawsuits.

terms.label: political duties
terms.gloss: Discretionary duties an officer performs for the President, which courts will not control, unlike ministerial duties fixed by law.

terms.label: auxiliary writ
terms.gloss: A writ a court issues to help it use jurisdiction it already has, not to start a new case (today's All Writs Act).

terms.label: assessment (tax)
terms.gloss: An official determination of how much tax or charge each property owes.

terms.label: abutting
terms.gloss: Directly bordering, as land along a street.

terms.label: pleading stage
terms.gloss: The start of a lawsuit, when the court looks only at the complaint's allegations, assuming them true, before any evidence.

terms.label: bitter with the sweet
terms.gloss: Arnett plurality's theory: someone who accepts a government job created by statute must also accept the statute's limited firing procedures. Loudermill rejected it.

terms.label: pleading standard
terms.gloss: The rule for how much detail a complaint must allege to proceed; it was more lenient in 1985 than today.

terms.label: reputational-liberty claim
terms.gloss: A due process claim that government publicly damaged one's reputation in connection with firing, harming the liberty to find other work.

terms.label: Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act
match: personal responsibility and work opportunity reconciliation act
terms.gloss: The 1996 federal welfare reform law that replaced AFDC with TANF block grants, adding work requirements and time limits.

terms.label: Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF)
terms.gloss: The welfare program created in 1996: federal block grants that states use for time-limited cash aid with work requirements.

terms.label: block grants
terms.gloss: Lump sums of federal money given to states for a broad purpose, leaving states much choice in how to spend them.

terms.label: adverse-action notice
terms.gloss: Written notice that an agency is reducing, ending, or denying a benefit, with reasons and how to appeal.

terms.label: bad-conduct discharge
terms.gloss: A punitive release from military service, less severe than a dishonorable discharge, that can cost veterans' benefits.

terms.label: dishonorable discharge
terms.gloss: The most severe punitive release from military service, for serious offenses, stripping benefits.

terms.label: forfeiture of pay
terms.gloss: A military punishment taking away part or all of a service member's pay.

terms.label: convening authority
terms.gloss: The commander who orders a court-martial, picks its members, and can reduce its sentence.

terms.label: Court of Military Review
terms.gloss: The intermediate military appeals court for each service (now Courts of Criminal Appeals), staffed mainly by officers.

terms.label: Court of Military Appeals
terms.gloss: The top military appeals court, with civilian judges serving fixed terms (now the Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces).

terms.label: commissioned officer
terms.gloss: A military officer appointed by the President, with Senate consent, under a formal commission.

terms.label: detailed (assigned)
terms.gloss: Assigned temporarily to a particular post or duty.

terms.label: nonjudicial punishment
terms.gloss: Minor military discipline a commander imposes without a court-martial.

terms.label: judge-alone trial
terms.gloss: A trial decided by a judge without a jury or panel of members.

terms.label: aggrandizement
terms.gloss: One branch of government seizing power belonging to another.

terms.label: Price Administrator
terms.gloss: The federal official who set wartime maximum prices under the 1942 Emergency Price Control Act.

terms.label: protest (formal objection)
terms.gloss: A formal written objection to an official action. Under the 1942 price law, filing one with the Price Administrator was the required first step to challenge a price rule.

terms.label: officially noticed
terms.gloss: Facts an agency takes into account without formal proof, like a court's judicial notice.

terms.label: free exercise
terms.gloss: The First Amendment's protection of the right to practice one's religion.

terms.label: discretionary-ministerial distinction
terms.gloss: Officials are often immune for discretionary (judgment) acts but not for ministerial acts, duties the law spells out exactly.

terms.label: governmental vs. proprietary
terms.gloss: An old immunity distinction between core government functions (immune) and business-like activities (often not).

terms.label: declaration (pleading)
terms.gloss: In older common-law procedure, the plaintiff's first written statement of the claim, like today's complaint.

terms.label: duty to speak
terms.gloss: A legal obligation to disclose a fact, arising from things like a special relationship or one's own misleading statements.

terms.label: Court of General Sessions
terms.gloss: The District of Columbia's former local trial court for smaller civil and criminal cases.

terms.label: meaningful choice
terms.gloss: A real ability to bargain or go elsewhere; its absence is the 'procedural' half of unconscionability.

terms.label: loan-shark laws
terms.gloss: Laws capping interest rates and banning abusive lending (usury laws).

terms.label: substantive one-sidedness
terms.gloss: Terms unreasonably favorable to one side, the 'substantive' half of unconscionability.

terms.label: Parental Kidnaping Prevention Act
terms.gloss: A 1980 federal law (28 U.S.C. § 1738A) requiring each state to enforce qualifying custody orders from other states and limiting when another state may change them.

terms.label: rule of decision
terms.gloss: The legal rule a court applies to decide a case; here, a duty binding state courts rather than a basis for a separate federal lawsuit.

terms.label: continuing jurisdiction
terms.gloss: A court's ongoing power to revisit and modify its own order (such as a custody order) after it is entered.

terms.label: implied remedy
terms.gloss: A right to sue that a court reads into a statute even though the statute does not expressly create one; the question is whether Congress meant to allow it.

terms.label: prospective rule
terms.gloss: A rule that applies only to future cases or conduct, not to things that already happened.

terms.label: inducement of breach of contract
terms.gloss: A tort: intentionally persuading someone to break a contract with another person, who can then sue the persuader.

terms.label: business torts
terms.gloss: Civil wrongs that harm a company's commercial interests, such as interfering with contracts or unfair competition.

terms.label: Conformity Act
terms.gloss: An 1872 federal statute, later replaced by the Federal Rules, that told federal courts in non-equity cases to follow, as nearly as possible, the procedure of the state where they sat.

terms.label: Erie policies
terms.gloss: The 'twin aims' of Erie v. Tompkins: discouraging forum shopping and avoiding unequal treatment of state-law claims depending on whether they land in state or federal court.

terms.label: superseded
terms.gloss: Replaced by something newer; a superseded statute or agreement no longer governs because a later one has taken its place.

terms.label: International Chamber of Commerce
terms.gloss: A Paris-based business organization whose court of arbitration supplies widely used rules and administration for international arbitrations.

terms.label: void
terms.gloss: Of no legal effect at all, as if it never existed; a void judgment (for example, from defective service) can be attacked at any time, unlike one that is merely wrong.

terms.label: dwelling or usual place of abode
terms.gloss: Under the federal service rule, the home where a person actually lives; papers may be left there with a suitable resident instead of handing them to the defendant.

terms.label: failure to prosecute
terms.gloss: A plaintiff's failure to move its own case forward with reasonable speed; a court may dismiss the case for it.

terms.label: Rule 83
terms.gloss: The federal civil rule letting individual courts adopt local rules and regulate practice where the national rules are silent.

terms.label: adversary hearing
terms.gloss: A hearing at which both sides can appear and argue before the court decides.

terms.label: closed-end investment company
terms.gloss: A fund that raises money by selling a fixed number of shares and invests it; investors trade those shares rather than redeeming them from the fund.

terms.label: jury demand
terms.gloss: A party's formal request for a jury trial; without a timely demand, the right to a jury is waived in federal court.

terms.label: legal issues (law vs. equity)
terms.gloss: Issues of the kind historically tried in courts of law, such as claims for money damages; under the Seventh Amendment these carry a right to a jury.

terms.label: Beacon Theatres and Dairy Queen
terms.gloss: Supreme Court cases (1959, 1962) holding that when legal and equitable claims are joined, the jury must decide the common legal issues first, so equity cannot swallow the jury right.

terms.label: demand on the board (or excuse)
terms.gloss: Before a shareholder may sue on the company's behalf, she must ask the directors to sue, or show why asking would be pointless.

terms.label: consensual encounter
terms.gloss: A police contact a reasonable person would feel free to end or ignore; it is not a seizure and needs no suspicion.

terms.label: conversion to summary judgment
terms.gloss: If a court considers evidence beyond the complaint when ruling on a motion to dismiss, it must treat the motion as one for summary judgment (Rule 12(d)).

terms.label: immunity from suit vs. from liability
terms.gloss: Immunity from suit protects against having to go through litigation at all, so it can be appealed immediately; a defense to liability only defeats the claim at the end.

terms.label: Air Transportation Safety and System Stabilization Act
match: air transportation safety and system stabilization act
terms.gloss: A 2001 federal law passed after September 11 that created a victim compensation fund and sent 9/11-related lawsuits to one federal court.

terms.label: exclusive federal cause of action
terms.gloss: A right to sue that exists only under federal law and must be brought in a designated federal court.

terms.label: State Defense Emergency Act and Disaster Act
terms.gloss: New York statutes protecting people who carry out emergency and disaster response from liability for ordinary negligence.

terms.label: governmental-function defense
terms.gloss: A defense shielding public bodies from liability for discretionary acts that only government performs, as opposed to ordinary proprietary activities.

terms.label: Stafford Act
terms.gloss: The federal disaster-relief statute (42 U.S.C. § 5121 et seq.); § 305 bars claims based on the federal government's discretionary disaster-assistance decisions.

terms.label: discretionary function
terms.gloss: A government decision involving real judgment or policy choice, as opposed to following a mandatory rule; such decisions are commonly shielded from suit.

terms.label: derivative immunity
terms.gloss: Protection a private contractor may borrow from the government when it was carrying out the government's own protected decision.

terms.label: Boyle (government contractor defense)
terms.gloss: Boyle v. United Technologies (1988): a contractor can escape state-law liability if the government approved reasonably precise specifications, the work followed them, and it warned the government of dangers the government did not know.

terms.label: agreement in principle
terms.gloss: An announcement that parties agree on main terms; whether it is already a binding contract or just a step toward one depends on their intent.

terms.label: definitive merger agreement
terms.gloss: The final, detailed signed contract combining two companies, usually following preliminary agreements.

terms.label: knowing interference with contract
terms.gloss: The tort of intentionally inducing a breach of a contract the defendant knows exists, making the defendant liable to the injured party.

terms.label: objective intent
terms.gloss: Contract formation turns on what the parties' words and conduct would reasonably signal, not on secret private intentions.

terms.label: express reservation
terms.gloss: A clear statement that a party does not mean to be bound until a condition (such as signing a formal document) is met, or that it keeps a particular right.

terms.label: nonterminable
terms.gloss: A contract that cannot be ended at will by one party; interference with such a contract is not excused as fair competition.

terms.label: broad-form submission
terms.gloss: In Texas, how the judge puts questions to the jury; a broad-form submission asks a few general questions instead of many narrow ones.

terms.label: Revlon duties
terms.gloss: Revlon v. MacAndrews & Forbes (Del. 1986): once a company is for sale, its directors must seek the best price for shareholders.

terms.label: harmful error
terms.gloss: A trial mistake serious enough that it probably affected the result, so an appeals court will correct it; the opposite of harmless error.

terms.label: cumulative evidence
terms.gloss: Evidence that merely repeats what other admitted evidence already shows, so its admission or exclusion usually makes no difference.

terms.label: juror misconduct
terms.gloss: Improper behavior by a juror, such as outside contact or concealing bias, that can justify setting a verdict aside.

terms.label: pecuniary interest
terms.gloss: A financial stake in the outcome; a judge with one should not hear the case.

terms.label: consequential loss
terms.gloss: Indirect harm flowing from the wrong, such as lost opportunities, beyond the direct value lost.

terms.label: replacement cost
terms.gloss: What it would cost to obtain an equivalent substitute; here, the cost of finding oil reserves to replace those Pennzoil lost.

terms.label: reform and affirm
terms.gloss: An appellate court's modifying a judgment (for example, reducing damages) and then upholding it as modified.

terms.label: subsequent history
terms.gloss: What happened in a case after the decision being studied, such as later appeals, bankruptcy or settlement.

terms.label: lease bonus
terms.gloss: The up-front payment a company makes to win a mineral lease, separate from rent and royalties.

terms.label: Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act
terms.gloss: The federal law governing leasing and drilling for oil and gas on the seabed beyond state waters.

terms.label: Coastal Zone Management Act
terms.gloss: A federal law letting coastal states object to federal activities, such as offshore drilling plans, that are inconsistent with their approved coastal programs.

terms.label: consistency certification
terms.gloss: A company's statement that its plan fits the state's coastal-management program; the state may object, and the Secretary of Commerce may override.

terms.label: Outer Banks Protection Act
terms.gloss: A 1990 federal law that temporarily barred approval of drilling plans off North Carolina pending further environmental review.

terms.label: total breach
terms.gloss: A breach so serious that it substantially defeats the contract's purpose, letting the other side stop performing and seek full remedies such as restitution.

terms.label: sovereign acts doctrine
terms.gloss: A defense that the government is not liable for breaching a contract when it acts in its general public capacity, rather than targeting the contract.

terms.label: § 13(b)
terms.gloss: The FTC Act provision letting the FTC seek injunctions in federal court; courts long read it to allow refunds too, until the Supreme Court rejected that in 2021.

terms.label: infomercial
terms.gloss: A long television advertisement styled like a program.

terms.label: substantiation
terms.gloss: Under FTC law, the evidence an advertiser must have before making a claim; health claims need competent and reliable scientific proof.

terms.label: placebo
terms.gloss: A fake treatment used for comparison in a study; improvement from belief alone is the 'placebo effect'.

terms.label: randomized double-blind study
terms.gloss: A study where subjects are randomly assigned and neither they nor the researchers know who gets the real treatment, so belief cannot skew the results.

terms.label: statistically significant
terms.gloss: A difference between groups large enough that it is unlikely to be due to chance alone.

terms.label: asset freeze
terms.gloss: A court order stopping a defendant from moving or spending money so it stays available to pay any eventual judgment.

terms.label: deception (FTC)
terms.gloss: Misleading conduct: under the FTC Act, a material representation, omission or practice likely to mislead reasonable consumers.

terms.label: overall impression
terms.gloss: The FTC judges an ad by the total message it conveys to consumers, not by isolated fine print.

terms.label: express and implied claims
terms.gloss: An express claim says something directly; an implied claim conveys it indirectly. Obvious claims can be judged without consumer surveys.

terms.label: establishment claim
terms.gloss: An ad claim that scientific tests prove a product works; the advertiser must have the specific proof it claims. A plain efficacy claim just says it works.

terms.label: competent and reliable scientific evidence
terms.gloss: The FTC standard for health claims: tests done by qualified people using methods accepted in the field.

terms.label: privy
terms.gloss: Someone so closely connected to a party (for example, a successor or controller) that a judgment binds them too.

terms.label: individual liability
terms.gloss: Holding a company officer personally responsible for the company's violations, here requiring participation or control plus knowledge.

terms.label: trial by consent before a magistrate
terms.gloss: When all parties agree, a magistrate judge may try the case and enter judgment instead of a district judge.

terms.label: adoption
terms.gloss: A legal process making someone a child's parent with all parental rights and duties.

terms.label: holding oneself out
terms.gloss: Presenting oneself publicly as having a status (here, as a child's father), which others may rely on.

terms.label: O.C.G.A. § 13-3-44
terms.gloss: Georgia's statute adopting promissory estoppel: a promise that reasonably induces reliance is enforceable if needed to avoid injustice.

terms.label: stipulated judgment
terms.gloss: A judgment whose terms (here, an alternative amount) the parties agreed to in advance.

terms.label: set aside the verdict
terms.gloss: To cancel the jury's decision so that it no longer has effect.

terms.label: bump stock
terms.gloss: A rifle stock attachment that harnesses recoil so the trigger repeatedly bumps against the shooter's stationary finger, letting a semiautomatic rifle fire very rapidly.

terms.label: semiautomatic
terms.gloss: A firearm that fires one round per trigger pull and reloads itself; an automatic weapon (machine gun) keeps firing while the trigger is held.

terms.label: machine gun
terms.gloss: Under federal law, a weapon that fires more than one shot automatically by a single function of the trigger; civilians generally cannot possess new ones.

terms.label: Firearm Owners Protection Act
terms.gloss: A 1986 federal law that, among other things, banned civilian possession of machine guns made after that year.

terms.label: Federal Vacancies Reform Act
terms.gloss: The 1998 law letting the President name temporary acting officials to fill Senate-confirmed posts, with eligibility and time limits.

terms.label: Rule 25(d)
terms.gloss: The federal civil rule automatically substituting a new officeholder as party when a sued official leaves office.

terms.label: likelihood of success
terms.gloss: For a preliminary injunction, the challenger must show it will probably win on the merits.

terms.label: oral (trial-type) hearing
terms.gloss: Formal, trial-like agency procedure with live testimony; required only when a statute clearly demands it, otherwise written comments suffice.

terms.label: Little Tucker Act
terms.gloss: The companion law letting federal district courts hear smaller (up to $10,000) money claims against the United States.

terms.label: United States v. Eaton
terms.gloss: An 1898 case holding that a subordinate temporarily performing a superior's duties does not thereby become a principal officer needing Senate confirmation.

terms.label: civil investigative demand
terms.gloss: An agency's order, like a subpoena, requiring a company to hand over documents or answer questions in an investigation.

terms.label: for-cause removal (inefficiency, neglect, malfeasance)
terms.gloss: Removal protection allowing the President to fire an official only for specific misconduct like inefficiency, neglect of duty or wrongdoing in office, not for policy disagreement.

terms.label: Myers and Free Enterprise Fund
terms.gloss: Myers v. United States (1926) recognized broad presidential removal power; Free Enterprise Fund (2010) struck down two layers of removal protection.

terms.label: prudential concerns
terms.gloss: Court-made, discretionary reasons for declining to decide a case (as opposed to strict constitutional limits), such as lack of a real adversary.

terms.label: staggered terms / partisan balance
terms.gloss: Features of independent commissions: members' terms end at different times and no more than a set number can belong to one party.

terms.label: Financial Stability Oversight Council
terms.gloss: A body of federal financial regulators created by Dodd-Frank that can veto CFPB rules threatening the financial system.

terms.label: Tenure of Office Act
terms.gloss: An 1867 law requiring Senate consent to remove cabinet officers, later viewed as unconstitutional.

terms.label: term of court
terms.gloss: A fixed period during which a court sits to hear cases.

terms.label: legal separation
terms.gloss: A court decree letting spouses live apart with set rights and duties while remaining legally married.

terms.label: cruelty
terms.gloss: A traditional ground for separation or divorce: treatment by a spouse that endangers health or makes living together unsafe.

terms.label: absolute divorce
terms.gloss: A full divorce ending the marriage, as opposed to a separation.

terms.label: New York Supreme Court
terms.gloss: Despite its name, New York's general trial court; its highest court is the Court of Appeals.

terms.label: general original jurisdiction
terms.gloss: A trial court's power to hear virtually every kind of case in the first instance.

terms.label: matrimonial
terms.gloss: Relating to marriage, such as divorce or separation actions.

terms.label: Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp.
terms.gloss: A 2006 Supreme Court case holding that Title VII's 15-employee threshold is an element of the claim, not a limit on the court's jurisdiction.

terms.label: land patent
terms.gloss: A government document transferring public land to a private owner; for mines, it gives full title to a mining claim.

terms.label: Revised Statutes
terms.gloss: The 1870s official compilation of federal statutes, a predecessor of today's U.S. Code.

terms.label: adverse suit
terms.gloss: A lawsuit by a rival mining claimant, brought while a patent application is pending, to decide who has the better right of possession.

terms.label: Land Department
terms.gloss: The historical federal office (in the Interior Department) that handled sales and patents of public land.

terms.label: court of competent jurisdiction
terms.gloss: Any court that has the legal power to hear the type of case; the phrase points to existing rules rather than creating new federal jurisdiction.

terms.label: federal ingredient
terms.gloss: From Osborn v. Bank of the United States: a case may arise under federal law when federal law forms an original part of it; Shoshone refused to read the jurisdictional statute that broadly.

terms.label: Osborn v. Bank of the United States
terms.gloss: An 1824 case reading the Constitution's 'arising under' clause to cover any case with a federal ingredient.

terms.label: local mining customs
terms.gloss: Rules adopted by miners in a district about locating and keeping claims, which federal law recognized.

terms.label: lifetime employment
terms.gloss: A promise of a job for life; courts often demand clear proof and real consideration before enforcing one.

terms.label: forbearance from a claim as consideration
terms.gloss: Giving up a legal claim can be consideration for a promise if the claim was genuinely doubtful or honestly believed in.

terms.label: nuisance claim (settlement)
terms.gloss: A weak claim made mainly to extract a settlement because defending it costs more than paying; not the property-law tort of nuisance.

terms.label: personal-services agreement
terms.gloss: A contract under which a performer agrees to work exclusively for a company, such as a record label.

terms.label: advance
terms.gloss: An up-front payment to an artist, normally recouped from royalties later earned.

terms.label: synchronization license
terms.gloss: Permission to pair a recording with moving images, such as in a film or TV show.

terms.label: unexecuted
terms.gloss: Not signed; to 'execute' a document is to sign it to make it legally effective.

terms.label: four corners rule
terms.gloss: Interpreting a written document from its text alone, without outside evidence, when it is clear on its face.

terms.label: Pacific Gas & Electric
terms.gloss: A 1968 California case allowing evidence outside the document to show a meaning the contract language can reasonably bear.

terms.label: remitted
terms.gloss: Sent back to a lower court for further action.

terms.label: Higher Education Act
terms.gloss: The 1965 federal law creating federal student-aid and loan programs; its Title IV covers student loans.

terms.label: HEROES Act
terms.gloss: A 2003 law letting the Secretary of Education waive or modify student-aid rules during war or national emergency so borrowers are not left worse off.

terms.label: Title IV
terms.gloss: The part of the Higher Education Act governing federal student aid, including student loans.

terms.label: Pell Grant
terms.gloss: A federal need-based grant for low-income college students.

terms.label: adjusted gross income
terms.gloss: A tax-law measure of income after certain deductions, used here to set eligibility.

terms.label: expedited review
terms.gloss: Fast-tracked consideration on a shortened schedule.

terms.label: loan servicing
terms.gloss: Handling borrowers' accounts and collecting payments for the loan's owner, for a fee.

terms.label: MCI (meaning of "modify")
terms.gloss: MCI v. AT&T (1994): the power to 'modify' allows only moderate changes, not fundamental transformation.

terms.label: King v. Burwell
terms.gloss: A 2015 case on Affordable Care Act subsidies, cited for treating questions of vast economic importance as ones Congress usually decides itself.

terms.label: West Virginia v. EPA
terms.gloss: The 2022 case formally naming the major questions doctrine, where Justice Gorsuch tied it to Article I nondelegation concerns.

terms.label: in lieu of
terms.gloss: Instead of; in place of.

terms.label: neutral (in war)
terms.gloss: A country or its citizens not taking part in a war; their ships and trade are normally protected from seizure by the belligerents.

terms.label: belligerent
terms.gloss: A nation engaged in war, which under the law of nations may stop and search ships.

terms.label: protest (maritime)
terms.gloss: A ship master's sworn statement explaining events at sea, such as why the ship went to a port.

terms.label: assessors
terms.gloss: People appointed by a court to calculate the amount of damages.

terms.label: remisier
terms.gloss: In Singapore and Malaysia, a self-employed stockbroker's agent who brings in clients and earns a share of commissions.

terms.label: listed company
terms.gloss: A company whose shares trade on a stock exchange.

terms.label: placement shares / IPO
terms.gloss: In an initial public offering, a company sells new shares; 'placement' shares are allocated directly to selected investors.

terms.label: entire agreement clause
terms.gloss: A contract term stating that the written document is the parties' whole agreement, aimed at excluding outside promises.

terms.label: High Court (Singapore)
terms.gloss: Singapore's main trial-level court for major civil cases; appeals go to the Court of Appeal.

terms.label: bifurcation
terms.gloss: Splitting a trial into separate stages, such as deciding liability first and the amount of damages (quantum) later.

terms.label: quantum
terms.gloss: The amount of damages, as opposed to liability.

terms.label: custom
terms.gloss: A practice so well established in a trade that the parties are taken to have agreed to it.

terms.label: term implied in law
terms.gloss: A term the law reads into every contract of a given type for policy reasons, regardless of the particular parties' intent.

terms.label: officious bystander test
terms.gloss: An English-law test: a term is implied if, had a bystander suggested it, both parties would have said 'of course'.

terms.label: Unfair Contract Terms Act
terms.gloss: A UK-derived statute, also in force in Singapore, limiting clauses that exclude or restrict liability.

terms.label: exclusion clause
terms.gloss: A contract term excluding or limiting one party's liability.

terms.label: Luxor v. Cooper
terms.gloss: A 1941 English case holding that an estate agent's commission depends on the contract's terms; the principal generally may refuse the deal without owing commission.

terms.label: want of consideration
terms.gloss: The defense that a promise is unenforceable because nothing was given in exchange for it.

terms.label: brought error
terms.gloss: Took the case to a higher court by writ of error to review mistakes in the record.

terms.label: charitable subscription
terms.gloss: A promise to donate to a charity, church or school; courts often enforce these even without a bargain.

terms.label: gift promise
