terms.gloss: A transfer, or promise of one, made for nothing in return; a gift promise traditionally lacks consideration, while a completed gift takes effect.

terms.label: Electronic Communications Privacy Act
terms.gloss: A 1986 federal law banning unauthorized interception of electronic communications.

terms.label: fresh review
terms.gloss: Review without deference to the lower court's view, also called de novo.

terms.label: reasonably prudent user
terms.gloss: The objective standard of an ordinary careful person in the same situation.

terms.label: ProCD and Hill
terms.gloss: ProCD v. Zeidenberg and Hill v. Gateway (7th Cir.): terms shipped with a product are binding if the buyer can review them and return the product but keeps it.

terms.label: summary trial (FAA § 4)
terms.gloss: A quick trial under the Federal Arbitration Act to decide whether an arbitration agreement was actually made.

terms.label: presumptively arbitrable
terms.gloss: Under a broad arbitration clause, disputes are assumed to belong in arbitration unless clearly outside it.

terms.label: Williston
terms.gloss: Samuel Williston, a leading contracts scholar whose treatise argued that promising extra pay for already-owed work lacks consideration.

terms.label: Restatement § 89
terms.gloss: The Restatement (Second) of Contracts section letting a change to a contract not yet fully performed bind without new consideration if fair and equitable given circumstances the parties did not anticipate.

terms.label: improper threat
terms.gloss: A threat (such as to breach a contract in bad faith) that can make a resulting agreement voidable for duress.

terms.label: Austin Instrument v. Loral
terms.gloss: A 1971 New York case finding economic duress where a supplier's threat to stop deliveries left the buyer no reasonable alternative.

terms.label: Alaska Packers (fishermen case)
terms.gloss: Alaska Packers' Ass'n v. Domenico (1902): fishermen who demanded more pay mid-season could not enforce the promise, since they already owed the work.

terms.label: federal-incorporation cases
terms.gloss: Cases, such as Osborn, holding that suits involving corporations chartered by Congress arise under federal law because federal law created the corporation.

terms.label: Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co.
terms.gloss: A 1940 Supreme Court case: a contractor doing work validly authorized and directed by the federal government is not liable for carrying out that work.

terms.label: United States v. Booker
terms.gloss: A 2005 Supreme Court case that fixed the unconstitutional mandatory federal Sentencing Guidelines by striking the provisions making them binding, leaving them advisory.

terms.label: identified in interest
terms.gloss: So closely connected to a party in an earlier case, such as an employer sued only for its employees' acts, that the earlier judgment binds or protects it too.

terms.label: derivative liability
terms.gloss: Liability that exists only because someone else, such as an employee or agent, is liable; if that person did nothing wrong, the one held responsible for them is not liable either.

terms.label: disorderly conduct
terms.gloss: A minor criminal offense for disturbing public order, such as fighting or unruly behavior in public.

terms.label: peace officer
terms.gloss: A person with legal authority to keep public order and make arrests, such as a police officer.

terms.label: directly and collaterally estopped
terms.gloss: Barred both from suing again on the same claim and from re-arguing facts the earlier court already decided.

terms.label: transaction (claim preclusion)
terms.gloss: In claim preclusion, the real-world events behind a lawsuit; claims arising from the same events generally must all be brought in one suit.
terms.context: adjudication of this transaction|change the underlying transaction|this repeated transaction|same transaction

terms.label: Hague Service Convention
terms.gloss: A 1965 treaty setting how lawsuit papers must be formally delivered to defendants in other member countries, mainly through each country's designated Central Authority.

terms.label: Central Authority
terms.gloss: The office each country designates under the Hague Service Convention to receive foreign lawsuit papers and arrange their formal delivery.

terms.label: notification au parquet
terms.gloss: A French-style practice of serving a foreign defendant by leaving papers with a local public official, which can count as service before the defendant actually learns of the suit.

terms.label: administrator (of an estate)
terms.gloss: A person a court appoints to manage a dead person's estate, including suing on the estate's behalf.

terms.label: involuntary agency
terms.gloss: Treating one company as another's agent for receiving lawsuit papers because of their close relationship, even though it was never formally appointed.

terms.label: office of discount and deposit
terms.gloss: A branch office of the Bank of the United States that made loans and took deposits.

terms.label: amended bill
terms.gloss: A revised complaint in an equity case; in old equity practice the complaint was called a 'bill'.

terms.label: taken as confessed
terms.gloss: Treated as admitted because the defendant did not properly answer them, much like a default.

terms.label: warrant of attorney
terms.gloss: A formal written authorization for a lawyer to appear and act for a party; here, a corporate document authorizing counsel to sue.

terms.label: courts of record
terms.gloss: Regular courts whose proceedings are formally recorded and whose judgments have lasting legal force.

terms.label: named on the record
terms.gloss: Formally listed as a party in the case papers; Osborn read the Eleventh Amendment as protecting only a state so named.

terms.label: specie
terms.gloss: Coined money, such as gold or silver coins, as opposed to paper notes.

terms.label: McCulloch v. Maryland
terms.gloss: The 1819 Supreme Court case holding that Congress could create a national bank and that states could not tax it.

terms.label: Bank of the United States v. Deveaux
terms.gloss: An 1809 Supreme Court case holding the first Bank charter's 'sue and be sued' clause did not itself open the federal courts to the Bank.

terms.label: rate of return
terms.gloss: The percentage profit on its property value that regulators allow a utility to earn through its rates.

terms.label: course of post
terms.gloss: By return mail in the normal way; a request for an answer 'in course of post' meant reply promptly by the next post.

terms.label: bill (of exchange)
terms.gloss: A written order to pay a set sum at a later date; here, payment due two months after delivery.

terms.label: conditional rule (rule nisi)
terms.gloss: An English court order granting relief, such as a new trial, unless the other side shows good reason why not.

terms.label: discharge the rule
terms.gloss: Cancel a conditional court order, so the relief it offered (here a new trial) is refused.

terms.label: Easter Term
terms.gloss: One of the fixed yearly sittings of the old English common-law courts.

terms.label: 1 & 2 Vict. c.110 (Judgments Act 1838)
terms.gloss: An 1838 English statute that, among other things, made court judgments carry interest at four percent a year.

terms.label: Cumber v. Wane
terms.gloss: A 1721 English case applying Pinnel's rule to hold that a smaller promissory note could not satisfy a larger debt.

terms.label: Queen's Bench Division
terms.gloss: A division of England's High Court that hears ordinary civil cases and some appeals.

terms.label: M.R. (Master of the Rolls)
terms.gloss: Master of the Rolls, the senior judge presiding in the English Court of Appeal.

terms.label: nominee
terms.gloss: A person designated to receive payment or act on someone else's behalf.

terms.label: sham plea
terms.gloss: A plea built on a convenient fiction, such as claiming a creditor took a hat or wine as payment, so a smaller settlement would count as giving 'something different'.

terms.label: leave (sought or denied)
terms.gloss: Permission from a court to take a step, such as appealing or proceeding; when a higher court 'denied leave', it refused to hear an appeal.

terms.label: ordinary fraud
terms.gloss: Fraud based on a false statement about a present or past fact, as opposed to promissory fraud about a future promise.

terms.label: Alabama constitutional immunity
terms.gloss: Alabama's constitution bars suits against the state and its agencies, including state universities, though officials can be sued personally for fraud.

terms.label: opening brief
terms.gloss: The appealing party's first written argument; issues not raised there generally cannot be added later in a reply.

terms.label: direct appellate review
terms.gloss: A Massachusetts procedure letting the state's highest court take an appeal straight from the trial court, skipping the intermediate Appeals Court.

terms.label: Fortune v. National Cash Register
terms.gloss: A 1977 Massachusetts case holding an employer breached good faith by firing a salesman to avoid paying commissions he had already earned.

terms.label: franchise (business)
terms.gloss: A business arrangement in which a company licenses its name, methods and support to an operator who runs an outlet in return for fees.
terms.context: Dairy Mart|principally received franchise fees|business-format|particular franchises|franchise policy

terms.label: delegation (of legislative power)
terms.gloss: Congress handing an agency or official power to make binding rules; allowed only if Congress supplies an 'intelligible principle' to guide it.

terms.label: A.O. Smith
terms.gloss: A.O. Smith Corp. v. FTC (3d Cir. 1976), holding that ordinary costs of complying with a regulation are generally not irreparable harm.

terms.label: Ohio v. EPA
terms.gloss: A 2024 Supreme Court order pausing an EPA air-pollution rule because challengers were likely to win and faced very large compliance costs.

terms.label: rule of reason
terms.gloss: The antitrust approach that judges a business practice by weighing its actual harms to competition against its benefits, rather than condemning it automatically.

terms.label: National Industrial Recovery Act
terms.gloss: A 1933 New Deal law letting the President approve industry 'codes of fair competition'; struck down in Schechter.

terms.label: incipient restraints
terms.gloss: Practices that have not yet harmed competition but tend toward it; the FTC may stop them early.

terms.label: substantive rules
terms.gloss: Agency rules that create binding legal duties with the force of law, as opposed to procedural rules or interpretive guidance.
terms.context: carry out that function|§ 6\(g\)|agency|Commission|FTC|rulemaking|power to make|delegation

terms.label: mental incompetence
terms.gloss: Lacking the mental capacity to understand or make a legal decision; a contract made while incompetent may be cancelled.

terms.label: adjudicated insane / incompetent
terms.gloss: Formally declared mentally incompetent by a court; afterward the person's contracts are generally void, not just voidable.

terms.label: chargeable with awareness
terms.gloss: Treated by law as knowing something because the information was available to it, whether or not anyone actually knew.

terms.label: actuarial
terms.gloss: Relating to statistical calculations of life expectancy and risk used to fund pensions and insurance.

terms.label: volitional
terms.gloss: Relating to the ability to control one's own actions and choices, as distinct from understanding them.

terms.label: AG (Aktiengesellschaft)
terms.gloss: A stock corporation under Swiss or German law, roughly like a U.S. corporation.

terms.label: cantonal
terms.gloss: Belonging to one of Switzerland's cantons (states); cantonal courts decide cases before any appeal to the Federal Supreme Court.

terms.label: Obergericht
terms.gloss: A Swiss canton's High Court, which hears appeals from its trial courts (here, the canton of Zug).

terms.label: subsidiary constitutional appeal
terms.gloss: A Swiss backup appeal available only when the ordinary appeal is not, limited to claims that constitutional rights were violated.

terms.label: principle of trust
terms.gloss: Swiss interpretation rule: absent proof of what both sides actually meant, a contract means what a reasonable person would understand from its words and context.

terms.label: party compensation
terms.gloss: The Swiss term for money a court orders one side to pay toward the other's legal fees.

terms.label: prima facie case
terms.gloss: Enough evidence that, if not answered, would let a party win; failing to make one means losing without the other side needing to respond.

terms.label: escalation mechanism
terms.gloss: A contract term that adjusts the price automatically when specified costs rise.

terms.label: resale (seller's remedy)
terms.gloss: A seller's remedy when a buyer wrongly refuses goods: resell them in good faith and recover the shortfall from the contract price.

terms.label: reciprocal purchasing (reciprocity)
terms.gloss: An arrangement in which a company buys from a supplier on the understanding that the supplier buys from it; it can violate antitrust law, especially when coerced.

terms.label: official comments (UCC)
terms.gloss: Explanatory notes written by the UCC's drafters, which courts use to interpret the code's text.

terms.label: § 8.2-202 (UCC § 2-202)
terms.gloss: Virginia's UCC § 2-202, the sales parol evidence rule: a final writing cannot be contradicted by earlier agreements but may be explained by trade usage, course of dealing and consistent extra terms.

terms.label: § 8.1-205 (UCC § 1-205)
terms.gloss: Virginia's version of the UCC rule defining usage of trade and course of dealing and ranking them below express terms.

terms.label: § 8.2-209 (UCC § 2-209)
terms.gloss: Virginia's version of UCC § 2-209, which lets parties modify a sales contract without new consideration.

terms.label: § 8.2-706 (UCC § 2-706)
terms.gloss: Virginia's version of UCC § 2-706, letting a seller resell refused goods and recover the gap between contract and resale price.

terms.label: Kelly v. Kosuga
terms.gloss: A 1959 Supreme Court case holding that a buyer cannot avoid paying for goods merely because the deal involved an antitrust violation, unless enforcing it would itself carry out the illegality.

terms.label: Perma Life
terms.gloss: Perma Life Mufflers v. International Parts (1968), limiting the defense that a plaintiff who took part in an illegal arrangement cannot sue for antitrust damages.

terms.label: towage
terms.gloss: Pulling a vessel or floating structure by tug; towage contracts set the tug owner's duties and liability.

terms.label: London Court of Justice
terms.gloss: The contract's name for the High Court of Justice in London, England's main civil trial court.

terms.label: arrest (of a vessel)
terms.gloss: Seized by court order in a maritime case, so the ship itself stands as security for the claim.

terms.label: released on security
terms.gloss: Freed from court seizure after the owner posted a bond or other guarantee covering the claim.

terms.label: limitation of liability (shipowner)
terms.gloss: Under the federal Limitation of Liability Act, a shipowner can ask an admiralty court to cap its total liability at the vessel's value and gather all claims into one proceeding.

terms.label: salvage
terms.gloss: A reward owed under maritime law to someone who saves a ship or cargo from danger at sea.

terms.label: Bisso v. Inland Waterways
terms.gloss: A 1955 Supreme Court case holding that towing companies cannot contract out of liability for their own negligence in U.S. towage.

terms.label: day in court
terms.gloss: A real opportunity to present one's case to a court.

terms.label: named plaintiffs
terms.gloss: The class members who actually bring and run a class action on behalf of the whole group.

terms.label: legitimate nondiscriminatory reason
terms.gloss: The lawful explanation an employer must offer once an employee presents a prima facie case of discrimination.

terms.label: General Telephone Co. v. Falcon
terms.gloss: A 1982 Supreme Court case holding that one person's discrimination claim does not automatically justify a class action for all similar employees.

terms.label: blackballing
terms.gloss: Being collectively shut out, here by racetracks jointly refusing to let a driver race.

terms.label: batture
terms.gloss: Land built up by river deposits between the low-water line and the levee, here along the Mississippi in New Orleans.

terms.label: venue fiction
terms.gloss: An old pleading practice of alleging that events happened in the court's own county, which the defendant could not deny, so claims that could arise anywhere could be sued on there.

terms.label: justification
terms.gloss: A defense admitting the act but claiming it was legally authorized or excused.

terms.label: local action
terms.gloss: A lawsuit, especially for injury to land, that by tradition can be brought only where the land lies.

terms.label: quare clausum fregit
terms.gloss: Latin, 'because he broke the close': the traditional common-law suit for unlawful entry onto another's land.

terms.label: waste
terms.gloss: A suit against someone in possession of land, such as a tenant, for damaging or neglecting it.

terms.label: juries of the vicinity
terms.gloss: The old practice of drawing jurors from the neighborhood where events happened, because they were expected to know the facts.

terms.label: general or natural law
terms.gloss: Broad principles of justice and reason thought to exist independently of any particular statute or court decision.

terms.label: Mostyn v. Fabrigas
terms.gloss: A 1774 English case in which Lord Mansfield allowed suit in England for a wrong committed abroad, reasoning broadly about transitory actions.

terms.label: Doulson v. Matthews
terms.gloss: A 1792 English case reaffirming that trespass to land abroad cannot be sued on in England.

terms.label: realty
terms.gloss: Real property: land and things attached to it; Arkansas law here treated growing crops as part of the land.

terms.label: bank holding company
terms.gloss: A company that owns or controls one or more banks and is regulated by the Federal Reserve.

terms.label: closely related to banking
terms.gloss: The Bank Holding Company Act test for which non-banking businesses a bank holding company may enter.

terms.label: Regulation Y
terms.gloss: The Federal Reserve's regulation governing bank holding companies, including its list of permitted non-banking activities.
The Bank Holding Company Act provision for court review of Federal Reserve orders, making the Board's findings conclusive if supported by substantial evidence.

terms.label: § 553(c) (APA)
terms.gloss: The APA provision requiring agencies to let the public comment on proposed rules and to explain final rules.

terms.label: § 557(c) (APA)
terms.gloss: The APA provision requiring formal agency decisions to state findings and reasons on all material issues.

terms.label: closed record
terms.gloss: The fixed set of evidence presented at a formal agency hearing, to which the decision must be confined.

terms.label: National Courier
terms.gloss: National Courier Ass'n v. Board of Governors (D.C. Cir. 1975), which set guides for deciding when an activity is closely related to banking.

terms.label: managerial employees
terms.gloss: Workers who make or carry out company policy with real discretion; Bell Aerospace held they are excluded from the NLRA's protections.

terms.label: certified the union
terms.gloss: Officially recognized the union as the employees' bargaining representative after it won the election.

terms.label: §§ 8(a)(5) and (1)
terms.gloss: NLRA provisions making it an unfair labor practice to refuse to bargain with the union and to interfere with employees' labor rights.

terms.label: enforcement (of an NLRB order)
terms.gloss: NLRB orders are not self-executing: the Board asks a federal appeals court to enforce them, while the employer may petition the court to review them.

terms.label: supervisors (NLRA)
terms.gloss: Under the NLRA, employees with authority to hire, fire, direct or discipline others using independent judgment; they are excluded from the Act's protections.

terms.label: House managers
terms.gloss: House members on the conference committee, whose explanation of the compromise bill courts treat as legislative history.

terms.label: Wyman-Gordon
terms.gloss: The company in NLRB v. Wyman-Gordon (1969), a split Supreme Court decision on whether the NLRB could announce a general rule in a case without using rulemaking procedures.

terms.label: Packard
terms.gloss: Packard Motor Car Co. v. NLRB (1947), holding foremen were protected 'employees' under the NLRA, which Congress then reversed in Taft-Hartley.

terms.label: reopening the record
terms.gloss: Allowing new evidence to be added after a hearing has closed.

terms.label: impasse
terms.gloss: In labor law, a genuine deadlock after good-faith bargaining, which can let an employer impose its final offer.

terms.label: unanimous consent
terms.gloss: A Senate procedure where business goes forward if no senator objects, without a formal vote.

terms.label: intersession / intrasession recess
terms.gloss: An intersession recess is the break between Congress's formal yearly sessions; an intrasession recess is a break within a session.

terms.label: sine die
terms.gloss: Latin, 'without a day': an adjournment ending a session with no set day to return.

terms.label: New Process Steel
terms.gloss: New Process Steel v. NLRB (2010), holding the five-member NLRB cannot act with only two members; it needs a quorum of three.

terms.label: § 10(e) (NLRA)
terms.gloss: The NLRA provision on court enforcement of Board orders, which bars objections not first raised before the Board unless extraordinary circumstances excuse it.

terms.label: extraordinary circumstances
terms.gloss: Unusual, serious situations that justify departing from a normal rule, such as the bar on raising arguments that were not made earlier.

terms.label: Evans v. Stephens
terms.gloss: A 2004 Eleventh Circuit decision upholding a recess appointment of a judge made during a break within a Senate session.

terms.label: Adjournments Clause
terms.gloss: The constitutional rule that neither house of Congress may adjourn for more than three days during a session without the other's consent.

terms.label: Wirt
terms.gloss: William Wirt, U.S. Attorney General, whose 1823 opinion said the President may fill during a recess vacancies that arose before it.

terms.label: knowingly and willfully
terms.gloss: Acting with awareness of what one is doing and deliberately, not by accident or mistake.

terms.label: Criminal Appeals Act
terms.gloss: A 1907 federal law letting the United States appeal directly to the Supreme Court when a trial court dismissed criminal charges by holding a statute invalid.

terms.label: Wayman v. Southard
terms.gloss: An 1825 case in which Chief Justice Marshall said Congress may let others 'fill up the details' of a law while it decides the important matters itself.

terms.label: United States v. Eaton
terms.gloss: An 1892 case holding that violating an agency regulation is not a crime unless Congress itself made it one.

terms.label: implied license
terms.gloss: Permission to use property inferred from the owner's conduct, such as long tolerance, rather than granted expressly.

terms.label: Aurora and Field
terms.gloss: The Brig Aurora (1813) and Field v. Clark (1892), upholding laws whose operation depended on the President finding specified facts.

terms.label: SORNA
match: sex offender registration and notification act
terms.gloss: The 2006 federal law requiring convicted sex offenders to register, and keep their registration current, where they live, work or study.

terms.label: pre-Act offenders
terms.gloss: People convicted of covered sex offenses before SORNA was enacted in 2006.

terms.label: interim rule
terms.gloss: A rule an agency puts into effect immediately, before or while taking public comment, until a final rule replaces it.

terms.label: residential reentry center
terms.gloss: A halfway house where federal prisoners finish their sentences while returning to the community.

terms.label: § 2250(a)
terms.gloss: The federal crime of knowingly failing to register, or update a registration, as SORNA requires, for example after traveling between states.

terms.label: time served
terms.gloss: A sentence equal to the time already spent in custody, so no further prison time.

terms.label: Reynolds v. United States
terms.gloss: A 2012 Supreme Court case holding SORNA's duties did not apply to pre-Act offenders until the Attorney General said so.

terms.label: general and limited partner
terms.gloss: For diversity jurisdiction, a partnership is a citizen of every state where any partner, general (managing) or limited (passive investor), is a citizen.

terms.label: opportunism
terms.gloss: Exploiting a contract's gaps or the other side's mistake to grab gains the bargain did not give.

terms.label: exclusive dealership
terms.gloss: An arrangement giving a dealer the sole right to sell a maker's products in an area, with an implied duty to promote them.

terms.label: curative instruction
terms.gloss: A judge's instruction telling the jury to ignore improper evidence or remarks, meant to undo their effect.

terms.label: duplicative
terms.gloss: Compensating the same loss twice.

terms.label: Missouri Approved Instruction
terms.gloss: Missouri's official pattern jury instructions, which trial courts must use where one applies.

terms.label: informal verdict
terms.gloss: A jury verdict not in proper legal form, such as one mixing findings with suggestions. A judge may fix it only if the jury's intent is clear.

terms.label: plain view
terms.gloss: A rule letting police seize evidence without a warrant when its criminal nature is obvious and they see it from a place they are lawfully in.

terms.label: suppress (evidence)
terms.gloss: To exclude evidence from a criminal trial because the police got it illegally.

terms.label: facially inadequate
terms.gloss: Plainly inadequate on its face: obviously defective as written or designed, without needing proof about how it worked in a particular case.

terms.label: England reservation
terms.gloss: From England v. Louisiana State Board of Medical Examiners (1964). A litigant sent to state court by federal abstention may reserve federal issues for a federal court to decide later.

terms.label: involuntary bankruptcy
terms.gloss: A bankruptcy case started by a debtor's creditors rather than by the debtor itself, forcing court-supervised handling of its debts.

terms.label: Bank Holding Company Act
terms.gloss: A federal law regulating companies that own banks. Its 1970 amendments bar banks from certain coercive 'tying' practices and let injured customers sue.

terms.label: commercially unreasonable (sale)
terms.gloss: Under the UCC, a creditor selling a debtor's collateral must use commercially reasonable methods and terms. A sale that falls short can make the creditor liable.

terms.label: relitigation exception
terms.gloss: An Anti-Injunction Act exception. A federal court may block a state case when that is needed to protect or carry out a judgment the federal court already entered.

terms.label: transfer (of venue)
terms.gloss: Moving a pending lawsuit from one federal district court to another, for convenience or because the first court is the wrong place.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 1406(a)
terms.gloss: A federal statute telling a court in which venue is improper to dismiss the case, or to transfer it to a district where it belongs.

terms.label: related-case order
terms.gloss: A court order marking separate lawsuits as connected so that the same judge handles them, which saves effort.

terms.label: scheduling order
terms.gloss: A court order setting deadlines for the steps in a case, such as discovery, motions and trial.

terms.label: Atlantic Marine
terms.gloss: A 2013 Supreme Court decision holding that a valid forum-selection clause should control transfer decisions except in extraordinary cases.

terms.label: nonsignatory
terms.gloss: A party who did not sign the contract in question, and so is generally not bound by its terms.

terms.label: Sinochem
terms.gloss: A 2007 Supreme Court decision allowing a court to dismiss for an inconvenient forum before deciding whether it has jurisdiction.

terms.label: closely related party
terms.gloss: A doctrine some courts use to bind a non-signer to a forum-selection clause when its ties to the deal or a signer made being bound foreseeable.

terms.label: contacts (with a state)
terms.gloss: A defendant's own connections with a state, such as business, visits or conduct there. They decide whether that state's courts may hear claims against it.

terms.label: derivative claimant
terms.gloss: A relative, such as a spouse or child, whose claim depends on injury to someone else, for example a claim for loss of companionship.

terms.label: American Pipe tolling
terms.gloss: A rule from American Pipe v. Utah (1974). Filing a class action pauses the filing deadline (statute of limitations) on class members' federal claims.

terms.label: Amchem
terms.gloss: Amchem Products v. Windsor (1997). The Supreme Court rejected a huge asbestos class settlement because members' interests conflicted and were not separately represented.

terms.label: Wal-Mart (v. Dukes)
terms.gloss: Wal-Mart v. Dukes (2011). The Supreme Court refused class certification because millions of separate manager decisions lacked a common question.

terms.label: admission of liability
terms.gloss: A formal acknowledgment of legal fault. Settlements usually disclaim one, so that paying does not count as admitting wrongdoing.

terms.label: Department of Fair Employment and Housing
match: department of fair employment and housing
terms.gloss: California's agency (now the Civil Rights Department) that investigates job and housing discrimination complaints under state law.

terms.label: JAMS
terms.gloss: A large private provider of arbitration and mediation services (formerly Judicial Arbitration and Mediation Services). It has its own procedural rules.

terms.label: carveout
terms.gloss: An exception that removes certain claims or matters from a contract term, such as from a duty to arbitrate.

terms.label: duty to read
terms.gloss: The rule that a person who signs a contract is generally bound by its terms, even without reading them.

terms.label: fraud in the execution
terms.gloss: Fraud that tricks a person about the nature of what they are signing, so they do not realize it is a contract. Such an agreement is void.

terms.label: California Civil Code § 1717
terms.gloss: A California statute that makes one-sided contract fee clauses work both ways: whichever side wins a suit on the contract can recover its lawyers' fees.

terms.label: depublication
terms.gloss: A California Supreme Court order removing a lower court's opinion from the official reports, so it cannot be cited as precedent, without reviewing its result.

terms.label: custom-house weight
terms.gloss: The weight recorded by customs officials when the goods were imported, used here as the agreed measure for the price.

terms.label: condition (contract)
terms.gloss: An event that must happen before a party has to perform. If it never happens, the duty to perform may never arise.

terms.label: mercantile
terms.gloss: Commercial: having to do with merchants and trade.

terms.label: conformity
terms.gloss: Matching what the contract required. A demand for conformity asks that the goods or work be brought into line with the agreed terms.

terms.label: letter of intent
terms.gloss: A preliminary document, often not fully binding, that outlines the main terms of a proposed deal before the final contract is signed.

terms.label: asset (purchase) agreement
terms.gloss: A contract to buy a business's assets, such as its inventory, contracts and goodwill, rather than its stock.

terms.label: three-tier system
terms.gloss: Alcohol regulation that keeps producers, wholesale distributors and retailers separate, so suppliers must sell through independent wholesalers.

terms.label: state-controlled system
terms.gloss: In 'control states' such as Michigan, the state itself is the wholesaler of spirits and uses private agents to distribute them.

terms.label: ground of appeal (moyen)
terms.gloss: In French cassation practice, a distinct legal argument attacking the lower decision. The court rules on each ground separately.

terms.label: former French Civil Code article 1184
terms.gloss: A provision of the old French Civil Code. A party whose contract was not performed could force performance if still possible, or end the contract with damages.

terms.label: lack of legal basis
terms.gloss: A French ground for annulment: the lower court failed to make the factual findings needed to justify how it applied the law.

terms.label: proportionality exception
terms.gloss: A rule added to French law in 2016. A court may refuse to force performance when its cost to the debtor is clearly out of proportion to the creditor's benefit.

terms.label: certified conflict
terms.gloss: A lower appeals court's formal statement that its ruling conflicts with other appellate decisions, which sends the question to the state supreme court.

terms.label: general relief
terms.gloss: A catch-all request in a pleading for any other relief the court finds just. It can support an award beyond the sums specifically named.

terms.label: merchants' written confirmation
terms.gloss: Under the UCC, a written confirmation sent between merchants can satisfy the writing requirement even against the recipient, unless the recipient objects within ten days.

terms.label: limited-purpose public figure
terms.gloss: Someone who is a public figure only for a particular public controversy they joined. They must prove actual malice to win a libel suit about it.

terms.label: material fact
terms.gloss: A fact that could change the outcome under the governing law. Only disputes over such facts prevent summary judgment.

terms.label: state of mind
terms.gloss: What a person knew, intended or believed at a given time, such as whether a publisher doubted a story's truth.

terms.label: Celotex
terms.gloss: Celotex v. Catrett (1986), on what a party seeking summary judgment must show first. It may point to the other side's lack of evidence.

terms.label: Matsushita
terms.gloss: A 1986 Supreme Court antitrust case allowing summary judgment where a claimed conspiracy made no economic sense and stronger evidence was lacking.

terms.label: specific gifts (bequests)
terms.gloss: Gifts in a will of particular items or amounts to named people. They are paid before the leftover (residue) is distributed.

terms.label: common fund
terms.gloss: A single pool of money shared by several claimants, so awarding more to one necessarily leaves less for the others.

terms.label: alternative writ
terms.gloss: A preliminary order that temporarily halts a lower court and requires it to stop or explain itself. The final order is the 'peremptory' writ.

terms.label: California Code of Civil Procedure § 389
terms.gloss: California's joinder statute at the time. It required bringing in parties needed for a complete decision, while allowing cases among present parties to go on where others could be protected.

terms.label: small-claims court
terms.gloss: A simplified, informal court for low-value disputes, often without lawyers.

terms.label: purposes-and-objectives preemption
terms.gloss: Striking down a state law because it obstructs the goals of a federal law, even though it does not directly conflict with the federal text.

terms.label: bilateral (individual) arbitration
terms.gloss: Arbitration between only the two parties to the contract, one claim at a time, as opposed to class arbitration.

terms.label: Rule 12(c)
terms.gloss: The federal rule allowing a party to ask for judgment based only on the complaint and answer, once the pleadings are closed.

terms.label: admission (in a pleading)
terms.gloss: Accepting an allegation as true in a pleading. An admitted fact needs no proof.

terms.label: legal conclusion
terms.gloss: A statement about what the law is or how it applies, as opposed to a statement of fact.

terms.label: 'the document speaks for itself'
terms.gloss: A common, widely criticized answer that neither admits nor denies a description of a document, saying only that the document speaks for itself.

terms.label: (insurance) policy
terms.gloss: The insurance contract, which sets out who and what it covers and how much it will pay.

terms.label: named insured
terms.gloss: The person listed in an insurance policy as the policyholder. They have the fullest rights under it.

terms.label: permissive use (omnibus clause)
terms.gloss: Car insurance usually covers anyone driving with the owner's permission. A driver who strays beyond that permission may lose the coverage.

terms.label: destroy diversity
terms.gloss: Adding a party from the same state as someone on the other side ends complete diversity, so the federal court loses its diversity jurisdiction.

terms.label: Dead Man Rule
terms.gloss: A rule barring an interested witness from testifying against a dead person's estate about dealings with that person.

terms.label: absentee (party)
terms.gloss: A person with an interest in a case who is not a party to it.

terms.label: coverage
terms.gloss: The protection an insurance policy or settlement provides: who and what it pays for.

terms.label: deputized
terms.gloss: Given official authority to act as a deputy. Here, a local officer was authorized to work as a federal agent.

terms.label: Drug Enforcement Administration
terms.gloss: The federal agency that enforces drug laws.

terms.label: trademark dilution
terms.gloss: Weakening a famous mark's distinctiveness, or tarnishing it, through unrelated use, even without confusing customers.

terms.label: Rules 12(b)(2) and 12(b)(3)
terms.gloss: Federal rules letting a defendant seek dismissal before answering, for lack of personal jurisdiction (12(b)(2)) or improper venue (12(b)(3)).

terms.label: fortuitous (contacts)
terms.gloss: Happening by chance rather than through the defendant's deliberate choice. Chance contacts do not support jurisdiction.

terms.label: passive website
terms.gloss: A site that only posts information for visitors, with no transactions. Under Zippo it generally does not support personal jurisdiction.

terms.label: bid bond
terms.gloss: A guarantee, usually from a surety company, that a winning bidder will sign the contract, or pay a penalty if it backs out.

terms.label: unilateral offer
terms.gloss: An offer that can be accepted only by doing the requested act, not by promising to do it.

terms.label: Restatement § 45
terms.gloss: The Restatement rule that once someone begins the performance a unilateral offer invites, the offer cannot be revoked while they finish.

terms.label: Restatement (Second) § 87(2)
terms.gloss: A Second Restatement rule. An offer the offeror should expect to be relied on before acceptance is binding, as an option, to the extent needed to avoid injustice.

terms.label: special demurrer
terms.gloss: In California, an early objection that a pleading is unclear or uncertain, rather than legally insufficient. It is lost if not raised in time.

terms.label: artisan's (possessory) lien
terms.gloss: A worker's right to keep goods they repaired or processed until they are paid for that work.

terms.label: stipulated sum
terms.gloss: An amount fixed in the contract in advance as damages for breach. It is enforced as liquidated damages or struck down as a penalty.

terms.label: variable cost
terms.gloss: Costs that rise and fall with the amount of work done, such as labor and bags. They are saved if the work is never done.

terms.label: Circuit Rule 18
terms.gloss: A Seventh Circuit rule that normally sends a retrial on remand to a different district judge. Here the court said it did not apply.

terms.label: Magnuson-Stevens Act
terms.gloss: The main federal law governing fishing in U.S. ocean waters, carried out through regional councils and the National Marine Fisheries Service.

terms.label: National Marine Fisheries Service
terms.gloss: The Commerce Department agency that regulates commercial fishing in federal waters.

terms.label: Brand X
terms.gloss: A 2005 Supreme Court decision letting an agency's reasonable reading override a court's earlier interpretation, unless the court had found the statute clear.

terms.label: Trade Act of 1974
terms.gloss: A federal trade law that, among other things, gives cash allowances and other help to workers who lose their jobs because of import competition.

terms.label: trade readjustment allowances
terms.gloss: Federal weekly payments under the Trade Act to workers displaced by imports, mostly paid after their unemployment benefits run out.

terms.label: Hunt (associational standing test)
terms.gloss: Hunt v. Washington State Apple Advertising Commission (1977). It set the three-part test for when an organization may sue on behalf of its members.

terms.label: Warth
terms.gloss: Warth v. Seldin (1975). An organization could not seek damages for members when each member's injury and amount needed individual proof.

terms.label: live claims
terms.gloss: Claims that are still unresolved and still matter to the parties, as opposed to moot ones.

terms.label: deferred action
terms.gloss: A discretionary decision by immigration authorities not to seek a person's removal for a period. It gives no legal status and can be revoked.

terms.label: DAPA
terms.gloss: Deferred Action for Parents of Americans and Lawful Permanent Residents (2014). The program for parents of citizens and green-card holders was blocked in court and never took effect.

terms.label: lawful permanent resident
terms.gloss: A noncitizen allowed to live and work in the U.S. permanently: a green-card holder.

terms.label: enforcement priority
terms.gloss: The categories of people immigration authorities choose to pursue first for removal, such as those with serious criminal records.

terms.label: work authorization
terms.gloss: Federal permission for a noncitizen to work legally in the U.S.

terms.label: lawful presence
terms.gloss: A designation that the government tolerates a person's presence for certain purposes, such as some benefits. It is not lawful immigration status.

terms.label: nationwide injunction
terms.gloss: A court order blocking a policy everywhere, not just as it affects the parties who sued.

terms.label: alternative holding
terms.gloss: A separate reason a court gives that is enough on its own to support the result.

terms.label: Massachusetts v. EPA
terms.gloss: A 2007 Supreme Court case letting Massachusetts challenge the EPA over climate change, giving states special leeway on standing.

terms.label: 8 U.S.C. § 1252(g)
terms.gloss: An immigration provision barring courts from hearing claims by or for noncitizens over decisions to start removal proceedings, decide cases or carry out removal orders.

terms.label: substantive rule
terms.gloss: An agency rule that creates binding rights or duties, like a statute. It generally requires notice and comment.

terms.label: procedural-rule exception
terms.gloss: An APA exemption from notice and comment for rules about an agency's own internal procedures, as opposed to people's rights.

terms.label: substantial-impact approach
terms.gloss: A Fifth Circuit test treating a rule as substantive, and so requiring notice and comment, if it substantially affects people's rights or interests.

terms.label: public-benefits exception
terms.gloss: The APA exemption from notice and comment for rules about public grants, benefits or contracts.

terms.label: Sentencing Reform Act of 1984
terms.gloss: A 1984 federal law that created the U.S. Sentencing Commission, binding sentencing guidelines and supervised release, and phased out federal parole.

terms.label: Sentencing Guidelines
terms.gloss: Rules written by the Sentencing Commission that give a sentencing range for each case based on the crime and the defendant's record. They were binding until 2005.

terms.label: Sentencing Commission
terms.gloss: An independent federal agency, placed in the judicial branch, that writes the federal Sentencing Guidelines.

terms.label: determinate sentence
terms.gloss: A fixed prison term that is actually served, rather than one a parole board can cut short.

terms.label: departure (sentencing)
terms.gloss: A sentence outside the Guidelines range, allowed for unusual circumstances the Commission did not adequately consider.

terms.label: aggravating or mitigating circumstances
terms.gloss: Facts that make a crime or offender more blameworthy (aggravating) or less (mitigating), which can raise or lower a sentence.

terms.label: Judicial Conference
terms.gloss: The policymaking body of the federal courts, chaired by the Chief Justice.

terms.label: recidivist
terms.gloss: A repeat offender.

terms.label: Incompatibility Clause
terms.gloss: A constitutional clause barring members of Congress from holding other federal offices at the same time.

terms.label: Hayburn's Case
terms.gloss: A 1792 episode in which federal judges refused to act as pension commissioners whose decisions others could revise. It is an early separation-of-powers precedent.

terms.label: nonadjudicatory
terms.gloss: Not involving deciding cases, such as administrative or rulemaking work.

terms.label: conflict certiorari
terms.gloss: Florida Supreme Court review granted to resolve conflicting decisions between Florida appeals courts.

terms.label: Second / Third District (Florida)
terms.gloss: Florida's intermediate appeals courts, the District Courts of Appeal, which sit between the trial courts and the Florida Supreme Court.

terms.label: open account
terms.gloss: A running credit account in which a buyer receives goods now and pays the balance later; suing on an open account means suing to collect that unpaid balance.

terms.label: collection suit
terms.gloss: A lawsuit brought to collect money a person or business claims it is owed.

terms.label: perpetuating testimony
terms.gloss: Recording a witness's sworn testimony before a lawsuit exists, under Federal Rule 27, so it is preserved if the witness may become unavailable.

terms.label: pre-complaint discovery
terms.gloss: Court-ordered fact-gathering before any lawsuit is filed. Federal courts generally do not allow it, apart from narrow tools like Rule 27.

terms.label: civil-rights claim
terms.gloss: A lawsuit seeking a remedy when government officials violate a person's constitutional or statutory rights, commonly brought under 42 U.S.C. section 1983.

terms.label: insured
terms.gloss: The person or business covered by an insurance policy.

terms.label: insurer
terms.gloss: The insurance company that issues a policy and pays covered losses.

terms.label: syllabus
terms.gloss: A summary of the legal holdings printed at the head of a court opinion. In Ohio at the time, the syllabus, not the opinion's discussion, stated the binding law.

terms.label: disenfranchisement
terms.gloss: Taking away a person's right to vote, for example because of a felony conviction.

terms.label: restoration of civil rights
terms.gloss: Giving back rights a person lost on a felony conviction, such as voting, serving on a jury, or holding office.

terms.label: poll tax
terms.gloss: A fee charged as a condition of voting. The Twenty-Fourth Amendment bans it in federal elections, and Harper v. Virginia (1966) struck it down in state elections.

terms.label: Twenty-Fourth Amendment
terms.gloss: The 1964 constitutional amendment forbidding denial of the vote in federal elections 'by reason of failure to pay any poll tax or other tax.'

terms.label: wealth discrimination
terms.gloss: Treating people differently by how much money they have. Wealth is not a 'suspect' classification, though some poverty-based barriers to voting or courts are struck down.

terms.label: access to courts
terms.gloss: The constitutional principle that people cannot be shut out of the justice system, such as denied an appeal, merely because they cannot afford its costs.

terms.label: community service
terms.gloss: Unpaid work for the public good that a court can order as part of, or in place of, a criminal sentence.

terms.label: legislative/adjudicative distinction
terms.gloss: The due-process rule that government decisions setting general rules for many people need no individual hearings, while decisions about particular individuals do.

terms.label: Richardson v. Ramirez
terms.gloss: Richardson v. Ramirez (1974): the Fourteenth Amendment lets states deny the vote to people convicted of felonies, even after they finish their sentences.

terms.label: Harper
terms.gloss: Harper v. Virginia Board of Elections (1966): struck down poll taxes in state elections, holding that wealth has nothing to do with fitness to vote.

terms.label: Griffin
terms.gloss: Griffin v. Illinois (1956): a state that allows criminal appeals cannot deny one to a defendant just because he cannot afford a trial transcript.

terms.label: Bearden
terms.gloss: Bearden v. Georgia (1983): a state cannot jail a person for failing to pay a fine he genuinely cannot afford without considering alternatives.

terms.label: notice and hearing
terms.gloss: The core of procedural due process: being told what the government is doing to you and getting a fair chance to contest it before a neutral decision-maker.

terms.label: dial-around compensation
terms.gloss: Payments federal law requires long-distance carriers to make to payphone owners for calls placed from their phones using access codes or toll-free numbers.

terms.label: aggregator
terms.gloss: A firm that takes over many small claims from their owners, by assignment, in order to sue on them together.

terms.label: collection assignment
terms.gloss: A transfer of a claim to someone just so they can sue and collect it, with the money going back to the original owner.

terms.label: Vermont Agency
terms.gloss: Vermont Agency of Natural Resources v. United States ex rel. Stevens (2000): a private whistleblower may sue for fraud on the government because the law partly assigns him the government's injury.

terms.label: striking class allegations
terms.gloss: A court order removing a complaint's class-action claims, which in effect denies class treatment and leaves only the named plaintiffs' own claims.

terms.label: death-knell doctrine
terms.gloss: A rejected theory that denying class certification could be appealed at once when it effectively ended the case because individual claims were too small to pursue.

terms.label: Coopers & Lybrand v. Livesay
terms.gloss: Coopers & Lybrand v. Livesay (1978): rejected the death-knell doctrine; an order denying class certification is not a final, immediately appealable decision.

terms.label: improvident
terms.gloss: Ill-considered or mistaken, such as a class ruling a court got wrong.

terms.label: Marine Mammal Protection Act
terms.gloss: A 1972 federal law generally banning the harassing, harming, or killing of marine mammals, with exemptions such as for national defense.

terms.label: environmental assessment
terms.gloss: A shorter NEPA study an agency prepares to decide whether a project's environmental effects are significant enough to require a full environmental impact statement.

terms.label: finding of no significant impact
terms.gloss: An agency's NEPA conclusion, after an environmental assessment, that its action will not significantly affect the environment, so no full impact statement is required.

terms.label: Council on Environmental Quality
terms.gloss: A White House office that writes the regulations agencies follow to comply with NEPA, including alternative arrangements in emergencies.

terms.label: likelihood of success on the merits
terms.gloss: The requirement that a party seeking an injunction before trial show it will probably win the case in the end.

terms.label: military deference
terms.gloss: Courts' practice of giving heavy weight to military leaders' professional judgments about what readiness and national defense require.

terms.label: administrative segregation
terms.gloss: Holding a prisoner in isolation, apart from the general population, for administrative rather than formally disciplinary reasons.

terms.label: Prison Litigation Reform Act (PLRA)
terms.gloss: A 1996 federal law limiting prisoner lawsuits, including requiring prisoners to use available prison grievance procedures before suing over prison conditions.

terms.label: judicial screening
terms.gloss: PLRA provisions requiring judges to review prisoner complaints early and dismiss those that are frivolous or fail to state a claim.

terms.label: Dairy Queen v. Wood
terms.gloss: Dairy Queen v. Wood (1962): extended Beacon Theatres, guaranteeing a jury on legal issues even when a case is mostly equitable.

terms.label: intertwinement
terms.gloss: When the same disputed facts decide both a preliminary issue, such as exhaustion or jurisdiction, and the main merits of the claim.

terms.label: threshold issue
terms.gloss: A preliminary question, such as jurisdiction or exhaustion, that a court decides before reaching the merits of a claim.

terms.label: Prison Rape Elimination Act
terms.gloss: A 2003 federal law addressing sexual abuse in prisons; it led to special rules for how prisoners report such abuse.

terms.label: Katchen v. Landy
terms.gloss: Katchen v. Landy (1966): a bankruptcy court could decide, without a jury, a trustee's claim against a creditor who had filed its own claim against the bankrupt's estate.

terms.label: Tull v. United States
terms.gloss: Tull v. United States (1987): the Seventh Amendment gives a jury right on whether a defendant is liable for civil penalties under the Clean Water Act.

terms.label: Granfinanciera
terms.gloss: Granfinanciera, S.A. v. Nordberg (1989): a bankruptcy trustee's fraudulent-transfer suit against a noncreditor is a legal claim carrying a jury right.

terms.label: gray market
terms.gloss: Genuine goods imported outside the manufacturer's authorized distribution channels, such as cars built for foreign markets and brought in without U.S. certification.

terms.label: formal execution
terms.gloss: Signing the final written contract. If parties say they will not be bound until then, there is no contract before signing.

terms.label: oral contract
terms.gloss: An agreement made in spoken words rather than in a signed writing; usually enforceable unless a law such as the statute of frauds requires a writing.

terms.label: negotiated (check)
terms.gloss: Never cashed or deposited. A check that is 'negotiated' has been transferred or presented for payment.

terms.label: deadlock
terms.gloss: A standstill in which co-owners or directors with equal votes cannot make a decision.

terms.label: full-performance exception
terms.gloss: The idea that once one side has fully performed its part of an unwritten agreement, the statute of frauds may no longer bar enforcing it.

terms.label: E-SIGN Act
match: electronic signatures in global and national commerce act
terms.gloss: The federal E-SIGN Act (2000): gives electronic records and signatures the same legal effect as paper ones, when a person adopts them with intent to sign.

terms.label: electronic signature
terms.gloss: Under E-SIGN, a sound, symbol, or process attached to an electronic record and adopted by a person with intent to sign it.

terms.label: electronic record
terms.gloss: Information created or stored electronically, such as an audio file or email.

terms.label: judicial stipulation
terms.gloss: A binding agreement or admission parties make formally in court, such as a settlement stated on the record under oath.

terms.label: memorandum (statute of frauds)
terms.gloss: A signed writing, even an informal note or check, that records an agreement's essential terms and so satisfies the statute of frauds.

terms.label: Suez Canal cases
terms.gloss: Cases holding that the 1956-57 closure of the Suez Canal did not excuse shipping contracts, because the longer route around Africa's Cape of Good Hope remained available.

terms.label: contingency
terms.gloss: A possible future event. An unforeseen contingency is one the parties did not anticipate or allocate risk for in their contract.

terms.label: rate recovery
terms.gloss: A regulated utility's ability to pass costs on to customers through the rates its regulators approve.

terms.label: Atomic Energy Commission (AEC)
terms.gloss: The federal agency (1946-1974) that both promoted and regulated civilian nuclear power; its duties then passed to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and an energy-research agency.

terms.label: Nuclear Waste Policy Act of 1982
terms.gloss: The 1982 federal law making the national government responsible for building permanent storage for spent nuclear fuel, paid for by fees on utilities.

terms.label: code of fair competition (Petroleum Code)
terms.gloss: Under the National Industrial Recovery Act, industry-wide rules on production, prices, and labor approved by the President and enforceable as law.

terms.label: unfair trade practice
terms.gloss: Business conduct that a law or industry code declares unfair to competitors or consumers, such as the oil code's label for producing above assigned quotas.

terms.label: embargo
terms.gloss: A government ban on trade with certain places or in certain goods.

terms.label: The Brig Aurora
terms.gloss: The Brig Aurora (1813): upheld a law letting the President revive a trade embargo once he found a fact Congress had specified.

terms.label: Field v. Clark
terms.gloss: Field v. Clark (1892): upheld letting the President suspend tariff exemptions upon finding that foreign countries' duties were unequal, treating him as a fact-finder, not lawmaker.

terms.label: Martin v. Mott
terms.gloss: Martin v. Mott (1827): the President's decision that an emergency justified calling out the militia was conclusive; courts presume he found the required facts.

terms.label: inventory plaintiffs
terms.gloss: People who had already filed asbestos claims through the class lawyers; their cases were settled separately from the class settlement.

terms.label: attorney-client relationship
terms.gloss: The formal relationship in which a lawyer agrees to represent a client, owing that client loyalty and care.

terms.label: enhanced risk
terms.gloss: A claim for compensation because exposure raised one's chance of developing a disease later, though no disease has yet appeared.

terms.label: exposure-only
terms.gloss: Describes class members who had been exposed to asbestos but had not yet developed any illness from it.

terms.label: manageability (trial management)
terms.gloss: Rule 23(b)(3)(D)'s concern with whether a class case could practically be tried; it drops out when a class is formed only to settle.

terms.label: logically antecedent
terms.gloss: Something that must be decided first because other questions depend on its answer.

terms.label: on-sale bar
terms.gloss: The patent rule that an invention cannot be patented if it was sold or offered for sale more than one year before the patent application.

terms.label: experimental use
terms.gloss: An exception to the on-sale bar for sales or uses made mainly to test and perfect an invention rather than to profit from it.

terms.label: § 1338(a)
terms.gloss: 28 U.S.C. § 1338(a): gives federal courts jurisdiction over cases arising under patent law and makes it exclusive, so state courts cannot hear them.

terms.label: case within a case
terms.gloss: In a legal-malpractice suit, proving the client would have won the original case if the lawyer had acted properly, by in effect retrying it.

terms.label: Grable
terms.gloss: Grable & Sons v. Darue Engineering (2005): set the test for when a state-law claim 'arises under' federal law because it turns on a substantial, disputed federal issue.

terms.label: subsistence allowance
terms.gloss: The part of a worker's wages a statute protects from garnishment so the worker can live on it.

terms.label: release bond
terms.gloss: Money or a surety's promise posted with the court so that seized property is released while the case continues.

terms.label: summary affirmance
terms.gloss: An appeals court decision upholding a lower court without full briefing, argument, or a written explanation.

terms.label: summary action
terms.gloss: Government action, such as a seizure, taken immediately without a prior hearing, allowed only in emergencies or special situations.

terms.label: adequate state ground
terms.gloss: The rule that the U.S. Supreme Court will not review a state-court decision that rests on a state-law basis sufficient by itself to support the result.

terms.label: Atomic Energy Act
terms.gloss: The 1954 federal law comprehensively regulating civilian nuclear materials and facilities, administered at first by the Atomic Energy Commission.

terms.label: effluent
terms.gloss: Waste liquid or gas discharged into the environment from a plant or facility.

terms.label: Federal Water Pollution Control Act
terms.gloss: The main federal water-pollution law, rewritten in 1972 and later called the Clean Water Act; it forbids discharging pollutants into navigable waters without a permit.

terms.label: source, special nuclear, and byproduct materials
terms.gloss: Atomic Energy Act categories: uranium and thorium ores (source), enriched uranium and plutonium (special nuclear), and radioactive materials produced by nuclear processes (byproduct).

terms.label: Nuclear Regulatory Commission
terms.gloss: The independent federal agency created in 1974 that took over the AEC's licensing and safety regulation of civilian nuclear power.

terms.label: interpretive aids
terms.gloss: Sources beyond a statute's words, such as committee reports and floor debates, used to work out its meaning.

terms.label: notwithstanding clause
terms.gloss: Statutory wording such as 'notwithstanding any other provision of law', making a provision override conflicting laws.

terms.label: reorganization plan
terms.gloss: A presidential plan, under authority from Congress, restructuring executive agencies; Reorganization Plan No. 3 of 1970 created EPA.

terms.label: Northern States Power v. Minnesota
terms.gloss: A 1971 federal appeals decision, affirmed by the Supreme Court in 1972, holding that federal law preempted Minnesota's stricter limits on nuclear-plant radioactive discharges.

terms.label: Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA)
terms.gloss: The 1976 federal law giving EPA power to regulate chemicals, including a specific ban and cleanup regime for PCBs.

terms.label: hardship (ripeness)
terms.gloss: The ripeness question whether delaying court review would seriously harm the party challenging an agency action.

terms.label: informal hearing
terms.gloss: A hearing at which interested people can present their views orally, which TSCA requires before EPA issues certain rules.

terms.label: noncitizen
terms.gloss: A person who is not a citizen of the United States.

terms.label: removal period
terms.gloss: The 90-day period after a final deportation order during which immigration law directs the government to detain and remove the person.

terms.label: detention
terms.gloss: Holding a person in government custody, for example while immigration proceedings are pending or before deportation.

terms.label: Linda R. S. v. Richard D.
match: linda r. s. v. richard d.
terms.gloss: Linda R. S. v. Richard D. (1973): a mother lacked standing to force prosecution of her child's father for unpaid support; private citizens lack a cognizable interest in another's prosecution.

terms.label: nonreviewability
terms.gloss: The principle that some government decisions are not subject to court review at all.

terms.label: § 1252(f)(1)
terms.gloss: An immigration-law provision barring lower federal courts from ordering officials to stop carrying out certain removal provisions, except for individual noncitizens.

terms.label: universal vacatur
terms.gloss: A court's setting aside of a rule or policy entirely, for everyone, not just for the parties who sued.

terms.label: Castle Rock
terms.gloss: Town of Castle Rock v. Gonzales (2005): a woman had no due-process property interest in police enforcement of her restraining order.

terms.label: detainer
terms.gloss: A request from one authority, such as immigration officers, asking a jail or prison to hold a person, or give notice before release, so it can take custody.

terms.label: recidivism
terms.gloss: Repeat offending; committing new crimes or violations after an earlier one.

terms.label: suspending and dispensing powers
terms.gloss: The English king's claimed powers to suspend laws entirely or excuse individuals from obeying them; the 1689 English Bill of Rights condemned them as illegal.

terms.label: prime broker
terms.gloss: A firm that provides a hedge fund with bundled services such as holding its assets, settling trades, and lending.

terms.label: antifraud provisions
terms.gloss: Securities-law provisions banning false statements or misleading omissions of important facts in selling securities or advising investors.

terms.label: Investment Advisers Act of 1940
terms.gloss: The federal law regulating people paid to give investment advice, including banning advisers from defrauding clients.

terms.label: initial decision
terms.gloss: An administrative law judge's first ruling in an agency case, which the agency's leadership can then review, adopt, or change.

terms.label: double for-cause protection
terms.gloss: An official removable only for good cause by another official who is also removable only for good cause; the Supreme Court held this unconstitutional in 2010.

terms.label: common-law fraud
terms.gloss: The traditional court-made claim for knowingly false statements of fact that another person relies on to their harm.

terms.label: core bankruptcy proceeding
terms.gloss: A matter central to administering a bankruptcy case, which a bankruptcy judge may finally decide.

terms.label: Atlas Roofing
terms.gloss: Atlas Roofing Co. v. OSHRC (1977): Congress may assign new statutory 'public rights' cases, such as workplace-safety penalties, to an agency without a jury.

terms.label: vice-admiralty courts
terms.gloss: British colonial courts that tried trade and customs cases without juries, a grievance listed in the Declaration of Independence.

terms.label: Crowell
terms.gloss: Crowell v. Benson (1932): allowed an agency to find facts in some disputes between private parties, subject to court review.

terms.label: Murray’s Lessee
terms.gloss: Murray's Lessee v. Hoboken Land & Improvement Co. (1856): an early public-rights case allowing the government to collect a debt from a customs collector without a court trial.

terms.label: proprietary capacity
terms.gloss: The government acting like a private party, such as an owner or contractor, rather than as sovereign lawmaker or law enforcer.

terms.label: postmaster
terms.gloss: The official in charge of a local post office; first-class postmasters ran the largest offices and were appointed by the President with Senate consent.

terms.label: supplemental petition
terms.gloss: A filing that adds facts or claims based on events after the original complaint was filed.

terms.label: confession of error
terms.gloss: The government's formal admission to an appeals court that a lower-court ruling in its favor was wrong.

terms.label: Executive Vesting Clause
terms.gloss: Article II's first sentence: 'The executive Power shall be vested in a President.' Taft read it as granting real powers, including removal.

terms.label: rider
terms.gloss: A provision attached to a bill on a different subject, often a funding bill, so the President must accept it to get the rest.

terms.label: United States v. Perkins
terms.gloss: United States v. Perkins (1886): when Congress gives a department head power to appoint an inferior officer, it may limit that head's power to remove the officer.

terms.label: Marbury
terms.gloss: Marbury v. Madison (1803): the Supreme Court case establishing judicial review; it also said an officer appointed for a fixed term had a vested right to his commission.

terms.label: royal prerogative
terms.gloss: Powers the English Crown held by tradition rather than by act of Parliament.

terms.label: spoils system
terms.gloss: The practice of handing government jobs to political supporters and firing the other party's appointees after elections.

terms.label: clerk of superior court
terms.gloss: The clerk of a North Carolina county's trial court (the superior court), an official with power to receive certain resignations and fill vacancies.

terms.label: oath of office
terms.gloss: The formal promise an official swears on taking office, a step needed to begin serving.

terms.label: duty to mitigate
terms.gloss: After the other side breaches, the injured party cannot recover for losses it could reasonably have avoided, such as costs of continuing unwanted work.

terms.label: countermand
terms.gloss: To cancel or withdraw an order or offer before it is acted on.

terms.label: acceptance by conduct
terms.gloss: Accepting an offer by doing something rather than saying something; it works when the offer invites it and the act clearly signals agreement.

terms.label: Restatement § 45
terms.gloss: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 45: if an offer can be accepted only by full performance, starting performance keeps the offer from being revoked while the offeree finishes.

terms.label: Restatement § 62
terms.gloss: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 62: if an offer allows acceptance by promise or by performance, beginning performance counts as acceptance and implies a promise to finish.

terms.label: fitness (ripeness)
terms.gloss: In deciding whether a challenge is ripe, whether the issue is ready for a court now, usually because it is mainly legal and needs no further facts.

terms.label: prudential limits
terms.gloss: Limits on who may sue that courts have created themselves, beyond the Constitution's minimum requirements, such as the usual bar on asserting other people's rights.

terms.label: reprocessing (nuclear fuel)
terms.gloss: Chemically treating used nuclear fuel to recover its still-valuable uranium and plutonium, which also reduces the waste left to store.

terms.label: reracking
terms.gloss: Replacing the storage racks in a nuclear plant's spent-fuel pool with denser ones, so more used fuel can be kept on site.

terms.label: service mark
terms.gloss: Like a trademark, but identifying a business's services (such as restaurant services) rather than physical goods.

terms.label: trade dress
terms.gloss: The distinctive look of a product or its packaging (shape, colors, design) that identifies its source and is protected like a trademark.

terms.label: trade-secret misappropriation
terms.gloss: Wrongfully taking or using a business's confidential information, such as formulas or methods, that gives it a competitive edge.

terms.label: pendent appellate jurisdiction
terms.gloss: An appeals court's discretionary power to decide an issue not otherwise appealable yet because it is closely tied to an issue properly on immediate appeal.

terms.label: exclusive of interest and costs
terms.gloss: The amount counted for federal jurisdiction leaves out interest and court costs; only the value of the claim itself counts.

terms.label: separate and distinct claims
terms.gloss: Claims by different people that each rest on their own rights; for federal jurisdiction, each must meet the dollar threshold on its own.

terms.label: spurious class action
terms.gloss: Under the pre-1966 Rule 23, a class suit joining people with separate claims that shared a common question; it worked like ordinary joinder.

terms.label: permissive joinder
terms.gloss: Allowing, but not requiring, several parties to join in one suit because their claims arise from the same events and share a common question.

terms.label: Snyder v. Harris
terms.gloss: Snyder v. Harris (1969): class members cannot add their separate claims together to meet the federal amount-in-controversy requirement.

terms.label: Clark v. Paul Gray
terms.gloss: Clark v. Paul Gray, Inc. (1939): each plaintiff with a separate claim must meet the jurisdictional amount; those who fall short are dismissed.

terms.label: Supreme Tribe of Ben-Hur v. Cauble
terms.gloss: Supreme Tribe of Ben-Hur v. Cauble (1921): in a class action, only the named representatives' citizenship counts for diversity jurisdiction.

terms.label: permission to sue (right-to-sue notice)
terms.gloss: The EEOC's notice that a worker may now go to court; a Title VII suit normally cannot be filed without it.

terms.label: across-the-board class
terms.gloss: A former Fifth Circuit practice letting one employee who suffered discrimination represent a class attacking all of an employer's discriminatory practices, even different ones.

terms.label: intentional discrimination
terms.gloss: Deliberately treating someone worse because of a protected trait (also called disparate treatment), as opposed to a neutral policy with unequal effects.

terms.label: affirmative action
terms.gloss: Here, court-ordered changes requiring an employer to take positive steps, such as revised recruiting or hiring, to remedy past discrimination.

terms.label: Burdine
terms.gloss: Texas Dept. of Community Affairs v. Burdine (1981), setting how the burden of proof shifts between worker and employer in intentional-discrimination cases.

terms.label: final judgment on the merits
terms.gloss: A court's conclusive decision on the substance of the claims, not a dismissal on a technicality; only such judgments bar later suits.

terms.label: actually and necessarily determined
terms.gloss: The core test for issue preclusion: the issue was genuinely contested and decided, and the earlier judgment depended on that decision.

terms.label: federal (intergovernmental) immunity
terms.gloss: The constitutional rule that states may not tax the federal government directly or discriminate against it or those who deal with it.

terms.label: Commissioner v. Sunnen
terms.gloss: Commissioner v. Sunnen (1948): collateral estoppel does not apply in tax cases when the controlling legal principles have significantly changed since the first case.

terms.label: United States v. Moser
terms.gloss: United States v. Moser (1924): applied preclusion against the government, while noting that a pure ruling of law may be reargued in later suits on unrelated claims.

terms.label: administrative remedy
terms.gloss: A way to get relief from a government agency itself, such as a refund procedure, rather than from a court.

terms.label: import agent
terms.gloss: A middleman who arranges overseas purchases for a buyer for a fee, without buying and reselling the goods itself.

terms.label: conforming goods
terms.gloss: To meet the contract's description and specifications; goods that do are 'conforming', and buyers may reject goods that do not.

terms.label: debit memorandum
terms.gloss: A notice a buyer sends its supplier deducting amounts, for example for defective goods, from what the buyer owes or billing the supplier for them.

terms.label: passage of title
terms.gloss: The moment legal ownership of goods transfers from seller to buyer, which can decide where a sale legally happened and who bears risks.

terms.label: UCC §§ 2-714 and 2-715
terms.gloss: UCC provisions letting a buyer who kept defective goods recover for the defect (2-714), plus incidental and consequential damages (2-715).

terms.label: accepting buyer
terms.gloss: Under the UCC, a buyer who kept the goods instead of rejecting them; it can still recover damages for defects if it gives timely notice.

terms.label: natural and probable consequence
terms.gloss: The traditional test (from Hadley v. Baxendale) allowing damages only for losses that ordinarily follow a breach or that both sides could foresee.

terms.label: reasonable (fair) certainty
terms.gloss: The rule that lost profits must be proved by evidence giving a rational basis for the amount, not left to speculation.

terms.label: thrift (savings and loan)
terms.gloss: A savings and loan association or savings bank: an institution that mainly takes deposits and makes home mortgage loans.

terms.label: FSLIC
match: federal savings and loan insurance corporation
terms.gloss: The former federal agency that insured deposits at savings and loans; Congress abolished it in 1989.

terms.label: liquidate
terms.gloss: To shut down an insolvent institution and sell off its assets to pay its debts.

terms.label: supervisory merger
terms.gloss: A regulator-arranged takeover in which a healthy buyer absorbed a failing thrift, often in return for federal help and favorable accounting.

terms.label: supervisory goodwill
terms.gloss: The amount by which a buyer's price for a failing thrift exceeded the fair value of its assets, which regulators let the buyer count as capital.

terms.label: purchase accounting
terms.gloss: A merger accounting method that records the acquired company's assets at fair value and books any extra price paid as goodwill.

terms.label: capital requirements
terms.gloss: Rules requiring a bank or thrift to keep a minimum cushion of its own funds (capital) relative to its assets; 'tangible' and 'core' capital are categories that count toward it.

terms.label: capital credit
terms.gloss: A regulator's agreement to count federal assistance toward an institution's capital, helping it meet capital requirements.

terms.label: generally accepted accounting principles
terms.gloss: The standard rules accountants use for financial statements; regulators' own accounting rules for thrifts could differ from them.

terms.label: recapitalization
terms.gloss: Raising new money, for example from investors, to restore an institution's capital.

terms.label: Court of Federal Claims
terms.gloss: The federal court that hears money claims against the United States, including contract claims; it was earlier called the Claims Court.

terms.label: reserved-powers doctrine
terms.gloss: The doctrine that a government cannot contract away essential sovereign powers, such as the power to legislate, so such promises are unenforceable.

terms.label: express delegation
terms.gloss: The argument that an agency may surrender a sovereign power by contract only if Congress expressly authorized it to do so.

terms.label: sovereign power
terms.gloss: The government's inherent authority to govern, including making and changing laws.

terms.label: public and general (act)
terms.gloss: The sovereign-acts test: the government may use the defense only for a broad law aimed at the public, not one targeted at relieving it of its own contracts.

terms.label: Bank Board
terms.gloss: The Federal Home Loan Bank Board, the agency that then regulated savings and loans and oversaw the FSLIC.

terms.label: payable against documents
terms.gloss: Payment due when the seller hands over the shipping documents (bill of lading, insurance, invoice), not when the goods arrive.

terms.label: Law Lords
terms.gloss: The senior judges who sat in the House of Lords as the United Kingdom's highest court.

terms.label: Sale of Goods Act
terms.gloss: The English statute (1893) codifying the law on sales of goods, including the seller's duty to arrange reasonable carriage.

terms.label: deposited in court
