terms.gloss: Money paid into the court's custody while a dispute is pending, to be released to whichever side wins.

terms.label: land contract
terms.gloss: A purchase of land paid in installments to the seller, who keeps legal title until the full price is paid.

terms.label: recordable restriction
terms.gloss: A limit on land use put in a form that can be filed in public land records, so later buyers have notice and may be bound.

terms.label: subsequent purchasers
terms.gloss: Later buyers of the land; a restriction binds them only if property-law rules make it 'run with the land', not merely as a contract between the original parties.

terms.label: disproportionate hardship
terms.gloss: A ground for equity to refuse specific enforcement: compliance would burden the defendant far more than it would benefit the plaintiff.

terms.label: judgment roll
terms.gloss: The official file of pleadings, findings, and judgment; an appeal on it alone argues only that the findings do not support the judgment.

terms.label: affirmed as modified
terms.gloss: The appeals court changed part of the judgment (here, reducing the amount) and upheld the rest.

terms.label: Department One
terms.gloss: One of the panels into which the California Supreme Court then divided its justices to hear cases.

terms.label: representation determination
terms.gloss: The NLRB's decision about which workers form a bargaining unit and may vote on a union; it cannot be appealed directly to a court.

terms.label: enforcement (of an NLRB order)
terms.gloss: The NLRB cannot enforce its own orders; it asks a federal court of appeals to order compliance.

terms.label: Adjournment Clause
terms.gloss: Constitutional provisions on congressional breaks: neither house may adjourn more than three days without the other's consent, and a bill can be pocket-vetoed during an adjournment.

terms.label: Attorney General opinion
terms.gloss: A formal legal opinion by the U.S. Attorney General advising the President or agencies; persuasive, but not binding on courts.

terms.label: Pay Act
terms.gloss: A federal law limiting salary payments to certain recess appointees, which assumes recess appointments can occur in various situations.

terms.label: NLRB v. Noel Canning
terms.gloss: NLRB v. Noel Canning (2014): recess appointments may be made during intrasession recesses of ten days or more, but not during pro forma sessions.

terms.label: proposed rule
terms.gloss: A draft regulation an agency publishes for public comment before deciding whether to adopt it as a final rule.

terms.label: appropriations
terms.gloss: Money Congress allots by law for government spending; appropriations laws can also forbid an agency from spending on certain things.

terms.label: APA § 706(1)
terms.gloss: The APA provision directing courts to 'compel agency action unlawfully withheld or unreasonably delayed'.

terms.label: APA § 706(2)
terms.gloss: The APA provision directing courts to set aside agency actions that are arbitrary, unlawful, or made without required procedures.

terms.label: approved state plan (OSHA § 18)
terms.gloss: Under § 18 of the OSH Act, a state may run its own workplace-safety program if it is federally approved as at least as effective as federal standards.

terms.label: unreasonable delay
terms.gloss: Agency foot-dragging that a court may remedy under APA § 706(1) by ordering the agency to act.

terms.label: Michigan Franchise Investment Law
terms.gloss: A Michigan statute regulating the sale of franchises and protecting franchisees, for example against misrepresentation.

terms.label: direct appeal (to the Supreme Court)
terms.gloss: An appeal the Supreme Court was required to hear, unlike discretionary certiorari review; Congress almost entirely abolished these in 1988.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 1254(2)
terms.gloss: A former provision (eliminated in 1988) giving a right of appeal to the Supreme Court when a federal appeals court held a state statute unconstitutional.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 2103
terms.gloss: The statute, as then in force, letting the Supreme Court treat a mistakenly filed appeal as a petition for certiorari.

terms.label: jurisdictional statement
terms.gloss: The document that began a direct appeal to the Supreme Court, explaining why the Court had jurisdiction and should hear the case.

terms.label: random and attenuated contacts
terms.gloss: Chance or remote connections to a state that the defendant did not deliberately create; not enough for jurisdiction.

terms.label: transfer (of venue)
terms.gloss: Moving a case to a more convenient federal court under the change-of-venue statute, rather than dismissing it.

terms.label: petition for hearing
terms.gloss: The request (now called a petition for review) asking the California Supreme Court to take a case.

terms.label: extraordinary relief
terms.gloss: Immediate review of a trial-court ruling through a special writ such as mandate, instead of waiting for an ordinary appeal after final judgment.

terms.label: initial disclosures
terms.gloss: Information each side must give the other early in a federal case without being asked, such as relevant parties, witnesses, and documents.

terms.label: Federal Rule 15(c)
terms.gloss: Federal rule letting an amended pleading 'relate back' to the original filing date; changing a defendant requires timely notice and a mistake about identity.

terms.label: mistake (about a party’s identity)
terms.gloss: Under Rule 15(c), a misunderstanding about who the proper defendant was, including a deliberate choice made on a mistaken view of the parties' roles.

terms.label: undue delay
terms.gloss: Unjustified lateness in asking for something, such as permission to amend, which can justify denying the request.

terms.label: Nelson v. Adams USA
terms.gloss: Nelson v. Adams USA (2000): a party added after judgment to collect fees, not because of an original mistake, got no relation back.

terms.label: Telecommunications Act of 1996
terms.gloss: Federal law that sought to open local phone markets to competition, requiring incumbent carriers to share their networks with new entrants.

terms.label: incumbent carriers
terms.gloss: The established regional local-phone companies (the 'Baby Bells') that held monopolies before 1996.

terms.label: parallel conduct
terms.gloss: Competitors acting alike, such as staying out of each other's markets, without proof they agreed to; alone it does not prove an antitrust conspiracy.

terms.label: concerted action (antitrust)
terms.gloss: Action taken by agreement among two or more firms, which Sherman Act § 1 requires, as opposed to independent decisions.

terms.label: market allocation
terms.gloss: An agreement among competitors to divide territories or customers so they do not compete with each other; illegal under antitrust law.

terms.label: Conley v. Gibson
terms.gloss: Conley v. Gibson (1957), which said a complaint survives unless 'no set of facts' could support it; Twombly retired that phrase.

terms.label: forfeiture
terms.gloss: Losing a right, here the lease, as the penalty for breaking one of its conditions.

terms.label: exclusive right
terms.gloss: A right that belongs to one party alone, so no one else may exercise it; here, a claimed sole right to sell soft drinks in the building.

terms.label: oral agreement
terms.gloss: An agreement made in spoken words rather than in a signed writing.

terms.label: fraud, accident, or mistake
terms.gloss: Traditional equitable grounds for correcting (reforming) or setting aside a written contract that does not state the real agreement.

terms.label: building permit
terms.gloss: Official approval required before constructing or altering a building.

terms.label: abate
terms.gloss: To stop or put an end to something, here a use that violated zoning.

terms.label: Swinton v. Whitinsville Savings Bank
terms.gloss: Swinton v. Whitinsville Savings Bank (Mass. 1942): a seller had no duty to disclose hidden termites; the classic rule that bare silence is not fraud.

terms.label: half-truth (partial disclosure)
terms.gloss: A statement that is literally true but misleading because it leaves out facts needed to avoid a false impression; the law treats it like a lie.

terms.label: representations
terms.gloss: Statements of fact one party makes to persuade another to enter a deal; false ones can support fraud or rescission.

terms.label: articles of agreement
terms.gloss: A written contract setting out the parties' terms in numbered clauses.

terms.label: partnership deed
terms.gloss: A formal sealed document creating a business partnership and setting its terms.

terms.label: security (for payment)
terms.gloss: Something that guarantees payment, such as a surety's promise, a bond, or a claim on property, so the creditor can collect if the debtor defaults.

terms.label: sealing and delivery
terms.gloss: The old formalities for executing a deed: sealing it and handing it over, which made it binding.

terms.label: action of debt
terms.gloss: An old common-law form of lawsuit to recover a fixed sum owed; here Kingston used it to sue on the agreement.

terms.label: concurrent conditions
terms.gloss: Duties to be performed at the same time, like payment and delivery; a party ready and offering to perform may sue if the other refuses.

terms.label: Lord Mansfield
terms.gloss: William Murray, Chief Justice of the King's Bench from 1756 to 1788, the English judge who did much to shape modern commercial and contract law.

terms.label: preliminary examination
terms.gloss: A hearing after a criminal charge where a judge decides whether there is probable cause to send the case to trial.

terms.label: bound over
terms.gloss: Ordered to stand trial after a preliminary examination found enough evidence.

terms.label: information (criminal charge)
terms.gloss: A formal criminal charge filed by a prosecutor rather than by grand jury indictment.

terms.label: carrying concealed weapons
terms.gloss: The crime of carrying a hidden weapon on one's person or in a vehicle without legal authorization.

terms.label: enumeration (statutory list)
terms.gloss: The specific items a statute lists by name.

terms.label: McBoyle v. United States
terms.gloss: McBoyle v. United States (1931): a federal law on stolen 'motor vehicles' did not cover airplanes, read in light of the listed land vehicles.

terms.label: did not sit / participate
terms.gloss: Took no part in hearing or deciding the case.

terms.label: census
terms.gloss: The constitutionally required count of every person in the country, taken every ten years.

terms.label: apportionment
terms.gloss: Dividing House of Representatives seats among the states according to population counted in the census.

terms.label: citizen voting-age population
terms.gloss: The number of adult citizens in an area, used to judge whether districts dilute minority votes under the Voting Rights Act.

terms.label: Enumeration Clause
terms.gloss: The constitutional provision (Art. I, § 2) requiring an 'actual Enumeration' of the population every ten years as Congress directs.

terms.label: Census Act
terms.gloss: The federal statute directing how the Commerce Secretary runs the census, including using records and reporting planned questions to Congress.

terms.label: extra-record discovery
terms.gloss: Gathering evidence beyond the agency's official record, such as testimony from officials; allowed only on a strong showing of bad faith.

terms.label: contemporaneous record
terms.gloss: The reasons and documents an agency produced when it decided, not justifications created later for litigation.

terms.label: Census Act § 6(c)
terms.gloss: Census Act provision telling the Secretary to use existing administrative records, where possible, instead of asking direct questions.

terms.label: Census Act § 141(f)
terms.gloss: Census Act provision requiring the Secretary to report planned census subjects and questions to Congress years in advance.

terms.label: manageable standard
terms.gloss: Legal criteria clear enough for judges to apply; without them a matter may be unreviewable.

terms.label: Bureau of Land Management
terms.gloss: The Interior Department agency that manages most federal public lands, mainly in the West.

terms.label: multiple use and sustained yield
terms.gloss: The mandate to manage public lands for many uses at once (recreation, grazing, minerals, wildlife) while keeping their resources productive over time.

terms.label: wilderness study area
terms.gloss: Federal land found to have wilderness qualities, managed to preserve them until Congress decides whether to designate it as wilderness.

terms.label: nonimpairment
terms.gloss: FLPMA's command to manage study areas so as not to impair their suitability for designation as wilderness.

terms.label: supplementation (NEPA)
terms.gloss: Preparing an updated environmental analysis when significant new information arises while a federal action is still underway.

terms.label: APA § 551(13)
terms.gloss: The APA's definition of 'agency action': a rule, order, license, sanction, relief, or the equivalent, or a denial of these, or a failure to act.

terms.label: discrete agency action
terms.gloss: A specific, identifiable act, such as issuing a particular rule, that § 706(1) requires, as opposed to broad program-wide failings.

terms.label: programmatic attack
terms.gloss: A lawsuit challenging an agency's overall running of a program instead of specific decisions; courts generally reject these under the APA.

terms.label: Lujan v. National Wildlife Federation
terms.gloss: 1990 Supreme Court case refusing to let challengers attack the BLM's whole land-management program instead of specific actions.

terms.label: land-use plan
terms.gloss: A BLM document setting long-term goals and permitted uses for an area of public land.

terms.label: implementation decision
terms.gloss: A specific on-the-ground agency choice carrying out a plan, such as closing a route, as distinct from approving the plan itself.

terms.label: Marsh v. Oregon Natural Resources Council
match: marsh v. oregon natural resources council
terms.gloss: Marsh v. Oregon Natural Resources Council (1989): agencies must take a hard look at significant new information while a project, there a dam, is still underway.

terms.label: Ohio Forestry Ass’n v. Sierra Club
terms.gloss: Ohio Forestry Ass'n v. Sierra Club (1998): a challenge to a forest plan was not ripe until specific actions were taken under it.

terms.label: categorical exclusion
terms.gloss: Categories of agency actions found to have no significant environmental effect, so they skip detailed NEPA review.

terms.label: administrative appeal
terms.gloss: Asking a higher authority within the agency to review a decision before going to court.

terms.label: Federal Power Commission
terms.gloss: The federal agency, replaced in 1977 by FERC, that regulated interstate natural-gas pipelines and electricity.

terms.label: curtailment
terms.gloss: Cutting back gas deliveries to some customers during a shortage, under a plan ranking who loses service first.

terms.label: end-use priorities
terms.gloss: Ranking customers by what they use gas for, such as home heating versus industrial boiler fuel, rather than by their contract rights.

terms.label: interruptible service
terms.gloss: Service sold on the condition that the supplier may cut it off when supplies are short.

terms.label: Natural Gas Act § 19(b)
terms.gloss: The Natural Gas Act provision letting a party harmed by a Commission order petition a court of appeals for review.

terms.label: Natural Gas Act §§ 4 and 5 proceedings
terms.gloss: Natural Gas Act procedures: in § 4 cases the pipeline files and must prove its plan reasonable; in § 5 cases the Commission or a complainant starts and bears the burden.

terms.label: pre-enforcement review
terms.gloss: Challenging a rule in court before the agency applies or enforces it against the challenger.

terms.label: hardship (ripeness)
terms.gloss: The ripeness question whether delaying court review would seriously harm the challenger now, for example by forcing costly changes.

terms.label: CBS v. United States
terms.gloss: Columbia Broadcasting System v. United States (1942) allowed immediate review of FCC regulations that directly disrupted broadcasters' contracts.

terms.label: contract abrogation
terms.gloss: Government action cancelling or overriding existing private contracts.

terms.label: WARN Act
match: worker adjustment and retraining notification act
terms.gloss: 1988 federal law requiring larger employers to give 60 days' notice before plant closings or mass layoffs, with backpay owed for violations.

terms.label: plant closing
terms.gloss: Under WARN, shutting down a site or unit in a way that costs 50 or more workers their jobs.

terms.label: mass layoff
terms.gloss: Under WARN, a large layoff at one site without a full closing (generally at least 50 workers forming a third of the workforce, or 500).

terms.label: North Star Steel Co. v. Thomas
terms.gloss: North Star Steel Co. v. Thomas (1995), a WARN Act case about the filing deadline that recognized unions among the permitted plaintiffs.

terms.label: exclusive representation
terms.gloss: The labor-law rule that a union chosen by a majority represents all workers in the unit, and the employer must deal with it alone.

terms.label: adversity (adverseness)
terms.gloss: The requirement that opposing parties have real stakes and argue each side vigorously, which Article III cases need.

terms.label: collective-bargaining representative
terms.gloss: The union chosen by workers to negotiate wages and conditions with the employer on behalf of all of them.

terms.label: construction permit / operating license
terms.gloss: The two separate nuclear approvals: one to build a reactor and, later, one to run it.

terms.label: Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards
terms.gloss: A statutory panel of experts that reviews the safety of proposed nuclear reactors and advises the Commission.

terms.label: licensing board
terms.gloss: Panels of the nuclear agency that hold trial-like hearings on license applications.

terms.label: Appeal Board
terms.gloss: A review body inside an organization that hears appeals from a first-level decision, here in the nuclear agency or in a trade association's arbitration.

terms.label: fuel cycle
terms.gloss: The stages of nuclear fuel's life, from mining through reprocessing to waste disposal.

terms.label: generic rulemaking
terms.gloss: Deciding a recurring issue once, by a rule that applies to all cases, instead of relitigating it in each license hearing.

terms.label: cost-benefit analysis
terms.gloss: Weighing a project's expected costs, including environmental harms, against its benefits.

terms.label: contentions (licensing)
terms.gloss: In nuclear licensing, specific issues an intervenor formally raises for the board to decide; they must be adequately supported.

terms.label: reissued patent
terms.gloss: A corrected replacement patent granted after the owner surrenders the original because of a fixable error, such as a defective description of the invention.

terms.label: specification (patent)
terms.gloss: The written part of a patent that describes the invention and how to make and use it.

terms.label: prior use (patent defense)
terms.gloss: A patent defense that others were already using the invention before the patent holder claimed it, so it was not new and the patent is invalid.

terms.label: trial error
terms.gloss: A legal mistake made during a trial, such as admitting improper evidence, that can overturn a conviction without any finding that the defendant is innocent.

terms.label: postconviction proceedings
terms.gloss: A separate case, after the ordinary appeal is over, in which a convicted person asks a court to set the conviction aside.

terms.label: Exoneration Act (Colorado, 2013)
terms.gloss: Colorado's 2013 law compensating people imprisoned for a felony who prove, by clear and convincing evidence, that they were actually innocent.

terms.label: Medina test
terms.gloss: From Medina v. California (1992): a state criminal-procedure rule violates due process only if it offends a deeply rooted, fundamental principle of justice, judged largely by history.

terms.label: survivors (wrongful-death claimants)
terms.gloss: Family members whom the law allows to sue for losses caused by a relative's death.

terms.label: consumer-protection laws
terms.gloss: Statutes, usually state laws, that forbid unfair or deceptive business practices and let harmed consumers sue.

terms.label: redhibition
terms.gloss: A Louisiana civil-law claim letting a buyer undo a sale, or get the price reduced, because the thing sold had a hidden defect.

terms.label: Eisen v. Carlisle & Jacquelin
terms.gloss: A 1974 Supreme Court class-action case, often read as forbidding judges to decide certification based on who is likely to win on the merits.

terms.label: precedential force
terms.gloss: The power of a court decision to bind later courts. A vacated (cancelled) opinion has none.

terms.label: immaturity (immature tort)
terms.gloss: Lack of a track record: a new kind of injury claim that has not been tried individually enough for courts to know how proof and outcomes typically go.

terms.label: bifurcation
terms.gloss: Splitting one case into separate trials for different issues, such as liability first and damages later.

terms.label: exclusions (opt-outs)
terms.gloss: Class members who asked to be left out of the settlement, keeping their right to sue on their own.

terms.label: statutory notice to state attorneys general
terms.gloss: Under the Class Action Fairness Act, defendants must notify state and federal officials of a proposed class settlement so they can object.

terms.label: average wholesale price (AWP)
terms.gloss: A published list price for a drug that Medicare and insurers used to set reimbursement. It could sit far above what doctors actually paid.

terms.label: Medicare Part B
terms.gloss: The part of the federal Medicare health program for older and disabled people that covers doctor services, including drugs given in a doctor's office.

terms.label: Medigap
terms.gloss: Private supplemental insurance that pays some or all of the share of costs Medicare leaves to the patient.

terms.label: total (comprehensive) peace
terms.gloss: A settlement that resolves every possible claim against the defendant, which is why defendants pay more for broader classes.

terms.label: ALI aggregate-litigation principles
terms.gloss: Draft recommendations from the American Law Institute on group lawsuits, persuasive to courts but not binding law.

terms.label: assigned debt
terms.gloss: A debt the original creditor transferred to someone else, here a collection agency, who can then sue to collect it.

terms.label: motion to dissolve (an attachment)
terms.gloss: A request asking the court to cancel an attachment and free the seized property.

terms.label: Sniadach v. Family Finance Corp.
terms.gloss: A 1969 Supreme Court case holding that freezing a worker's wages before any hearing on the debt violated due process.

terms.label: prejudgment claim and delivery
terms.gloss: California's procedure letting a plaintiff seize specific personal property, much like replevin, before the case is decided.

terms.label: summary measures
terms.gloss: Quick government or court action taken without a full hearing first, justified only in true emergencies.

terms.label: bankruptcy priority
terms.gloss: The order in which creditors are paid in bankruptcy. An earlier attachment can give a creditor a better place in line.

terms.label: probable-validity hearing
terms.gloss: A hearing before seizure at which the creditor must show the debt claim is probably valid.

terms.label: new Bivens context / special factors
terms.gloss: Courts extend Bivens only to situations like past Bivens cases. In a new setting, 'special factors' such as national security weigh against creating a damages remedy.

terms.label: Bell v. Wolfish
terms.gloss: A 1979 Supreme Court case: detainees awaiting trial cannot be punished, and restrictions unrelated to a legitimate goal suggest punishment.

terms.label: pretrial detainee
terms.gloss: A person held in custody who has not been convicted of anything, such as someone awaiting trial.

terms.label: Ziglar v. Abbasi
terms.gloss: The 2017 Supreme Court decision in the 9/11-detainee suit Turkmen v. Hasty, sharply limiting new Bivens damages claims, especially against senior policymakers.

terms.label: Citizenship Clause
terms.gloss: The Fourteenth Amendment's opening sentence: people born in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction are citizens.

terms.label: Nationality Act of 1940
terms.gloss: The federal law declaring who is a citizen at birth, including people born in the United States; its birthright rule is carried forward today in 8 U.S.C. § 1401.

terms.label: complete relief
terms.gloss: A remedy that fully fixes the plaintiffs' own injuries. The Court treated it as the outer limit of what a court may order.

terms.label: Grupo Mexicano v. Alliance Bond Fund
terms.gloss: A 1999 Supreme Court case: federal courts' equity powers extend only to remedies traditionally available in English equity courts around 1789.

terms.label: founding era
terms.gloss: The time the Constitution and first federal laws were adopted, around 1789, used here as the benchmark for what remedies courts may give.

terms.label: Ex parte Young
terms.gloss: A 1908 Supreme Court case allowing suits to stop state officials from enforcing unconstitutional laws, despite state sovereign immunity.

terms.label: antisuit injunction
terms.gloss: Traditional equity orders stopping a party, such as an official, from bringing an enforcement action; Ex parte Young suits were seen as this kind of relief.

terms.label: bill of peace
terms.gloss: An old English equity procedure letting one suit settle the rights of a large, united group at once; a forerunner of the class action.

terms.label: partial stay
terms.gloss: Suspending only part of a court order, here the part protecting people beyond the plaintiffs, while the rest stays in force.

terms.label: interim ruling / emergency review
terms.gloss: Temporary orders deciding who wins while a case is pending, before a final decision on the merits; the Supreme Court issues these on emergency applications.

terms.label: Civil Rights Act of 1866
terms.gloss: The first federal civil rights law, declaring persons born in the United States citizens and guaranteeing equal rights to contract and own property.

terms.label: United States v. Wong Kim Ark
terms.gloss: An 1898 Supreme Court case holding that a child born in the United States to Chinese immigrant parents was a citizen under the Citizenship Clause.

terms.label: Rule 71
terms.gloss: The federal rule letting a nonparty who benefits from a court order enforce it as if a party.

terms.label: plaintiff with standing
terms.gloss: A plaintiff legally entitled to sue because he or she suffered a concrete injury the court can remedy.

terms.label: assume a note
terms.gloss: To take over responsibility for paying someone else's promissory notes (written promises to repay debts).

terms.label: demand for performance
terms.gloss: A formal request that the other side perform; a statute here required one before a contract with no fixed deadline could support a suit for money.

terms.label: Article 2 (UCC)
terms.gloss: The part of the Uniform Commercial Code that governs contracts for the sale of goods.

terms.label: measure (of damages)
terms.gloss: The formula a court uses to calculate damages, here the contract price minus the resale price.

terms.label: installment agreement
terms.gloss: A purchase paid off in regular payments over time, usually with added credit charges.

terms.label: credit (service) charge
terms.gloss: The extra cost charged for buying on credit and paying over time, beyond the cash price.

terms.label: official comment (UCC)
terms.gloss: Explanatory notes written with the UCC by its drafters; courts use them to interpret the Code.

terms.label: Campbell Soup Co. v. Wentz
terms.gloss: A 1948 federal appeals case refusing to order farmers to perform a one-sided carrot-supply contract, cited in the UCC comment on unconscionability.

terms.label: Appellate Term
terms.gloss: A New York appeals court that hears appeals from lower-level local courts.

terms.label: net cost / reasonable profit
terms.gloss: The seller's actual costs plus a fair margin, a remedy replacing an unconscionable price.

terms.label: billing
terms.gloss: In theater, being named in a show's advertising and programs, valuable publicity for a performer's career.

terms.label: master (of a ship)
terms.gloss: The captain of a merchant ship, who hired and paid the crew.

terms.label: guinea
terms.gloss: An old British gold coin worth 21 shillings (£1 1s.), so thirty guineas equaled £31 10s.

terms.label: usage (commercial custom)
terms.gloss: An established business custom that can show what parties meant or what terms they assumed, such as how merchants treated a particular kind of note.

terms.label: entire (indivisible) contract
terms.gloss: A contract to be performed completely before any payment is earned; partial performance earns nothing under it.

terms.label: implied undertaking
terms.gloss: A promise the law infers from conduct, such as paying fair value for work accepted, rather than one stated in words.

terms.label: laws of Oléron
terms.gloss: A medieval code of sea law from the French island of Oléron, long influential on English maritime customs, including sailors' wages.

terms.label: Salkeld (reports)
terms.gloss: An early-1700s English volume of reported court decisions, compiled by William Salkeld.

terms.label: documentary-style
terms.gloss: The release's description of the film. The court read it as covering a film in the form of a factual report, even with a fictional lead character.

terms.label: denied as moot
match: denied all pending motions as moot
terms.gloss: The court did not decide the other requests because dismissing the cases made them pointless.

terms.label: license (government permit)
terms.gloss: Official government permission to do something otherwise forbidden, here to operate a dam or a radio station, for a fixed term.

terms.label: Federal Power Act
terms.gloss: The federal law under which a federal commission licenses hydroelectric dams; it gave states and cities a preference among equally qualified applicants.

terms.label: municipal preference
terms.gloss: A Federal Power Act tiebreaker favoring state and city applicants for a dam license when their plans are as good as a private company's.

terms.label: incumbent (licensee)
terms.gloss: The current license holder, here the company already running the dam and seeking renewal.

terms.label: declaratory proceeding/order
terms.gloss: An agency proceeding that settles a legal question in advance, here what the statute meant, without deciding a specific license.

terms.label: deferential standard
terms.gloss: Review in which the court upholds the agency's view if reasonable, even if the court might have chosen differently.

terms.label: Electric Consumers Protection Act of 1986
terms.gloss: A 1986 federal law that ended the municipal preference in dam relicensing, but expressly left the Merwin dispute out.

terms.label: party preclusion
terms.gloss: Binding the specific parties to an earlier decision of an issue between them, so they cannot relitigate it.

terms.label: administrative adjudication
terms.gloss: An agency deciding a particular case, like a court, rather than making general rules.

terms.label: Retail, Wholesale (factors)
terms.gloss: A 1972 D.C. Circuit case listing factors, like reliance and burden, for when an agency may apply a new rule retroactively.

terms.label: second impression
terms.gloss: The dissent's term for a case reversing an already-established rule, contrasted with a 'first impression' case deciding a new question.

terms.label: Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act
terms.gloss: The 1938 federal law giving the FDA power to regulate foods, drugs, medical devices, and cosmetics for safety.

terms.label: device (FDA)
terms.gloss: Under the food and drug law, an instrument or product intended to affect the body's structure or function without working chemically as a drug.

terms.label: therapeutic claims
terms.gloss: Statements by a seller that a product treats, prevents, or cures a disease, which traditionally triggered FDA authority.

terms.label: Chevron's first step
terms.gloss: The first question in the former Chevron test: did Congress clearly answer this question? If so, the agency must follow that answer.

terms.label: affidavit of merit
terms.gloss: A sworn statement from a qualified doctor, required by some states with a malpractice complaint, saying the claim has reasonable grounds.

terms.label: Federal Rules (of Civil Procedure)
terms.gloss: The Federal Rules of Civil Procedure: the nationwide rules governing how civil lawsuits proceed in federal court.

terms.label: conversion (Rule 12(d))
terms.gloss: Under Rule 12(d), if a court considers material outside the pleadings on a motion to dismiss, it must treat it as summary judgment, giving both sides chance to present evidence.

terms.label: Rule 12(d)
terms.gloss: The federal rule converting a motion to dismiss into summary judgment if the court considers evidence outside the pleadings.

terms.label: Rule 7
terms.gloss: The federal rule listing which papers count as pleadings: mainly the complaint and the answer.

terms.label: Rule 17
terms.gloss: The federal rule on who may sue, letting executors, guardians, trustees, and similar representatives sue for others.

terms.label: Sibbach test
terms.gloss: From Sibbach v. Wilson (1941): a Federal Rule is valid if it really regulates procedure, the manner and means of enforcing rights.

terms.label: manner and means
terms.gloss: The procedural process by which rights are enforced, as opposed to the rights and remedies themselves.

terms.label: Walker v. Armco Steel
terms.gloss: A 1980 Supreme Court case applying a state rule on when a suit counts as begun for the state limitations period, because Rule 3 did not address it.

terms.label: Woods v. Interstate Realty
terms.gloss: A 1949 Supreme Court case: a business barred from state court for not registering in the state was also barred from federal diversity court there.

terms.label: Shady Grove v. Allstate
terms.gloss: A 2010 Supreme Court case: Rule 23 allowed a class action in federal court despite a New York law barring that kind of class action.

terms.label: outside the pleadings
terms.gloss: Material not in the complaint or answer. On a motion to dismiss, considering it requires converting to summary judgment.

terms.label: willfully, wantonly and maliciously
terms.gloss: A traditional phrase alleging intentional, reckless, and spiteful conduct, which can support punitive damages.

terms.label: assault and battery
terms.gloss: Assault is putting someone in fear of imminent harmful contact; battery is the harmful or offensive contact itself. Both are torts and crimes.

terms.label: wrongful attachment
terms.gloss: Seizing or tying up someone's property through attachment without a valid claim, for which the victim may recover damages.

terms.label: sheriff
terms.gloss: A county law officer who, among other duties, carries out court orders such as attachments.

terms.label: mortgage / home-equity loan
terms.gloss: A loan secured by real estate, such as a home, which lets the lender force a sale of the property if the loan is not repaid.

terms.label: insecurity clause
terms.gloss: A loan term letting the lender demand full repayment if something, like a lien, makes it feel the loan is no longer safe.

terms.label: incipient lien
terms.gloss: A claim on property that is not yet a final lien but would ripen into one if the plaintiff wins.

terms.label: vendor's lien
terms.gloss: A seller's claim against goods sold on credit until paid, giving the seller an existing interest in them.

terms.label: technical default
terms.gloss: Breaking a loan term other than missing payments, such as letting a lien attach, which can let the lender demand repayment.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 2403(b)
terms.gloss: The federal law letting a state join a federal case to defend a state statute's constitutionality.

terms.label: double damages
terms.gloss: A statutory remedy awarding twice the actual loss, here against someone who sued without probable cause.

terms.label: advice-of-counsel defense
terms.gloss: A defense that the person acted in good faith on a lawyer's advice, which can defeat claims requiring malice.

terms.label: liberal pleading
terms.gloss: The modern approach requiring only a short statement of the claim, rather than detailed facts, so cases are decided on merits rather than technicalities.

terms.label: Dioguardi v. Durning
terms.gloss: A 1944 federal appeals case letting an awkwardly written complaint proceed under the new, liberal Federal Rules pleading standard.

terms.label: severance pay
terms.gloss: Money owed to a worker upon being let go, sometimes required by law.

terms.label: Telephone Consumer Protection Act
terms.gloss: A 1991 federal law restricting unwanted telemarketing calls and junk faxes, with statutory damages for each violation.

terms.label: opt-out notice
terms.gloss: Under the junk-fax law, a required statement telling recipients how to stop future faxes.

terms.label: named parties
terms.gloss: The plaintiffs and defendants actually listed in the case, as opposed to unnamed class members.

terms.label: Phillips Petroleum v. Shutts
terms.gloss: A 1985 Supreme Court case allowing a state court to bind out-of-state class members if they receive notice and a chance to opt out.

terms.label: Taylor v. Sturgell
terms.gloss: A 2008 Supreme Court case rejecting broad 'virtual representation'; nonparties are generally not bound by judgments, with limited exceptions such as class actions.

terms.label: Committee Note
terms.gloss: An official explanation written by the drafters of a Federal Rule; courts use it to interpret the rule.

terms.label: free alongside ship (FAS)
terms.gloss: A shipping term: the seller pays to deliver goods to the dock beside the ship; the buyer bears loading and later costs.

terms.label: warranty that goods match their description
terms.gloss: A warranty, imposed by the sales statute, that goods sold by description will match that description. Modern law treats such a description as an express warranty.

terms.label: hundredweight
terms.gloss: A unit of weight equal to 100 pounds in the United States, used here to price the chickens.

terms.label: circuit judge sitting as trial judge
terms.gloss: An appeals judge temporarily assigned to hear a case in the trial court.

terms.label: notorious (trade usage)
terms.gloss: So widely known in the trade that anyone in it is presumed to know it.

terms.label: final-payment certificate
terms.gloss: An architect's written approval that construction is complete, which the contract made a condition of the final payment.

terms.label: counterperformance
terms.gloss: What the other party must do in return under a contract, here the owner's payment.

terms.label: collateral (independent) promise
terms.gloss: A promise whose breach gives a right to damages but does not excuse the other side from performing.

terms.label: willful transgressor
terms.gloss: Someone who knowingly and deliberately departs from the contract; such a party gets no leniency under substantial performance.

terms.label: appeal stipulation (New York)
terms.gloss: In New York, the appellant's agreement that if the new-trial order is affirmed, final judgment will be entered against it rather than a new trial.

terms.label: definitive contract
terms.gloss: A final, detailed written agreement, which parties sometimes say must be signed before they are bound.

terms.label: escrow agent
terms.gloss: A neutral third party holding money or documents until the conditions of a deal are met.

terms.label: closing
terms.gloss: The time when a sale is completed: the price is paid and ownership is transferred.

terms.label: memorial (of an agreement)
terms.gloss: A writing that records a deal already made, rather than a condition that must be signed before any deal exists.

terms.label: firm conviction of mistake
terms.gloss: The clear-error test: an appeals court reverses a factual finding only if left with a definite and firm conviction that a mistake was made.

terms.label: prevention or excuse
terms.gloss: Doctrines excusing an unmet contract condition, for example because the other party itself prevented it from occurring.

terms.label: unique goods
terms.gloss: Goods with no real substitute available, such as a one-of-a-kind item, so money damages would not adequately compensate.

terms.label: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA)
terms.gloss: The 1990 federal law forbidding discrimination against people with disabilities, including in businesses open to the public.

terms.label: Access Board
terms.gloss: A federal agency that writes minimum accessibility guidelines that agencies like the Justice Department then adopt as binding standards.

terms.label: technical manual
terms.gloss: Official guidance documents the Justice Department issued to explain how to comply with the ADA's accessibility standards.

terms.label: Perez v. Mortgage Bankers Association
terms.gloss: A 2015 Supreme Court case: agencies need not use notice and comment to change an interpretive rule, overturning the D.C. Circuit's Paralyzed Veterans doctrine.

terms.label: with Senate consent (advice and consent)
terms.gloss: The Constitution's requirement that the President appoint major federal officers only with Senate approval.

terms.label: appraisers
terms.gloss: Appraisers are neutral experts who estimate the value of property; an appraisal is their valuation. Here a court appointed them to value land being taken.

terms.label: disinterested
terms.gloss: Having no personal stake in the outcome; impartial (not 'uninterested').

terms.label: substitution (of parties)
terms.gloss: Replacing a party who has died with the people who now hold the interest, so the case can continue.

terms.label: officer (of the United States)
terms.gloss: A government post with significant legal authority. The Constitution requires such officers to be appointed by the President (with Senate consent), courts, or department heads.

terms.label: exclusive legislation (District Clause)
terms.gloss: The Constitution's grant to Congress of full lawmaking power over the District of Columbia, combining national and local government powers.

terms.label: speculative enhancement
terms.gloss: Added value caused by the government project itself, which owners generally cannot claim in compensation.

terms.label: royal mines
terms.gloss: Gold and silver deposits that English law reserved to the Crown, or to colonial proprietors, rather than the landowner.

terms.label: third-party priorities
terms.gloss: Which of several competing claimants to the same property has the stronger, earlier right.

terms.label: warrant (land)
terms.gloss: An official authorization to survey public land for grant to a private person, a step before issuing a patent.

terms.label: rents, issues and profits
terms.gloss: Old legal phrase for all income produced by land, such as rent and crops.

terms.label: prepayment
terms.gloss: Paying off a loan before its due date. Lenders may forbid it or charge a fee, because they lose expected interest.

terms.label: default (on a loan)
terms.gloss: Failing to make required loan payments or meet other loan terms, which gives the lender remedies such as demanding full repayment.

terms.label: waive noncompliance
terms.gloss: To choose not to enforce one's right after the other side breaks a term.

terms.label: assignment of rents
terms.gloss: A loan term transferring a property's rental income to the lender, which can collect rents directly from tenants after default.

terms.label: one-form-of-action rule
terms.gloss: A California rule generally requiring a lender to pursue a single foreclosure action on the property, rather than separate suits, to recover a secured debt.

terms.label: nonjudicial remedies
terms.gloss: Remedies a lender can use without suing, such as a trustee's sale or notifying tenants to pay rent to the lender.

terms.label: trustee's sale
terms.gloss: A foreclosure sale held by the trustee under a deed of trust, without a court case.

terms.label: Pacific Gas & Electric Co. v. Thomas Drayage
terms.gloss: A 1968 California Supreme Court case requiring judges to consider outside evidence of meaning before deciding contract words are unambiguous.

terms.label: Iqbal v. Hasty
terms.gloss: The Second Circuit's 2007 ruling in a similar 9/11-detention suit, later reversed by the Supreme Court as Ashcroft v. Iqbal.

terms.label: Mitchell v. W.T. Grant Co.
terms.gloss: A 1974 Supreme Court case upholding seizure of goods before a hearing where the seller had a lien, the issue was documentary, a judge approved, and a bond was posted.

terms.label: Fuentes v. Shevin
terms.gloss: A 1972 Supreme Court case striking down laws letting sellers seize goods bought on credit without any prior hearing.

terms.label: North Georgia Finishing v. Di-Chem
terms.gloss: A 1975 Supreme Court case striking down a garnishment of a company's bank account issued by a clerk without notice, a hearing, or judicial oversight.

terms.label: Frothingham v. Mellon
terms.gloss: A 1923 Supreme Court case refusing a taxpayer's challenge to a federal spending law; courts decide only a party's own concrete injury.

terms.label: Smyth v. Ames
terms.gloss: An 1898 Supreme Court case upholding an injunction against enforcing Nebraska railroad rates, later debated as a possible early broad injunction.

terms.label: Califano v. Yamasaki
terms.gloss: A 1979 Supreme Court case holding that a federal court may certify a nationwide class.

terms.label: Devlin v. Scardelletti
terms.gloss: A 2002 Supreme Court case letting an unnamed class member who objected to a settlement appeal without formally joining the case.

terms.label: strip search
terms.gloss: A search requiring a person to remove clothing so officials can inspect the body for hidden items.

terms.label: civil immigration detainee
terms.gloss: A noncitizen held while immigration proceedings are pending. The detention is civil, not punishment for a crime.

terms.label: rational-relationship standard
terms.gloss: A test asking whether a restriction is reasonably related to a legitimate goal, such as prison security; it gives officials substantial leeway.

terms.label: statelessness
terms.gloss: Having no nationality, so that no country recognizes the person as its citizen.

terms.label: New Mexico Rule 9(k)
terms.gloss: A New Mexico pleading rule requiring a copy of a written instrument that a claim is founded on to be attached to the complaint.

terms.label: telex
terms.gloss: A typed message sent over a teleprinter network, a common way to exchange written business offers before email.

terms.label: dispersal (of wheelchair seating)
terms.gloss: Spreading wheelchair seating across different sections and price levels rather than clustering it in one place.

terms.label: comparable sightlines
terms.gloss: A view of the event from a wheelchair space comparable to other spectators' views, including over people standing.

terms.label: integration (of seating)
terms.gloss: Placing wheelchair seating among the general seats rather than segregating it.

terms.label: civil judgment
terms.gloss: A court order to pay money, enforceable like a judgment in a private lawsuit and separate from the criminal sentence.

terms.label: core liability
terms.gloss: The basic common questions of whether defendants' shared conduct was wrongful, proposed to be tried once for the whole class.

terms.label: intended use
terms.gloss: What a maker means a product to do. FDA power over a drug or device depends on the product's intended use.

terms.label: combination products
terms.gloss: Products that combine a drug and a device, regulated under rules for both.

terms.label: public utility districts
terms.gloss: Local government bodies that supply electricity; as public entities they could claim the Federal Power Act's municipal preference.

terms.label: Bonneville Power Administration
terms.gloss: A federal agency selling low-cost hydroelectric power in the Northwest, with priority access for public utilities.

terms.label: best practicable notice
terms.gloss: Rule 23's standard for class notice: the best notice practicable in the circumstances, including individual notice to members reasonably identifiable.

terms.label: resurvey grant
terms.gloss: A new official survey and grant of land that replaced the earlier grant of the same tract.

terms.label: Court of Appeal certification
terms.gloss: A request to send the case to California's intermediate appeals court for review, which the appellate department could grant or refuse.

terms.label: unsecured
terms.gloss: Not backed by collateral: the creditor has no claim on specific property unless it wins a judgment.

terms.label: professional services corporation
terms.gloss: A corporation formed by licensed professionals, such as doctors, to run their practice.

terms.label: forum-concentration factor
terms.gloss: Rule 23(b)(3)'s consideration of whether it is desirable to gather the claims in one particular court.

terms.label: Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services
match: centers for medicare and medicaid services
terms.gloss: The federal agency that runs Medicare and Medicaid.

terms.label: assigned error
terms.gloss: An appellant must formally list the specific mistakes it claims the lower court made; unlisted points are generally not reviewed.

terms.label: class waiver
terms.gloss: A contract term in which a person gives up the right to bring or join a class or group action, so each claim must be pursued alone.

terms.label: individual arbitration
terms.gloss: Arbitration in which each person's claim is heard separately, not combined with anyone else's.

terms.label: tying arrangement
terms.gloss: Forcing customers who want one product to also take a second one; it can violate antitrust law when the seller has power in the first product's market.

terms.label: market power
terms.gloss: A company's ability to raise prices or impose terms without losing much business to competitors.

terms.label: prospective waiver
terms.gloss: Giving up a legal right in advance, before any claim exists, for example in a contract signed when a job or purchase begins.

terms.label: formation defect
terms.gloss: A problem in how a contract was made, such as fraud or duress, that can make it unenforceable.

terms.label: Rule 8(d)(3)
terms.gloss: Part of the federal pleading rule allowing a party to state as many separate claims or defenses as it has, even inconsistent ones.

terms.label: Federal Rule of Evidence 412
terms.gloss: The 'rape shield' rule, which generally bars evidence of an alleged sexual-misconduct victim's other sexual behavior or predisposition, with narrow exceptions.

terms.label: freedom of association
terms.gloss: The constitutional right, drawn from the First Amendment, to join with others for shared purposes without undue government interference.

terms.label: proportionality (discovery)
terms.gloss: The requirement that discovery be reasonable compared with the case's needs and stakes and the burden on the person producing it.

terms.label: state failure-to-warn law
terms.gloss: State tort law making manufacturers liable for injuries caused by inadequate warnings about a product's risks.

terms.label: Markman v. Westview Instruments
terms.gloss: A 1996 Supreme Court case holding that judges, not juries, decide what the words of a patent claim mean.

terms.label: brute facts
terms.gloss: Bare historical facts (who said or did what), as opposed to their legal meaning; traditionally decided by juries.

terms.label: counselor privilege
terms.gloss: A claimed rule protecting confidential communications between a person and a counselor from forced disclosure in a lawsuit.

terms.label: FERPA
terms.gloss: The Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, a federal law limiting disclosure of students' education records without consent.

terms.label: nonprivileged
terms.gloss: Not protected by a legal privilege (such as attorney-client), so open to discovery if relevant.

terms.label: special proceeding
terms.gloss: In New York, a streamlined court case begun by petition rather than a full lawsuit, used for particular statutory remedies.

terms.label: Chief Administrative Judge
terms.gloss: The official who runs the day-to-day administration of New York's state court system.

terms.label: affidavit of service
terms.gloss: A sworn statement by a process server saying when, where, and how court papers were delivered to a defendant.

terms.label: index number
terms.gloss: The number a New York court assigns to identify a case file.

terms.label: answer (to a complaint)
terms.gloss: A defendant's formal written response to a complaint; a fresh time to answer lets the defendant defend the case.

terms.label: gross ton
terms.gloss: A 'long' ton of 2,240 pounds, traditionally used for iron and steel.

terms.label: jury instructions
terms.gloss: The judge's directions telling the jury what law to apply in deciding the case.

terms.label: prevention doctrine
terms.gloss: A contract rule that a party who prevents or hinders the other side's performance cannot hold the other side liable for failing to perform.

terms.label: constable
terms.gloss: A local law-enforcement officer who serves court papers and carries out court orders, such as seizing property.

terms.label: justice's court
terms.gloss: A local court run by a justice of the peace, handling small civil claims and minor offenses.

terms.label: out-of-pocket loss
terms.gloss: Money actually lost, as opposed to merely failing to earn an expected profit.

terms.label: conscious ignorance
terms.gloss: Knowingly contracting despite limited knowledge of a fact; a party who does so generally bears the risk of being wrong.

terms.label: most-favored-customer clause
terms.gloss: A clause promising a buyer prices or terms at least as good as those the seller gives other customers.

terms.label: side letter
terms.gloss: A separate written agreement made alongside a main contract, adding to or clarifying its terms.

terms.label: estoppel by contract
terms.gloss: A rule barring a party from contradicting facts or characterizations it agreed to in a contract.

terms.label: Robinson-Patman Act
terms.gloss: A 1936 federal antitrust law forbidding sellers from charging different buyers different prices for the same goods where that harms competition.

terms.label: predicting state law (Erie guess)
match: predicted how indiana courts would rule
terms.gloss: When a state's courts have not settled an issue, a federal court applying that state's law must forecast how its highest court would decide.

terms.label: conflict-of-laws rules
terms.gloss: Rules deciding which state's or country's law applies when a case touches more than one place.

terms.label: consumer protection act
terms.gloss: A state law forbidding unfair or deceptive business practices and letting consumers sue over them.

terms.label: well-pleaded facts
terms.gloss: Specific factual allegations in a complaint, not bare conclusions, which a court accepts as true when deciding a motion to dismiss.

terms.label: educational malpractice
terms.gloss: A claim that a school taught badly; courts generally refuse to hear it because judging teaching quality is beyond their role.

terms.label: incorporated by reference / integral
terms.gloss: On a motion to dismiss, a court may look only at the complaint plus documents it incorporates, refers to, or depends on heavily.

terms.label: possessory right
terms.gloss: A right to possess specific property; the tort of conversion requires interference with such a right.

terms.label: consumer fraud
terms.gloss: Deceiving consumers in commercial dealings, as forbidden by consumer-protection laws.

terms.label: H-2A visa
terms.gloss: A U.S. visa letting foreign workers enter temporarily for seasonal farm work sponsored by an employer.

terms.label: farm labor contractor
terms.gloss: A business that recruits, hires, and supplies workers to farms or other employers.

terms.label: minimum wage
terms.gloss: The lowest hourly pay employers must legally pay, set by federal and state law.

terms.label: wrongful act (duress)
terms.gloss: In duress law, improper pressure (not necessarily a crime or tort) used to force someone's agreement.

terms.label: hard bargaining
terms.gloss: Tough but legitimate negotiating pressure, which does not make a contract invalid for duress.

terms.label: Odorizzi factors
terms.gloss: From Odorizzi v. Bloomfield School District (Cal. Ct. App. 1966): signs of undue influence, such as unusual time or place, urgency, multiple persuaders, and absent advisers.

terms.label: California Civil Code § 1575
terms.gloss: California's statute defining undue influence, including abusing trust or authority and taking grossly oppressive advantage of another's weakness or distress.

terms.label: obstruction of justice
terms.gloss: Interfering with investigations or legal proceedings, for example by falsifying records or pressuring witnesses; a federal crime.

terms.label: 18 U.S.C. § 1519
terms.gloss: A federal crime of knowingly falsifying, hiding, or destroying records intending to obstruct a federal investigation or matter, even one not yet begun.

terms.label: 18 U.S.C. § 1512
terms.gloss: The federal witness-tampering law, covering intimidating or corruptly persuading people to keep information from investigators or proceedings.

terms.label: 18 U.S.C. § 1001
terms.gloss: The federal crime of knowingly making a materially false statement to federal officials in a matter within their authority.

terms.label: 18 U.S.C. § 1503
terms.gloss: The general federal obstruction-of-justice law, which the Supreme Court (in Aguilar) read to require a link to a pending judicial proceeding.

terms.label: corrupt persuasion
terms.gloss: Trying to get a witness to lie or hold back information through intimidation or improper persuasion; a form of witness tampering.

terms.label: summary order
terms.gloss: A short, unsigned appellate ruling that resolves issues without a full published opinion and generally is not binding precedent.

terms.label: published opinion
terms.gloss: An appellate opinion issued for official reporting, which serves as binding precedent in that court's circuit.

terms.label: official proceeding
terms.gloss: A formal government proceeding, such as a court case, grand jury, or congressional or agency hearing.

terms.label: inconsistent verdicts
terms.gloss: Jury verdicts that seem logically at odds, such as convicting one alleged conspirator while acquitting the others; courts generally let them stand.

terms.label: jury lenity
terms.gloss: A jury's choice to acquit out of mercy or compromise despite evidence of guilt; courts do not second-guess it.

terms.label: substantial right
terms.gloss: A right important enough that an error affecting it may require reversal; errors that do not affect one are ignored as harmless.

terms.label: security for expenses
terms.gloss: A requirement that a plaintiff post money or a bond to cover the defendant's legal costs if the plaintiff loses.

terms.label: irreparable (harm)
terms.gloss: Harm that cannot be undone or adequately fixed later, whether by money or by a later appeal.

terms.label: nuisance-value settlement
terms.gloss: A payment made just to make a weak lawsuit go away, because fighting it would cost more.

terms.label: collateral right
terms.gloss: Under Cohen, a right separate from the main merits (here, security for expenses) that can be appealed immediately because it would be lost by waiting.

terms.label: procedural (vs. substantive)
terms.gloss: About how a case is conducted in court (forms, timing, methods), not the underlying rights; under Erie, federal courts use federal procedure but state substantive law.

terms.label: state-created right
terms.gloss: A legal right that exists because of state law, such as a contract or trust claim, rather than federal law.

terms.label: diverse citizenship
terms.gloss: The parties being citizens of different states, which lets a federal court hear a state-law case (diversity jurisdiction).

terms.label: outcome-determinative test
terms.gloss: York's test: a federal court in a diversity case must follow a state rule if ignoring it would significantly change the outcome compared with state court.

terms.label: local prejudice
terms.gloss: Bias of state courts or juries against out-of-state parties, the traditional reason for allowing diversity jurisdiction.

terms.label: prime contractor
terms.gloss: The company that contracts directly with a project's owner and hires subcontractors for parts of the work.

terms.label: independent jurisdictional basis
terms.gloss: A separate ground for federal jurisdiction (such as a federal question or diversity) that a claim has on its own, apart from its link to another claim.

terms.label: affirmative relief
terms.gloss: A court award giving a party something (money or an order), beyond simply defeating or reducing the opponent's claim.

terms.label: transaction or occurrence
terms.gloss: The set of events underlying a claim; counterclaims arising from the same transaction or occurrence are compulsory.

terms.label: logical-relationship test
terms.gloss: A broad test treating claims as part of the same transaction if they are logically connected and share facts and evidence.

terms.label: foundation (evidence)
terms.gloss: Preliminary testimony showing an item of evidence is what it claims to be and meets the conditions for admitting it.

terms.label: settlement-discussion exclusion
terms.gloss: Statements made while negotiating a settlement, which generally cannot be used at trial to prove liability.

terms.label: harmless (error)
terms.gloss: A trial error that did not affect the outcome, so it does not require a new trial.

terms.label: polling the jury
terms.gloss: Asking each juror individually in court whether they agree with the announced verdict.

terms.label: cross-default provision
terms.gloss: A contract term making a default on one contract count as a default on another, allowing termination or withholding on both.

terms.label: process (court papers)
terms.gloss: The summons and complaint or other court papers that formally notify a defendant of a lawsuit.

terms.label: waiver of notice
terms.gloss: Agreeing in advance to give up the right to be formally notified of a lawsuit or proceeding.

terms.label: conditional sale
terms.gloss: A sale on credit in which the seller keeps ownership until the buyer finishes paying.

terms.label: notes (debt)
terms.gloss: Debt instruments: a borrower's written promises (here a corporation's) to repay investors, who are the noteholders.

terms.label: exchange offer
terms.gloss: A proposal letting investors swap their securities for different ones or cash, often in a debt restructuring.

terms.label: 9 U.S.C. § 16
terms.gloss: The FAA provision allowing an immediate appeal when a court refuses to compel arbitration.

terms.label: UCC § 2-602
terms.gloss: The UCC rule that a buyer must reject defective goods within a reasonable time after delivery and notify the seller.

terms.label: UCC § 2-711
terms.gloss: The UCC provision giving a buyer who rightfully rejects goods a security interest in them for money already paid.

terms.label: ProCD v. Zeidenberg
terms.gloss: A 1996 Seventh Circuit case holding that a buyer who keeps software after a chance to read enclosed license terms accepts those terms.

terms.label: rolling contract
terms.gloss: A contract formed in stages: terms arrive with the product, and the buyer accepts them by keeping it past a return period.

terms.label: Klocek v. Gateway
terms.gloss: A 2000 federal trial-court case in Kansas rejecting Hill's approach: the buyer's order was the offer, and enclosed terms were mere proposals needing express agreement.

terms.label: Doctor's Associates v. Casarotto
terms.gloss: A 1996 case holding states cannot single out arbitration clauses for special requirements, like extra-prominent notice.

terms.label: Shearson/American Express v. McMahon
terms.gloss: A 1987 case holding that civil RICO claims can be sent to arbitration.

terms.label: confirmation (UCC)
terms.gloss: A written message sent after a deal is made confirming its terms; UCC § 2-207 addresses terms added in such confirmations.

terms.label: J. (English judge)
terms.gloss: 'J.' after an English judge's name stands for 'Justice', a judge of the High Court, the main trial-level court.

terms.label: Taylor v. Caldwell
terms.gloss: An 1863 English case excusing both sides when the music hall to be rented burned down; the origin of the impossibility doctrine.

terms.label: foundation of the contract
terms.gloss: Krell's idea that a contract is excused when a state of affairs both sides treated as its basis disappears through no one's fault.

terms.label: The Moorcock
terms.gloss: An 1889 English case implying an unstated contract term needed to make the deal work as both parties must have intended.

terms.label: FLSA § 216(b)
terms.gloss: The FLSA provision letting employees sue for themselves and other 'similarly situated' workers who choose to join.

terms.label: NLRA § 7
terms.gloss: The NLRA section guaranteeing employees' rights to organize, bargain collectively, and act together 'for mutual aid or protection'.

terms.label: NLRA § 8(a)(1)
terms.gloss: The NLRA provision making it an unfair labor practice for an employer to interfere with employees' § 7 rights.

terms.label: D.R. Horton
terms.gloss: A 2012 NLRB decision holding that requiring employees to waive class and collective actions violated the NLRA; Epic Systems rejected it.

terms.label: general counsel memorandum (NLRB)
terms.gloss: Guidance from the NLRB's General Counsel, the official who decides which labor cases to prosecute; it is not binding law.

terms.label: opt in / opt out
terms.gloss: In group litigation, whether people must sign up to be included (opt in, as in FLSA actions) or are included unless they exclude themselves (opt out, as in class actions).

terms.label: genus (statutory interpretation)
terms.gloss: The general category a court infers from a list of specific items when applying ejusdem generis to read a catchall phrase.

terms.label: budget authority / direct spending
terms.gloss: Budget categories: spending set in yearly appropriations, spending required by permanent law (such as entitlements), and tax breaks benefiting very few people.

terms.label: disapproval bill
terms.gloss: A bill Congress could pass to undo a presidential cancellation; like any bill, it went to the President, who could veto it.

terms.label: Presentment Clause
terms.gloss: The constitutional rule (Art. I, § 7) that every bill passed by both Houses must go to the President for signature or veto before becoming law.

terms.label: Powell v. McCormack
terms.gloss: A 1969 case holding the House could not exclude an elected member who met the Constitution's qualifications, supporting his claim to his seat and salary.

terms.label: vote nullification
terms.gloss: Under Raines and Coleman, legislators may have standing only if votes that would have decided a measure were deprived of all effect.

terms.label: § 402 discharge permit
terms.gloss: The Act's permit program (NPDES) allowing pollutant discharges only within limits written into each permit.

terms.label: best practicable control technology currently available
match: best practicable control technology currently available
terms.gloss: The Act's first-stage pollution standard, based on what the best existing treatment technology in an industry can achieve.

terms.label: § 301 (Clean Water Act)
terms.gloss: The Act's section requiring dischargers to meet effluent limits, the technology-based pollution-control standards.

terms.label: state certification
terms.gloss: A state's right under the Act to certify that a federal discharge permit complies with state water-quality law; the state may waive it.

terms.label: Regional Administrator (EPA)
terms.gloss: The EPA official heading one of its regional offices, who issues permits for that region.

terms.label: upset (permit)
terms.gloss: An unintentional, temporary breach of permit limits caused by factors beyond the permit holder's control, which a permit may excuse.

terms.label: bypass
terms.gloss: Deliberately routing waste around treatment equipment, allowed only in narrow circumstances such as avoiding severe property damage.

terms.label: excursion
terms.gloss: A time when discharges exceed permit limits.

terms.label: APA §§ 554-558
terms.gloss: APA sections on formal, trial-type agency hearings: § 554 (adjudications), § 556 (hearings and the exclusive record), § 557 (decisions), § 558 (licenses).

terms.label: license (agency)
terms.gloss: Government permission to do something; the APA treats permits as licenses and has special rules for first-time applications.

terms.label: combination of functions
terms.gloss: An agency official both investigating a matter and then deciding it; generally allowed unless it creates an unacceptable risk of bias.

terms.label: Withrow v. Larkin
terms.gloss: A 1975 case holding that combining investigative and adjudicative functions in one agency does not by itself violate due process.

terms.label: bias
terms.gloss: Prejudgment or partiality in a decision-maker that may deny a fair hearing.

terms.label: lognormal distribution
terms.gloss: A statistical pattern in which the logarithms of measurements follow a bell curve; common for pollution data with occasional high readings.

terms.label: outlier
terms.gloss: A data point far from the others, often excluded from analysis as unrepresentative.

terms.label: citizen suits
terms.gloss: The Clean Water Act lets private citizens sue violators of permit limits even if the government chooses not to prosecute.

terms.label: shutting in a well
terms.gloss: Closing an oil or gas well so it stops producing.

terms.label: Gramm-Rudman-Hollings Act
match: balanced budget and emergency deficit control act
terms.gloss: A 1985 law setting yearly federal deficit targets and requiring automatic across-the-board spending cuts if they were missed.

terms.label: sequestration (budget)
terms.gloss: A presidential order automatically cancelling budget funds across programs to meet a deficit target.

terms.label: Congressional Budget Office (CBO)
terms.gloss: Congress's nonpartisan office that estimates the costs of legislation and budget outcomes.

terms.label: Comptroller General
terms.gloss: The head of the GAO, appointed for a 15-year term and removable by Congress through impeachment or by joint resolution for specified causes.

terms.label: General Accounting Office (GAO)
terms.gloss: Congress's auditing and investigative agency (now the Government Accountability Office), which checks how federal money is spent.

terms.label: statutory standing
terms.gloss: Whether a statute gives this particular plaintiff a right to sue, separate from constitutional standing.

terms.label: structural violation
terms.gloss: A breach of the Constitution's arrangement of powers among the branches, rather than of an individual right.

terms.label: moral turpitude
terms.gloss: Conduct regarded as deeply dishonest or depraved, such as fraud.

terms.label: inefficiency / neglect of duty
terms.gloss: Grounds for removing an official 'for cause': incompetent performance of official duties, or failing to perform them.

terms.label: veto override
terms.gloss: Congress enacting a vetoed bill anyway by a two-thirds vote in each House.

terms.label: INS v. Chadha
terms.gloss: A 1983 case striking down the one-House legislative veto: Congress can act with binding effect only by passing both Houses and presenting the measure to the President.

terms.label: Seila Law v. CFPB
terms.gloss: A 2020 case holding the President must be able to fire, at will, the single director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

terms.label: non-Article III judges
terms.gloss: Judges of courts created by Congress, such as the Tax Court, who lack the Constitution's life tenure and salary protections.

terms.label: civil servant
terms.gloss: A government employee hired through the merit system rather than appointed for political reasons.

terms.label: originalist
terms.gloss: Interpreting the Constitution according to the meaning its words had when adopted.

terms.label: The Federalist
terms.gloss: Essays by Hamilton, Madison, and Jay (1787-88) urging ratification of the Constitution, used as evidence of its original meaning.

terms.label: Civil Service Reform Act
terms.gloss: A 1978 law creating the system through which most federal employees challenge firings, generally before the Merit Systems Protection Board.

terms.label: emergency rulings
terms.gloss: Quick Supreme Court orders, often with little explanation, on requests to pause lower-court rulings while a case continues.

terms.label: acknowledgment
terms.gloss: A seller's signed return confirming it accepts a buyer's purchase order and its terms.

terms.label: practical foreclosure (of a claim)
terms.gloss: Blocking someone from pursuing a claim indirectly, for example through prohibitive costs, as opposed to expressly forbidding it.

terms.label: factual estoppel (issue preclusion)
terms.gloss: The rule that a party may not relitigate a fact actually decided against it in an earlier case.

terms.label: on other grounds
terms.gloss: Reversed for reasons different from the issue being discussed, so the lower court's view on that issue is neither approved nor necessarily rejected.

terms.label: terms by conduct (§ 2-207(3))
terms.gloss: Under UCC § 2-207(3), when the forms don't create a contract but the parties act as if they had one, the contract is the agreed terms plus UCC default rules.

terms.label: reviewed anew (de novo)
terms.gloss: Looked at from scratch, giving no deference to the lower court's conclusion; the same as 'de novo' review.

terms.label: reply (brief)
terms.gloss: The last brief in a round of briefing, filed by the side that made the motion or brought the appeal, answering the other side's opposing brief.

terms.label: opposition (brief)
terms.gloss: The brief a party files arguing that the court should deny the other side's motion.

terms.label: offset (right of offset)
terms.gloss: A right to reduce what you owe someone by what they owe you, so only the difference is paid; also called setoff.

terms.label: recant
terms.gloss: To formally take back an earlier statement or testimony.

terms.label: Judicial Council
terms.gloss: A body of federal judges in each circuit that administratively handles complaints of judicial misconduct; it does not correct rulings.

terms.label: right to counsel of choice
terms.gloss: A party's (limited) right to be represented by the lawyer it picks, which can yield to ethics rules and court needs.

terms.label: Drug Experience Reports
terms.gloss: Reports to the FDA of suspected harmful effects of a drug.

terms.label: New York Division of Human Rights
terms.gloss: New York State's agency that investigates and decides discrimination complaints under state law.

terms.label: New York Court of Appeals
terms.gloss: New York's highest court, despite its name.

terms.label: arbitrator
terms.gloss: A private, neutral person chosen to decide a dispute outside court.

terms.label: historically legal / equitable
terms.gloss: Whether a claim or defense belonged to the old common-law courts (mostly money damages, with juries) or to the old equity courts (orders, no juries).

terms.label: equitable defense
terms.gloss: A defense that came from the old equity courts, such as fraud in obtaining a contract, rather than from the common-law courts.

terms.label: bill (complaint in equity)
terms.gloss: The written complaint that started a case in a court of equity.

terms.label: restrain / restraint (injunction)
terms.gloss: For a court to forbid someone from doing something, by an injunction.

terms.label: Lord Chancellor
terms.gloss: England's highest judicial officer, who headed the Court of Chancery (equity) and heard appeals from vice-chancellors.

terms.label: personal services (contract)
terms.gloss: A contract for someone's own work or talent, like singing; courts will not order such a person to perform.

terms.label: negative promise (negative covenant)
terms.gloss: A promise not to do something, such as not to perform for anyone else; courts may enforce it by injunction.

terms.label: affirmative promise
terms.gloss: A promise to do something, such as to sing at a theatre, as opposed to a promise not to do something.

terms.label: in-house counsel
terms.gloss: A lawyer employed full-time by a company, whose one client is that employer.

terms.label: wrongful discharge in violation of public policy
terms.gloss: A tort claim by an employee fired for refusing to break the law or for obeying a duty the law imposes for the public's benefit.

terms.label: crime-fraud exception
terms.gloss: An exception to attorney-client privilege for communications in which the client sought help to commit a crime or fraud.

terms.label: professional discipline
terms.gloss: Penalties by the bar or courts against a lawyer for ethical violations, from reprimand to disbarment.

terms.label: assigned justice (sitting by assignment)
terms.gloss: A judge from another court temporarily assigned to sit on a court and vote in a case.

terms.label: option (to buy)
terms.gloss: A contract right to buy property on set terms within a set time, which the holder may choose to use (exercise) or not.

terms.label: assessments (property)
terms.gloss: Charges a government levies on property, such as for local improvements, on top of ordinary taxes.

terms.label: month-to-month tenancy
terms.gloss: A rental that renews each month and can be ended by either side on short notice.

terms.label: installment land contract
terms.gloss: A purchase where the buyer takes possession and pays the price over time, getting the deed only after the last payment.

terms.label: Westlaw citation (WL)
terms.gloss: A citation to the Westlaw legal database, used for decisions not published in an official reporter.

terms.label: airworthiness certificate
terms.gloss: An FAA document certifying an aircraft is safe to fly for a particular kind of use.

terms.label: public-use aircraft
terms.gloss: An aircraft flown for government purposes, which falls under different federal rules than private commercial flights.

terms.label: hull insurance
terms.gloss: Insurance covering physical damage to or loss of the aircraft itself.

terms.label: fleet policy
terms.gloss: One insurance policy covering a group of vehicles or aircraft owned or operated by the insured.

terms.label: third-party claim
terms.gloss: A defendant's claim bringing a new party into the lawsuit, such as an insurer said to owe the money at issue.

terms.label: implied at law
terms.gloss: Imposed by the law itself because fairness requires it, not because the parties actually agreed.

terms.label: co-insured
terms.gloss: A party protected by an insurance policy alongside the named insured.

terms.label: type rating
