terms.gloss: An extra pilot qualification required to fly a particular large aircraft model.

terms.label: astreinte
terms.gloss: In French law, a court-ordered penalty for each day a party fails to obey an order, used to pressure compliance.

terms.label: merits court
terms.gloss: In French procedure, the court that decides the full dispute, as opposed to a judge granting quick provisional relief.

terms.label: urgent judge (juge des référés)
terms.gloss: A French judge who grants fast, provisional orders in urgent matters without deciding the full case.

terms.label: serious contestation
terms.gloss: In French emergency procedure, a genuine dispute about the obligation that would normally stop the urgent judge from acting.

terms.label: rapporteur
terms.gloss: The judge in a French high court who studies a case and reports on it to the other judges.

terms.label: avocat général
terms.gloss: An official at a French high court who gives an independent opinion on how the case should be decided.

terms.label: branches (of a cassation ground)
terms.gloss: The separate parts of a legal ground of challenge argued before France's Court of Cassation.

terms.label: bar admission
terms.gloss: Being licensed to practice law after passing the bar exam and character review.

terms.label: Arizona Revised Statutes § 25-318
terms.gloss: Arizona's statute directing courts to divide a couple's community property in a divorce.

terms.label: lump sum
terms.gloss: Paying an amount all at once rather than in installments.

terms.label: survivorship (right of)
terms.gloss: In joint tenancy, when one co-owner dies the other automatically owns the whole property, regardless of any will.

terms.label: will
terms.gloss: A legal document saying who gets a person's property at death.

terms.label: substitution (of parties)
terms.gloss: Replacing a party who died with someone, such as an executor, who continues the case.

terms.label: Civil Code § 1624 / Code Civ. Proc. § 1973
terms.gloss: California's statute-of-frauds provisions then requiring certain agreements, such as ones about land or wills, to be in writing.

terms.label: resulting trust
terms.gloss: A trust the law presumes when one person pays for property titled in another's name, so the titleholder holds it for the payer.

terms.label: part performance
terms.gloss: An exception to the statute of frauds: an oral land deal can be enforced if a party acted on it, for example by taking possession or improving the land.

terms.label: reciprocal (testamentary) agreement
terms.gloss: Coordinated wills or an agreement about how two people will leave property to each other or to others.

terms.label: medically needy
terms.gloss: A Medicaid category for people whose income is too high for regular eligibility but whose medical bills are large.

terms.label: Legal Services Corporation
terms.gloss: A federally funded nonprofit that gives grants to legal-aid organizations serving low-income people.

terms.label: Title XX (Social Security Act)
terms.gloss: A part of the Social Security Act giving states grants for social services, which here helped fund legal aid.

terms.label: no-fee terms
terms.gloss: Contract terms barring a legal-aid group from seeking or accepting court-awarded fees against the state.

terms.label: Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 178–179
terms.gloss: Sections stating when courts refuse to enforce a contract term on public-policy grounds, by weighing the interest in enforcement against the policy.

terms.label: visiting district judge
terms.gloss: A trial judge temporarily sitting on an appeals court panel (sitting by designation).

terms.label: stock purchase agreement
terms.gloss: A contract to buy a company by buying its shares, setting the price, conditions, and each side's promises.

terms.label: materially disproportionate
terms.gloss: Hurting the company significantly worse than comparable businesses, which brings an otherwise excluded event back into the MAE definition.

terms.label: ordinary-course covenant
terms.gloss: A seller's promise to keep running the business normally, consistent with past practice, until the sale closes.

terms.label: in all material respects
terms.gloss: Compliance standard satisfied unless a failure is significant; small departures don't count.

terms.label: reasonable best efforts
terms.gloss: A contractual duty to take all reasonable steps to achieve a goal, such as getting financing.

terms.label: debt commitment letter
terms.gloss: Lenders' signed promise to lend a set amount on agreed terms to fund a deal, subject to conditions.

terms.label: condition to closing
terms.gloss: Something that must happen before a party is obligated to complete the deal.

terms.label: termination fee
terms.gloss: An agreed payment owed if a deal is called off in specified circumstances, such as the buyer failing to get financing.

terms.label: outside date
terms.gloss: The deadline in a deal contract after which a party may terminate if closing hasn't happened.

terms.label: revolver (revolving credit line)
terms.gloss: A credit line a company can borrow from, repay, and borrow again up to a limit.

terms.label: EBITDA
terms.gloss: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization: a common measure of a company's operating profit used in loan terms.

terms.label: covenant-testing holiday
terms.gloss: A period during which a borrower's financial ratios are not tested, so a weak quarter can't trigger a loan default.

terms.label: addbacks
terms.gloss: Amounts added back to earnings (EBITDA) for loan-calculation purposes, making the borrower look more profitable.

terms.label: regression evidence
terms.gloss: Statistical analysis estimating how much of a change was caused by particular factors.

terms.label: durational significance
terms.gloss: The requirement that harm to a business last long enough, usually years, to count as a material adverse effect.

terms.label: contempt of Congress
terms.gloss: A vote by a house of Congress declaring that someone defied its subpoena, which can lead to prosecution.

terms.label: false statement (crime)
terms.gloss: The federal crime of knowingly lying to federal officials or Congress about a material matter.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 1826(a) (recalcitrant witnesses)
terms.gloss: Lets a court confine a witness who refuses without just cause to testify before a grand jury, until they comply.

terms.label: hermetically sealed (branches)
terms.gloss: A phrase from Supreme Court cases: the branches overlap somewhat and are not completely isolated from one another.

terms.label: warrant
terms.gloss: A court order authorizing a search or an arrest; judges review applications for them.

terms.label: Watergate
terms.gloss: The 1970s Nixon scandal, including the firing of a special prosecutor, that led Congress to create the independent counsel.

terms.label: Convention history
terms.gloss: Records of the 1787 Constitutional Convention, used to understand what the drafters meant.

terms.label: bonding (surety bond)
terms.gloss: Acting as surety: guaranteeing that a contractor will finish the work and pay its subcontractors and suppliers.

terms.label: Federal Rule 13(h) (adding parties)
terms.gloss: Lets new parties be added to a counterclaim or crossclaim under the joinder rules (Rules 19 and 20).

terms.label: Federal Rules 19 and 20 (joinder)
terms.gloss: Rule 19 requires joining parties needed for a fair result; Rule 20 permits joining parties whose claims share a transaction and a common question.

terms.label: logical relationship test
terms.gloss: The test asking whether claims share enough facts and issues that trying them together makes sense.

terms.label: 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 5301
terms.gloss: Pennsylvania's statute listing bases for general jurisdiction, including a foreign corporation's registration to do business there.

terms.label: consent (to jurisdiction)
terms.gloss: Agreeing to be sued in a court, which allows jurisdiction even without other connections.

terms.label: Pike balancing
terms.gloss: Test from Pike v. Bruce Church (1970): a neutral state law is invalid if its burden on interstate commerce clearly exceeds its local benefits.

terms.label: fictional presence
terms.gloss: The old legal fiction that a corporation doing business in a state was 'present' there and so could be sued there.

terms.label: Shaffer v. Heitner
terms.gloss: 1977 decision holding that all assertions of state-court jurisdiction must meet International Shoe's fairness standards.

terms.label: Wilson Tariff Act
terms.gloss: An 1894 law applying antitrust prohibitions to conspiracies involving imported goods.

terms.label: Antidumping Act (1916)
terms.gloss: A 1916 law making it unlawful to sell imports in the U.S. far below their foreign-market price intending to injure U.S. industry.

terms.label: pretrial statement
terms.gloss: A filing before trial listing each side's claims, witnesses and evidence, which can limit what is used at trial.

terms.label: check prices
terms.gloss: Minimum export prices set under Japanese government arrangements for goods sold abroad.

terms.label: cartel
terms.gloss: A group of competitors agreeing to fix prices, limit output, or divide markets instead of competing.

terms.label: antitrust injury
terms.gloss: Harm of the kind antitrust laws prevent, flowing from what makes the conduct anticompetitive; a plaintiff must show it to sue.

terms.label: horizontal conspiracy
terms.gloss: An agreement among competitors at the same level of the market, such as rival manufacturers.

terms.label: incremental cost
terms.gloss: The extra cost of producing one more unit; prices below it are often viewed as predatory.

terms.label: free riding
terms.gloss: Benefiting from others' efforts or sacrifices without contributing; here, a cartel member cheating while others take losses.

terms.label: sovereign compulsion
terms.gloss: A defense that a foreign government required the challenged conduct, so the companies should not be liable for it.

terms.label: Ministry of International Trade and Industry
match: ministry of international trade and industry
terms.gloss: Japan's former government ministry that guided industrial and trade policy, including export price arrangements.

terms.label: per-occurrence limit
terms.gloss: An insurance cap on the amount paid for any single incident.

terms.label: inventory claims
terms.gloss: Cases a lawyer already has filed or lined up for existing clients, as opposed to claims of the future class.

terms.label: global settlement
terms.gloss: A settlement meant to resolve all present and future claims against a defendant at once.

terms.label: Trilateral Settlement Agreement
terms.gloss: A backup deal among Fibreboard and its two insurers, made at class counsel's insistence, promising $2 billion toward claims if the global settlement failed.

terms.label: mandatory class
terms.gloss: A class action whose members cannot opt out, so all are bound by the result.

terms.label: constructive bankruptcy
terms.gloss: Using a class settlement to achieve what bankruptcy would, without the protections of a bankruptcy case.

terms.label: agent for service (of process)
terms.gloss: A person a business designates in a state to receive legal papers on its behalf.

terms.label: qualification statute (foreign corporations)
terms.gloss: A state law requiring an out-of-state corporation doing business there to register (qualify), often barring unqualified companies from suing in state courts.

terms.label: S.C. Code § 36-2-719
terms.gloss: South Carolina's version of UCC § 2-719, letting contracts limit remedies and exclude consequential damages.

terms.label: grave danger
terms.gloss: The severe workplace risk OSHA must show to issue an emergency temporary standard.

terms.label: sent down (mandate)
terms.gloss: When the Supreme Court formally transmits its judgment to the lower court, making it effective.

terms.label: American Rescue Plan
terms.gloss: The 2021 federal COVID-19 relief law.

terms.label: awarding body
terms.gloss: The public agency that awards and pays for a public works contract.

terms.label: Division of Labor Standards Enforcement
terms.gloss: California's state agency that enforces wage-and-hour and prevailing-wage laws.

terms.label: predeprivation / postdeprivation hearing
terms.gloss: A hearing before (pre) or soon after (post) the government takes someone's property, as due process may require.

terms.label: dominion
terms.gloss: Control or ownership of property.

terms.label: distributorship
terms.gloss: An arrangement letting a business resell a supplier's products, often for a commission or discount.

terms.label: amortization
terms.gloss: Paying off a loan through regular installments over time.

terms.label: price escalation
terms.gloss: Raising a contract price during performance, often allowed by a clause tying price to costs.

terms.label: price protection
terms.gloss: A supplier's practice of holding the old price for materials a buyer already committed to jobs at that price, despite a price increase.

terms.label: posted price
terms.gloss: The seller's officially listed price at a given time.

terms.label: express terms
terms.gloss: Terms actually written or stated in a contract, as opposed to implied ones.

terms.label: immemorial custom
terms.gloss: An old common-law test requiring a custom to have existed 'beyond memory'; the UCC dropped it.

terms.label: trade code
terms.gloss: A written set of rules an industry adopts for its members' dealings.

terms.label: concurred specially
terms.gloss: Agreed with the court's result and reasoning but wrote separately to add or stress a point.

terms.label: federal district court
terms.gloss: A federal trial court for a particular region (district).

terms.label: Federal Employers’ Liability Act (FELA)
terms.gloss: A 1908 federal law letting injured railroad workers, or their estates, sue the railroad that employs them for injuries caused even partly by its negligence.

terms.label: speculation
terms.gloss: Guesswork not supported by enough evidence; a verdict or damages award resting only on speculation cannot stand.

terms.label: unimpeached
terms.gloss: Not discredited by the other side, for example by showing the witness was biased, mistaken or inconsistent.

terms.label: disinterested witness
terms.gloss: A witness with no personal stake in the outcome, whose testimony is therefore more readily trusted.

terms.label: interested witness
terms.gloss: A witness with a personal stake in the case's outcome, such as a manager defending his own decision, whom a jury may choose to disbelieve.

terms.label: union grievance
terms.gloss: A formal complaint brought through a labor union under its contract with the employer.

terms.label: protected age (protected class)
terms.gloss: Being in the group a discrimination law protects; under the ADEA, being 40 or older.

terms.label: Missouri Merchandising Practices Act
terms.gloss: Missouri's consumer-protection law, letting buyers sue sellers who use deception or unfair practices in selling goods or services.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 1447(e)
terms.gloss: Provision letting a federal court, after removal, either refuse to add a defendant who would destroy diversity, or allow it and send the case back to state court.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 1653
terms.gloss: Statute allowing parties to fix defective allegations of jurisdiction in their pleadings, in trial or appellate courts.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b)(3)
terms.gloss: Provision letting a defendant remove a case within 30 days after an amended pleading or other paper first shows the case has become removable.

terms.label: superseding complaint
terms.gloss: A new version of the complaint that completely replaces the earlier one; the old version stops having any effect.

terms.label: operative pleading
terms.gloss: The version of a complaint or other pleading currently in force in the case.

terms.label: substantial predominance
terms.gloss: A ground in § 1367(c) for declining supplemental jurisdiction: the state-law claims dominate the case and overshadow the federal claim.

terms.label: constitutional case (Article III case)
terms.gloss: The whole dispute a federal court may hear under Article III, which can include related state claims arising from the same facts as a federal claim.

terms.label: Rockwell International Corp. v. United States
terms.gloss: A 2007 Supreme Court decision that, in a case filed in federal court, jurisdiction is judged by the amended complaint rather than the original one.

terms.label: Carnegie-Mellon University v. Cohill
terms.gloss: A 1988 Supreme Court decision that a federal court declining to keep leftover state claims in a removed case may send them back to state court rather than dismiss them.

terms.label: time-of-filing rule
terms.gloss: The rule that diversity jurisdiction depends on the parties' citizenship when the suit was filed; later changes in citizenship do not affect it.

terms.label: forum manipulation
terms.gloss: Changing claims or parties tactically to steer a case into, or out of, a preferred court.

terms.label: late (tardy) acceptance
terms.gloss: An acceptance arriving after the offer's deadline; it usually makes no contract, though it may act as a new offer the other side can accept.

terms.label: ex rel.
terms.gloss: Latin 'on the relation of': a suit brought in the government's name by a private person, the relator, who supplied the information.

terms.label: False Claims Act
terms.gloss: A federal law making anyone who knowingly submits false claims for government money liable for up to triple damages plus penalties; private whistleblowers may sue on the government's behalf.

terms.label: 31 U.S.C. § 3729 (False Claims Act liability)
terms.gloss: The False Claims Act's liability section; (a)(1) covered presenting a false claim to a government official, (a)(2) using a false record to get a claim paid, and (c) defined 'claim'.

terms.label: appropriated funds (appropriation)
terms.gloss: Money Congress (or a legislature) formally sets aside by law for government spending.

terms.label: material falsity
terms.gloss: Whether a falsehood was important enough to affect the government's decision to pay; trivial falsehoods do not create liability.

terms.label: contracting officer
terms.gloss: A government official with legal authority to sign, manage and pay government contracts.

terms.label: contracting warrant
terms.gloss: The formal written grant of authority that lets a contracting officer bind the government to contracts.

terms.label: cost-plus (contract)
terms.gloss: Pricing where the buyer pays the seller's actual costs plus an added fee or percentage for overhead and profit.

terms.label: fixed price
terms.gloss: A set contract price that stays the same whatever the seller's actual costs turn out to be.

terms.label: Allison Engine Co. v. United States ex rel. Sanders
terms.gloss: A 2008 Supreme Court decision holding that False Claims Act § 3729(a)(2) did not require presenting the claim to the government itself, but did require intent that the government pay it.

terms.label: commercial bribery
terms.gloss: Secretly paying someone's employee or agent to act against that employer's interests in a business deal; a crime in New York.

terms.label: Penal Law section 439
terms.gloss: The New York criminal-code section then making commercial bribery a crime.

terms.label: lawful (or illegal) on its face
terms.gloss: Judged by the contract's own terms: a facially lawful promise requires nothing illegal, even if a party later acts illegally in performing it.

terms.label: depository (escrow holder)
terms.gloss: Someone who simply holds money or property for others, like a bank or escrow agent, without being a party to the underlying deal.

terms.label: contingent note payable
terms.gloss: A promise to pay money that comes due only if a stated event happens; here, if Miller left and took DeMuth's clients.

terms.label: termination for cause
terms.gloss: Firing for a reason the contract lists as justifying it, such as misconduct, rather than for no stated reason.

terms.label: special interrogatories (to a jury)
terms.gloss: Specific written questions the jury answers about particular facts, rather than only announcing which side wins.

terms.label: molded (verdict)
terms.gloss: Adjusted by the judge after the verdict to fit the law or the parties' agreement, for example reduced to an agreed maximum.

terms.label: judicial admission
terms.gloss: A statement of fact in a party's own pleading or in court that binds that party, so it cannot later argue the opposite.

terms.label: Shelley v. Kraemer
terms.gloss: A 1948 Supreme Court decision that courts may not enforce racially restrictive private agreements, because court enforcement is itself government ('state') action.

terms.label: Barrows v. Jackson
terms.gloss: A 1953 Supreme Court decision extending Shelley: courts may not award damages for breaking a racially restrictive covenant.

terms.label: Bowers v. Hardwick
terms.gloss: A 1986 Supreme Court decision, overruled in 2003, that upheld a state law criminalizing sodomy against a constitutional privacy challenge.

terms.label: nonactionable
terms.gloss: Not a valid basis for a lawsuit, even if the facts alleged are true.

terms.label: Pennsylvania Superior Court
terms.gloss: Pennsylvania's main intermediate appeals court, below the state Supreme Court; it usually sits in three-judge panels.

terms.label: finance lease
terms.gloss: A lease where a finance company buys equipment the customer chose from a supplier and leases it to the customer, mainly as a way of financing it.

terms.label: securitized pool
terms.gloss: A bundle of many loans or leases sold together to investors, who are paid from the borrowers' payments; a trustee holds the bundle for them.

terms.label: Cal. UCC § 9403 (waiver-of-defense clause)
terms.gloss: California's version of UCC § 9-403: a debtor's promise not to raise defenses against a later assignee is enforceable if the assignee paid value in good faith without notice of problems.

terms.label: Cal. UCC § 10407 ('hell or high water')
terms.gloss: California's version of UCC § 2A-407: in a non-consumer finance lease, once the lessee accepts the goods, its promises to pay become irrevocable and unaffected by complaints about the goods.

terms.label: Cal. UCC §§ 9405 and 9406
terms.gloss: Assignment rules: § 9405 makes good-faith changes to an assigned contract binding on the assignee; § 9406 lets a debtor pay the original creditor until notified of the assignment.

terms.label: former § 9206
terms.gloss: The California provision in force before July 2001 that contained the same rule enforcing waiver-of-defense clauses for good-faith assignees.

terms.label: irrevocable and independent
terms.gloss: Once the lessee accepts the goods, it must keep paying regardless of complaints about the goods or the supplier.

terms.label: possessory claim
terms.gloss: A claim by someone else that they own, or have a right to hold, the property involved.

terms.label: account (UCC)
terms.gloss: Under the UCC, a right to be paid for goods sold or leased or services provided, even if not yet earned.

terms.label: incidental appeal (French)
terms.gloss: In French procedure, a cross-appeal: the responding party's own challenge to parts of the lower court's decision.

terms.label: ground (and branches) of cassation
terms.gloss: In French Court of Cassation practice, a 'ground' (moyen) is a legal argument attacking the lower judgment; its 'branches' are separate sub-arguments.

terms.label: former French Civil Code arts. 1134, 1142, 1184
terms.gloss: Pre-2016 French contract rules: art. 1134 made agreements binding like law on the parties; 1142 turned unperformed duties to act into damages; 1184 let the unpaid party choose enforcement or dissolution.

terms.label: article 700 (French Code of Civil Procedure)
terms.gloss: The French rule letting a court order the losing party to pay part of the winner's unrecoverable legal costs, such as lawyers' fees.

terms.label: annotation (of a judgment)
terms.gloss: A note entered in the margin of the original lower-court judgment recording that it has been partly quashed.

terms.label: installment price
terms.gloss: A price paid in a series of scheduled payments over time rather than all at once.

terms.label: commencement of performance
terms.gloss: Starting to do the promised work; an offer may say that beginning performance itself counts as accepting it.

terms.label: judicial demand
terms.gloss: In Louisiana, the filing of the lawsuit; interest on the judgment runs from that date.

terms.label: rendered judgment (appellate)
terms.gloss: The appeals court itself entered the final judgment for the winning side, instead of sending the case back for another trial.

terms.label: parish (Louisiana)
terms.gloss: A Louisiana parish is the equivalent of a county in other states.

terms.label: termination of parental rights
terms.gloss: A court order permanently ending a parent's legal relationship with a child, which must happen before someone else can adopt the child.

terms.label: stepparent adoption
terms.gloss: Adoption of a child by the spouse of the child's legal parent, usually with simplified procedures.

terms.label: presumed paternity
terms.gloss: The rule that a married woman's husband is legally presumed to be the father of her child unless that is disproved.

terms.label: best interests of the child
terms.gloss: The standard for custody decisions: the court chooses what will be best for the child's welfare, not what the parents want or agreed.

terms.label: surrogacy
terms.gloss: An arrangement in which a woman agrees to become pregnant and give birth to a child for another person or couple to raise.

terms.label: direct certification (New Jersey)
terms.gloss: The New Jersey Supreme Court's agreeing to hear a case straight from the trial court, skipping the intermediate Appellate Division.

terms.label: serious neglect
terms.gloss: A parent's serious failure to give a child basic care, food, safety or supervision; a legal ground for ending parental rights.

terms.label: unfit (parent)
terms.gloss: Legally incapable of properly caring for a child, for example because of abuse, neglect or severe incapacity.

terms.label: Parentage Act (New Jersey)
terms.gloss: New Jersey's law for establishing who a child's legal parents are and for settling custody and support between them.

terms.label: natural parent
terms.gloss: A biological parent, as opposed to an adoptive parent or stepparent.

terms.label: sperm-donor statute
terms.gloss: A New Jersey law providing that a man who donates sperm through a doctor for a married woman's artificial insemination is not the child's legal father.

terms.label: baby-selling laws
terms.gloss: Laws making it a crime to pay or accept money for handing over a child for adoption.

terms.label: acknowledgment (seller's form)
terms.gloss: The seller's form replying to a purchase order, confirming the sale and often adding the seller's own printed terms.

terms.label: expressly conditional acceptance
terms.gloss: Under UCC § 2-207(1), a reply saying it accepts only if the other side agrees to its added terms; it is a counteroffer, not an acceptance.

terms.label: suit at law
terms.gloss: A case seeking a legal remedy such as money damages, historically heard in courts of law rather than courts of equity.

terms.label: in default (of arbitration)
terms.gloss: Here, not having lost the right to arbitrate, for example by delaying or by fighting the case in court instead.

terms.label: UCC § 2-201 (statute of frauds for goods)
terms.gloss: The UCC's statute of frauds: sales of goods for $500 or more need a signed writing, but a merchant who ignores a written confirmation loses that defense.

terms.label: Dorton v. Collins & Aikman Corp.
terms.gloss: A 1972 Sixth Circuit battle-of-the-forms case reading § 2-207's 'expressly conditional' proviso narrowly.

terms.label: Roto-Lith, Ltd. v. F.P. Bartlett & Co.
terms.gloss: A 1962 First Circuit case, later overruled, treating a reply that added terms as a counteroffer accepted by taking the goods, so the last form's terms won.

terms.label: unlawful assembly
terms.gloss: A crime of gathering with others in a way that threatens public peace or aims at unlawful action.

terms.label: petit theft
terms.gloss: Theft of low-value property, a minor crime (also called petty theft or petit larceny).

terms.label: generally applicable law
terms.gloss: A law that applies to everyone and does not target speech or the press; applying it to the press usually does not violate the First Amendment.

terms.label: N.W.2d (case citation)
terms.gloss: Abbreviation for the North Western Reporter, Second Series, the book series printing decisions of Minnesota and nearby state courts; '481 N.W.2d 840' means volume 481, page 840.

terms.label: summarily reversed
terms.gloss: Reversed without full briefing or argument, because existing precedent clearly decided the question.

terms.label: Owen Equipment & Erection Co. v. Kroger
terms.gloss: A 1978 Supreme Court decision that a plaintiff cannot use ancillary jurisdiction to sue a nondiverse third-party defendant in a diversity case.

terms.label: United States v. Sherwood
terms.gloss: A 1941 Supreme Court decision that the Court of Claims could hear claims only against the United States, not against private parties joined with it.

terms.label: United States v. Yellow Cab Co.
terms.gloss: A 1951 Supreme Court decision allowing private defendants to bring in the United States under the FTCA to share liability (contribution).

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 1346(b)
terms.gloss: The FTCA's jurisdiction provision, giving federal district courts exclusive power over damages claims against the United States for its employees' torts.

terms.label: exclusive federal jurisdiction
terms.gloss: The rule that certain claims, such as FTCA suits, may be heard only in federal court, never in state court.

terms.label: Federal Rules 14 and 20
terms.gloss: Rule 14 lets a defendant bring in a third party who may owe it for the claim (impleader); Rule 20 lets multiple plaintiffs or defendants join in one suit.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 1338(b)
terms.gloss: Statute giving federal courts jurisdiction over unfair-competition claims joined with a related patent, copyright or trademark claim.

terms.label: registrar (of motor vehicles)
terms.gloss: A state official who keeps official records; under nonresident-motorist statutes, the motor-vehicle registrar acted as an out-of-state driver's agent to receive court papers.

terms.label: return receipt
terms.gloss: A postal card signed by the recipient and mailed back to the sender, proving the item was delivered.

terms.label: citizen of a State (for diversity)
terms.gloss: For diversity jurisdiction, a U.S. citizen is a citizen of the state where he or she is domiciled.

terms.label: residence
terms.gloss: Where a person is actually living; unlike domicile, it requires no intent to stay indefinitely.

terms.label: intent to remain
terms.gloss: A plan to stay in a place indefinitely, which together with living there establishes domicile.

terms.label: derivative domicile
terms.gloss: The old rule that a wife automatically took her husband's domicile; modern law rejects it.

terms.label: nationality
terms.gloss: Which country a person is a citizen of; distinct from domicile, the place a person lives intending to stay.

terms.label: exclusive distributor
terms.gloss: A company given the sole right to sell a manufacturer's products in a territory.

terms.label: consigned stock
terms.gloss: Goods placed with a seller to sell on the owner's behalf, while the owner keeps ownership until they are sold.

terms.label: inadequate warnings (failure to warn)
terms.gloss: A product-liability claim that the maker failed to give adequate warnings or instructions about a product's dangers.

terms.label: Charles Gendler & Co. v. Telecom Equipment Corp.
terms.gloss: A 1986 New Jersey Supreme Court decision on when a foreign maker whose products reach New Jersey through distributors may be sued there.

terms.label: fractured decision
terms.gloss: A decision in which no single rationale wins a majority of the Justices, though a majority agrees on the result.

terms.label: track system
terms.gloss: Placing students in separate curricular tracks by perceived ability; the trial court found Washington's version discriminatory.

terms.label: excessive (award)
terms.gloss: Too high to be supported by the evidence, allowing the judge to reduce it or order a new trial.

terms.label: objective manifestation (objective theory)
terms.gloss: In contract law, what a party outwardly says or does, judged as a reasonable person would understand it; that, not secret intentions, controls.

terms.label: duplicate recovery
terms.gloss: Compensating the same loss twice, which damages rules forbid.

terms.label: out-of-pocket expenses
terms.gloss: Money actually spent, as opposed to profits that might have been earned.

terms.label: nonfinal order
terms.gloss: A court order that does not end the case; normally reviewable only later, on appeal from the final judgment.

terms.label: N.Y. CPLR § 5601(d)
terms.gloss: New York rule letting an appeal from a final judgment also bring up an earlier nonfinal Appellate Division order that necessarily affected it.

terms.label: Designated Judge
terms.gloss: A lower-court judge temporarily assigned to sit on New York's Court of Appeals to fill a vacancy.

terms.label: extraordinary (consequential) losses
terms.gloss: Unusual losses beyond the normal results of a breach; recoverable only if both parties contemplated them when contracting.

terms.label: Bituminous Coal Act of 1937
terms.gloss: A New Deal law stabilizing the soft-coal industry by setting minimum prices through a code, taxing coal sold outside it, and exempting coal producers used themselves.

terms.label: code (coal-pricing code)
terms.gloss: The Act's system of minimum prices and marketing rules binding coal producers who joined it.

terms.label: producer-consumer exemption
terms.gloss: The Act's exemption for coal mined by a company that consumes all of it itself rather than selling it.

terms.label: captive coal
terms.gloss: Coal mined by or for a company for its own use rather than for sale on the market.

terms.label: National Motor Vehicle Theft Act
terms.gloss: The 1919 'Dyer Act' making it a federal crime to transport a motor vehicle across state lines knowing it was stolen.

terms.label: residual phrase (catchall)
terms.gloss: General words at the end of a list, like 'any other self-propelled vehicle', meant to cover things not specifically named.

terms.label: Animal Welfare Act
terms.gloss: The federal law setting standards for humane treatment of animals by dealers, exhibitors and research facilities, enforced by USDA through licenses and penalties.

terms.label: general statement of policy
terms.gloss: An agency's announcement of how it plans to use its discretion; not binding, so the APA exempts it from notice and comment.

terms.label: book value
terms.gloss: A company's or share's value as shown in its accounts (assets minus debts), which can differ greatly from market price.

terms.label: express trustee
terms.gloss: A trustee appointed deliberately by a written trust, as opposed to someone the law merely treats as a trustee.

terms.label: short-swing profit rule
terms.gloss: A rule making insiders hand over to the company any profit from buying and selling its shares within six months.

terms.label: secured (debt)
terms.gloss: Backed by collateral, here the house, which the lender can sell if the loan is not repaid.

terms.label: wrongful foreclosure
terms.gloss: A claim that a lender foreclosed illegally, for example in breach of its promises or of required procedures.

terms.label: slander of title
terms.gloss: A claim that someone maliciously made false statements disparaging a person's ownership of property, causing financial loss.

terms.label: unreasonable collection
terms.gloss: A Texas claim that a creditor used outrageous, harassing tactics to collect a debt.

terms.label: Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 26.02
terms.gloss: Texas's statute of frauds for loans: loan agreements over $50,000 must be in a signed writing to be enforceable.

terms.label: financial accommodation
terms.gloss: In the Texas statute, a lender's agreement to give a borrower some financial benefit, such as delaying payment or foreclosure.

terms.label: prime contract
terms.gloss: The main contract between a project owner (such as the government) and the contractor, who may then hire subcontractors to do parts of it.

terms.label: modification (of a contract)
terms.gloss: A change to the terms of an existing contract; whether it binds can turn on consideration, writing requirements, good faith, or duress.

terms.label: UCC § 1-103(b)
terms.gloss: The UCC provision keeping general legal principles, such as duress, fraud, and incapacity, in force unless the Code specifically displaces them.

terms.label: Restatement §§ 175–176
terms.gloss: Restatement (Second) of Contracts duress rules: § 175 lets a party avoid assent induced by an improper threat leaving no reasonable alternative; § 176 lists improper threats, including bad-faith threatened breach.

terms.label: factual issue vs. legal issue
terms.gloss: A factual issue asks what happened and is for the jury or trial judge, whose answer appeals courts rarely disturb; a legal issue asks what the law requires, which appeals courts decide themselves.

terms.label: defense verdict
terms.gloss: A verdict or judgment in the defendant's favor, meaning the plaintiff recovers nothing.

terms.label: forfeiture (of an argument)
terms.gloss: Losing the right to raise an argument by failing to present it properly or in time, for example not raising it in the lower courts or briefs.

terms.label: special parole
terms.gloss: A period of supervision after prison that federal drug laws once required; violating its conditions could send the person back to prison.

terms.label: guilty plea
terms.gloss: A defendant's formal admission in court that he committed the charged crime, which takes the place of a trial.

terms.label: possession with intent to distribute
terms.gloss: The drug crime of holding illegal drugs while planning to sell or pass them to others; punished more severely than simple possession.

terms.label: Rule 41(e) (criminal)
terms.gloss: The federal criminal rule (now Rule 41(g)) letting a person ask a court to order the government to return seized property.

terms.label: warranted search
terms.gloss: A search authorized in advance by a judge's warrant, which requires probable cause.

terms.label: common trust fund
terms.gloss: A fund in which a bank pools many small trusts for investment; Mullane involved a court proceeding settling its accounts for all beneficiaries at once.

terms.label: insertion order
terms.gloss: An advertising-industry order setting the price, volume, and other terms for running a client's ads; once signed, it works as the parties' contract.

terms.label: signed-modification requirement
terms.gloss: A contract term saying changes count only if put in a signed writing (a 'no oral modification' clause); many courts let parties waive it by later agreement or conduct.

terms.label: Restatement § 89
terms.gloss: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 89: a change to a not-yet-completed contract binds without new consideration if fair in light of unforeseen circumstances, or if the other side materially relied on it.

terms.label: dram-shop liability
terms.gloss: Liability of a seller of alcohol for harm caused by serving someone who is already visibly drunk.

terms.label: marker (casino credit)
terms.gloss: A casino IOU: a signed credit slip letting a gambler get chips now and pay later, enforceable much like a check.

terms.label: countercheck
terms.gloss: A check a gambler writes at the casino to get chips on credit; the casino deposits it later and can sue on it if it bounces.

terms.label: vigorish
terms.gloss: The commission a casino or bookmaker takes on bets; in baccarat, the house's cut of certain winning bets.

terms.label: primary jurisdiction
terms.gloss: A doctrine under which a court leaves a dispute, at least at first, to a specialized regulatory agency (such as a state casino commission) instead of deciding it itself.

terms.label: Casino Control Commission
terms.gloss: New Jersey's agency that licenses and regulates Atlantic City casinos.

terms.label: predicting state law
terms.gloss: When a federal court applies state law that the state's highest court has not settled, it must forecast how that court would rule (an 'Erie guess').

terms.label: change order
terms.gloss: A signed written amendment to a construction contract that changes the work or the price.

terms.label: nonresponsive (bid)
terms.gloss: Describes a bid that fails to meet the essential requirements of the request for bids, so it cannot be accepted as submitted.

terms.label: Procurement Code
terms.gloss: A state statute, such as New Mexico's, governing how public bodies buy goods and construction, including rules on opening, correcting, and withdrawing bids.
A New Mexico statute making government bodies immune from contract suits unless the claim is based on a valid written contract.

terms.label: Rule 1-012(B)(6)
terms.gloss: New Mexico's counterpart to federal Rule 12(b)(6): dismissal of a complaint that fails to state a claim on which relief can be granted.

terms.label: Restatement § 155
terms.gloss: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 155: a court may reform a writing that, because of both parties' mistake, fails to express what they actually agreed.

terms.label: Restatement § 157
terms.gloss: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 157: a party's carelessness in not catching a mistake does not bar relief unless it amounts to bad faith or unfair dealing.

terms.label: Third Civil Chamber
terms.gloss: The chamber of France's Court of Cassation that hears civil cases about property, construction, and leases.

terms.label: quash (a decision)
terms.gloss: For France's Court of Cassation, to annul a lower court's decision for legal error, usually sending the case to another court to decide again.

terms.label: later/specific-over-general canons
terms.gloss: Interpretive rules: when two laws truly conflict, the more specific one, or the later-enacted one, usually controls.

terms.label: Winter
terms.gloss: Winter v. NRDC (2008): a preliminary injunction requires likely success, likely irreparable harm, a favorable balance of equities, and consistency with the public interest.

terms.label: declaration (sworn statement)
terms.gloss: A written statement signed under penalty of perjury, used as evidence much like an affidavit.

terms.label: Authorization for Use of Military Force
match: authorization for use of military force
terms.gloss: The 2001 congressional resolution letting the President use force against those responsible for the September 11 attacks; the government relied on it to detain suspected enemies.

terms.label: Combatant Status Review Tribunals
terms.gloss: Military panels created in 2004 to decide whether Guantanamo detainees were 'enemy combatants'; detainees had no lawyer and limited access to evidence.

terms.label: tribunal personal representative
terms.gloss: A military officer assigned to help a detainee before a status tribunal; expressly not a lawyer or advocate for the detainee.

terms.label: Detainee Treatment Act
terms.gloss: A 2005 law that, among other things, removed federal courts' power to hear Guantanamo detainees' habeas cases and gave the D.C. Circuit limited review of tribunal decisions.

terms.label: Military Commissions Act
terms.gloss: A 2006 law that set up military trials for detainees and, in section 7, stripped courts of habeas jurisdiction over alien detainees, including in pending cases.

terms.label: Suspension Clause
terms.gloss: Article I, § 9, cl. 2 of the Constitution: the privilege of habeas corpus may not be suspended except when rebellion or invasion requires it for public safety.

terms.label: Rasul
terms.gloss: Rasul v. Bush (2004): the federal habeas statute let Guantanamo detainees challenge their detention in federal court.

terms.label: Hamdi
terms.gloss: Hamdi v. Rumsfeld (2004): a U.S. citizen held as an enemy combatant must get notice and a fair chance to contest the basis for detention before a neutral decision-maker.

terms.label: Hamdan
terms.gloss: Hamdan v. Rumsfeld (2006): the Detainee Treatment Act's removal of habeas jurisdiction did not reach pending cases, and the President's military commissions were unlawful as set up.

terms.label: Eisentrager
terms.gloss: Johnson v. Eisentrager (1950): German prisoners convicted by a U.S. military commission and held in occupied Germany could not seek habeas in U.S. courts.

terms.label: Insular Cases
terms.gloss: Early-1900s Supreme Court decisions holding that only 'fundamental' constitutional rights automatically apply in U.S. territories not headed for statehood.

terms.label: Reid
terms.gloss: Reid v. Covert (1957): American civilians abroad (military spouses) could not be tried by court-martial without the Constitution's jury-trial protections.

terms.label: Petition of Right
terms.gloss: A 1628 English statute Parliament forced on Charles I, condemning imprisonment without stated cause, among other royal abuses.

terms.label: Habeas Corpus Act of 1679
terms.gloss: The English statute that strengthened habeas corpus by setting deadlines and penalties so jailers had to bring prisoners before a court promptly.

terms.label: collateral review
terms.gloss: A separate later proceeding, such as habeas, that challenges a conviction or detention outside the ordinary direct appeal.

terms.label: exhaust (a remedy)
terms.gloss: To use up an available remedy or procedure first, before going to court for other relief.

terms.label: Statement and Account Clause
terms.gloss: Article I, § 9, cl. 7 of the Constitution: a regular statement and account of all public money received and spent must be published from time to time.

terms.label: Central Intelligence Agency Act
terms.gloss: A 1949 law letting the CIA spend money secretly, accounted for only on the Director's certificate rather than through ordinary public accounts.

terms.label: Flast v. Cohen
terms.gloss: Flast v. Cohen (1968): a federal taxpayer may challenge a congressional spending law that allegedly violates a specific limit on the spending power, such as the Establishment Clause.

terms.label: taxing and spending power
terms.gloss: Congress's constitutional power to impose taxes and to spend money for the general welfare (Article I, § 8, cl. 1).

terms.label: Fair Debt Collection Practices Act
terms.gloss: A 1977 federal law banning abusive, deceptive, or unfair debt-collection practices and letting consumers sue collectors for damages and attorney's fees.

terms.label: § 1391(b)(2)
terms.gloss: The federal venue provision allowing suit in any district where a substantial part of the events or omissions giving rise to the claim occurred.

terms.label: Leroy
terms.gloss: Leroy v. Great Western United Corp. (1979): read the old 'where the claim arose' venue rule narrowly, usually pointing to one place, with emphasis on fairness to defendants.

terms.label: bona fide error defense
terms.gloss: An FDCPA defense: a collector is not liable if the violation was unintentional and came from a genuine mistake despite reasonable procedures to avoid it.

terms.label: Collector of Customs
terms.gloss: The federal official in charge of a customs port, who collected import duties and held or sold imported goods under the customs laws.

terms.label: reasonable inferences
terms.gloss: Conclusions logically drawn from the facts alleged or shown; on motions to dismiss or for summary judgment they are drawn in favor of the non-moving party.

terms.label: odd lot / round lot
terms.gloss: An odd lot is a stock trade of fewer than 100 shares; a round lot is a trade in units of 100.

terms.label: odd-lot differential
terms.gloss: The extra per-share charge odd-lot dealers added to the round-lot price, on top of ordinary brokerage commissions.

terms.label: death-knell doctrine
terms.gloss: A since-rejected theory allowing an immediate appeal of an order denying class status, because with tiny individual claims that order effectively ended the case.

terms.label: Rule 23(b)(1) and (b)(2)
terms.gloss: Rule 23(b)(1) covers classes where separate suits would risk inconsistent results; (b)(2) covers classes seeking an injunction or declaration about conduct affecting the whole group.

terms.label: fluid recovery
terms.gloss: Using unclaimed class damages for a general benefit to the class or similar people (here, lowering future odd-lot charges) instead of paying identified individuals.

terms.label: legal conclusions
terms.gloss: Statements that simply assert a legal result (e.g., 'defendant assaulted me') without the underlying facts; courts need not accept them as true.

terms.label: appointment (of trust property)
terms.gloss: Exercising a power of appointment: directing who will receive property, here trust assets, that the power-holder controls.

terms.label: McGee
terms.gloss: McGee v. International Life (1957): California could hear a suit against a Texas insurer that solicited and kept a single insurance contract with a Californian.

terms.label: republication
terms.gloss: The wills doctrine that re-executing a will or related document treats it as newly made at the later date, which can change the law that governs it.

terms.label: coercive relief
terms.gloss: A court order backed by enforcement power that forces a party to pay or act, such as a damages judgment or injunction.

terms.label: conflict (of laws)
terms.gloss: A real difference between the laws of two places that would change the result, forcing a court to choose which law applies.
terms.context: (choice of law|choice-of-law|other states’|another state|forum law|Kansas|established conflict|applicable laws)

terms.label: acceptance (of a bill)
terms.gloss: The drawee's signed promise on a bill of exchange to pay it when due; the acceptor then becomes primarily liable to whoever holds the bill.

terms.label: bill of discovery
terms.gloss: An old equity proceeding forcing a party to answer questions or produce documents under oath for use in another case.

terms.label: certificate of division
terms.gloss: A historical procedure: when the two judges of a federal circuit court disagreed on a legal question, they sent it to the Supreme Court for an answer.

terms.label: Court of Errors
terms.gloss: New York's highest court until 1847 (the Court for the Correction of Errors), later replaced by the Court of Appeals.

terms.label: value (for negotiable paper)
terms.gloss: Something given in exchange that the law recognizes; a holder of a bill or note must have given value, such as cancelling an existing debt, to take it free of earlier defenses.
terms.context: \b(holders?|negotiable|paper|old debt|existing debt|antecedent debt|question was value|valuable consideration)\b

terms.label: infirmities
terms.gloss: Defects or defenses attached to an instrument, such as fraud in the deal that produced it.

terms.label: antecedent equities
terms.gloss: Defenses arising from earlier dealings between the original parties, such as fraud in the land sale, which a protected holder takes free of.

terms.label: discount (selling paper)
terms.gloss: Selling a note or bill before it is due for less than its face value, the buyer profiting from the difference.

terms.label: article 78 proceeding
terms.gloss: New York's special court proceeding for challenging a decision by a government or similar body as arbitrary, unlawful, or procedurally improper.

terms.label: Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA)
terms.gloss: The federal law giving states special-education money on condition that they provide disabled children a free appropriate public education, with procedures parents can enforce.

terms.label: expert fees
terms.gloss: Payments to hired specialists who advise or testify; normally not shifted to the losing side beyond small statutory witness allowances.

terms.label: impartial hearing
terms.gloss: IDEA's administrative hearing before a neutral officer, where parents can challenge a school district's decisions about their child.

terms.label: Crawford Fitting
terms.gloss: Crawford Fitting Co. v. J.T. Gibbons (1987): courts may not shift expert-witness fees beyond the small statutory witness fee without explicit statutory or contractual authority.

terms.label: Casey (W. Va. Univ. Hospitals)
terms.gloss: West Virginia University Hospitals v. Casey (1991): § 1988's 'attorney's fee' did not include expert fees; Congress then amended § 1988 to allow them.
28 U.S.C. § 1821, which sets the small daily attendance fee and travel allowance paid to witnesses.

terms.label: Spending Clause
terms.gloss: Congress's power to spend for the general welfare; conditions attached to federal money for states work like contract terms, so they must be stated clearly.

terms.label: clear notice
terms.gloss: The Spending Clause rule that a statute must tell states unambiguously what obligations they accept by taking federal money.

terms.label: free appropriate public education
terms.gloss: IDEA's core guarantee: special education and related services meeting a disabled child's needs, at public expense.

terms.label: Marek v. Chesny
terms.gloss: Marek v. Chesny (1985): where a statute defines attorney's fees 'as part of costs,' those fees count as costs under the federal settlement-offer rule.

terms.label: Smith v. Robinson
terms.gloss: Smith v. Robinson (1984): held the education law then in force allowed no attorney's fees to winning parents; Congress overturned it in 1986.

terms.label: Affordable Care Act (ACA)
terms.gloss: The 2010 federal health-insurance law ('Obamacare'), which expanded coverage through subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and a requirement that individuals have insurance.

terms.label: individual mandate
terms.gloss: The ACA's § 5000A(a) requirement that most people have health insurance; from 2019 the penalty for not complying was zero.

terms.label: shared-responsibility payment
terms.gloss: The ACA's tax-like penalty for going without required health insurance; Congress cut it to $0 starting in 2019.

terms.label: pocketbook injury
terms.gloss: A direct financial loss, the classic kind of concrete injury that supports standing.

terms.label: classified civil service
terms.gloss: The government workforce hired on merit, often through examinations, and given job protections, as opposed to political appointees; 'classified' employees are those covered by these rules.

terms.label: reduction in force
terms.gloss: A layoff of government employees because of budget cuts or reorganization, not their performance or conduct.

terms.label: loyalty board
terms.gloss: Panels under President Truman's 1947 loyalty program that decided whether there were reasonable grounds to believe a federal employee disloyal; the Loyalty Review Board heard appeals.

terms.label: Executive Order 9835
terms.gloss: President Truman's 1947 order creating the federal employee loyalty program, allowing dismissal on reasonable grounds to believe a person disloyal.

terms.label: treason
terms.gloss: The crime of making war against the United States or aiding its enemies; the only crime the Constitution defines.

terms.label: Lloyd-LaFollette Act
terms.gloss: A 1912 law protecting classified federal employees from removal except for causes promoting the efficiency of the service, with notice and a chance to answer in writing.

terms.label: Lovett
terms.gloss: United States v. Lovett (1946): a law cutting off pay to three named federal employees branded disloyal was an unconstitutional bill of attainder, punishment without trial.

terms.label: proscription
terms.gloss: A formal ban; here, barring a person from future federal employment.

terms.label: United Public Workers
terms.gloss: United Public Workers v. Mitchell (1947): upheld the Hatch Act's limits on federal employees' political activity.

terms.label: guilt by association
terms.gloss: Judging a person disloyal or guilty because of the groups or people they associate with, rather than their own acts.

terms.label: blocked / frozen property
terms.gloss: Frozen by government order: the owner, such as a foreign government, cannot transfer or use the property without a government license.

terms.label: Algerian declarations (Algiers Accords)
terms.gloss: The January 1981 agreements, mediated by Algeria, in which the U.S. and Iran arranged the hostages' release and sent claims to an international tribunal.

terms.label: Iran–United States Claims Tribunal
terms.gloss: An international arbitration tribunal in The Hague, created by the 1981 accords, to decide claims between Americans and Iran.

terms.label: Trading With the Enemy Act
terms.gloss: A 1917 law giving the President wartime powers over enemy property, including 'vesting' (taking title to) it for the United States.

terms.label: vesting power
terms.gloss: The power to take ownership of foreign property for the United States, not merely to freeze it.

terms.label: Hostage Act
terms.gloss: An 1868 law directing the President to demand release of citizens unjustly imprisoned by foreign governments and to use means short of war to free them.

terms.label: executive agreement
terms.gloss: An international agreement made by the President alone, without the Senate's two-thirds treaty approval.

terms.label: International Claims Settlement Act
terms.gloss: A 1949 law creating a commission to divide money received in claims settlements among Americans with claims against foreign governments.

terms.label: Pink
terms.gloss: United States v. Pink (1942): upheld an executive agreement with the Soviet Union settling claims and gave it the force of law over contrary state policy.

terms.label: Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (FSIA)
terms.gloss: A 1976 law setting when foreign states can be sued in U.S. courts, with exceptions such as commercial activity, and taking immunity decisions away from the State Department.

terms.label: absolute sovereign immunity
terms.gloss: The older rule that a foreign government could never be sued without its consent, later replaced by a 'restrictive' rule allowing suits over commercial acts.

terms.label: revival (of a law)
terms.gloss: Bringing an expired or suspended law back into force, for example when a statute provides that old restrictions return after a stated event.

terms.label: brig
terms.gloss: A two-masted sailing ship.

terms.label: cleared (port)
terms.gloss: Obtained official customs permission to leave port.

terms.label: sentence (admiralty)
terms.gloss: In old admiralty cases the 'sentence' was the court's final decree, here condemning the cargo; 'sentence affirmed' means the Supreme Court upheld it.

terms.label: the Convention (CISG)
terms.gloss: Here, the CISG: the 1980 treaty governing international sales of goods between businesses in member countries.

terms.label: MCC-Marble
terms.gloss: MCC-Marble Ceramic Center v. Ceramica Nuova D'Agostino (11th Cir. 1998): under the CISG, evidence of the parties' actual intent can override written terms; the U.S. parol evidence rule does not apply.

terms.label: seniority system
terms.gloss: Workplace rules giving longer-serving employees priority for jobs, promotions, and layoff protection; here seniority was counted within one department.

terms.label: Title VII § 703(h)
terms.gloss: The part of Title VII that protects a genuine (bona fide) seniority system, even one with unequal racial effects, unless it was created or kept with intent to discriminate.

terms.label: Teamsters (1977)
terms.gloss: International Brotherhood of Teamsters v. United States (1977): a bona fide seniority system is lawful under Title VII even if it carries forward the effects of earlier discrimination.

terms.label: Commissioner of Internal Revenue
terms.gloss: The head of the Internal Revenue Service, named as the government's party in federal tax cases.

terms.label: tax incidence
terms.gloss: Who bears the legal duty to pay tax on income; here, whether Sunnen rather than his wife owed tax on the royalties.

terms.label: Clifford–Horst line
terms.gloss: Supreme Court tax cases (Helvering v. Clifford, Helvering v. Horst) holding that a person who keeps control of income cannot avoid tax by assigning it to family members.

terms.label: Dobson
terms.gloss: Dobson v. Commissioner (1943): appeals courts should give strong deference to Tax Court decisions, overturning them only for clear legal error.

terms.label: immunity from judicial process
terms.gloss: Protection from being subject to court orders at all; Nixon claimed a sitting President could not be compelled by a court.

terms.label: chambers
terms.gloss: A judge's private office; a matter handled 'in chambers' is heard privately, outside open court.

terms.label: sealed (records)
terms.gloss: Kept confidential by court order, so the public and others cannot see it.

terms.label: compulsory process
terms.gloss: A criminal defendant's Sixth Amendment right to have the court order witnesses or evidence produced for the defense.

terms.label: Court-packing plan
terms.gloss: President Franklin Roosevelt's failed 1937 plan to add Justices to the Supreme Court so it would uphold New Deal laws.

terms.label: Burr proceedings
terms.gloss: Aaron Burr's 1807 treason trial, where Chief Justice Marshall ruled that President Jefferson could be subpoenaed to provide evidence.

terms.label: implied duty of marketability
terms.gloss: A Kansas rule read into oil-and-gas leases: the producer must pay the costs of making gas sellable and cannot deduct them from owners' royalties.

terms.label: Comcast (2013)
terms.gloss: Comcast Corp. v. Behrend (2013): before certifying a class, courts must rigorously check that damages can be measured class-wide consistent with the theory of liability.

terms.label: special session
terms.gloss: A meeting of a legislature called outside its regular schedule, often to handle a particular matter.

terms.label: public facilities district
terms.gloss: A special local government body created under Washington law to build and own public facilities, here the baseball stadium.

terms.label: bond validation action
terms.gloss: A Washington lawsuit procedure letting a government get a binding court ruling that its bonds are valid before relying on them.

terms.label: public purpose
terms.gloss: A use benefiting the public generally; government may spend tax money only for public purposes, not mainly for private benefit.

terms.label: gift of public funds
terms.gloss: Washington's constitutional ban (article VIII, sections 5 and 7) on governments giving away public money or property, or lending public credit, to private parties.

terms.label: tax uniformity
terms.gloss: A state constitutional rule that taxes on the same class of property or activity be applied at the same rate.

terms.label: peppercorn
terms.gloss: From the old saying that even a peppercorn can be consideration: courts usually ask only whether something was exchanged, not whether the bargain was fair.

terms.label: time-and-materials contract
terms.gloss: A pricing method where the customer pays for actual hours worked at set rates plus materials used, instead of a fixed price.

terms.label: Louisiana Civil Code
terms.gloss: Louisiana's main body of private law, organized as a code in the French and Spanish civil-law tradition rather than built mainly from judges' decisions.

terms.label: stipulation pour autrui
terms.gloss: Louisiana's term for a contract term giving a benefit to a third person, who can then enforce it, like a third-party beneficiary.

terms.label: selective enforcement
terms.gloss: An agency's choice about which violations to pursue; choosing not to enforce does not change what the law requires.

terms.label: then-required amount (diversity)
terms.gloss: The minimum value a claim had to exceed for a federal court to hear it on diversity grounds, then $10,000 (now $75,000).

terms.label: agreed final judgment
terms.gloss: A judgment entered with the parties' consent, ending the case on terms they accepted.

terms.label: demand for assurances
terms.gloss: Under UCC § 2-609, a party with reasonable grounds to doubt the other's performance may demand adequate assurance and suspend its own performance until it comes.

terms.label: wager
terms.gloss: A bet. Contracts that were really bets on price changes, with no intent to deliver goods, were illegal under some state laws.

terms.label: commodity futures
terms.gloss: Contracts to buy or sell goods like cotton at a set price on a future date; some old state laws banned such deals when used for gambling.

terms.label: crop share
terms.gloss: An arrangement where a tenant farmer pays rent with a share of the crop rather than cash.

terms.label: inadequate damages
terms.gloss: Courts order specific performance only when money damages would not fully make the buyer whole, as when the goods cannot be bought elsewhere.

terms.label: retained (a lawyer)
terms.gloss: Hired a lawyer or law firm to represent you in a matter.

terms.label: Court of Appeal (France)
terms.gloss: In France, the intermediate appeals court that rehears both facts and law after a first-level court decides.

terms.label: individual-house construction contract
terms.gloss: A French statutory contract type in which a builder agrees to build a house for a set price, with strong legal protections for the owner.

terms.label: coercive monetary penalty (astreinte)
terms.gloss: In French law, an astreinte: a court-ordered payment that keeps growing for each day or period a party fails to obey.

terms.label: substitute damages
terms.gloss: Money awarded in place of the promised performance, measured by the loss caused, as distinct from making the debtor pay the agreed price itself.

terms.label: 2016 reforms (French contract law)
terms.gloss: France's 2016 overhaul of the contract-law part of its Civil Code, modernizing and renumbering rules such as former article 1134.

terms.label: collective bargaining agreement
terms.gloss: A contract between an employer and a union setting wages, job rights, and seniority for the workers the union represents.

terms.label: Railway Labor Act
terms.gloss: A 1926 federal law governing labor relations in railroads (and later airlines), including union representation and how disputes are resolved.

terms.label: National Railroad Adjustment Board
terms.gloss: A federal board under the Railway Labor Act that resolves disputes between railroads and employees over interpreting their labor agreements.

terms.label: indispensable (party)
terms.gloss: So essential to a case that, if it cannot be brought in, the lawsuit should not go forward without it.

terms.label: statutory service agent
terms.gloss: A person a corporation names under state law to receive lawsuits and legal papers on its behalf in that state.

terms.label: adequate and independent state ground
terms.gloss: A state-law basis that alone supports a state court's judgment; the U.S. Supreme Court will not review a judgment resting on one.

terms.label: Canada Malting (1932)
terms.gloss: Canada Malting Co. v. Paterson Steamships (1932): a U.S. court could decline a suit between foreigners over events abroad, even though plaintiffs preferred U.S. law.

terms.label: commitment (to jail)
terms.gloss: An order sending a person to jail or custody.

terms.label: Botsford (1891)
terms.gloss: Union Pacific Railway v. Botsford (1891): without a statute, federal courts could not order a plaintiff to undergo a medical examination.

terms.label: offeree
terms.gloss: The person to whom an offer is made, who has the power to accept it.

terms.label: Commission of Appeals (Texas)
terms.gloss: A former panel of Texas judges that helped the overloaded Texas Supreme Court by recommending decisions the Supreme Court could adopt.

terms.label: return promise
terms.gloss: A promise given in exchange for the other side's promise; when acceptance takes this form, it usually must be communicated.

terms.label: trial without a jury
terms.gloss: A bench trial: the judge alone decides the facts as well as the law.

terms.label: Carlill v. Carbolic Smoke Ball Co.
match: carlill v. carbolic smoke ball co.
terms.gloss: An 1893 English case: an offer made to the public could be accepted by doing the requested act, without first notifying the offeror.

terms.label: charge (on property)
terms.gloss: A payment obligation attached to property, so whoever takes the property takes it subject to that duty, here the widow's support.

terms.label: unduly influenced
terms.gloss: Made because someone improperly pressured the person, overpowering free choice; a will made that way can be set aside.

terms.label: legal maxim
terms.gloss: A short traditional statement of legal principle, such as 'no one may profit from his own wrong'.

terms.label: racial gerrymander
terms.gloss: A district drawn mainly on the basis of race without sufficient justification, which violates equal protection.

terms.label: remedial plan
terms.gloss: A replacement district map drawn to fix a plan a court found unlawful.

terms.label: associational injury
terms.gloss: Harm to the right to join with others for political ends, such as party organizing, fundraising, and campaigning.

terms.label: Article I, § 2
terms.gloss: The constitutional clause providing that House members are chosen every two years 'by the People' of the states.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 1253
terms.gloss: The statute allowing a direct appeal to the Supreme Court from a three-judge district court's order granting or denying an injunction.

terms.label: packing (districts)
terms.gloss: Concentrating a party's voters into a few districts so they win those by huge margins and waste votes.

terms.label: entrenchment
terms.gloss: Using district lines to lock a party into power so it cannot easily be voted out.

terms.label: judicially manageable standards
terms.gloss: Clear legal tests courts can apply consistently; their absence is a main sign that an issue is a political question for other branches.

terms.label: Gill v. Whitford (2018)
terms.gloss: Gill v. Whitford (2018): voters challenging a partisan map must show harm in their own district; the Court decided standing, not whether such claims can be heard.

terms.label: proportional representation
terms.gloss: A system where a party wins seats in proportion to its share of the vote; the Constitution does not require it.

terms.label: viewpoint discrimination
terms.gloss: Government treating speech or speakers differently because of the opinions they express, which the First Amendment almost always forbids.

terms.label: Guarantee Clause
terms.gloss: Article IV, § 4: the United States guarantees every state a republican form of government; courts treat claims under it as nonjusticiable.

terms.label: 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1)
terms.gloss: The federal law making it a crime for anyone convicted of a crime punishable by more than a year in prison to possess a gun.

terms.label: sentence enhancement
terms.gloss: A longer sentence imposed because of a defendant's prior convictions or other aggravating facts.

terms.label: business-offense exception
terms.gloss: The federal gun law's exclusion of antitrust and similar business-regulation crimes from the convictions that trigger the gun ban.

terms.label: soft referral
terms.gloss: In international adoption, informally identifying or reserving a specific child for prospective parents before the official steps allow it.

terms.label: home study
terms.gloss: An assessment of prospective adoptive parents and their home, required before an adoption can be completed.

terms.label: strike (evidence)
terms.gloss: To remove material from the court record so the court does not consider it.

terms.label: procedural redressability
terms.gloss: For a claim that an agency skipped a required procedure, the plaintiff need not prove the proper procedure would change the result, only that it could.

terms.label: unfair method of competition
terms.gloss: Business conduct the FTC Act forbids because it harms competition, as defined case by case by the FTC and courts.

terms.label: unfair or deceptive act or practice
match: unfair or deceptive act or practice
terms.gloss: Conduct the FTC Act bans because it misleads or unfairly harms consumers.

terms.label: FTC Act § 6(g)
terms.gloss: The FTC Act provision letting the Commission make rules and regulations for the purpose of carrying out the Act.

terms.label: Fair Packaging and Labeling Act
terms.gloss: A 1966 federal law requiring accurate labeling of consumer products and giving the FTC and FDA rulemaking power to enforce it.

terms.label: self-defense
terms.gloss: The right to use reasonable force, even deadly force if necessary, to protect oneself or others from an imminent threat.

terms.label: Revised Statutes § 753
terms.gloss: The federal habeas statute then in force, letting federal courts free prisoners held for acts done under U.S. law or in violation of it.

terms.label: traverse
terms.gloss: A formal written denial of facts stated in the other side's pleading; in habeas, the prisoner's reply to the jailer's return.

terms.label: implied powers
terms.gloss: Powers not spelled out in the Constitution or a statute but reasonably inferred as necessary to carry out the powers that are.

terms.label: circuit attendance (riding circuit)
terms.gloss: The former duty of Supreme Court Justices to travel and sit as judges in the regional federal circuit courts.

terms.label: breach of the peace
terms.gloss: Disturbing public order, for example by violence; keeping the peace means preventing such disturbances.

terms.label: Fugitive Slave Act
terms.gloss: Federal laws (1793, 1850) requiring return of people who escaped slavery; federal officers enforcing them were sometimes prosecuted by Northern states.

terms.label: nullification
terms.gloss: South Carolina's 1832 claim that a state could void federal tariff laws; Congress responded in 1833 with laws protecting federal officers.

terms.label: McLeod controversy
terms.gloss: An 1840s dispute after New York prosecuted British subject Alexander McLeod for acts done under British orders; it led Congress to expand federal habeas in 1842.

terms.label: federal common-law crimes
terms.gloss: Power to punish crimes Congress has not defined; since 1812 federal courts have had none, so every federal crime must be written in a statute.

terms.label: 21 U.S.C. § 342(a)(4)
terms.gloss: The food-law clause treating food as adulterated if prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions that may make it harmful.

terms.label: 21 U.S.C. § 371(a)
terms.gloss: The food-and-drug law section letting the FDA issue regulations for the Act's efficient enforcement.

terms.label: insanitary
terms.gloss: Unsanitary: unclean or unhealthy conditions that may contaminate food.

terms.label: concise general statement
terms.gloss: The explanation of a final rule's basis and purpose that APA § 553(c) requires an agency to publish with it.

terms.label: finality order
terms.gloss: An SEC order declaring that an administrative law judge's initial decision has become the Commission's final action.

terms.label: industry bar
terms.gloss: An order barring a person from working in the investment industry.

terms.label: officer (vs. employee)
terms.gloss: An Officer of the United States must be appointed by the President, a court, or a department head; mere government employees need not be.

terms.label: significant authority
terms.gloss: Buckley v. Valeo's test: an official who exercises significant authority under federal law is an 'officer' who must be properly appointed.

terms.label: Freytag (1991)
terms.gloss: Freytag v. Commissioner (1991): Tax Court special trial judges are officers, because they hold continuing offices and exercise significant discretion.

terms.label: Germaine (1879)
terms.gloss: United States v. Germaine (1879): an officer holds a continuing position established by law, not a temporary or occasional task.

terms.label: Merit Systems Protection Board
terms.gloss: An independent federal agency that hears federal employees' appeals of firings and similar actions, including cases about ALJs.

terms.label: good-cause protection
terms.gloss: A rule that an official can be removed only for a good reason, such as misconduct, not at will.

terms.label: government-contractor defense
terms.gloss: Protects a government contractor from state-law design-defect claims if the government approved reasonably precise specifications, the product met them, and the maker warned of dangers known to it but not the government.

terms.label: manufacturing defect
terms.gloss: A product-liability claim that a particular item departed from its intended design during production, making it more dangerous than intended.

terms.label: reasonably precise specifications
terms.gloss: Under the government-contractor defense, detailed product requirements the government actually reviewed and approved, rather than vague goals left to the contractor.

terms.label: procurement
terms.gloss: The government's buying of goods or services, such as military supplies, through contracts.

terms.label: consolidation (of cases)
terms.gloss: Combining separate cases or applications so they are heard and decided together; 'unconsolidated' cases stay formally separate even if heard side by side.

terms.label: multidistrict record
terms.gloss: The shared pretrial evidence file from multidistrict litigation, where many similar federal suits are gathered before one judge.

terms.label: latent risk
terms.gloss: A hidden danger that is not apparent at the time and shows up only later, such as a disease with a long delay.

terms.label: companion decision
terms.gloss: A related case decided at the same time by the same court, usually in a separate opinion.

terms.label: uninsured-motorist coverage
terms.gloss: Car-insurance coverage that pays the policyholder when injured by a driver who has no insurance.

terms.label: stacking (insurance)
terms.gloss: Adding together the coverage limits of several insurance policies or vehicles to get a larger total payout for one accident.

terms.label: false conflict
terms.gloss: A case where two states' laws differ but only one state actually has an interest in applying its law, so there is no real clash.

terms.label: significant contacts (choice of law)
terms.gloss: The Hague plurality's test: a state may apply its own law only if it has a significant contact, or several, creating state interests, so the choice is neither arbitrary nor fundamentally unfair.

terms.label: Leflar's choice-influencing considerations
terms.gloss: A choice-of-law method by Professor Robert Leflar weighing predictability, interstate order, simplicity, the forum's interests, and which law is the 'better rule.'

terms.label: better rule of law
terms.gloss: Leflar's fifth factor: a court may prefer the law it judges sounder or more modern when choosing among states' laws.

terms.label: dismissal stipulation
terms.gloss: A signed agreement by the parties to end a lawsuit, which takes effect once filed with or entered by the court.

terms.label: entered (court)
