terms.gloss: Formally recorded on the court's docket, which is what makes a judgment or order official.

terms.label: unsecured creditor
terms.gloss: Someone owed money without a lien or collateral backing the debt, so with no claim to any particular property.

terms.label: Rule 66
terms.gloss: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 66, governing court-appointed receivers in federal lawsuits.

terms.label: winding up
terms.gloss: Closing down an arrangement in an orderly way: finishing business, paying costs, and returning property.

terms.label: trust account
terms.gloss: A bank account in which a lawyer holds clients' money, kept separate from the lawyer's own funds.

terms.label: Code of Civil Procedure section 1281.2
terms.gloss: The California statute directing courts to order arbitration when a valid arbitration agreement exists, unless grounds exist to refuse.

terms.label: backpay
terms.gloss: Wages an employee would have earned between being fired and a decision in the case.

terms.label: California Arbitration Act
terms.gloss: California's own statute governing arbitration agreements and procedures, found in the Code of Civil Procedure.

terms.label: Civil Rights Act of 1991
terms.gloss: A federal law strengthening job-discrimination remedies, including damages under Title VII, and encouraging arbitration 'where appropriate.'

terms.label: FAA employment exemption
terms.gloss: Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, which excludes certain workers' employment contracts (such as transportation workers') from the Act.

terms.label: contract defenses
terms.gloss: Standard reasons a contract can't be enforced, such as fraud, duress, or unconscionability.

terms.label: Civil Code sections 1668 and 3513
terms.gloss: California statutes voiding contracts that excuse someone from liability for fraud or legal violations, and barring private waiver of laws made for a public purpose.

terms.label: award (arbitration)
terms.gloss: An arbitrator's final written decision resolving the dispute.

terms.label: postdispute agreement
terms.gloss: An agreement made after a dispute has already arisen, when both sides know what is at stake, rather than signed in advance as a job condition.

terms.label: Civil Code section 1670.5
terms.gloss: The California statute letting a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable contract, cut out the unconscionable term, or limit its effect.

terms.label: collateral illegality
terms.gloss: An unlawful term incidental to a contract's main purpose, which can be cut out, unlike illegality that runs through the whole deal.

terms.label: permeated by an unlawful purpose
terms.gloss: So shot through with an unfair or illegal aim that no single term can be cut out to save the rest.

terms.label: drafter
terms.gloss: The party who wrote the contract; courts often read unclear terms against it and refuse to reward its overreaching.

terms.label: repeat player
terms.gloss: A party, like an employer, that uses the same arbitrators repeatedly, raising concern they may favor it to win future business.

terms.label: vindicate (a right)
terms.gloss: To enforce a legal right and make it effective in practice.

terms.label: capital (partnership)
terms.gloss: Money or property a partner has invested in the firm, normally returned when the partner leaves.

terms.label: withdrawal benefits
terms.gloss: Payments a partnership agreement gives a partner who leaves the firm, such as a share of future profits.

terms.label: receivables
terms.gloss: Money owed to a business for work already done or billed but not yet paid.

terms.label: rule 1-500
terms.gloss: California's former lawyer-ethics rule barring agreements that restrict a lawyer's right to practice after leaving a firm, with listed exceptions.

terms.label: Business and Professions Code § 16602
terms.gloss: California statute letting partners agree not to compete within a defined area when a partnership dissolves or a partner leaves; an exception to California's ban on noncompetes.

terms.label: shipping documents
terms.gloss: Papers such as the bill of lading and insurance certificate that represent goods in transit; handing them over lets the buyer claim the cargo and triggers payment.

terms.label: speech (House of Lords)
terms.gloss: In the House of Lords, each judge's separate opinion was called a 'speech.'

terms.label: supervening
terms.gloss: Happening after the contract was made, unexpectedly and outside the parties' control.

terms.label: enemy-payment restrictions
terms.gloss: Wartime laws forbidding trade with or payments to people in enemy-controlled territory without government license.

terms.label: Board of Trade license
terms.gloss: Permission from Britain's Board of Trade, a government department, needed in wartime to deal with parties in enemy territory.

terms.label: Chandler v. Webster
terms.gloss: A 1904 English case holding that when a contract is frustrated, losses lie where they fall, so money already paid cannot be recovered; Fibrosa overruled it.

terms.label: coronation cases
terms.gloss: Early-1900s English cases over rooms rented to watch Edward VII's coronation procession, cancelled when he fell ill; they shaped the doctrine of frustration.

terms.label: prepaid freight
terms.gloss: Shipping charges paid in advance, which by long custom the carrier keeps even if the goods are lost: an exception to recovering money paid.

terms.label: risk of loss
terms.gloss: Who bears the loss if goods are damaged or destroyed before the buyer takes them over.

terms.label: Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943
terms.gloss: A British statute letting courts adjust money paid under a frustrated contract, including letting the payee keep some to cover its expenses.

terms.label: allowing the appeal
terms.gloss: British phrasing for the appeals court ruling in favor of the party who appealed, overturning the decision below.

terms.label: Arms Export Control Act
terms.gloss: The federal law governing U.S. sales and exports of weapons and military equipment to foreign governments.

terms.label: Foreign Military Sales Program
terms.gloss: A program in which foreign governments buy U.S. defense equipment through the U.S. government, which contracts with the suppliers.

terms.label: Letter of Offer and Acceptance
terms.gloss: The government-to-government agreement setting the terms of a Foreign Military Sales purchase.

terms.label: agency boards (contract appeals)
terms.gloss: Boards of contract appeals: agency tribunals that hear contractors' appeals from contracting officers' decisions.

terms.label: derivative rights
terms.gloss: Rights that come through someone else's rights, and so are usually no greater than theirs.

terms.label: acceptance record
terms.gloss: In French construction law, the formal report (procès-verbal de réception) in which the owner accepts the finished work, with or without reservations.

terms.label: chamber of the Court of Cassation
terms.gloss: Divisions of France's Court of Cassation, its highest court for civil and criminal cases; each handles a field, such as construction and property (Third Civil) or business (Commercial).

terms.label: tacit renewal
terms.gloss: Automatic renewal of a contract for another term unless a party gives notice to end it.

terms.label: obligation to act
terms.gloss: French 'obligation de faire,' a duty to do something; under old article 1142 its breach generally led only to damages, not forced performance.

terms.label: price claim
terms.gloss: A suit for the agreed contract price itself, as opposed to damages for loss caused by a breach or termination.

terms.label: fixed-term contract
terms.gloss: A contract running for a set period, which normally can't be ended early at will without consequences.

terms.label: guardianship
terms.gloss: A court-ordered arrangement in which a guardian manages the affairs of someone legally unable to manage them.

terms.label: restoration (rescission)
terms.gloss: Giving back what one received under a contract, usually required before a court will undo (rescind) it.

terms.label: ratification
terms.gloss: Approving an act after the fact so it becomes binding, as when a person confirms a contract once able to understand it; 'unratifiable' means it cannot be saved that way.

terms.label: director (corporate)
terms.gloss: A member of a company's board, elected by shareholders to oversee the business.

terms.label: lay witness
terms.gloss: A non-expert witness who testifies about what they personally saw or experienced.

terms.label: prescription drug
terms.gloss: A drug that may legally be sold only with a licensed medical professional's prescription.

terms.label: § 701(a) (FDCA)
terms.gloss: The FDCA's general provision letting the FDA issue regulations for efficient enforcement of the Act.

terms.label: § 701(e) (FDCA)
terms.gloss: The FDCA's formal procedure for certain rules, with public objections, an evidentiary hearing on request, and direct court of appeals review.

terms.label: Durham-Humphrey Amendment
terms.gloss: A 1951 FDCA amendment creating the legal category of prescription-only drugs.

terms.label: access (copyright)
terms.gloss: In copyright, proof the defendant had a reasonable chance to hear or see the plaintiff's work, which with similarity can show copying.

terms.label: independent creation
terms.gloss: Creating a similar work on one's own without copying, which is a complete defense to copyright infringement.

terms.label: unlawful appropriation
terms.gloss: Arnstein's second step: whether the defendant took enough of the protected expression that ordinary audiences would find the works too similar.

terms.label: striking similarity
terms.gloss: Resemblance so close it can only be explained by copying, which can prove copying even without evidence of access.

terms.label: expert witness
terms.gloss: A witness with special knowledge, like a doctor or musicologist, allowed to give opinions to help the factfinder.

terms.label: chain of title
terms.gloss: The sequence of transfers of ownership of a right or property; someone 'in the chain' claims through an earlier owner.

terms.label: nonfederal claims
terms.gloss: Claims based on state law, which a federal court may hear only with an independent jurisdictional basis or a rule allowing them alongside federal claims.

terms.label: Rule 43
terms.gloss: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 43 on taking testimony, which prefers live testimony in open court (Rule 26 covers depositions); old Rule 43(b) let a party question an adverse party as a hostile witness.

terms.label: slightest-doubt standard
terms.gloss: The Second Circuit's old approach that summary judgment was improper if there was even the slightest doubt about the facts.

terms.label: extraordinary review
terms.gloss: Review through a special order like mandamus, used to correct a lower court's action before the case ends.

terms.label: absent defendant
terms.gloss: A defendant who is not physically in the state where sued, so jurisdiction must rest on contacts or other ties.

terms.label: corporate registration consent
terms.gloss: Jurisdiction based on a state law treating a company's registration to do business there as consent to be sued there on any claim; the Supreme Court allowed it in Mallory v. Norfolk Southern (2023).

terms.label: utterance
terms.gloss: A spoken statement; here, each alleged defamatory remark.

terms.label: substantive evidence
terms.gloss: Evidence that can be used to prove the facts at issue, as opposed to evidence usable only to attack a witness's credibility.

terms.label: same transaction
terms.gloss: A test allowing related claims to be joined in one suit if they arise from the same event or connected series of events.

terms.label: subject of action
terms.gloss: Under code pleading, the underlying right or property the lawsuit is about; claims connected to it could be joined.

terms.label: malicious procurement of a warrant
terms.gloss: Wrongfully getting legal process, like an arrest warrant, issued against someone without probable cause.

terms.label: CARES Act
match: coronavirus aid, relief, and economic security act
terms.gloss: A March 2020 federal COVID-19 relief law that, among much else, briefly barred evictions from federally backed rental housing.

terms.label: Public Health Service Act
terms.gloss: A 1944 federal law on public health; its section 361 lets the government make rules to stop communicable diseases spreading into or between states.

terms.label: clear congressional authorization
terms.gloss: The major questions principle: an agency needs Congress's clear permission before claiming power of vast economic or political significance.

terms.label: quarantine
terms.gloss: Separating and restricting the movement of people exposed to a contagious disease.

terms.label: federal-state balance
terms.gloss: The constitutional division of power between the national government and the states (federalism).

terms.label: premium tax credit
terms.gloss: An Affordable Care Act tax subsidy that lowers the cost of health insurance bought on an exchange for qualifying households.

terms.label: refundable (tax credit)
terms.gloss: A refundable credit pays out money even if it exceeds the tax a person owes.

terms.label: Section 36B
terms.gloss: The Internal Revenue Code section that creates the Affordable Care Act's premium tax credits.

terms.label: Halbig
terms.gloss: Halbig v. Burwell, a D.C. Circuit case on the same tax-credit question, where a panel ruled against the IRS before rehearing was granted.

terms.label: qualified individual
terms.gloss: Affordable Care Act term for a person eligible to buy coverage on an exchange, defined by residence in the state that set it up.

terms.label: applicable taxpayer
terms.gloss: Under Section 36B, a taxpayer whose household income falls within the range eligible for a premium tax credit.

terms.label: on call
terms.gloss: Required to be available to respond to work if called, even while not actively working.

terms.label: Interpretative Bulletin
terms.gloss: An agency publication explaining how it reads a statute; informal guidance that does not bind courts.

terms.label: compensable
terms.gloss: Counted as work that must be paid for.

terms.label: § 12(2) (Securities Act)
terms.gloss: The 1933 Act's remedy (now § 12(a)(2)) letting a buyer undo a purchase made by prospectus or oral communication with a material misstatement or omission.

terms.label: material misstatement
terms.gloss: A false statement or missing fact important enough that a reasonable buyer would consider it in deciding whether to buy.

terms.label: material adverse change
terms.gloss: A significant negative development in a business's condition, often a contract trigger for adjusting or exiting a deal.

terms.label: controlling shareholder
terms.gloss: An owner with enough shares to control the company.

terms.label: secondary market
terms.gloss: Trading of securities between investors after the issuer first sells them.

terms.label: post-enactment
terms.gloss: Written after a law was passed, so weak evidence of what the enacting legislature meant.

terms.label: Uniform Securities Act
terms.gloss: A model state securities law adopted by many states, with a civil remedy similar to § 12.

terms.label: public offering
terms.gloss: A sale of securities to the general public, which must be registered with the SEC unless exempt.

terms.label: confirmation slip
terms.gloss: A broker's written notice confirming the details of a completed securities trade.

terms.label: Naftalin
terms.gloss: United States v. Naftalin (1979), holding that the 1933 Act's antifraud section, § 17(a), reaches fraud in ordinary trading, not just initial offerings.

terms.label: expenditure (campaign)
terms.gloss: Money spent to influence a federal election, as defined by campaign-finance law.

terms.label: membership-communications exception
terms.gloss: A FECA exception letting an organization communicate with its own members about elections without the spending counting as an expenditure.

terms.label: major-purpose test
terms.gloss: The rule that a group is a political committee only if its main purpose is nominating or electing candidates.

terms.label: lobbying
terms.gloss: Trying to influence legislators or officials on policy issues.

terms.label: administrative complaint
terms.gloss: A complaint filed with an agency, asking it to investigate and act, rather than with a court.

terms.label: informational injury
terms.gloss: Being denied information a statute requires to be made public, which can count as an injury for standing.

terms.label: antecedent
terms.gloss: Logically prior; a question that must be answered first.

terms.label: colorblind (Constitution)
terms.gloss: The view that the Constitution forbids government from classifying people by race at all.

terms.label: mutually exclusive
terms.gloss: Two applications where granting one necessarily rules out the other, as when two stations would interfere on one frequency.

terms.label: designation for hearing
terms.gloss: The FCC's formal order setting an application for a hearing and listing what the applicant must prove.

terms.label: adversely affected
terms.gloss: Harmed by an agency decision in a way that allows a court challenge.

terms.label: grant on examination
terms.gloss: Approval of an application on the papers alone, without a hearing.

terms.label: vested right
terms.gloss: A settled, owned right that cannot be taken away without due process; broadcast licensees own no such right in a frequency.

terms.label: Wage Stabilization Board
terms.gloss: A Korean War-era federal agency that recommended settlements in labor disputes to control wage-driven inflation.

terms.label: Commander-in-Chief power
terms.gloss: The President's constitutional role as head of the armed forces.

terms.label: Selective Service Act
terms.gloss: The federal draft law, which also let the government order or seize plants refusing to fill defense orders.

terms.label: theater of operations
terms.gloss: An area where military forces are actively engaged in war.

terms.label: historical gloss
terms.gloss: Frankfurter's idea that a long, consistent practice known to and accepted by Congress can help define a branch's constitutional power.

terms.label: Midwest Oil
terms.gloss: United States v. Midwest Oil (1915), upholding presidential withdrawals of public land because Congress had long acquiesced in the practice.

terms.label: zone of twilight
terms.gloss: Jackson's second category: when Congress has neither granted nor denied power, the President and Congress may share authority and the line is unclear.

terms.label: concurrent authority
terms.gloss: Power that two branches (or governments) hold at the same time over the same subject.

terms.label: Curtiss-Wright
terms.gloss: United States v. Curtiss-Wright (1936), upholding broad presidential power in foreign affairs acting under a congressional delegation.

terms.label: Little v. Barreme
terms.gloss: An 1804 case: when Congress authorized seizing ships sailing to France, a captain who followed a presidential order to seize a ship from France was liable.

terms.label: War Claims Act of 1948
terms.gloss: A federal law setting up a commission to pay certain World War II claims by internees, POWs, and religious groups from seized enemy assets.

terms.label: tenure (office)
terms.gloss: The length of time, and the security, with which an official holds office.

terms.label: Bakke
terms.gloss: Regents of the University of California v. Bakke (1978): struck down a medical school's racial quota, but Justice Powell allowed race as one factor to pursue student diversity.

terms.label: Grutter
terms.gloss: Grutter v. Bollinger (2003): upheld a law school's individualized, race-conscious admissions for diversity, expecting such preferences to be unnecessary in twenty-five years.

terms.label: Bostock
terms.gloss: Bostock v. Clayton County (2020): firing someone for being gay or transgender is sex discrimination under Title VII, because sex is a but-for cause of the decision.

terms.label: commerce power (Commerce Clause)
terms.gloss: Congress's constitutional power to regulate trade and transportation among the states, including railways carrying goods across state lines.

terms.label: pledge a husband's credit
terms.gloss: A wife's former legal power to buy household necessaries on her husband's account, making him liable to pay the seller.

terms.label: maintenance (spousal support)
terms.gloss: A spouse's legal duty to provide financial support for the other spouse.

terms.label: Married Women's Property Act 1882
terms.gloss: An English statute letting married women own property and make contracts in their own names, which coverture had largely prevented.

terms.label: separate estate
terms.gloss: Property a married woman owned for herself, free of her husband's legal control.

terms.label: obligation of honour
terms.gloss: A promise binding only morally, not legally, so a court will not enforce it.

terms.label: authorities (legal sources)
terms.gloss: Earlier court decisions and other legal sources a lawyer or judge cites to support an argument.

terms.label: allow an appeal
terms.gloss: English phrasing meaning the appeal succeeds and the lower court's decision is overturned.

terms.label: express and implied terms
terms.gloss: Express terms are stated outright; implied terms are unstated but treated as part of a contract because the circumstances necessarily show the parties meant them.

terms.label: Title VIII (Fair Housing Act)
terms.gloss: The part of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, known as the Fair Housing Act, banning racial and other discrimination in renting or selling housing.

terms.label: dignitary wrong
terms.gloss: A tort that injures a person's dignity or honor, such as insult or humiliating discrimination, rather than body or property.

terms.label: detention-of-goods exception
terms.gloss: An FTCA exception keeping the United States immune from suits over customs or law-enforcement officers' detention of property.

terms.label: FTCA judgment bar (§ 2676)
terms.gloss: The FTCA rule that a judgment in an FTCA suit against the United States blocks a later suit over the same subject against the individual federal employee.

terms.label: appeal of right
terms.gloss: An appeal the appeals court must hear, as opposed to one it may accept or refuse.

terms.label: open-end investment fund
terms.gloss: A mutual fund that continuously sells new shares and buys them back at their current value.

terms.label: net asset value
terms.gloss: A fund's per-share worth: its investments minus its debts, divided by shares outstanding.

terms.label: sales charge
terms.gloss: A commission (a 'load') added to the price of mutual fund shares.

terms.label: restricted securities
terms.gloss: Stocks or bonds that cannot be freely resold to the public, which makes them harder to sell and to value.

terms.label: derivative count
terms.gloss: A claim shareholders bring on the company's (here, the Fund's) behalf, with any recovery going to the company.

terms.label: contingent liability
terms.gloss: A possible debt that depends on some future event, such as losing a lawsuit.

terms.label: class representatives
terms.gloss: The named plaintiffs who sue on behalf of the whole class and must protect its interests.

terms.label: undue burden
terms.gloss: In discovery, a demand so costly or difficult compared with its value that a court may limit it or shift its cost.

terms.label: responding party
terms.gloss: The party asked to answer or produce information in discovery.

terms.label: fungible
terms.gloss: Interchangeable with other units of the same kind; one dollar is as good as any other.

terms.label: allowance of claims
terms.gloss: The bankruptcy process of deciding whether a creditor's claim against the estate is valid and how much it is worth.

terms.label: Bankruptcy Clause
terms.gloss: The constitutional provision letting Congress make uniform national bankruptcy laws.

terms.label: Katchen v. Landy
terms.gloss: A 1966 Supreme Court case holding that a creditor who files a claim in bankruptcy can have related disputes decided without a jury.

terms.label: acre-foot
terms.gloss: A volume of water that would cover one acre one foot deep, about 326,000 gallons.

terms.label: presumption of correctness
terms.gloss: Treating someone's findings, here the special master's, as right unless the challenger shows they are wrong.

terms.label: recklessness
terms.gloss: Knowingly ignoring a substantial risk of harm: worse than carelessness, short of acting on purpose.

terms.label: conforming (goods)
terms.gloss: Goods that meet the contract's requirements, such as the agreed size and condition.

terms.label: perpetuity and alienation restrictions
terms.gloss: Rules voiding future property interests that might take effect too far in the future (perpetuities) or that tie up property so no one can sell it for too long (alienation).

terms.label: life in being
terms.gloss: A person alive when an interest is created; perpetuity rules measure the allowed waiting period from such a life.

terms.label: special undertaking
terms.gloss: An extra promise by a professional to guarantee a particular result, beyond the ordinary duty of care.

terms.label: Massachusetts Civil Rights Act
terms.gloss: A Massachusetts law letting people sue anyone, including private parties, who interferes with their legal rights by threats, intimidation, or coercion.

terms.label: advisory jury
terms.gloss: A jury whose verdict only advises the judge, who decides the claim; used for claims with no jury right.

terms.label: remoteness (of damages)
terms.gloss: Harm too indirect or far removed from the breach or wrong for the law to allow recovery.

terms.label: natural and probable consequences
terms.gloss: Results that ordinarily and predictably follow from an act, such as a breach; contract damages are limited to these.

terms.label: symbolic speech
terms.gloss: Conduct meant to express a message, such as flag burning, which the First Amendment can protect like words.

terms.label: heckler's veto
terms.gloss: Silencing a speaker because of the hostile reaction of opponents, letting the crowd effectively veto the speech.

terms.label: Michigan v. Long
terms.gloss: A 1983 case: the Supreme Court presumes a state decision rests on federal law unless it clearly rests on independent state-law grounds.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 2241
terms.gloss: The federal habeas corpus statute, letting people held in custody ask a federal court to rule on whether the detention is lawful.

terms.label: Non-Detention Act (§ 4001(a))
terms.gloss: A 1971 federal law providing that no citizen shall be imprisoned or detained by the United States except under an Act of Congress.

terms.label: Ex parte Quirin
terms.gloss: A 1942 Supreme Court case upholding military trial of Nazi saboteurs, including one claimed U.S. citizen, as unlawful enemy combatants.

terms.label: Ex parte Milligan
terms.gloss: An 1866 Supreme Court case holding that a civilian could not be tried by a military commission where ordinary courts were open.

terms.label: suspension of habeas corpus
terms.gloss: The Constitution lets Congress suspend habeas corpus, the right to challenge detention in court, only in cases of rebellion or invasion when public safety requires.

terms.label: some-evidence standard
terms.gloss: A very deferential review standard asking only whether any evidence at all supports the government's decision.

terms.label: neutral decisionmaker
terms.gloss: An impartial judge or official with no stake in the outcome, a basic requirement of due process.

terms.label: Geneva Conventions
terms.gloss: International treaties setting rules for treating prisoners of war, wounded soldiers, and civilians in armed conflict.

terms.label: prisoner of war
terms.gloss: A captured member of enemy armed forces, entitled under the Geneva Conventions to specific protections and a hearing if status is doubtful.

terms.label: military tribunal
terms.gloss: A military court or hearing body, rather than a civilian court, that decides cases involving military matters or enemy fighters.

terms.label: PATRIOT Act
terms.gloss: The 2001 antiterrorism law that, among much else, allowed limited detention of suspected terrorist noncitizens.

terms.label: preventive detention
terms.gloss: Holding someone to prevent future harm rather than to punish a proven crime.

terms.label: private attorney general doctrine
terms.gloss: A former judge-made rule awarding attorney's fees to private plaintiffs who vindicated important public policies; the Supreme Court ended it in Alyeska (1975).

terms.label: Alyeska Pipeline v. Wilderness Society
terms.gloss: A 1975 Supreme Court case holding federal courts cannot make losers pay winners' attorney's fees without a statute authorizing it.

terms.label: Handicapped Children's Protection Act
terms.gloss: A 1986 law allowing attorney's fees for parents who win suits under the special-education law now called IDEA.

terms.label: digital penetration
terms.gloss: In sexual-assault law, penetration with a finger or fingers.

terms.label: immunity from prosecution
terms.gloss: A formal grant protecting someone from being prosecuted, often given so a witness cannot refuse to testify on Fifth Amendment grounds.

terms.label: declination (to prosecute)
terms.gloss: A prosecutor's decision not to bring charges.

terms.label: Pennsylvania Constitution Article I, Section 9
terms.gloss: The Pennsylvania Constitution's rights of the accused, including due process ('law of the land') and protection against self-incrimination.

terms.label: Santobello v. New York
terms.gloss: A 1971 Supreme Court case holding that prosecutors must keep promises made to induce a guilty plea.

terms.label: administrative feasibility
terms.gloss: Whether there is a practical, reliable way to identify who belongs to a class.

terms.label: ascertainability
terms.gloss: A requirement some courts impose that class membership be definable or identifiable; its meaning varies among courts.

terms.label: issue certification
terms.gloss: Certifying a class only for particular shared issues, such as liability, leaving the rest for individual proceedings.

terms.label: price premium
terms.gloss: The extra amount consumers paid because of a product's claimed feature, here the 'natural' label.

terms.label: memorandum disposition
terms.gloss: A short, usually unpublished appellate ruling that resolves issues without setting binding precedent.

terms.label: insured / insurer
terms.gloss: The insured is the person covered by an insurance policy; the insurer is the company that pays covered losses.

terms.label: certification for interlocutory appeal
terms.gloss: A trial judge's certification (28 U.S.C. § 1292(b)) that a key legal question deserves immediate appeal before the case ends; the appeals court may then accept it.

terms.label: minority shareholders
terms.gloss: Owners of less than a controlling share of a corporation's stock.

terms.label: amenable to process
terms.gloss: Subject to being served with legal papers and sued in a particular place.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 1453(b)
terms.gloss: CAFA's removal provision letting any defendant remove a qualifying class action without the others' consent, even if it is from the forum state.

terms.label: Shamrock Oil & Gas Corp. v. Sheets
terms.gloss: A 1941 Supreme Court case holding that an original plaintiff facing a counterclaim cannot remove the case to federal court.

terms.label: unanimity rule (removal)
terms.gloss: The rule that all defendants must consent before a case can be removed to federal court.

terms.label: antiremoval presumption
terms.gloss: The idea that removal statutes should be read narrowly, resolving doubts in favor of sending cases back to state court.

terms.label: new-source performance standards
terms.gloss: National emission limits for newly built or modified industrial sources of air pollution.

terms.label: lowest achievable emission rate
terms.gloss: The strictest pollution limit achieved in practice, required for new major sources in polluted areas.

terms.label: major (stationary) source
terms.gloss: A factory or facility emitting enough pollution (here at least 100 tons a year) to trigger the Act's permit requirements.

terms.label: traditional tools of statutory construction
terms.gloss: Ordinary methods of reading statutes, such as text, structure, context, and canons, used before deciding a law is ambiguous.

terms.label: obviousness (patent)
terms.gloss: An invention cannot be patented if it would have been obvious to a skilled person given earlier inventions and publications (prior art).

terms.label: Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences
match: board of patent appeals and interferences
terms.gloss: The Patent Office's internal appeals body (now the Patent Trial and Appeal Board) reviewing examiners' rejections.

terms.label: APA § 559
terms.gloss: The APA section saying the Act does not limit additional requirements 'recognized by law' and that later statutes must expressly depart from it.

terms.label: Court of Customs and Patent Appeals
match: court of customs and patent appeals
terms.gloss: A former specialized federal appeals court for patent and customs cases, replaced by the Federal Circuit in 1982.

terms.label: priority dispute (patent interference)
terms.gloss: A contest between inventors over who invented something first and so deserves the patent.

terms.label: 35 U.S.C. §§ 141 and 145
terms.gloss: Two routes for rejected patent applicants: § 141 appeals straight to the Federal Circuit; § 145 sues in district court, where new evidence is allowed.

terms.label: 29 U.S.C. §§ 482–483
terms.gloss: LMRDA sections: § 482 lets a union member complain to the Secretary of Labor, who may sue to overturn an election; § 483 makes that the exclusive remedy.

terms.label: 28 U.S.C. § 1337
terms.gloss: The statute giving federal district courts jurisdiction over cases arising under federal laws regulating commerce.

terms.label: presumption of reviewability
terms.gloss: The principle that agency actions are subject to court review unless Congress clearly says otherwise.

terms.label: statutory preclusion (of review)
terms.gloss: A statute's barring of court review of an agency action (APA § 701(a)(1)).

terms.label: presumptively valid
terms.gloss: Treated as valid unless and until someone proves otherwise.

terms.label: internal remedies
terms.gloss: Complaint procedures inside an organization, here a union, which members must use before going to the government or court.

terms.label: post roads
terms.gloss: Routes designated by Congress for carrying mail, under its constitutional postal power.

terms.label: verified bill
terms.gloss: A complaint in an equity case whose facts are sworn to be true under oath.

terms.label: combination (concerted action)
terms.gloss: A group acting together for a common purpose; in older law, similar to a conspiracy.

terms.label: public nuisance
terms.gloss: An unreasonable interference with rights common to the public, such as blocking a road or river, which courts could order stopped.

terms.label: summarily
terms.gloss: Quickly, by a judge alone, without a full trial or jury.

terms.label: security clearance
terms.gloss: Government permission for a person or company to access classified information, granted after a background investigation.

terms.label: Communist front
terms.gloss: An organization the government viewed as secretly controlled by the Communist Party behind a non-Communist face.

terms.label: informant
terms.gloss: A person who secretly supplies information to investigators.

terms.label: National Security Act
terms.gloss: The 1947 law reorganizing the military and intelligence agencies, creating the Defense establishment, CIA, and National Security Council.

terms.label: Armed Services Procurement Act
terms.gloss: A 1947 law governing how the military buys goods and services from contractors.

terms.label: placer-mining laws
terms.gloss: Federal laws letting private people claim and buy public land containing loose surface mineral deposits, extended in 1897 to oil land.

terms.label: withdrawal (of public land)
terms.gloss: An executive order temporarily closing public land to private claims, sale, or settlement.

terms.label: location (mining claim)
terms.gloss: Staking and recording a mining claim on public land, the first step toward acquiring it.

terms.label: quarter section
terms.gloss: A 160-acre parcel, one quarter of a square-mile section in the federal land survey.

terms.label: tacit (implied) consent
terms.gloss: Approval inferred from silence or conduct rather than stated outright.

terms.label: reservation (public land)
terms.gloss: Public land set aside by the government for a specific use, such as an Indian reservation, military post, or bird refuge.

terms.label: practical construction
terms.gloss: Interpreting a law by how officials have long actually applied it without objection.

terms.label: Article IV, § 3 (Property Clause)
terms.gloss: The constitutional provision giving Congress power to dispose of and regulate federal land and property.

terms.label: railroad land grant
terms.gloss: Public land Congress gave railroad companies by statute to encourage building lines.

terms.label: Stuart v. Laird
terms.gloss: An 1803 case upholding Supreme Court Justices' circuit duty largely because the practice had long been accepted.

terms.label: classified information
terms.gloss: Government information officially restricted for national-security reasons; only people with the right security clearance may see it.

terms.label: multiple hearsay (hearsay within hearsay)
terms.gloss: A statement passed along through two or more people before being written down or repeated, which makes it even harder to test than ordinary hearsay.

terms.label: compulsory reference
terms.gloss: A court order, made without the parties' consent, sending disputed issues to a referee or master; if it finally decided the facts, it would displace the jury.

terms.label: trial calendar
terms.gloss: The court's schedule of cases waiting to be tried; restoring a case to it means letting it go to trial in the normal way.

terms.label: agency or instrumentality (FSIA)
terms.gloss: Under the FSIA, a separate entity owned or controlled by a foreign state, such as a state-owned company; it can be served by more flexible methods than the state itself.

terms.label: Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations
terms.gloss: The 1961 treaty governing diplomacy; among other things it makes embassy premises inviolable, so the host country's officials may not enter or interfere with them.

terms.label: inviolability (diplomatic)
terms.gloss: The protection of embassy premises and diplomatic papers from entry, search, or interference by the host country.

terms.label: diplomatic channels
terms.gloss: Sending legal papers through the U.S. State Department, which delivers them to the foreign government through official government-to-government communication.

terms.label: Rooker-Feldman doctrine
terms.gloss: The rule that lower federal courts cannot act as appeals courts over completed state-court judgments; only the U.S. Supreme Court can review those.

terms.label: Heck v. Humphrey
terms.gloss: Heck v. Humphrey (1994): a prisoner cannot sue under § 1983 if winning would necessarily imply an outstanding conviction or sentence is invalid; that must go through habeas.

terms.label: Wilkinson v. Dotson
terms.gloss: Wilkinson v. Dotson (2005): prisoners could use § 1983 to challenge parole procedures because winning would bring only a new hearing, not necessarily earlier release.

terms.label: District Attorney's Office v. Osborne
terms.gloss: District Attorney's Office v. Osborne (2009): the Constitution gives prisoners no freestanding right to DNA testing, though state testing procedures must be fundamentally fair.

terms.label: Brady claim
terms.gloss: A claim that prosecutors violated due process by suppressing evidence favorable to the defendant and material to guilt or punishment (Brady v. Maryland).

terms.label: chain of custody
terms.gloss: An unbroken record of who has held a piece of evidence since it was collected, showing it has not been tampered with.

terms.label: Texas Court of Criminal Appeals
terms.gloss: Texas's highest court for criminal cases; Texas has two top courts, one for civil and one for criminal matters.

terms.label: medical authorization
terms.gloss: Signed forms by which a patient permits doctors or hospitals to release her medical records to another party.

terms.label: request for production
terms.gloss: A formal discovery demand that the other side produce specified documents, which must be answered within thirty days under the federal rules.

terms.label: electronically stored information (ESI)
terms.gloss: Discoverable material kept electronically, such as emails, databases, and files; the federal rules have special provisions for searching and producing it.

terms.label: search terms
terms.gloss: Agreed keywords and date ranges used to search large email or document collections for material to produce in discovery.

terms.label: predictive coding
terms.gloss: Computer-assisted review in which software, trained on sample documents a lawyer has tagged, ranks large document sets by likely relevance.

terms.label: Rule 26(f)
terms.gloss: The federal rule requiring parties to meet early and plan discovery, including how electronic information will be preserved, searched, and produced.

terms.label: meet and confer
terms.gloss: A required good-faith discussion between opposing lawyers to try to resolve a discovery dispute before asking the court to step in.

terms.label: horizontal merger
terms.gloss: A combination of direct competitors at the same level of business, such as two shoe retailers, which can reduce competition between them.

terms.label: vertical merger / vertical integration
terms.gloss: A merger between a supplier and its customer, such as a shoe manufacturer buying shoe stores; it can shut rival suppliers out of those outlets.

terms.label: Expediting Act
terms.gloss: A 1903 federal law sending government civil antitrust cases directly from the trial court to the Supreme Court; amended in 1974 to route most through the courts of appeals.

terms.label: incipiency (antitrust)
terms.gloss: The early stage of a trend; Section 7 lets courts stop mergers likely to harm competition before the harm fully develops.

terms.label: relevant market
terms.gloss: The products and area in which a court measures competition, since a merger's effect depends on whom the merging firms actually compete with.

terms.label: submarket
terms.gloss: A narrower group of products within a broad market, such as children's shoes, that courts may treat as a separate area of competition.

terms.label: geographic market
terms.gloss: The area, national or local, where buyers can practically turn to other sellers; competition is measured within it.

terms.label: failing-company defense
terms.gloss: An antitrust doctrine allowing an otherwise doubtful merger when one firm would likely go out of business anyway and no less harmful buyer exists.

terms.label: oligopoly
terms.gloss: A market dominated by a few large sellers, which may compete less vigorously than many smaller ones would.

terms.label: reasonable probability (Clayton Act)
terms.gloss: Section 7's standard: the government must show a merger will probably, not certainly or merely possibly, lessen competition.

terms.label: equitable distribution
terms.gloss: Dividing a couple's marital property at divorce fairly, though not necessarily equally, as New Jersey courts do.

terms.label: plenary trial
terms.gloss: A full trial with live testimony and complete hearing of the evidence, rather than a decision on written papers.

terms.label: mutual cancellation
terms.gloss: Both parties agreeing to end a contract and release each other from it.

terms.label: marital estate
terms.gloss: The property a couple acquired during marriage that is subject to division at divorce.

terms.label: interim support
terms.gloss: Temporary support payments ordered while a divorce case is still pending; the payer may ask for credit for them against what is finally owed.

terms.label: estate rights (of a spouse)
terms.gloss: A spouse's legal rights in the other spouse's property at death, such as a guaranteed share of the estate, which can be waived by agreement.

terms.label: substantial credible evidence
terms.gloss: The appellate standard for upholding a trial judge's fact findings: enough believable evidence supports them, even if the appeals court might have decided differently.

terms.label: interspousal immunity
terms.gloss: The old rule barring spouses from suing each other in tort or enforcing certain contracts between them, now largely abandoned.

terms.label: transmutation (of property)
terms.gloss: Spouses changing the character of property, for example from separate to community property; California requires an express writing to do it.

terms.label: new business rule
terms.gloss: The traditional doctrine that a business with no operating history cannot recover lost profits because they are too speculative; Maryland refused to make it absolute.

terms.label: willful breach
terms.gloss: A deliberate failure to perform a contract; unlike a good-faith shortfall, it can bar the breaching party from recovering for substantial performance.

terms.label: delay damages
terms.gloss: Compensation for losses caused by late completion, here measured by the property's rental value and actual expenses.

terms.label: Restatement (Second) of Agency
terms.gloss: A 1958 American Law Institute summary of agency law; its § 354 makes an agent who undertakes protective action liable for harm when others rely on it and the agent fails to act.

terms.label: H.R. Moch Co. v. Rensselaer Water Co.
terms.gloss: Moch (1928): a water company that contracted with a city was not liable to a resident whose building burned for lack of hydrant water.

terms.label: equitable adjustment
terms.gloss: A court-fashioned change to contract obligations that fairly shares an unexpected loss, instead of fully enforcing or fully excusing the contract.

terms.label: underwrite (insurance)
terms.gloss: For an insurer, to evaluate a risk and agree to issue and stand behind the policy; fresh underwriting means re-deciding whether to insure.

terms.label: evidence of insurability
terms.gloss: Proof, such as a health questionnaire, that the insured is still an acceptable risk, often required to revive a lapsed policy.

terms.label: postdating (a check)
terms.gloss: Dating a check later than the day it is written; a bank may pay it early unless the customer has given the bank notice of the later date.

terms.label: properly payable
terms.gloss: UCC phrase for a check the bank may pay and charge to the customer's account because the customer authorized it.

terms.label: negotiation (of a check)
terms.gloss: Transferring a check so that someone becomes its holder; for the payee, cashing or depositing it.

terms.label: standards of identity
terms.gloss: FDA rules defining what a product must contain to be sold under a given name, here what vitamin and mineral supplements could include.

terms.label: Public Law (number)
terms.gloss: The official numbering of an enacted federal statute: Public Law 94-278 was the 278th law passed by the 94th Congress.

terms.label: formal hearing procedure
terms.gloss: Trial-like agency proceedings with sworn testimony and cross-examination, far more elaborate than ordinary notice and comment.

terms.label: exceptions (to an ALJ decision)
terms.gloss: Written objections a party files to an administrative law judge's decision, asking the agency head to reject parts of it.

terms.label: variance (from a rule)
terms.gloss: Permission to depart from a regulation's general requirements if the applicant meets a stated standard.

terms.label: food additive
terms.gloss: Under the food statute, a substance added to food that experts do not generally recognize as safe; it needs FDA approval before use.

terms.label: generally recognized as safe (GRAS)
terms.gloss: If qualified experts generally agree a substance is safe for its intended use, it escapes the approval required for food additives.

terms.label: infirm (legally)
terms.gloss: Legally defective or invalid.

terms.label: found within (jurisdiction rule)
terms.gloss: Montana's jurisdiction rule reaching persons 'found within' the state, which its courts read to include companies doing business there.

terms.label: Helicopteros Nacionales de Colombia v. Hall
terms.gloss: Helicopteros (1984): a Colombian company's purchases and training trips in Texas were not enough for general jurisdiction there.

terms.label: weather working day
terms.gloss: A contract-defined workday on which weather permits construction; late-completion deductions were counted only on such days.

terms.label: debtor and creditor
terms.gloss: A relationship in which one simply owes money to the other; unlike a trust, it creates no duty to hold particular property for the creditor.

terms.label: face of the complaint
terms.gloss: What the complaint itself shows; a defense not apparent there must be raised in the defendant's answer or it is lost.

terms.label: battle of the forms
terms.gloss: The clash when buyer and seller exchange preprinted forms with conflicting terms; UCC § 2-207 decides which terms control.

terms.label: express assent
terms.gloss: Clear, affirmative agreement to a term, not just silence or keeping the product.

terms.label: arbitral stay
terms.gloss: A court order pausing a lawsuit while the dispute goes to arbitration.

terms.label: memorandum and order
terms.gloss: A trial judge's written ruling that explains its reasons and states what the court orders.

terms.label: employee (statutory)
terms.gloss: A worker hired to work under another's control. Statutes such as the NLRA and Title VII protect 'employees', so who counts as one decides who is covered.

terms.label: representation proceedings
terms.gloss: NLRB proceedings deciding which workers form a bargaining unit and whether a union represents them, usually through an election.

terms.label: master-servant relationship
terms.gloss: The traditional common-law employment relationship, defined mainly by the employer's right to control how the work is done.

terms.label: disability benefits
terms.gloss: Payments to a person whose medical condition keeps them from working, from Social Security or a private or employer plan; Social Security pays only if no substantial work in the economy is possible.

terms.label: vocational expert
terms.gloss: A job-market specialist who testifies at Social Security hearings about what work a claimant with given limitations could do and how many such jobs exist.

terms.label: nonadversarial
terms.gloss: A proceeding without two opposing sides; the judge investigates and develops the record instead of just refereeing a contest.

terms.label: sedentary, unskilled work
terms.gloss: Social Security job categories: sedentary work is done mostly sitting with light lifting; unskilled work can be learned in about a month.

terms.label: 42 U.S.C. § 405(g)
terms.gloss: The Social Security Act provision allowing court review of benefit decisions and making the agency's fact findings conclusive if supported by substantial evidence.

terms.label: categorical rule
terms.gloss: A bright-line rule applied the same way in every case, regardless of the particular circumstances.

terms.label: tolerance (food law)
terms.gloss: A formal, legally binding limit on a contaminant in food that FDA sets through rulemaking.

terms.label: poisonous or deleterious substance
terms.gloss: The food statute's phrase for harmful substances; food with added ones is adulterated, while unavoidable ones may be limited by tolerances.

terms.label: American Bus Ass'n v. United States
terms.gloss: A 1980 D.C. Circuit decision: an agency statement is a binding rule if it creates a present binding norm rather than leaving officials real discretion.

terms.label: lawfully present
terms.gloss: A designation treating a noncitizen as legally in the country for certain benefits, without granting permanent immigration status.

terms.label: post hoc rationalization
terms.gloss: Reasons offered after the fact, often by lawyers, to defend an agency decision; courts judge the decision only by reasons given when it was made.

terms.label: 8 U.S.C. § 1103(a)(1)
terms.gloss: The immigration-statute provision making the Attorney General's rulings on questions of immigration law controlling for the agency.

terms.label: animus
terms.gloss: Hostility or ill will toward a group; a government policy motivated by it can violate equal protection.

terms.label: Reno v. American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee
terms.gloss: Reno v. AADC (1999): sharply limited courts' power to hear claims that the government selectively targeted noncitizens for deportation.

terms.label: Immigration and Nationality Act (INA)
terms.gloss: The main federal immigration statute, governing admission, status, and removal of noncitizens.

terms.label: dissolve (an injunction)
terms.gloss: To end an injunction so it no longer restricts anyone.

terms.label: OMB Circular A-76
terms.gloss: A federal policy directing agencies to compare in-house costs with private bids when deciding whether to contract work out.

terms.label: Service Contract Act
terms.gloss: A 1965 federal law requiring private companies providing services to the government to pay their workers Labor Department-set prevailing wages and benefits.

terms.label: rebidding
terms.gloss: Reopening a government contract to fresh competition so bidders can submit new offers.

terms.label: wage determination
terms.gloss: The Labor Department's schedule of minimum wages and benefits a service contractor must pay workers in a given area.

terms.label: UAW v. Brock
terms.gloss: UAW v. Brock (1986): the Supreme Court reaffirmed that unions and associations may sue on behalf of their members.

terms.label: disappointed bidder
terms.gloss: A company that lost a government contract competition and may sue to challenge an unfair procurement process.

terms.label: charge (of discrimination)
terms.gloss: A formal complaint of discrimination filed with the EEOC, a required step before suing under Title VII.

terms.label: protected activity
terms.gloss: Actions the law shields from retaliation, such as filing a discrimination charge or supporting a coworker's complaint.

terms.label: Burlington Northern & Santa Fe Ry. v. White
terms.gloss: Burlington Northern (2006): Title VII forbids any employer retaliation that might dissuade a reasonable worker from making or supporting a discrimination charge.

terms.label: Trafficante v. Metropolitan Life Ins. Co.
terms.gloss: Trafficante (1972): a fair-housing case suggesting that 'person aggrieved' reaches as far as Article III standing allows.

terms.label: EEOC Compliance Manual
terms.gloss: The EEOC's guidance explaining how it interprets discrimination laws; persuasive to courts but not binding.

terms.label: terms or conditions of employment
terms.gloss: The pay, duties, and other features of a job; Title VII's discrimination ban focuses on these, while its retaliation ban reaches more broadly.

terms.label: third-party retaliation
terms.gloss: Punishing a worker's close associate, such as a fiancé, to get back at the worker who complained.

terms.label: customs collector
terms.gloss: The federal official at a port who assessed and collected import duties.

terms.label: bounty (subsidy)
terms.gloss: Government payments to encourage an activity, here subsidies to domestic sugar producers.

terms.label: enrolled bill (enrolled Act)
terms.gloss: The final official copy of a bill, signed by both Houses' presiding officers and approved by the President; courts treat it as conclusive proof of what Congress passed.

terms.label: presiding officers (of Congress)
terms.gloss: The Speaker of the House and the President of the Senate (or their stand-ins), whose signatures certify that a bill passed.

terms.label: Journal Clause
terms.gloss: Article I's requirement that each House of Congress keep and publish a journal of its proceedings.

terms.label: Board of General Appraisers
terms.gloss: The federal body, a forerunner of today's Court of International Trade, that heard importers' protests against customs assessments.

terms.label: treaty-making power
terms.gloss: The President's power to make treaties with foreign nations, valid only with approval by two-thirds of the Senate.

terms.label: contingent legislation
terms.gloss: A law that takes effect or changes when an official finds that specified facts exist; allowed because Congress itself made the policy choice.

terms.label: The Brig Aurora
terms.gloss: The Brig Aurora (1813): Congress could revive trade restrictions effective upon a presidential proclamation that stated conditions had occurred.

terms.label: separable (statutory provisions)
terms.gloss: Able to be cut out of a statute without bringing down the rest; courts strike only the invalid part if Congress would have wanted the remainder.

terms.label: General Welfare Clause
terms.gloss: Congress's constitutional power to tax and spend for the general welfare, which the sugar-bounty challenge would have tested.

terms.label: coordinate branches
terms.gloss: The three equal branches of government; courts respect Congress by not second-guessing its certified records.

terms.label: collateral impeachment
terms.gloss: Attacking the validity of an official record with outside evidence, here trying to prove a statute's text wrong with congressional journals.

terms.label: refund (of duties)
terms.gloss: Repayment of taxes or duties claimed to have been unlawfully collected.

terms.label: codes of fair competition
terms.gloss: Industry-wide rules on wages, hours, prices, and trade practices drafted under the NIRA and made legally binding by presidential approval.

terms.label: substantive counts
terms.gloss: Charges for actual offenses committed, as opposed to the separate charge of conspiring to commit them.

terms.label: United States v. Grimaud
terms.gloss: Grimaud (1911): upheld letting the Secretary of Agriculture make forest grazing rules, backed by criminal penalties, to carry out Congress's stated purposes.

terms.label: direct/indirect effects test
terms.gloss: The Court's 1930s test allowing federal regulation of local activity only if it directly affected interstate commerce; later abandoned.

terms.label: narrowing construction
terms.gloss: Reading a statute or rule more narrowly than its words might allow so that it stays within legal limits.

terms.label: 42 U.S.C. § 1985(3)
terms.gloss: A federal statute allowing suits against people who conspire to deprive others of equal protection; it requires facts showing an actual agreement.

terms.label: South Dakota Codified Laws (SDCL)
terms.gloss: The official collection of South Dakota's statutes.

terms.label: formulaic recitation
terms.gloss: Repeating a claim's legal elements in conclusory words without supporting facts, which modern pleading rules say is not enough.

terms.label: consequential recovery (damages)
terms.gloss: Recovery for losses that flow indirectly from a breach, such as an injury or death, rather than the promised service itself; contract law allows it only if foreseeable when contracting.

terms.label: stock-exchange acquisition
terms.gloss: Buying a company by giving its shareholders the buyer's own shares in exchange for theirs, instead of paying cash.

terms.label: Batson v. Kentucky
terms.gloss: The 1986 Supreme Court case barring race-based jury strikes. If an objector shows a strike looks racial, the striking side must give a race-neutral reason.

terms.label: prospective juror
terms.gloss: A person summoned for possible jury service who has not yet been chosen to sit on the jury.

terms.label: significant encouragement
terms.gloss: A state-action test: government is responsible for a private choice it coerced or strongly encouraged, not one it merely allowed.

terms.label: race-neutral explanation
terms.gloss: Under Batson, a reason for striking a juror that does not depend on race, which the striking side must give once the objector makes an initial showing.

terms.label: in the first instance
terms.gloss: First, before anyone else; for example, a lower court deciding a question before any appeals court reviews it.

terms.label: Section 1870 (28 U.S.C. § 1870)
terms.gloss: The federal statute giving each side in a federal civil case three peremptory challenges (removals of jurors without stating a reason).

terms.label: Lugar v. Edmondson Oil Co.
terms.gloss: A 1982 Supreme Court case setting a two-part state-action test: the harm must come from government-created rules, and the private party must fairly count as a government actor.

terms.label: presidential elector
terms.gloss: A person chosen to cast one of a state's votes for President in the Electoral College. Electors nominated by a party become electors only if their candidate wins the state.

terms.label: electoral vote
terms.gloss: The formal vote of each state's presidential electors in December after a presidential election; Congress counts the votes in January. In 2020 it was held on December 14.

terms.label: Board of State Canvassers
terms.gloss: The Michigan board that officially certifies statewide election results.

terms.label: impoundment
terms.gloss: A court order placing property, here voting machines, in official custody, usually to preserve it as evidence.

terms.label: cocounsel
terms.gloss: Lawyers who jointly represent the same client in a case.

terms.label: local counsel
terms.gloss: A lawyer admitted where the court sits who joins out-of-area lawyers on a case, often filing papers and handling local requirements.

terms.label: threshold barriers
terms.gloss: Preliminary obstacles, such as lack of standing or mootness, that can end a case before a court reaches whether the claims are true.

terms.label: continuing legal education
terms.gloss: Courses lawyers must take after admission to keep their licenses; here, extra hours were ordered as a sanction.

terms.label: wetlands
terms.gloss: Land saturated with water much of the year, like marshes and swamps; filling them without a federal permit can violate the Clean Water Act.

terms.label: Rivers and Harbors Act
terms.gloss: An 1899 federal law forbidding obstruction or filling of navigable waterways without permission from the Army Corps of Engineers.

terms.label: after-the-fact permit
terms.gloss: A permit issued after regulated work is already done, which can legalize the work instead of requiring it to be undone.

terms.label: action in debt
terms.gloss: An old English common-law lawsuit to recover a fixed or calculable sum owed, including statutory penalties. It was tried to a jury.

terms.label: Section 1319(d)
terms.gloss: The Clean Water Act provision letting courts impose civil penalties, then up to $10,000 per day of violation.

terms.label: Hepner and Regan
terms.gloss: Hepner v. United States (1909) and United States v. Regan (1914): Supreme Court cases treating government suits for statutory penalties like actions in debt, tried to juries.

terms.label: public-policy exception (full faith and credit)
terms.gloss: A claimed power of one state to refuse to honor another state's judgment that offends its own strong policies. The Supreme Court rejected it for judgments in Baker v. General Motors (1998).

terms.label: public-policy wrongful discharge
terms.gloss: An exception to at-will employment letting a fired worker sue if the firing violated an important public policy found in a statute, constitution or court decision.

terms.label: antisuit injunction
terms.gloss: A court order forbidding a party from bringing or continuing a lawsuit in another court.

terms.label: strangers (to a case)
terms.gloss: People who were not parties to a lawsuit and so generally are not bound by its judgment.

terms.label: equitable class
terms.gloss: The part of a class seeking injunctions or similar group-wide relief; members of such a class generally cannot opt out.

terms.label: fee benchmark
terms.gloss: In the Ninth Circuit, the starting presumption that common-fund attorney fees equal about 25 percent of the fund, adjustable up or down.

terms.label: cross-check
terms.gloss: Using a second fee method, usually lodestar, to test whether a percentage-of-fund award is reasonable.

terms.label: incentive award
terms.gloss: An extra payment to named class representatives for the time, effort and risk of bringing the case for the group.

terms.label: open and notorious
terms.gloss: Possession so obvious that a reasonably attentive owner would notice it, a requirement for gaining title by adverse possession.

terms.label: reply (pleading)
terms.gloss: A plaintiff's written pleading responding to new matter, such as a defense, raised in the defendant's answer.

terms.label: joined issue
terms.gloss: Took opposite positions on a point in the pleadings or at trial, making it a contested question the court must decide.

terms.label: monuments (boundary)
terms.gloss: Physical markers, natural or artificial, such as stones, fences or trees, used to fix property boundaries.

terms.label: Supreme Court of Errors
terms.gloss: The former name of Connecticut's highest court.

terms.label: found no error
terms.gloss: Connecticut's way of saying the trial court's judgment stands; in effect, the appeal was rejected and the judgment affirmed.

terms.label: Antiterrorism Act (ATA)
terms.gloss: A federal law letting U.S. nationals injured by international terrorism, or their survivors, sue in federal court for triple damages.

terms.label: Anti-Terrorism Clarification Act
terms.gloss: A 2018 law treating certain U.S. activities, or acceptance of certain U.S. aid, as a defendant's consent to be sued under the Antiterrorism Act.

terms.label: Promoting Security and Justice for Victims of Terrorism Act (PSJVTA)
match: promoting security and justice for victims of terrorism act
terms.gloss: A 2019 law deeming the PLO and PA to consent to U.S. jurisdiction in terrorism suits if they make certain payments or conduct certain activities in the U.S.

terms.label: Section 2334(e)
terms.gloss: The provision of the Antiterrorism Act, added by the PSJVTA, listing the conduct that counts as the PLO's and PA's consent to jurisdiction.

terms.label: Federal Rule 4(k)
terms.gloss: The federal rule on how far courts' power reaches: 4(k)(1)(A) borrows the local state courts' limits; 4(k)(1)(C) allows whatever reach a federal statute authorizes.

terms.label: reasonableness inquiry (jurisdiction)
terms.gloss: A possible extra step in personal-jurisdiction analysis asking whether suing the defendant in the forum is fair, weighing its burdens against the forum's and plaintiffs' interests.

terms.label: subconstitutional
terms.gloss: Below the level of the Constitution, such as ordinary statutes or international-law rules, so Congress can override them.

terms.label: evidence preponderated against
terms.gloss: The weight of the evidence pointed the other way. In Tennessee, an appeals court may reject a trial finding when the evidence preponderates against it.

terms.label: permission to appeal
terms.gloss: Leave from a higher court to hear an appeal it is not required to take.

terms.label: clean hands
terms.gloss: The equity principle that a court may refuse to help a party who acted wrongfully in the same matter; its absence is the 'unclean hands' defense.

terms.label: reciprocal-fee statute (ORS 20.096)
terms.gloss: An Oregon statute making a one-sided contract fee clause two-way: if only one party could recover fees, whichever side wins may.

terms.label: Section 31-51q
terms.gloss: A Connecticut statute making employers liable for disciplining workers for exercising free-speech rights, if the speech does not substantially interfere with their job.

terms.label: Section 31-49
terms.gloss: A Connecticut statute requiring employers to provide reasonably safe workplaces and competent co-workers.

terms.label: transferred appeal
terms.gloss: An appeal moved from Connecticut's intermediate Appellate Court directly to its Supreme Court.

terms.label: Sheets v. Teddy's Frosted Foods
terms.gloss: A 1980 Connecticut case recognizing a narrow claim for at-will employees fired in violation of important public policy.

terms.label: progressive discipline
terms.gloss: An employer system of increasingly serious steps, such as warnings, probation and then firing, for repeated problems.

terms.label: seal (notary's)
terms.gloss: An official stamp or embossed mark a notary places on a document to certify it.

terms.label: original-document (best evidence) rule
terms.gloss: The evidence rule requiring the original writing to prove its contents, though duplicates are usually allowed and a lost original's contents can be proved other ways.

terms.label: legal rate (of interest)
terms.gloss: The interest rate set by statute that applies when parties have not agreed on one.

terms.label: transfer taxes
terms.gloss: Taxes owed when real estate changes hands, usually a percentage of the price.

terms.label: Rule 54(d)
terms.gloss: The court rule letting the winning side recover ordinary court costs, such as filing fees, though not usually lawyer fees.

terms.label: cohabitant
terms.gloss: A partner who lives with someone in a marriage-like relationship without being married.

terms.label: uniquely federal interest
terms.gloss: An area, like federal contracts, so tied to national concerns that federal courts may create federal rules displacing state law there.

terms.label: official immunity
terms.gloss: Protection shielding government officials from personal liability for discretionary acts within their official duties.

terms.label: Feres doctrine
terms.gloss: The rule from Feres v. United States (1950) that service members cannot sue the federal government for injuries arising from military service.

terms.label: discretionary-function exception
terms.gloss: The Federal Tort Claims Act exception barring suits against the United States over employees' policy-based judgment calls.

terms.label: Death on the High Seas Act
match: death on the high seas act
terms.gloss: A 1920 federal law giving families a damages claim for deaths caused by wrongful acts on the high seas, beyond U.S. coastal waters.

terms.label: interstitial
terms.gloss: Filling small gaps in existing law, as courts routinely do, rather than creating major new rules.

terms.label: New York Banking Law § 100-c
terms.gloss: The New York statute authorizing common trust funds and setting their court-accounting and notice procedures.

terms.label: Pennoyer v. Neff
terms.gloss: An 1878 Supreme Court case tying state courts' power to their borders: an out-of-state defendant generally had to be served personally within the state.

terms.label: Grannis v. Ordean
terms.gloss: A 1914 Supreme Court case calling the opportunity to be heard the fundamental requirement of due process.

terms.label: McDonald v. Mabee
terms.gloss: A 1917 Supreme Court case holding newspaper notice could not replace personal service on a resident who had left the state; due process requires real notice where practical.

terms.label: Shaffer v. Heitner
terms.gloss: A 1977 Supreme Court case requiring every exercise of state-court jurisdiction, including over property, to satisfy the minimum-contacts fairness test.

terms.label: bill in chancery
terms.gloss: The opening pleading in a court of equity (chancery), roughly what is now called a complaint.

terms.label: federal Circuit Court (pre-1912)
terms.gloss: The original federal trial courts for major cases, including diversity suits, abolished at the start of 1912; not today's courts of appeals.

terms.label: joint interest
terms.gloss: An interest several people share together, so they must sue or be sued together as one side.

terms.label: general common law
terms.gloss: Under Swift v. Tyson, common law that federal judges decided for themselves, without following state courts. Erie abolished it in 1938.

terms.label: Judicial Code § 37
terms.gloss: The then-federal statute requiring dismissal of suits not really within federal jurisdiction, or where parties were improperly or collusively made or joined to create it.

terms.label: charter powers
terms.gloss: What a corporation may do under its charter, the founding document the state issues it; acts beyond it are 'ultra vires.'

terms.label: hack stand
terms.gloss: A public taxi stand where cabs wait for riders ('hack' is old slang for a taxi).

terms.label: nonresident-motorist statute
terms.gloss: A state law treating out-of-state drivers who use its roads as agreeing that a state official, here the Auditor, may receive court papers for them after an accident.

terms.label: artifice
terms.gloss: A clever trick or deceptive scheme.

terms.label: replication
terms.gloss: In old-style pleading, the plaintiff's written answer to the defendant's plea, for example denying its factual allegations.

terms.label: Ragan v. Merchants Transfer & Warehouse Co.
match: ragan v. merchants transfer & warehouse co.
terms.gloss: A 1949 Supreme Court case holding that a state rule starting a suit at service, for limitations purposes, governs in diversity cases despite Federal Rule 3.

terms.label: bailee for hire
terms.gloss: Someone paid to hold another's property, such as a parcel room; owes ordinary care and is liable for losses caused by negligence.

terms.label: Restatement § 211(3)
terms.gloss: A Restatement (Second) of Contracts rule: a standard-form term does not bind the signer if the drafter had reason to know the signer would have rejected it.

terms.label: machinegun
terms.gloss: Under federal law, any weapon that fires automatically more than one shot, without manual reloading, by a single function of the trigger.

terms.label: presumption against ineffectiveness
terms.gloss: An interpretive principle that courts should avoid readings that let a statute's evident purpose be easily evaded.

terms.label: purposive argument
terms.gloss: An argument that a statute should be read in light of its purpose, not just its words.

terms.label: Staples v. United States
terms.gloss: A 1994 gun case in which the Supreme Court described a machinegun as firing repeatedly with one trigger pull, unlike a semiautomatic.

terms.label: FDIC
terms.gloss: The federal agency that insures bank deposits and supervises many banks, with power to remove, ban and fine bank officials.

terms.label: 12 U.S.C. § 1818(e)
terms.gloss: The federal banking statute letting regulators remove and ban bank officials for misconduct that caused harm or brought them benefit, plus dishonesty or willful disregard.

terms.label: unsafe or unsound practices
terms.gloss: Banking-law term for imprudent conduct, contrary to accepted banking standards, that risks abnormal loss to a bank or its depositors.

terms.label: charge-off
terms.gloss: A bank's writing off a loan as a loss on its books because it is unlikely to be repaid.

terms.label: disability insurance (Social Security)
terms.gloss: Social Security payments to insured workers who can no longer work because of a long-term medical impairment, regardless of financial need.

terms.label: Social Security Administration
terms.gloss: The federal agency that runs Social Security retirement and disability programs.

terms.label: insured status
terms.gloss: Having worked and paid Social Security taxes long enough to qualify for benefits.

terms.label: medically determinable impairment
terms.gloss: A physical or mental condition shown by medically acceptable tests or clinical findings.

terms.label: substantial gainful work
terms.gloss: Meaningful paid work; being unable to do any such work is the core of the Social Security disability test.

terms.label: retroactive benefits
terms.gloss: Back payments covering the period benefits were wrongly cut off.

terms.label: Social Security Act
terms.gloss: The 1935 federal law creating Social Security; it limits court review of benefit decisions to specified routes.

terms.label: Section 405(h)
terms.gloss: The Social Security Act provision barring other routes into court, such as general federal-question jurisdiction, for benefit claims.

terms.label: Weinberger v. Salfi
terms.gloss: A 1975 Supreme Court case holding that Social Security claims must go through § 405(g), which requires a final agency decision on a presented claim.

terms.label: means-tested
terms.gloss: Available only to people whose income and assets are low enough.

terms.label: equitable jurisdiction
terms.gloss: A court's power to grant and oversee equity remedies, like specific performance, including continuing oversight of how parties perform.

terms.label: competent, credible evidence
terms.gloss: Ohio's deferential appellate standard: a trial finding stands if some reliable, believable evidence supports it.

terms.label: interlocking directors
terms.gloss: The same people serving on both companies' boards of directors.

terms.label: Restatement § 33
terms.gloss: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 33: terms must be reasonably certain, but a court can supply missing terms if the parties meant to be bound.

terms.label: UCC § 2-305
terms.gloss: The Uniform Commercial Code rule that a sale-of-goods contract can stand without a fixed price if the parties meant to deal; a reasonable price is supplied.

terms.label: open price term
terms.gloss: A contract term leaving price to be set later, for example by agreement or a market benchmark.

terms.label: Restatement § 362
terms.gloss: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 362: specific performance requires terms certain enough for a court to frame an order.

terms.label: Restatement § 152
terms.gloss: The Restatement rule allowing a contract to be undone when both sides were mistaken about a basic assumption that materially affects the deal, unless the harmed side bore that risk.

terms.label: Restatement § 376
terms.gloss: The Restatement rule that a party who undoes a contract for mistake can recover the value of benefits it conferred on the other side.

terms.label: Restatement § 371(b)
terms.gloss: The Restatement rule that restitution may be measured by how much the other party's property increased in value, not by what was spent.

terms.label: fair rental value
terms.gloss: What a reasonable tenant would pay to rent the property for that period.

terms.label: mixed question of law and fact
terms.gloss: A question that applies a legal standard to particular facts, such as whether conduct was reasonable; appeals courts give the trial court varying deference on it.

terms.label: judicially noticed
terms.gloss: Accepted a fact as true without formal proof because it is commonly known or easily verified.
